Ch. 1–2
2.2 Historical context: from seals to cryptographic
attestation
 Verifiable evidence in human affairs long predates cryptography: seals, notarized
registers, and double-entry bookkeeping all bind a claim to an artifact whose integrity can
be inspected by a third party, and all fail when the inspector trusts the maker of the artifact
more than the artifact. The computational reformulation of this problem begins with Ralph


=== PAGINA 45 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 45
Merkle's 1979 construction of hash-tree signatures, which allowed a single root hash to
commit to an arbitrarily large set of leaves so that the membership of any leaf — and any
tampering — could be demonstrated with a short proof path. The construction lay relatively
dormant until two industrializations: Git, released in 2005, made content addressing the
everyday substrate of software development by naming every commit, tree, and blob with
the hash of its contents; and the certificate-authority reform described below made Merkle
trees the audit substrate of the web's identity system. The pattern established in both cases
is the one this book generalizes: identity by content, and authority bounded by publicly
checkable structure.
 Certificate Transparency, deployed from 2013 and standardized in RFC 6962, is the
decisive precedent. It placed every publicly trusted TLS certificate into append-only,
publicly auditable Merkle-tree logs, so that a certification authority could still mis-issue a
certificate but could no longer mis-issue quietly: domain owners and monitors could detect
issuance the owner had not requested, and browsers could require proofs of inclusion [8].
The mechanism that made Certificate Transparency work was not cryptography alone but
the coupling of cryptography to publicity — an economy in which the cost of undetected
mis-issuance rose to prohibitive levels. Certificate Transparency Version 2.0, standardized
as RFC 9162, consolidated the design with the operational refinements of a decade of
deployment at web scale [99]. The lesson for agent infrastructure is procedural rather than
technical: evidence must be born into a public structure, not assembled retrospectively for
an auditor [8, 99].
 A parallel lineage hardened the device side. The Trusted Platform Module 2.0
specification defines a vendor-neutral hardware root of trust that measures boot
components and reports signed measurements, making the claim “this machine runs this
software” checkable by a remote verifier [101]. The Remote ATtestation procedureS
architecture, standardized as RFC 9334 in 2022, gave the field its shared vocabulary —
attester, verifier, relying party, and the distinction between evidence produced by the
attesting system and assertions made about it [100]. That distinction is exactly the one this
book applies to agents: an agent's self-description is an assertion, while a measurement of
its loaded model and policy is evidence. Device attestation never reached the application
layer of AI systems, however; the hardware root measures the boot chain, not the model.
 The last decade transposed these mechanisms to software supply chains and
messaging. Sigstore's Rekor provides a public transparency log for signatures and software
artifacts, with inclusion and consistency proofs that let any auditor detect log rewriting, and
the Open Source Security Foundation has documented operational use of Rekor in catching
malicious package releases [9, 10]. SLSA defines graduated levels of build provenance —
statements about how an artifact was produced and by whom — and in-toto standardizes
signed attestations about the steps of a software supply chain, so that the provenance of an


=== PAGINA 46 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 46
artifact becomes evidence rather than a claim [102, 103]. In messaging, WhatsApp
deployed key transparency in 2023, giving clients an auditable directory in which the
public key a user receives for a correspondent is provably the key that correspondent
registered, closing the gap between encrypted transport and authentic identity [11, 12].
Each system evidences one stratum — code, builds, or keys — and none evidences the
behavior of autonomous software acting on that stratum.
 Figure 2.1 places these milestones on a single timeline from 1979 to 2026, and the
pattern it displays is the argument of this section. Each generation of infrastructure narrows
the same gap: between what a system claims and what a third party can check, and between
evidence born at the moment of action and evidence assembled afterwards for the auditor.
The most recent nodes extend the pattern in two directions — post-quantum signature
standards, approved by NIST in 2024, future-proof the evidentiary layer itself [104, 105],
and agentic protocols such as the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent protocol
create the interconnection layer that now needs exactly this evidence [108, 110, 111]. What
no node on the timeline provides is the joining of the evidentiary lineage with the
governance lineage, and that joining is the work of Part II.
Figure 2.1 — Lineage of verifiability infrastructure, 1979–2026. Milestones from Merkle's certified signatures to
 post-quantum signatures and agentic protocols; each node is cited in Section 2.2.
 Viewed from the state's side of the ledger, the governance of AI systems has developed
along a largely non-cryptographic track. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework
organizes organizational practice around the functions Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage
[15]; ISO/IEC 42001:2023 defines management-system requirements for the AI lifecycle,
including documented controls and internal audit [16]; and the EU AI Act imposes on


=== PAGINA 47 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 47
high-risk systems duties of risk management, data governance, automatic logging, human
oversight, and robustness [17, 18, 19]. These instruments specify what must be true of an
organization; they largely leave open how the underlying artifacts are made
tamper-evident, which is precisely the question the transparency lineage answers. The VTK
hypothesis, stated here and developed throughout, is that the two tracks must be joined in a
single architecture rather than coordinated across separate ones: statutory duties supply the
demand for evidence, and the transparency lineage supplies its production [15, 16, 17].
2.3 The verification gap in AI agent stacks
 The security community has codified the agent threat surface faster than it has
architected against it. The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, whose
2025 edition placed prompt injection at rank one, catalogs the ways in which untrusted
content becomes instruction: direct injection through user-supplied text, indirect injection
through retrieved documents and tool outputs, and the disclosure or corruption of state that
follows [13]. The 2026 edition extends the catalog toward agentic concerns — memory
poisoning, tool misuse, and cascading failures in systems that compose models with each
other and with infrastructure [14]. The catalog is valuable as a taxonomy of failure, but a
taxonomy is not a control set: OWASP tells the engineer what goes wrong, and leaves open
the architectural question of what to build so that it cannot go wrong silently. That omission
is the space this book occupies.
 The tool layer illustrates the omission concretely. The Model Context Protocol,
published as a specification in 2025, standardizes stateful JSON-RPC 2.0 sessions between
LLM applications and servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts, and has become
the de facto interchange format of the agentic ecosystem [108]. Within months of its
adoption, researchers documented tool poisoning attacks: malicious instructions embedded
in tool descriptions, which the model consumes as instructions rather than as data, directing
it to exfiltrate session context, to misrepresent available functionality, or to shadow trusted
tools with attacker-controlled look-alikes [109]. The attack succeeds because the
description field is a representation with authority but no verifiable provenance —
precisely the pattern of the Bybit interface, relocated from the transaction to the tool
catalog. No MCP-level mechanism today allows a relying party to verify who authored a
tool description, when it changed, or what policy it satisfies [108, 109].
 One layer down, the model artifact itself is an unattested binary in most pipelines.
Serialized Python pickle files — the dominant distribution format for many model families
— allow arbitrary code execution at load time, and researchers have repeatedly
demonstrated the consequence: in February 2024, JFrog reported models on a public hub
whose loading executed silent malicious code [120], and in February 2025, ReversingLabs
catalogued further malicious models with payload-bearing serialized objects [119].


=== PAGINA 48 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 48
Platform-level defenses arrived after the fact: Hugging Face now scans pickle-based
uploads for dangerous constructs [118], and the PickleBall line of work proposes safer
deserialization with format-level constraints [121]. GGUF, the single-file container for
open-weight language models, removes the code-execution surface but not the provenance
problem: nothing in the container binds the weights to a publisher, a training-run identity,
or a policy [26, 27]. The artifact is content-addressable in principle and unaddressed in
practice — a gap that Chapter 10 turns into a product.
 Threat modeling has followed the same codify-without-architecting pattern. MITRE's
ATLAS matrix, at version 5.1.0, organizes the adversarial landscape for AI systems into 16
tactics and 84 techniques supported by 42 real-world case studies, giving defenders a
shared language for reconnaissance, initial access, model exfiltration, and persistence
[112]. The companion SAFE-AI framework extends the analysis to securing AI-enabled
systems end to end, and is explicit that controls must attach to the systems-engineering
lifecycle rather than to the model alone [113]. What ATLAS and SAFE-AI do not supply is
an evidence substrate: techniques are named, tactics sequenced, and case studies narrated,
but no mechanism in the framework proves that a given control operated during a given
action. The matrix tells an architect where the adversary will knock; it does not build the
door.
 The governance instruments, reviewed in Section 2.2 from the design side, look
different from the compliance side. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework asks
organizations to govern, map, measure, and manage, and its measurement function
presumes records that can support claims about system behavior [15]. ISO/IEC 42001:2023
makes the management system auditable in the management-system sense, with
documented-information requirements that map naturally onto evidence records [16]. The
EU AI Act goes furthest: Article 12 requires that high-risk systems log events
automatically over their lifetime, with conditions on the logs' sufficiency and integrity, and
the Act's phased timeline — entry into force in August 2024, general applicability from 2
August 2026, and high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 —
converts the logging duty into a near-term engineering requirement [17, 18, 19, 117].
 Logging, however, is not verification, and the difference is this section's conclusion. A
log is produced by the system it describes, stored where the operator controls, and read by
whoever the operator permits; it is assurance in evidentiary clothing. Verification requires
that the record be born with integrity guarantees — content addressing, signatures by
parties other than the writer, inclusion in infrastructure the operator cannot rewrite — and
that a third party be able to re-check the record without the operator's cooperation. The
instruments above demand evidence-shaped outputs while specifying none of the
mechanisms that make outputs evidentiary; the agent stacks reviewed below supply
mechanisms but not governance. The gap between the two lists is, in one sentence, the


=== PAGINA 49 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 49
market that the architecture of Part II addresses [15, 17].
2.4 Related systems and the identified gap
 Adjacent technical literature clusters into groups that each solve part of the problem,
and locating the gap requires saying precisely what each group does not do. Sandboxed
execution — from operating-system containers to WebAssembly — supplies containment
primitives that the VTK kernel layer reuses conceptually; containment bounds what a
deceived agent can do, but says nothing about the evidence trail of what it did, and
containment without evidence produces quiet failures. Policy engines and declarative
access-control models supply the style that constitution-as-code adopts — rules external to
code, evaluated at decision time — but the rules are typically governed by the same
operator the rules police, so the Bybit pattern of self-certification reappears at the policy
layer. Formal verification infrastructure, most prominently the Lean 4 proof assistant and
its mathematical library mathlib, supplies the strongest known form of artifact verification
for mathematical claims, and is the target environment of the program in Chapter 22 [62,
63, 124, 125].
 Blockchain-native security tooling addresses the human-approval gap that Chapter 1
identified. Transaction simulators model the state effects of a signed transaction before
execution; decoding layers translate opaque calldata into human-readable summaries; and
the clear-signing movement pushes decoded semantics onto the signing device itself, so
that the hardware wallet displays what the transaction does rather than a hash of what
someone claims it does [1, 38]. These are genuine advances, and the counterfactual analysis
of Chapter 7 shows the decoding gate to be the single most valuable control for the custody
class of incidents. The tooling nevertheless covers only the transaction domain: it has
nothing to say about the provenance of the models that may be generating the transactions,
the governance of the rules that decide which transactions are permitted, or the anchoring
of the resulting evidence [2, 6].
 A wave of 2025–2026 product launches constitutes the emerging agentic infrastructure
industry. Coinbase's AgentKit and its agentic wallets give AI agents authenticated,
monitored access to blockchain wallets, with telemetry and security monitoring aimed at
institutional deployments [115, 116]. Circle's Agent Stack provides infrastructure for
autonomous agent wallets and programmable wallet operations, positioning stablecoin rails
as a default settlement layer for agent-to-agent commerce [149]. These systems solve
access and transport — who the agent is, what it may touch, where value moves — and
their monitoring is, again, operator-controlled assurance rather than third-party-checkable
evidence. None of them binds the agent's model artifact to a policy, anchors its decisions
outside the operator's perimeter, or separates the definition of rules from the recording of
events.


=== PAGINA 50 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 50
 Industry frameworks one level higher confirm that the category is forming. The
Know-Your-Agent interoperability framework announced by Ant International, with Visa
and Mastercard as collaborators, in September 2026 extends the know-your-customer
tradition to autonomous agents, proposing interoperable verification of agent identity and
behavior across institutions [39, 40]. In media, the Coalition for Content Provenance and
Authenticity standardizes cryptographically signed provenance for digital content — origin
and edit history attached to images, video, and documents [114]. C2PA evidences content,
and Know-Your-Agent frameworks propose to evidence agents; neither evidences the
binding among a model, the policy under which it acts, and the evidence record of what it
did, and neither is designed to survive its own supply chain being compromised, which is
the failure class Chapter 1 documented. The pattern across the industry is consistent:
identity and provenance are being solved piecewise, and the joining layer is missing.
 Across all groups, the gap this book addresses can be stated in one sentence: no openly
specified, implementable stack unifies agent containment, model attestation, an
append-only causal evidence graph, quorum-based rule governance, and regulatory-grade
evidence export in one system whose authority is structurally separated from its witnesses.
Each ingredient exists separately in mature or emerging form; the unification — with the
discipline it imposes on who may define rules, who may witness events, and who may
change either — is the contribution. Stated as a binding requirement: end-to-end
verification means that the model hash binds to the policy version under which it was
loaded, the policy version binds to the quorum that enacted it, and the decision binds to an
anchored evidence record that names all three, with each link independently checkable by a
party that trusts none of the operators. No system surveyed in this chapter offers that chain,
and the survey above is offered as the falsifiable basis of that claim.
 The claim is necessarily modest in scope and aggressive only in integration. VTK is a
design and an early implementation [28], not a deployed system with production telemetry;
its governance claims rest on internal specifications [29, 31] whose epistemic status Section
1.5 fixed; and adoption data for agent-trust tooling generally remains thin — one industry
survey places verified-agent tooling at single-digit percentages of the adoption dimensions
it measures, which suggests that the market is earlier than the incident record implies [161].
What the design demonstrates today is that the unification is coherent, that it responds to
documented failure modes rather than to hypothetical ones, and that it is achievable with
standardized, independently evaluated components rather than with new cryptography
[104, 105]. With the vocabulary fixed, the lineage identified, the gap located, and the
epistemic rules stated, Part II can proceed to the architecture itself: Chapter 3 presents the
design principles and the six-layer trust stack, and Figure 3.1 gives the reader its single
most useful mental model [28].


=== PAGINA 51 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 51
PART II — ARCHITECTURE OF THE
VERIFIABLE TRUST KERNEL
Four chapters specify the machine. Chapter 3 states the six design principles with their
falsifiers and the four load-bearing elements. Chapter 4 grounds the pipeline in
cryptographic and systems foundations, from BLAKE3 and ML-DSA to transparency logs
and WebAssembly verification. Chapter 5 maps the Rust crate ecosystem and the
repository, including the TLA+-checked invariant set. Chapter 6 develops governance:
constitution-as-code, the authority–witness separation, the ADR-011 quorum decision, and
the VetoGraph lineage that connects governance to graph theory.
3. Design Principles and Load-Bearing Elements
3.1 Six design principles
 The architecture rests on six design principles that recur throughout the project corpus
and that the incident analysis of Chapter 7 treats as the specification against which failures
are judged [28, 31]. The principles are stated here as commitments with falsifiers rather
than as aspirations: for each, this section names the observation that would count as
evidence that VTK does not implement it. The discipline matters because trust architectures
are unusually prone to principle inflation, the gradual accumulation of slogans that no test
could ever embarrass. A principle that cannot be falsified is decoration; a principle that can
be falsified becomes a target for the test suite, the model checker, and the external auditor
alike. The six principles — prove rather than promise, fail-closed, honest status, separation
of powers, non-custodial operation, and layered verification — are therefore presented in a
fixed format: content, rationale, and falsifier.
 The first principle, prove rather than promise, holds that whenever a security-relevant
claim can be replaced by a checkable artifact, the artifact wins [28]. The claim that a model
is the one that was evaluated becomes a hash comparison; the claim that a signature was
approved by quorum becomes a verifiable multisignature record; the claim that a log was
not rewritten becomes a consistency proof against an externally witnessed tree head [8, 9].
Verbal assurance is not banned — operators still write documentation — but it is demoted
to commentary on artifacts rather than accepted as evidence in its own right. The principle
descends directly from the post-mortem observation that the largest losses in the incident
record occurred where a promise was the only control present [2, 96].
 Prove rather than promise also disciplines the project's own claims. Every capability
advertised for VTK — kernel containment, model attestation, WormGraph anchoring,
quorum governance — is expected to ship with the artifact that demonstrates it, and where


=== PAGINA 52 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 52
a capability is not yet demonstrated the architecture requires that it be labeled as pending
under the honest-status rule rather than silently implied [28, 31]. The falsifier is direct: if
any load-bearing security decision in a deployed VTK system cannot be traced to a
machine-checkable artifact, the principle is violated, and the implementation — not the
auditor — must change. Chapter 10 operationalizes the principle for model verification by
defining falsifiable success metrics for the MVP before implementation begins.
 The second principle, fail-closed, specifies the direction of every ambiguity: an action
that is not explicitly permitted is denied, and the denial itself becomes evidence [28].
Fail-closed behavior appears at every layer of the stack — the kernel denies unlisted
capability uses, the verifier rejects unparseable or unanchored records rather than admitting
them with a warning, and the governance layer treats a lapsed quorum as a freeze rather
than as an invitation to improvised action. The alternative, fail-open design, is attractive in
demonstrations and catastrophic in custody, because it converts every bug, every parser
quirk, and every outage into a potential authorization. The incident record supports the
strict reading: the StablR minting failure and the Bybit interface compromise both
succeeded through paths that a default-deny posture would have closed [2, 6, 33].
 Fail-closed is also the principle that makes the others testable. Because the permitted
set is enumerable, the denial path can be exercised systematically: the fuzz targets in the
repository hammer the verification functions with malformed inputs and require rejection,
and the kernel test suite asserts that out-of-envelope actions produce structured denial
events rather than undefined behavior [28]. The falsifier is correspondingly concrete: any
single demonstrated case in which an undefined, unlisted, or malformed input results in
permissive behavior — a successful signature over an undecoded payload, a model load
with a mismatched digest, an action taken while the constitution is unavailable — falsifies
the claim that VTK is fail-closed. Availability pressure is acknowledged as the historical
enemy of this principle, which is why Chapter 6 treats liveness explicitly rather than
pretending the trade-off away.
 The third principle, honest status, requires that the system report what is known, what
is partially established, and what is not known, using the same vocabulary for internal
displays and external reports [28, 31]. Verification results are three-valued rather than
binary: verified means re-derived from artifacts by executable checks; partial means some
gates passed and the remainder are named; pending means no evidence exists yet. The
governance interface applies the same discipline to invariants, distinguishing invariants
checked by the model checker from those covered only by unit tests and those merely
declared [28]. The contrast is with security interfaces that flatten everything to a green
checkmark — a presentation choice the Bybit case showed can be weaponized, since the
attacker controlled exactly what the approver saw [1, 2, 95].


=== PAGINA 53 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 53
 Honest status extends to the project's self-description. Where a component is a design
rather than an implementation, or an implementation rather than an audited one, the corpus
says so; the repository even carries a proposed registry for documenting fabricated or
unverified sources as such, an artifact whose existence encodes the principle [28]. The
falsifier is: any instance in which the system presents an unverified or partially verified
state as fully verified — a pending invariant displayed as checked, an unanchored record
rendered as anchored — refutes the implementation. This principle is the epistemic
foundation on which the verifiable trust layer stands, because a verifier that lies about its
own certainty is worse than no verifier at all: it manufactures false assurance with
cryptographic packaging.
 The fourth principle, separation of powers, divides authority from witness. The
authority — the ConstitutionStore — defines what events mean: the invariants, thresholds,
timelocks, and capability rules under which the system operates. The witness — a Safe
multisig in the reference deployment — attests that events occurred and approves
privileged actions under the rules the authority defines [25, 28]. The distinction sounds
scholastic until one observes that most multisignature custody systems conflate the two
roles, holding the rules in the same hands, and often the same hardware, as the keys that
approve events. The StablR post-mortem in Chapter 7 argues that this recorder-definer
collapse is precisely what converted a single compromised key into the unilateral minting
of thirteen and a half million dollars of stablecoins [6, 33].
 Structurally, the separation is enforced by making rules data and amendments events:
the ConstitutionStore is versioned and hashed, and every amendment requires quorum
under the project's decision record ADR-011, so the rulebook cannot drift silently [29]. The
falsifier follows: if the party that records history can also redefine what history should have
been — if a witness key set can alter thresholds, invariants, or capability rules without a
quorum-governed amendment — the separation is violated. Section 6.1 develops the role
model in detail, and Figure 6.1 there summarizes the topology. The principle is the
governance analogue of the non-custodial rule below: one prevents concentrated power
over assets, the other concentrated power over meaning.
 The fifth principle, non-custodial operation, holds that the architecture must not
concentrate custody of assets, or of the keys that control them, at any single point —
including its own runtime [28]. An agent operating under VTK spends through mediated,
policy-bounded transactions, and the reference custody design splits high-value keys across
independent operators using distributed-validator techniques, so that no operator, vendor,
or kernel instance ever holds a complete high-value secret [138, 139]. The principle is
aimed at a failure mode the agentic-AI market is currently reproducing at speed: platforms
that hold agent keys, define agent permissions, and audit their own behavior from the same
infrastructure, a pattern now visible across the emerging agentic-wallet offerings [115,


=== PAGINA 54 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 54
116]. Non-custodial operation is what makes the difference between an agent that uses a
treasury and a treasury that trusts an agent.
 The falsifier is: any single point — a key, a server, a vendor API, a kernel process —
whose compromise yields irrevocable control over assets or over the evidence layer itself.
Practical deployments will always retain some residual concentration, and the architecture's
response is to shrink and enumerate it rather than deny it: the trust-base inventory of
Chapter 4 and the threat model of Section 4.4 exist precisely to keep the residual visible. It
should be noted that non-custodial is a property of the design's target state; the
decentralization roadmap in Chapter 18 grades current components against it and records
the gaps. Where full non-custodial operation is not yet achievable, honest status requires
saying so [28].
 The sixth principle, layered verification, holds that no single check is sufficient and
that checks must be independent of the thing they check. The four-gate pipeline — hash,
signature, inclusion, quorum — is the canonical sequence, and it is deliberately redundant:
a payload must survive digest verification, signature verification, transparency-log
inclusion, and quorum evaluation before it is admissible [28]. Layering also has a temporal
sense: detection runs continuously at the kernel, post-selection verification runs at load and
approval time, and full third-party verification runs offline against anchored evidence. The
design inherits this redundancy from certificate-transparency deployments, where monitors
and gossip keep a log honest precisely because multiple independent observers check it [8,
11, 12].
 The falsifier is: any load-bearing claim accepted on the strength of a single gate — a
signature without inclusion, an inclusion proof without quorum context, a hash match
without signature attribution. When such an acceptance occurs in the reference
implementation, the layering claim is falsified and the pipeline must be corrected. Layered
verification is also the principle that converts the other five from intentions into an
architecture: prove rather than promise supplies the artifacts, fail-closed supplies the
default, honest status supplies the reporting vocabulary, separation of powers supplies the
governance topology, and non-custodial operation supplies the custody constraints. The
remainder of Part II is, in effect, the six principles unfolded into crates, schemas, and
decision records.
 Table 3.1 condenses the six principles into commitment and falsifier statements, and it
is intended to function as an audit checklist: each falsifier maps to specific tests,
model-checking runs, and review procedures in the repository [28, 29]. A falsifier that has
never been exercised is treated, under honest status, as an untested claim rather than a
satisfied requirement. The same table anchors the architecture's overall shape, which Figure
3.1 renders as a six-layer trust stack. Reading the figure from the bottom, payloads are


=== PAGINA 55 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 55
verified independently, constrained by the kernel, turned into signed evidence, registered
immutably, and judged against quorum-governed invariants, with the right-hand column
holding the external surfaces — the transparency log, independent witnesses,
browser-runnable verifiers, and the ConstitutionStore — that make the whole design
falsifiable from outside the vendor perimeter [28]. Every layer in the figure corresponds to
crates and schemas cataloged in Chapter 5, so the principles, the picture, and the code are
intended to remain one object viewed three ways.

3.2 The kernel of containment
 The kernel of containment is the layer at which an agent's statements about itself are
replaced by enforceable bounds. In the implemented design, arkhe-core defines the agent's
resource envelope — callable tools, data domains, network reach, spending authority —
and enforces a fail-closed policy: an action not explicitly permitted by the active
constitution is denied, and the denial itself becomes evidence [28]. The design borrows its
philosophy from decades of systems work on sandboxing and least privilege, but applies it
at the semantic boundary of agentic behavior. What is contained is not only memory and
processor time but authority: which counterparties may be contacted, which contracts may
be called, and which signatures may be produced on the agent's behalf. This reframing
matters because agentic failures rarely begin with memory corruption; they begin with an
agent exercising an authority nobody deliberately granted it.
 Four canonical types anchor the kernel's vocabulary, and they are deliberately austere.
A Session is a bounded execution context: a unit of agent activity with a start, an envelope,
and an auditable termination. A Principal is an identified actor — human, agent, or service
— carrying a cryptographic identity that evidence records can cite. A Capability is an
unforgeable reference to a specific right, such as invoking one tool or writing one memory
region, and a MemoryRegion is a declared, size-bounded span of storage that a session may
read or write [28]. These types live in arkhe-core/src/lib.rs, and their austerity is the point: a
kernel whose vocabulary fits in a paragraph is a kernel whose behavior can be stated in a
model checker, which is exactly where the project takes it next [28].


=== PAGINA 57 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 57
 Capability tokens are the mechanism that converts this envelope from documentation
into enforcement. Every privileged operation — contacting a domain, invoking a tool,
signing above a spending threshold — passes through a mediation point that consults the
active Capability Manifest and the constitution version in force before the operation
executes. The design follows the object-capability tradition in that rights are held rather
than asked for: there is no ambient authority that a persuasive prompt or a clever tool
description can summon, a property that matters given documented tool-poisoning attacks
against protocol-level tool registries [108, 109]. Mediation decisions are structured events,
so a denied action is as visible in the WormGraph as an executed one. Policy versioning
binds every decision to the constitution version under which it was taken, which lets an
auditor reconstruct not only what the agent did but under which rules.
 Fail-closed semantics at the kernel are specified more tightly than the slogan suggests.
The policy evaluator is total: every input, including malformed or adversarial ones, yields
exactly one of permit, deny, or escalate, and any internal error resolves to deny rather than
to a permissive fallback. Human-in-the-loop approvals resolve to denial on timeout — the
deny-on-timeout rule — so that silence can never be interpreted as consent [28]. Denials
are first-class evidence carrying the same schema as executions, which is what makes the
denial rate itself an auditable quantity. This is the layer where the fail-closed principle of
Section 3.1 stops being a preference and becomes a type-level property of the system.
 The kernel's behavior is pinned by a catalog of twenty numbered invariants, I-01
through I-20, defined formally in arkhe-core/src/invariants.rs and accompanied by TLA+
models that check them [28]. The invariant families include graph immutability and
append-only growth for the evidence layer, capability monotonicity and envelope
containment for sessions, fail-closed policy evaluation, quorum integrity for governance
actions, and anchoring consistency between internal records and external transparency logs.
Model checking complements testing rather than duplicating it: a unit test samples the state
space, while a model checker explores it exhaustively within stated bounds and returns
counterexamples when an invariant can be violated. The project's honest-status discipline
applies here as well, distinguishing invariants that are model-checked from those covered
only by unit tests and those so far merely declared [28, 31]. Section 5.4 describes how these
statuses are maintained in practice.
 The kernel is also where the architecture's threat model becomes concrete, and Figure
3.2 summarizes that model by placing four adversary classes against the layers of the agent
stack. The compromised signer (A1) holds a key inside an authorization threshold; the
interface adversary (A2) controls what an approver sees rather than what is signed; the
supply-chain adversary (A3) corrupts an artifact before deployment; and the governance
insider (A4) changes what the system's rules mean [28]. Each class exploits unverified
representations at a different layer, and the kernel is the first structural obstruction that


=== PAGINA 58 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 58
classes A2 and A3 encounter, because unmediated authority simply does not exist at this
layer. Section 4.4 develops the classes formally and maps each to the verification gate that
answers it; the immediate task, however, is the first artifact any deployment should verify
— the model file itself.
 Figure 3.2 — The agent stack and its attack surfaces. Four adversary classes (A1–A4) exploit unverified
 representations at different layers.
3.3 Model attestation: the model file as the first artifact
 Model attestation binds a model artifact to an identity that downstream policy can
reason about, and the design takes GGUF — the GPT-Generated Unified Format used by
llama.cpp and the dominant container for open-weight language models — as its canonical
target [26, 27]. A GGUF file is a single, self-describing binary: a fixed header carrying a
magic value and a version, a metadata section of key-value pairs recording architecture,
context length, and quantization, and a tensor directory of typed, offset-addressed entries
followed by the weight bytes themselves. The format carries data rather than executable
semantics, which keeps it clear of the deserialization hazards that afflict pickled model
formats — hazards that are not theoretical, since malicious pickle-based models have been
discovered on public model hubs [118, 119, 120] and hardened deserialization remains an
active research problem [121]. Choosing a data-only container is therefore itself a security
decision: it removes an entire class of before-the-first-token attacks from the default path.
 The attestation anchor is the SHA-256 hash of the file's bytes, which serves as a stable
identity that any party can re-derive offline. Local tooling reinforces the premise that this
identity is meaningful: Ollama's import path uses GGUF artifacts as provided, without
requantization or rewriting, so the file a user obtains is, byte for byte, the file that executes


=== PAGINA 59 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 59
[163]. This is why the project calls the model file the first artifact: before prompts are
written, tools are registered, or actions are authorized, there is a concrete object whose
integrity can and should be established. A deployment that later loads the model re-derives
the digest and compares it against an anchored attestation record, converting the claim we
believe we are running model X into the claim the bytes we loaded are provably the bytes
that were attested as model X.
 Attestation proceeds in three steps, each of which is implemented in the verification
crate described in Chapter 5. First, the digest is computed: the parser validates the header
(parse_header) and the digester streams the file (model_digest), so structure and identity
are established together. Second, the publisher's signature, license, declared training-data
status, and any declared safety evaluations are collected into an arkhe.attestation.* evidence
record with an explicit schema version [28, 70]. Third, the record is anchored in a
transparency log, so that its existence and timestamp are witnessed outside the operator's
perimeter [9]. The full JSON shape of the record appears as a listing in Section 5.3.
 Two limitations are acknowledged from the outset, because overstated attestation is
itself a trust hazard. Attestation establishes identity, not quality: a perfectly attested model
may still be malign, and the evidence record therefore includes declared evaluations rather
than certifications of behavior, with the honest-status vocabulary marking what each field
actually asserts [28, 31]. Attestation is also only as strong as the binding between the digest
and the executing process, which is why the kernel layer — not the attestation layer —
remains the ultimate enforcement point: an attested model still runs inside a session whose
capabilities, memory regions, and spending limits are independently bounded. The
architecture's position is that identity is a necessary substrate for quality assurance, not a
substitute for it, and that confusing the two is how checklists come to replace judgment.
 The scope of the promise is kept deliberately narrow. The MVP specified in Chapter 10
verifies that the file a user is about to run is the file that was attested — nothing more —
and it measures whether that narrow promise is one users value [31]. Keeping the promise
narrow is what makes it falsifiable: success and failure are defined as observable outcomes
(digest match, inclusion verified, user decision), not as sentiment. The attestation schema,
the verification functions, and the anchoring discipline are all designed so that this single
claim survives audit intact, and Chapter 4 supplies the cryptographic machinery on which it
rests.
 Attestation also has a lifecycle, and the design treats it as evidence rather than as state.
A model update is a new artifact with a new digest and a new attestation record, never a
mutation of the old one; supersession is expressed, WormGraph-style, by a new node that
references its predecessor, so that the question of which version was attested when always
has a cryptographic answer [28, 70]. Revocation propagates as evidence as well: a


=== PAGINA 60 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 60
publisher's revocation entry causes downstream policy to refuse the revoked digest at load
time, and the refusal is itself recorded. The design keeps the revocation problem tractable
by keeping the identity space small — digests, not names — because names can be reused
while digests cannot [9].
3.4 The WormGraph: an immutable causal evidence graph
 The WormGraph is the architecture's memory: an append-only directed graph in which
nodes represent events, decisions, artifacts, and evidence records, and edges represent
explicit causal or derivational dependencies [28, 70]. Each node carries the SHA-256 hash
of its canonical content, an Ed25519 signature over that hash plus metadata, references to
its parent nodes, and — where the node has been anchored — the index of its entry in a
transparency log [9]. The graph is a worm in the sense of write-once storage: history
accumulates and branches but is never rewritten. Errors are handled the way public ledgers
handle errors, by new entries that supersede rather than by edits that erase.
 The node anatomy rewards a closer look, because every field exists to answer an audit
question. The content hash answers the identity question; the signature over the canonical
body answers the attribution question; the parent references answer the provenance
question, tying each node to the events that caused it. The implementation models this as a
ProvenanceNode carrying a record_hash that binds metadata and content into a single
verifiable value, and the append-only evidence chain computes equivalent hashes for its
records [28]. An abridged evidence node, with its inclusion-proof and anchor fields,
appears as a listing in Section 4.2, where the anchoring machinery is presented.
 The causal structure is what makes the WormGraph more than a hash chain. Because
edges are first-class, an auditor can answer questions that flat logs cannot: which attestation
records contributed to this deployment decision; which constitution version was in force
along the path that produced this signature; which downstream artifacts must be
re-examined if this upstream model hash is revoked. The query layer supports cross-model
and cross-domain traversal, so that evidence produced by one agent run can be cited,
checked, and reused by another without either runtime trusting the other [28]. This is the
property the project calls semantic evidence, and it is the property the regulatory analysis
relies on when it argues that the architecture produces audit trails with legal texture rather
than undifferentiated event streams [17, 18, 28].
 Immutability inside the operator's infrastructure, however, is a claim that needs help
from outside it, and the WormGraph is designed to receive that help. Anchoring nodes to
external transparency logs converts internal append-only storage into externally detectable
append-only storage: an operator who silently rewrites the graph can no longer produce a
consistency proof against tree heads already witnessed by third parties [8, 9]. The storage


=== PAGINA 61 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 61
layer complements this with content addressing, so that payloads referenced by the graph
are themselves hash-named and can live in any store that respects their digest [28]. Section
4.2 develops the anchoring design in full, and the threat model of Section 4.4 prices what it
defends against.
 The graph also plays a coordination role that goes beyond record-keeping. Because the
WormGraph is append-only, content-addressed, and queryable, later project work treats it
as a shared environment on which multiple agents can coordinate stigmergically — leaving
traces that modify the conditions for subsequent traces — rather than communicating only
through message passing [28]. The governance documentation records this as a distinct
design decision with its own amendment record, and it is mentioned here because it
explains why the graph's query interface is a first-class component rather than an
afterthought. A memory that agents coordinate through must be exactly as trustworthy as
the agents themselves, which is the property the preceding paragraphs construct.
 A final design point concerns failure behavior. A node without an anchor is admissible
but visibly weaker, and consumers of the graph can demand anchoring for node kinds that
matter: governance events, attestations of deployed models, and signatures above threshold
[70]. Missing parents, malformed signatures, and unknown schema versions are not silently
tolerated; they surface as verification failures under the fail-closed rule, because a causal
graph that accepts broken edges is worse than one that refuses them. The result is a memory
whose trustworthiness is a property of every node individually and of the graph's structure
collectively — which is precisely what the governance layer of the next section needs to
stand on.
3.5 Invariant governance and the ConstitutionStore
 Governance closes the loop that the previous sections opened. Invariants are declared
in a constitution-as-code corpus held in the ConstitutionStore; each invariant is a
machine-checkable property over evidence records, and each amendment to the corpus is
itself an evidence event requiring quorum under the project's decision record ADR-011
[29]. The ConstitutionStore is versioned and hashed, so the rulebook in force at any
moment is an artifact rather than a memory. Nothing in the architecture's security story
survives the loss of this property: a rulebook that can drift silently is indistinguishable from
no rulebook at all.
 The separation of powers is enforced structurally rather than by convention. A Safe
multisig may witness that an event occurred and may approve privileged actions under the
rules, but only the ConstitutionStore, amended by quorum, may define what events mean
[25, 28]. The rationale is operational as well as philosophical: the post-mortem analysis in
Chapter 7 argues that low-threshold multisigs fail precisely when witnessing and authority


=== PAGINA 62 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 62
collapse into one small key set, as the StablR configuration did [6, 33]. Section 6.1
develops the full role model, and Chapter 7 supplies the counterfactual computations.
 Amendment is a workflow, not a keystroke. A proposed change to thresholds,
invariants, or capabilities enters as a proposal; approvals accumulate against the trust root;
the quorum requirement and the timelock — seven days for standard changes, fourteen for
critical ones — are checked by code rather than by custom; and the amended constitution
enters force as a new version with its own hash [28, 29]. Because each step is an evidence
event, the complete amendment history of the rulebook is itself auditable, and any
deployment's behavior can be reconstructed against the exact rules that were in force at the
time. This is the property that makes the record-keeping obligations discussed in Chapter 9
tractable rather than aspirational.
 The governance interface applies honest status to the rulebook itself. Invariants are
displayed with their verification provenance — checked by the model checker, covered by
tests, or declared — and the same status vocabulary is exposed programmatically through
the platform's query tools, so that external monitors see what internal reviewers see [28].
The display discipline is not cosmetic. A governance layer that renders its own uncertainty
as certainty would reproduce, inside the architecture, exactly the failure pattern that the
architecture exists to prevent.
 Constitution-as-code also disciplines the drafting of rules. Every invariant must cite its
basis — the incident, decision record, or external requirement that motivates it — which
turns the corpus into an argument map rather than a pile of assertions [28, 29]. Rules that
cannot state why they exist can be challenged and removed; rules that can state why can be
re-derived when circumstances change. Section 6.2 shows the discipline applied to the
most consequential rule in the system, the quorum threshold, and Section 6.3 supplies the
mathematics that makes the choice falsifiable.
 The ConstitutionStore's limits are acknowledged rather than hidden. It governs
meaning, not virtue: a quorum can still approve a bad rule, and the machinery will execute
it faithfully, which is why the governance layer is paired with the veto topology described
in Section 6.4 and audited against a real constitution in Chapter 20. It is also not yet a
decentralized protocol in itself; the decentralization roadmap in Chapter 18 grades the
current implementation against the non-custodial principle and records the gaps honestly
[28]. What the ConstitutionStore delivers today is narrower and therefore defensible: rules
as versioned, hashed, quorum-governed data, with an amendment trail that any third party
can replay.
3.6 Explicit non-goals


=== PAGINA 63 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 63
 A design is also defined by what it declines to include, and the architecture's exclusions
are load-bearing rather than incidental. The first non-goal is trusted hardware: attested
execution environments — enclaves and confidential virtual machines — are a
complementary containment technology with a different trust basis, and the design treats
them as pluggable strengthening rather than as a dependency [28]. The reason is evidential:
a hardware root of trust shifts the argument from checkable artifacts to vendor attestation,
and the supply-chain and side-channel posture of each enclave platform must be argued per
platform, per firmware version, and per vendor. Where deployments already operate
enclaves, the architecture records their attestation as additional evidence; it does not make
the correctness of its own claims depend on it.
 The second non-goal is blockchain settlement: the evidence registry is not a consensus
ledger. Anchoring uses established transparency-log infrastructure, whose append-only
Merkle trees and consistency proofs deliver auditability with far lower cost and latency
than consensus settlement [8, 9]. The trade is deliberate: trustless verification of every entry
is surrendered in exchange for detection of tampering by any auditor who retains a tree
head, which is the property the evidence layer actually needs. A settle-to-chain bridge
remains a defined extension for deployments whose auditors demand it, and the anchoring
interface is written so that such a bridge is an additional anchor kind rather than a redesign
[28].
 The third non-goal is zero-knowledge proofs, at least for the present sequencing. A
future direction is to attest that a payload satisfies a policy without disclosing the payload
itself, which would matter for commercially sensitive flows and for evidence that carries
personal data. The project's sequencing places general-purpose evidence integrity first,
however, because advanced cryptography only adds value once the governance layer that
makes its outputs meaningful is itself trustworthy [28]. A zero-knowledge proof of
compliance with a rulebook that can drift silently would certify compliance with nothing in
particular.
 A fourth exclusion follows from the universal-core thesis: the architecture ships
mechanisms, not policies. The crates verify, contain, record, and govern; the invariants,
thresholds, and capability rules that make a deployment concrete are local configuration,
owned by the deploying organization and expressed in the ConstitutionStore and its
Capability Manifests [28]. Shipping a reference policy would quietly re-centralize authority
in the vendor — precisely the recorder-definer collapse that the separation of powers
forbids — and would turn the sector adapters of Chapter 13 into forks of the core rather
than configurations of it. The design consequence is visible throughout Part IV: the
universal core is identical everywhere, and what varies is the local tier, never the
verification mathematics [28].


=== PAGINA 64 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 64
 The fifth exclusion is global identity. The architecture mints no universal registry of
agents; principals are cryptographic, and their meaning is fixed by the trust root of the
deployment that evaluates them, following the local-trust-root principle of the adaptation
analysis [28]. A global agent-identity registry would reintroduce a single point of
definitional power — who counts as a legitimate agent — that the governance design exists
to distribute, and industry interoperability efforts are converging on framework-level,
issuer-diverse approaches for the same reason [39]. Where cross-organization recognition
of agent identity is needed, it is achieved by anchored evidence and explicit cross-trust-root
acceptance, recorded as ordinary evidence events rather than as membership in a hidden
registry [28].
 Non-goals are maintained with the same discipline as requirements, because scope is a
security parameter. Each exclusion in this section carries an explicit re-entry criterion:
trusted hardware returns when a platform's attestation chain can be verified from public
roots; settlement returns when an auditor class requires it and accepts its costs;
zero-knowledge techniques return when the policy language they would compile is stable.
The honest-status rule applies to the boundary itself — components are not described as
supporting what they do not support — and the exclusion list is reviewed at each
constitution version. What the exclusions buy is a smaller surface to verify, and a smaller
surface is the one luxury a verification-first architecture cannot decline.
4. Cryptographic and Systems Foundations
4.1 Content addressing and signatures
 Two cryptographic primitives carry most of the architecture's daily load. SHA-256
provides content addressing: because the hash of an artifact is computed from its bytes,
identity and integrity collapse into one operation, and any party can re-derive it offline.
Ed25519 provides attribution: deterministic signatures, fast verification, and a public key
that serves as a stable actor identifier inside the WormGraph. The choice of Ed25519 over
ECDSA variants is pragmatic rather than ideological — deterministic signing removes a
class of nonce-reuse failures, and the scheme's verification cost suits the third-party
verification target of the principles [28]. All signature material in the evidence layer binds,
at minimum, the content hash, the author key, a timestamp, and the constitution version in
force.
 For large artifacts the architecture adds BLAKE3, a hash function designed around a
Merkle tree of fixed-size chunks, so that hashing parallelizes across cores and can be
verified incrementally as a stream [106]. The repository's storage layer implements content
addressing over both SHA-256 and BLAKE3, reserving the latter for high-throughput paths


=== PAGINA 65 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 65
such as digesting multi-gigabyte model files and indexing content-addressed chunks [28].
The division of labor is explicit rather than accidental: SHA-256 remains the canonical
identity for cross-tool compatibility and for transparency-log leaf entries, while BLAKE3
serves where throughput, not interoperability, is the binding constraint. Keeping two
algorithms with clearly separated roles is cheaper, in audit terms, than pretending one
algorithm is optimal everywhere.
 The second cryptographic axis is the post-quantum transition. NIST finalized the
module-lattice signature standard ML-DSA as FIPS 204, published on 13 August 2024,
alongside companion standards for key encapsulation and hashing [104, 105]. The
motivation for adopting lattice signatures in an evidence architecture is the
retroactive-forgery risk: evidence signed today may still be disputed in fifteen years, and a
signature scheme that a future quantum adversary could forge after the fact would hollow
out the entire WormGraph. The costs are real — lattice signatures and their public keys are
orders of magnitude larger than Ed25519 material, which inflates evidence records and
anchoring payloads — and the architecture treats those costs as parameters to be paid
selectively rather than uniformly [104].
 The transition mechanism is hybridization. The project's hybrid module follows the
composition pattern of X-Wing — the construction that pairs a classical primitive with a
lattice primitive so that the combination remains secure if either component survives —
and instantiates it for signatures by pairing Ed25519 with ML-DSA, while the standardized
X-Wing key encapsulation mechanism pairs X25519 with ML-KEM-768 for key
establishment [107]. In evidence terms, a hybrid-signed record carries two signatures over
the same canonical body, and verification succeeds only when the configured policy
accepts the combination; the signature-scheme field of the evidence schema makes the
combination explicit and versioned [28, 70]. Hybridization is thus not a hedge bolted on at
the end but a first-class state of the evidence format.
 The migration strategy proceeds in three stages. In the first stage, Ed25519 remains the
default for all evidence, keeping record sizes and verification costs low while post-quantum
tooling matures. In the second stage, governance-critical records — constitution
amendments, quorum approvals, model attestations for deployed systems — move to
hybrid signatures, because their required lifetime is the longest and their volume the lowest.
In the third stage, post-quantum-only profiles become available for deployments whose
threat model discounts classical forgery risks; schema versioning and the signature-scheme
field allow all three profiles to coexist and to be verified by the same code paths [28]. The
strategy's honesty requirement is that the stage of each record class be visible in its
evidence, not inferred.


=== PAGINA 66 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 66
 Table 4.1 summarizes the primitives, their roles, and their primary locations in the
repository. The table is intentionally short: a verification architecture benefits from a small,
boring cryptographic surface, because every additional primitive multiplies the audit
burden across native, WebAssembly, and formal-model representations. Each row's status
is reported under honest status, distinguishing standardized-and-deployed from
standardized-and-planned [28, 104]. The same table serves as the organizing checklist for
the test vectors of the crypto test suite.

4.2 Append-only logs and external anchoring
 Immutability inside the operator's infrastructure is a strong claim that requires evidence
outside it. The architecture therefore anchors WormGraph records to Sigstore's Rekor, an
implementation-independent transparency log in which entries live in an append-only
Merkle tree and are provable by inclusion proofs and consistency proofs [9]. An inclusion
proof demonstrates that a given entry is part of the signed tree head; a consistency proof
demonstrates that new tree heads extend previous ones, so that a log operator cannot
quietly rewrite history without detection by any auditor that has retained a prior tree head
[8, 9]. The pattern is inherited from Certificate Transparency, and its operational maturity
in the software-supply-chain setting — including the detection of malicious package
releases — is the reason the architecture treats it as substrate rather than as novelty [8, 10].
 The specification lineage matters for deployers choosing infrastructure. Certificate
Transparency was standardized in RFC 6962 and revised in RFC 9162, whose version 2
refines the tree hashing, the signed tree head structure, and the proof formats while
preserving the core property: an append-only, publicly auditable log whose behavior can be


=== PAGINA 67 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 67
checked from its outputs alone [8, 99]. Transparency logs of this family have since become
ordinary infrastructure — browser root programs, package registries, and key-transparency
deployments at messaging scale rely on the same audit pattern [11, 12]. The architecture's
anchoring format cites the log's identifier, tree size, and inclusion index, so that any verifier
can re-derive the proof against the live log or against a retained snapshot.
 The attestation vocabulary of the IETF's RATS architecture clarifies who is who in this
arrangement [100]. The agent runtime and its tooling act as attesters, producing evidence
about artifacts and actions; arkhe-verify — native or in-browser — acts as the verifier that
evaluates that evidence; and auditors, regulators, and counterparties act as relying parties
who accept the verifier's results on the strength of the anchored trail. Hardware roots of
trust slot into this vocabulary without restructuring it: a TPM 2.0 can anchor the identity of
the host that produces evidence, binding the attester role to a measured,
manufacturer-certified root [101]. Consistent with the non-goals of Section 3.6, the
architecture treats this as strengthening for deployments that already operate TPMs, not as a
requirement of the evidence layer.
 Figure 4.1 traces a single event through the resulting pipeline: the event is hashed (gate
one), the hash is signed (gate two), the signature enters an append-only log and acquires an
inclusion proof (gate three), and the record is judged against quorum-governed policy (gate
four), terminating in an external transparency anchor [28]. Each gate emits evidence, so the
pipeline's output is not a verdict but a chain of artifacts that any third party can replay.
Chapter 12 develops the four-gate pipeline as a verification contract in detail; here it serves
as the spine on which the anchoring design hangs. The figure's right-hand element — the
anchor — is the subject of the remainder of this section.
 Figure 4.1 — From event to anchor: the four-gate evidence pipeline (hash, signature, inclusion, quorum)
 terminating in an external transparency anchor.
 Anchoring gives the WormGraph a property that internal append-only storage cannot
achieve on its own: detectability of wholesale replacement. An operator who controls the
servers can silently truncate a private database, but cannot produce a valid consistency
proof from a rewritten history to tree heads already witnessed by third parties. The design


=== PAGINA 68 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 68
implication is that the anchoring interval — how often evidence is committed to the log —
is a security parameter, trading detection latency against operational cost [8, 28]. The
project corpus specifies continuous anchoring for governance-critical events and batched
anchoring for high-volume evidence, with the interval itself recorded in the constitution so
that weakening it is a governed change rather than an operational drift [28, 70].
 Anchoring is a role, not a vendor, and the interface is designed for plurality. Beyond
Rekor, the same anchor field can carry a DNSLink record mapping a domain to a content
identifier, a permanent-storage commitment on an archive chain, or a content-addressed
blob reference in a peer-to-peer store — each an external witness with different cost,
latency, and trust characteristics [136, 137, 142, 147]. What the anchor kinds share is the
property that matters: they are held by parties other than the operator and can be checked
by anyone. The following abridged listing shows a WormGraph evidence node at the end
of the pipeline, with its inclusion-proof and anchor fields populated:
{
"schema": "wormgraph.node/v1",
"id": "sha256:9f2c41aa...e17d", // SHA-256 of the canonical body
"type": "evidence.model_attestation",
"parents": ["sha256:41aa9f2c...07b3"], // causal dependencies
"payload_hash": "sha256:c3d977b1...5b02", // digest of the attested artifact
"signer": "ed25519:8b14d2a9...9f", // author public key
"signature": "ed25519:1f7c03ee...d2", // over the canonical body
"timestamp": "2026-09-15T14:03:22Z",
"inclusion_proof": {"log": "rekor", "tree_size": 48213, "leaf_hash":
"sha256:77b1...0a"},
"anchor": {"kind": "rekor", "index": 48213}
}
Two fields deserve comment. The inclusion_proof field carries the material a third party
needs to re-derive the node's membership in the log's Merkle tree without trusting the
operator, and the anchor field carries the log's stable coordinates so that the check can be
repeated years later. Both are optional at write time and checked at read time: a node
lacking them is admissible but visibly weaker, and policy can require them for node kinds
that matter [70]. This optional-but-checked pattern is the schema-level expression of honest
status — the record shows exactly what assurance it carries, no more and no less.
4.3 WebAssembly as the portable verification target
 The layered-verification principle requires, for its third-party clause, that verification
be executable by parties who hold no trust relationship with the operator. The architecture's
answer is arkhe-verify-wasm: the decoding and evidence-checking logic is compiled to
WebAssembly and executed in a sandbox — a browser tab, a worker, an embedder — with
no network access during verification [28]. A skeptical counterparty does not have to install
the operator's software, open a port, or accept a daemon; they open a page or run a static
binary and re-derive the verdict themselves. Verification that can be declined without cost


=== PAGINA 69 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 69
is verification that will be declined, and the design treats friction as the enemy of
third-party verification.
 WebAssembly is chosen because it is a mature, standardized compilation target with
near-native performance and a strong isolation story, and because it makes distribution
trivial: the verifier can be served as a static artifact whose own hash is itself
Rekor-anchored, closing the loop on verifier integrity [9, 28]. A third party who doubts the
verifier can check the verifier — the recursion is finite, ending at a small trusted computing
base consisting of a browser engine or a command-line build from source. The Rust crate
compiles to both native and wasm32 targets from one codebase, and determinism of the
verification functions makes the two targets equivalent in output, so that a browser verdict
and a native verdict can be compared byte for byte [28].
 The WebAssembly surface is deliberately narrow: four exports — verify_attestation,
verify_sha256, verify_signature, and verify_inclusion — mirroring the four verification
paths of the pipeline [28]. SHA-256 is implemented in the module with a pure-Rust crate;
Ed25519 verification runs against a pinned trust root; Merkle inclusion proofs are checked
against RFC 6962 tree mathematics; and attestation checking composes the three [8, 28].
The module's test suite carries more than eight unit tests covering the four paths, including
malformed-input cases whose required outcome is rejection — the fail-closed rule
expressed as a test matrix [28]. The same exports are what the user interface's verification
panel consumes, so the code path shown to end users and the code path offered to auditors
are the same code path.
 A concrete third-party workflow shows what the target buys. An auditor fetches the
verifier artifact, checks its pinned hash against the anchored record, runs it on the evidence
bundle in a disconnected environment, and compares the resulting verdict with the
operator's claims; every step is offline with respect to the operator. The same workflow,
repeated by a regulator, a counterparty, or a journalist, is the mechanism by which the
architecture's claims are kept cheap to check and expensive to fake [28, 102]. Nothing in
the workflow requires cooperation from the operator beyond publication of the anchored
artifacts, which is the definition of third-party verifiability the principle demands.
 Client-side re-verification becomes more consequential as client devices become
inference-capable. Browser-based inference engines already run multi-billion-parameter
language models in a tab via WebGPU, demonstrating that the machine which loads a
model can also be the machine that verifies it [148]. The verify-before-load flow follows
naturally: the attested digest is checked in the browser before the weights are handed to the
runtime, and the evidence card that results is itself a WormGraph artifact [28]. The pattern
generalizes beyond browsers — a CI runner, an edge device, or an organization's gateway
can all run the same verification module — which is the practical meaning of the universal


=== PAGINA 70 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 70
core: one verifier, many surfaces.
 The WebAssembly target does not dissolve the trust problem; it relocates and shrinks
it. The browser engine is part of the trusted base, as is the serving path that delivers the
verifier, which is why the verifier artifact is hash-pinned and anchored, and why
reproducible builds with supply-chain provenance — discussed in Section 5.4 — apply to
the verifier with special force [102]. A sufficiently motivated adversary who controls both
the operator and the user's software stack defeats client-side verification; the architecture's
response is honesty about the boundary rather than claims of omnipotence [31]. The claim
it does make is precise: verification no longer requires trusting the operator's servers, and
that removal is the difference between a security product and a security posture.
4.4 Threat model: adversary classes and the four gates
 The architecture assumes adversaries of four classes, labeled A1 through A4. The
compromised signer (A1) controls a key inside an authorization threshold — the StablR
class, where a single mint key controlled a one-of-three quorum [6, 33]. The interface
adversary (A2) controls what an approver sees rather than what is signed — the Bybit class,
in which a masked transaction interface deceived signers into approving a hostile transfer
[2, 5, 7]. The supply-chain adversary (A3) controls an artifact before deployment — a
poisoned model, a malicious dependency, a backdoored build — the class documented for
language-model applications by OWASP and for packages by the OpenSSF's transparency
work [10, 14]. The governance insider (A4) controls rule definition — the party who can
change what the system means.
 Each class is answered by a different gate of the four-gate pipeline, and the mapping is
the threat model's operational content. A1 is answered by the quorum gate: thresholds,
timelocks, and the witness-authority separation raise the cost of controlling a decision
beyond a single key [29]. A2 is answered by the signature gate together with independent
decoding — verification of what is actually signed, executed outside the interface that
displays it, using typed structured data so that the human-readable form is
cryptographically bound to the signed form [24, 38]. A3 is answered by the hash and
inclusion gates: a substituted artifact fails digest comparison, and an unanchored attestation
fails the visibility check that deployment policy can require [9]. A4 is answered by the
constitution machinery itself — versioned rules, quorum amendments, and timelocks — so
that changing what the system means is the most expensive action available in it [28, 29].
What the model does not assume is a trusted operator; the entire design exists because that
assumption fails [31].
 Table 4.2 states the mapping in audit form: adversary class, documented instance,
controlling gate, and residual risk. The residual-risk column is part of the model, not a


=== PAGINA 71 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 71
footnote to it — every control in the architecture leaves a remainder, and the purpose of the
table is to keep those remainders visible and priced [28, 31]. Threat taxonomies for
artificial-intelligence systems, such as MITRE ATLAS, overlay on this model by
classifying the techniques an adversary may use to reach each class; the classes here are
deliberately coarser, because they are keyed to gates rather than to techniques [112]. The
coarser grain is a feature for governance: techniques churn, gates do not.

 For class A3 the architecture also inherits the supply-chain frameworks that standardize
how build integrity is expressed. SLSA defines incremental levels for build provenance,
from provenance existence to hermetic, hardened builds, and the release pipeline is
expected to emit provenance at the level its operators can defend [102]. in-toto supplies the
attestation format for linking the steps of a software supply chain — source, build, package,
sign — into verifiable statements [103]. These frameworks answer a question the four gates
raise but do not themselves resolve: who vouches for the verifier and for the pipeline that
produced it. The answer, in the VTK's case, is the same machinery recursively — the
verifier artifact is hashed, signed, inclusion-proven, and quorum-released like any other
governed artifact [28].
 The threat model's boundaries are stated with equal care. It does not model a
nation-state adversary with sustained physical access to signer hardware as within the
mitigation envelope of quorum alone; it assumes endpoint compromise is possible — that
is A2's precondition — but not universal; and it treats collusion as an economic quantity,
priced by the thresholds of Section 6.3 rather than assumed away. The model also excludes,
by design, the case of a majority of governance signers acting honestly but wrongly: that is
a politics problem, and the architecture's answer is the amendment trail, the veto topology
of Section 6.4, and the auditability that makes wrongness visible rather than impossible
[28]. A threat model that promised more would itself be a promise, and the first principle of
Section 3.1 applies to the threat model too.
