SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 72
5. The Crate Ecosystem and Repository Map
5.1 Inventory and responsibilities
 The architecture is implemented as a family of Rust crates with deliberately narrow
interfaces, and the split follows the layer boundaries of Figure 3.1. Types and invariant
primitives live in arkhe-core; hashing and signing in arkhe-crypto; quorum and constitution
logic in arkhe-governance; evidence records and export in arkhe-evidence; the append-only
graph in arkhe-wormgraph; the browser-runnable decoder in arkhe-verify-wasm; the
orchestration CLI in arkhe-verify; and the Model Context Protocol server in arkhe-mcp
[28]. Rust is chosen for memory safety without a garbage collector, for a package
ecosystem that supports both native and wasm32 targets from one codebase, and for the
auditability that strong typing affords — the same reasons the systems-security community
has converged on the language for foundational components.
 Each crate's responsibility can be stated in a sentence, and the project treats that
statement as a contract. arkhe-core holds the canonical types and the invariant catalog;
arkhe-crypto implements the content addressing, the signature schemes, and their hybrid
composition; arkhe-governance owns the ConstitutionStore, the quorum evaluation of
ADR-011, and the amendment workflow; arkhe-evidence defines records and export
bundles; arkhe-wormgraph owns nodes, edges, and queries; arkhe-verify and
arkhe-verify-wasm expose the four verification paths to native and browser callers
respectively; and arkhe-mcp wraps verification and query tools as JSON-RPC methods for
language-model agents [28, 108]. Two supporting crates complete the picture:
arkhe-storage provides local and content-addressed persistence, and arkhe-verify-builder
— a newer addition — proposes and falsifies candidate verification instruments [28]. What
the map deliberately excludes is sector logic: adaptation to banking, pharmaceutical, or
government deployments happens by configuration in the local tier, not by forking the
crates — the sector-adapter pattern developed in Chapter 13 [28].
 Licensing is treated as part of the trust surface. The crates are dual-licensed under MIT
OR Apache-2.0, the disjunctive pattern that has become the default for Rust infrastructure
because it gives downstream users a choice of terms while both branches remain
compatible with GPLv3 licensing of derivatives under the Free Software Foundation's
published license-list guidance, a choice the project corpus documents explicitly [28]. A
cargo-deny policy file enforces the license whitelist and security advisories in continuous
integration, so that dependency drift against the policy is a build failure rather than a
discovery. For a project whose thesis is verifiability, licensing is not administrative trivia:
the right to run, inspect, and redistribute the verifier is what makes third-party verification
legally possible at all.


=== PAGINA 73 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 73
 Three implementation disciplines are specified across the family. First, no unsafe code
in the evidence path: crates that touch hashes, signatures, and graph mutation are written in
safe Rust, with any unavoidable unsafe confined to reviewed leaf code. Second,
determinism: verification functions are pure with respect to their inputs, which is what
makes the WebAssembly target equivalent to the native target and makes third-party
reproduction meaningful. Third, schema versioning: every evidence record and graph node
carries a schema version, so that the ecosystem can evolve without invalidating anchored
history [70]. These disciplines are internal project standards rather than externally audited
claims — a caveat the counterargument analysis in Chapter 24 develops — but they are
stated here because they define what the implementation is trying to be [28].
 Packaging discipline completes the inventory picture. Crates follow semantic
versioning with explicit deprecation, the public API of each crate is narrower than its
internal surface, and cross-crate dependencies point downward in the layer diagram only —
the governance crate may use crypto and core, but the crypto crate must never learn about
constitutions [28]. The discipline is what keeps the verification logic reusable across the
interfaces that Part IV will hang on it: command line, browser, protocol server, and the
sector adapters to come. A dependency that violated the downward-only rule would be a
design bug even if all its tests passed, and the workspace is structured so that the rule can
be checked mechanically [28].
5.2 Repository layout
 The repository is organized as a single Cargo workspace whose manifest lists more
than thirty-five members, arranged so that the directory tree mirrors the layered architecture
rather than the org chart of its authors [28]. The map rewards reading because the structure
encodes the argument of Part II: containment types and invariants at the core, cryptography
beneath verification, verification beneath governance, and interfaces — command line,
browser, protocol — as thin skins over the same verification functions. Table 5.1 presents
the repository map, listing the paths a reviewer should open first and the responsibility each
carries [28]. The table is deliberately confined to files that carry load-bearing logic or
policy; documentation and generated artifacts are omitted.

 Three files in the core repay the closest reading. lib.rs is where the canonical types of
Section 3.2 are defined, and its austerity — four types, no framework — is the design's first
testable claim. invariants.rs states I-01 through I-20 as formal definitions rather than
comments, so that the Rust compiler, the test suite, and the TLA+ models all consume the
same artifact [28]. kernel.rs implements the mediation points of Section 3.2: the gates
through which every privileged operation must pass, the deny-on-timeout rule, and the
emission of decision events into the evidence layer.
 The verification layer shows the same economy. The facade in arkhe-verify exposes
exactly four functions, and the specialized modules hang off it: gguf.rs parses GGUF
headers, computes model digests, and checks attestations, while merkle.rs implements RFC
6962 inclusion proofs against transparency-log tree mathematics [8, 26, 28]. The
WebAssembly crate re-exports the same four verification paths for browser execution, and
its test file demonstrates the project's testing discipline in miniature: more than eight unit
tests covering all four paths, each with malformed-input cases whose required outcome is
rejection [28]. One facade, four paths, two runtimes — the invariant that keeps the browser
verdict and the native verdict comparable.
 The governance and service layers complete the map. arkhe-governance embeds the
ADR-011 parameters — quorum bands and timelock durations — as configurable defaults
rather than magic numbers, and arkhe-wormgraph's node module binds metadata and
content into the record_hash that the evidence chain computes [28, 29]. arkhe-mcp wraps
the verification and query functions as protocol tools, including get_invariants, so that a
language-model agent can retrieve the invariant catalog with its honest status rather than
trusting a description of it [108]. The evidence crate's chain module computes the


=== PAGINA 75 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 75
append-only record hashes that link evidence entries, and the storage crate implements
content addressing over SHA-256 and BLAKE3, with an integration for content-addressed
peer storage on the roadmap [28, 106, 147].
 The repository's periphery is part of the architecture rather than decoration. Continuous
integration runs static analysis, fuzzing, tests, and builds; the release pipeline signs and
notarizes artifacts; the cargo-deny policy enforces licenses and advisories; and the docs
directory carries the amendment records — ADR-011 onward — whose content Chapter 6
argues is as load-bearing as any code [28, 29]. A verification catalog under docs collects
the execution evidence for claims about the system, and a proposed registry for fabricated
sources, pending ratification, would make the honest-status discipline explicit at the
repository level [28]. The fuzz targets aimed at the three verification functions are the
fail-closed rule converted into a standing adversarial workload.
 A reviewer's reading order falls out of the map naturally: the canonical types and
invariants first, because everything else references them; then the crypto crate, because its
choices constrain the evidence formats; then the verification facade and its GGUF and
Merkle modules, which are this book's running example; then governance, whose
parameters the earlier layers only consume [28]. The order is also the order of decreasing
certainty — types and invariants are the most stable, governance parameters the most likely
to evolve — and the repository is arranged so that the most volatile decisions live in the
most inspectable files, the amendment records. New contributors are expected to leave the
visit with one conviction: nothing load-bearing is hidden [28].
5.3 Data schemas
 Schemas are where the architecture's promises become machine-checkable, and the
project treats schema design as governance in miniature: a field that exists can be checked,
a field that does not exist cannot be lied about, and every schema carries a version so that
evolution does not orphan anchored history [70]. Two schemas carry most of the
interoperability weight: the arkhe.attestation.* family, which binds artifacts to publishers
and policy context, and the Capability Manifest, which states an agent's envelope in the
kernel's vocabulary [28]. The WormGraph node schema was shown in Section 4.2; the two
listings below complete the picture. Both are deliberately minimal, because the design adds
fields only when a verifier will actually consume them.
 Canonicalization is the quiet precondition beneath both schemas. Hashing a record
only means something if two implementations serialize the same logical record to the same
bytes, so the schemas fix key order, number formatting, and whitespace in a canonical
form, and signatures are computed over that form rather than over presentation variants
[70]. The canonicalization rule is itself versioned with the schema, and old canonical forms


=== PAGINA 76 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 76
remain verifiable forever — anchored history must not break when formats improve. These
are unglamorous decisions, but they are the difference between an evidence layer that
verifies and one that merely displays [28].
The listing below shows an abridged arkhe.attestation.model record — the attestation of a
quantized language-model artifact — with its digest, publisher, declared license and
training-data status, declared evaluations, constitution context, and anchoring coordinates:
{
"schema": "arkhe.attestation.model/v1",
"subject": "llama-3.1-8b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf",
"digest": {"alg": "sha256", "value": "9f2c41aa...e17d"},
"publisher": "ed25519:8b14d2a9...9f",
"signature": "ed25519:1f7c03ee...d2",
"license": "apache-2.0",
"training_data_status": "declared-undisclosed",
"evaluations": [
{"kind": "safety-suite", "version": "2026-06", "result_hash": "sha256:5c02..."},
{"kind": "capability-eval", "version": "2026-06", "result_hash": "sha256:a19d..."}
],
"constitution": "v3",
"anchor": {"kind": "rekor", "index": 48213, "inclusion_verified": true}
}
 Three fields carry the honesty of the record. training_data_status asserts what the
publisher declares, not what the verifier has established, and its vocabulary distinguishes
declared-complete from declared-undisclosed; evaluations carries hashes of evaluation
results rather than prose claims, so the underlying artifacts can be retrieved and checked;
and anchor carries the transparency-log coordinates that make the record's existence
externally witnessable [9, 28]. The record binds to the constitution version in force, which
is what lets a regulator ask not only whether a model was attested but under which policy
regime — the question Article 12 of the EU AI Act makes operational for high-risk
systems [17, 18]. The same record shape, with different kind fields, covers datasets, tools,
and agent builds, so that one verification path serves the whole artifact surface.
The Capability Manifest is the kernel-side counterpart: it states, in the envelope vocabulary
of Section 3.2, what a specific agent session may do. The abridged example below shows
tools, network domains, a spending bound, a memory region, the override quorum that may
change the manifest, and an expiry:
schema: arkhe.capability.manifest/v1
agent: arc://analyst-07
version: 12
tools: [verify_sha256, query_wormgraph, market_data_read]
network_allowed_domains: [api.venue.example, data.vendor.example]
spend: {asset: USDC, per_action_max: 250}
memory_regions: [{name: research-cache, bytes_max: 268435456}]
override: {quorum: "4-of-7", timelock_days: 7}
expires: "2026-12-31T00:00:00Z"


=== PAGINA 77 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 77
 The manifest is denied-by-default in interpretation: anything it does not grant is not
available, and its fields map directly onto kernel types — tools onto capabilities, network
domains into reach checks, the spend bound into signing limits, memory_regions into
MemoryRegion bounds [28]. The override block is the governance hook: changing the
manifest itself requires the quorum and timelock stated there, so that an agent's envelope
cannot be loosened by the same session that is bound by it. Expiry forces re-issuance under
the then-current constitution, which keeps envelopes synchronized with governance drift
rather than fossilizing them. Export bundles that assemble manifests, attestations, and
decision events for regulators are the subject of Chapter 9.
5.4 Testing and verification discipline
 The testing discipline is layered to mirror the architecture. Unit tests cover the four
verification paths, with more than eight tests in the WebAssembly module alone and
rejection cases specified alongside acceptance cases, so that fail-closed behavior is a tested
property rather than an intention [28]. Integration tests exercise the kernel's containment
logic and the WormGraph's structural guarantees — immutability, append-only growth,
and cross-verification of records — at the boundaries where components meet [28]. The
test suite is treated as part of the evidence surface: its results are artifacts, and its coverage
claims carry honest status like every other claim the project makes [31].
 Property-based testing generalizes the unit layer by asserting invariants over whole
families of inputs. The invariants of Section 3.2 double as properties: append-only
monotonicity for the graph, hash determinism for canonical serialization, round-trip fidelity
for record encoding and decoding, and envelope containment for generated operation
sequences against a simulated kernel. Where a property fails, the shrinking machinery of
the property framework reduces the failing case to a minimal reproducer, which then joins
the regression corpus as a unit test. The relationship is deliberate: properties state what
must always be true, units pin the historical edge cases, and the two layers cross-check each
other's blind spots [28].
 Fuzzing occupies the adversarial end of the spectrum. The repository carries fuzz
targets for the three verification functions — digest checking, signature checking, and
inclusion-proof checking — whose harnesses assert one thing: every input yields a
decision, and no malformed input yields permissive behavior [28]. This is the fail-closed
rule under sustained attack, and it is the cheapest continuous red team the project owns.
Inputs that survive fuzzing join the corpus; inputs that trigger rejections tighten the parser;
and the distinction between the two outcomes is exactly what the honest-status display
reports.


=== PAGINA 78 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 78
 Formal verification is applied where the cost of being wrong is highest. The invariant
catalog I-01 through I-20 is accompanied by TLA+ models, and model checking explores
the bounded state space of the kernel and governance protocols for counterexamples to
each invariant [28]. The method complements rather than replaces the dynamic layers: a
model checker proves properties of a model of the system, and the honest-status vocabulary
keeps that distinction visible — invariants are labeled by whether they are model-checked,
tested, or merely declared [28, 31]. Chapter 22 extends the same discipline to mathematical
claims, where the artifacts are Lean proofs rather than TLA+ traces; the verification posture
is identical.
 The build and release layer closes the supply-chain surface that class A3 exploits.
Builds aim for reproducibility — path remapping strips machine-specific identifiers so that
independent rebuilds can be compared by digest — and the release pipeline emits
provenance in the SLSA sense, stating what was built, from which sources, by which
pipeline [28, 102]. Attestation records for released artifacts follow the in-toto format so that
external tooling can consume them [103]. The verifier is itself a released artifact, and its
provenance is checked by the same pipeline it ships to verify — the recursion noted in
Section 4.3, made concrete here as build configuration rather than as aspiration.
 Verification discipline and management-system discipline are complements, not
substitutes. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 examinations address organizational controls —
access management, change management, incident response — that code alone cannot
provide, and regulated adopters of the architecture will typically operate both [170, 171].
The architecture's contribution is to make the technical layer of such audits cheap: where a
management system demands records, the WormGraph already holds them with signatures
and anchors attached. Chapter 9 develops this mapping for specific regulatory instruments;
the point here is that the testing layers above are what make the mapping honest rather than
decorative [28].
6. Governance: Constitution-as-Code, Quorum,
and VetoGraph
6.1 Authority and witness: a separation of powers
 The governance design begins from the observation that most multisignature systems
conflate two roles. Signers witness and authorize events, but the rules — who signs what,
with what threshold, subject to which exceptions — live in configuration controlled by
whoever deploys the wallet. The VTK's ConstitutionStore inverts this: rules are data,
versioned and hashed, and amendments are events that require the same evidentiary
discipline as any other action [28, 29]. A Safe multisig remains useful, but demoted to


=== PAGINA 79 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 79
witness: it records that something happened, while the ConstitutionStore records what it
meant [25]. The project's executive analysis names this separation the project's most
defensible architectural claim, precisely because it is the property that conventional custody
stacks lack [31].
 Figure 6.1 renders the separation as a topology: the ConstitutionStore declares policy at
the top; the Safe multisig witnesses events beside it; the WormGraph records what
happened; the verifiers re-derive what can be checked; and the VetoGraph — developed in
Section 6.4 — generalizes how vetoes propagate through the rule graph [28]. The figure is
deliberately institutional in its vocabulary, because the design's claim is that machine
governance can inherit the operating logic of institutional checks and balances without
inheriting their opacity. Reading the figure against Figure 3.1 shows the same stack from
the governance side: layers of verification below, roles above. The mapping is not
metaphorical; every box in the figure corresponds to a crate or schema cataloged in Chapter
5.
 Figure 6.1 — Separation of powers: the ConstitutionStore declares policy; the Safe multisig witnesses events;
 VetoGraph generalizes veto topology (cf. Chapter 20).
 The role model is stated in five parts, using the attester-verifier-relying-party
vocabulary of the IETF RATS architecture where the terms coincide [100]. The authority
(ConstitutionStore) declares invariants, thresholds, timelocks, and capability rules; it does
not sign events. The witness (Safe multisig) approves privileged events under the declared
rules; it does not define them. The recorder (WormGraph) appends evidence; it cannot edit.
The verifier (arkhe-verify, native or in-browser) re-derives checks; it cannot create state.
The relying party (auditor, regulator, counterparty) consumes the results; it cannot demand
privileged access to the operator's internals, only to the anchored evidence — which is the
point of anchoring [9, 100].
 Table 6.1 states the roles, their holders, and — critically — their explicit
non-capabilities. The non-capability column is the design: in the incidents of Chapter 7,
every collapse traced to a role quietly acquiring a non-capability, as when the recorder of
rules and the witness of events turned out to be the same three keys [6, 33]. A role table that


=== PAGINA 80 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 80
listed only powers would document the happy path; this one documents the failure paths it
forecloses [28]. The table is reviewed at each constitution version, and changes to it follow
the amendment workflow they describe.

 The separation earns its name through the checks each role imposes on the others. The
witness constrains the authority's operations by refusing actions that lack quorum under the
current version; the authority constrains the witness by making its approvals meaningless
without the constitution version they cite; the recorder constrains both by making their
interactions replayable; and the verifiers constrain the recorder by re-deriving its contents
from hashes and proofs [28]. No role can both define and record, both act and judge. This is
the structural insight that Section 3.1 stated as a principle, here unfolded into machinery,
and the remaining sections of this chapter parameterize it: Section 6.2 fixes the witness
quorum, Section 6.3 prices the parameter, and Section 6.4 generalizes the veto structure.
 Two practical consequences follow. For incident forensics, the separation means the
question of who changed what splits cleanly: witnesses attest occurrences, the authority's
versions bound interpretations, and the recorder holds the trace, so reconstruction never
depends on the goodwill of the operator under investigation [28]. For delegation, the
separation means that a deployer can grant a witness role to a vendor — who after all runs
infrastructure — without granting that vendor any voice in what the rules mean, and can
grant auditors full verification rights without granting them any operational power. Both
properties were missing in the custody stacks examined in Chapter 7, and their absence is
what turned operational incidents into governance failures [6, 33].
6.2 ADR-011: threshold choice under incident data
 Decision record ADR-011 fixes the quorum policy for privileged actions: thresholds of
4-of-7 or 5-of-7, with configurations below the two-thirds band of the active signer set
prohibited — for a seven-signer panel, any requirement of three approvals or fewer [29].


=== PAGINA 81 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 81
The policy is argued from incident data rather than from taste, and the decision record cites
its evidence the way a clinical guideline cites trials. The choice is presented not as
universally optimal but as a defensible default with explicit reasoning that deployers can
revisit under their own constitutions [29]. This section reconstructs the argument;
Appendix B reproduces the record itself.
 The lower bound comes from the StablR incident of May 2026, in which an attacker
who compromised a single key in a one-of-three multisig arrangement minted thirteen and
a half million dollars of stablecoins before the breach was contained [6, 33]. A one-of-three
threshold is trivially weak not because three is small but because one is: the quorum's
security reduces to the security of the single worst-kept key, and the multisig provides the
optics of distribution without its substance. At 3-of-7, three colluding or compromised keys
suffice — better, but still within reach of a focused campaign against a small signer set.
The two-thirds band, rounded down to four for a panel of seven, is where single-key and
small-coalition compromises stop being sufficient [29].
 The Bybit incident of February 2025 supplies the caution from the other direction: even
a threshold far above the band fails when the approval interface is subverted [2, 5, 7].
Signers approved a transaction whose displayed contents were not the contents signed, and
roughly one and a half billion dollars left custody to a state-sponsored attacker [93, 94].
Threshold arithmetic does not address this class — six honest signers approving a lie is still
a quorum — which is why ADR-011 treats thresholds as necessary and not sufficient, and
why the architecture pairs the quorum gate with independent decoding of what is actually
signed (Chapter 8) [1, 95]. The lesson the decision record draws is that interface trust and
threshold choice are orthogonal axes, and both must be defended [29].
 The upper bound of the band comes from liveness, which ADR-011 treats as a security
property rather than an operational nicety. A 6-of-7 wallet freezes if two keys are lost, and
with realistic per-key loss rates over a multi-year horizon, freeze risk is not negligible; a
frozen treasury is unavailable to its owners precisely when recovery matters most.
Availability failures also have security consequences, because custody decisions made
under freeze pressure are historically where corner-cutting happens. The band 4-of-7 to
5-of-7 is the project's balance point between the two failure directions — compromise and
freeze — and Section 6.3 prices that trade-off explicitly. The freeze asymmetry also
explains why the record fixes a default band rather than a single value: deployers with
strong key-hygiene operations can afford 5-of-7, while those managing dispersed, legally
independent signers may need the 4-of-7 end [29].
A threshold is a hypothesis about how many keys can be compromised
simultaneously. Incident data is the only honest source for that hypothesis, and
ADR-011 cites incidents the way a clinical guideline cites trials.


=== PAGINA 82 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 82
 Two implementation details complete the record. First, the threshold applies to the
active signer set, so that removing a stale or compromised signer is itself a governed
change rather than a silent reweighting. Second, the quorum gate composes with timelocks:
standard changes carry a seven-day delay and critical changes fourteen, so that even a
quorum-satisfying action remains visible — and anchorable, and challengeable — before it
takes effect [28, 29]. Threshold and timelock are therefore one control expressed in two
dimensions: how many must agree, and how long everyone else has to notice [29].
6.3 Quorum mathematics: security, availability, and
timelocks
 The threshold choice can be priced, and doing so exposes what the band 4-of-7 to
5-of-7 actually buys. Model each signer key as compromised independently with
probability p over the horizon of interest; the probability that an attacker controls an m-of-n
quorum is then the binomial tail — the sum over k from m to n of C(n,k) times pk times
(1-p)n-k. The independence assumption is an idealization — correlated compromise
through a shared vendor or fleet is precisely the failure mode the role separation of Section
6.1 addresses — but the model is still the honest first-order estimate, and its qualitative
behavior is robust. What follows uses p = 0.1 as an illustrative value; the point is the shape
of the curve, not the decimal places.
 The numbers are stark. At 1-of-3 — the StablR configuration — attacker control is
certain if any one of the three keys falls: the probability is 1-(1-p)3, which at p = 0.1 is 27.1
percent [6, 33]. At 4-of-7 the same model gives 0.43 percent; at 5-of-7 it gives 0.17 percent.
The move from one-of-three to four-of-seven therefore buys roughly a sixtyfold reduction
in attacker-control probability, and the move from four-of-seven to five-of-seven buys a
further factor of about two and a half. Below the two-thirds band the curve flattens into
irrelevance: no reasonable operations discipline compensates for a threshold that a single
adversary campaign can satisfy.
 The same mathematics prices the other failure direction. Model per-key loss — death,
departure, destroyed hardware, forgotten credentials — with probability q; the wallet
freezes when losses exceed n minus m, because no quorum can then be formed. At q =
0.05, a 4-of-7 panel freezes with probability about 0.02 percent, while a 5-of-7 panel
freezes with probability about 0.38 percent — a roughly twentyfold difference in the freeze
direction, bought with the factor-of-two-and-a-half security gain computed above [29]. The
band is thus not a taste preference but the visible elbow of two crossing curves: ADR-011
offers both points and requires deployers to choose with their own p and q in hand [29].
Availability engineering — key refresh, geographic distribution, documented recovery —
lowers q and moves the elbow, which is why the decision record treats custodial operations
as part of the security argument rather than as an afterthought.


=== PAGINA 83 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 83
 For high-value keys the architecture also borrows an implementation pattern from
proof-of-stake infrastructure: distributed validator technology splits a single validator key
into shares held by independent operators, using threshold cryptography so that the key as a
whole never exists in any one place and a minority of operators can neither sign nor freeze
the validator [138, 139]. Applied to agent custody, the analogy is direct: a
treasury-controlling key can be secret-shared across heterogeneous operators — different
jurisdictions, vendors, and hardware — so that the compromise of any single operator
yields shares, not authority. Empirical work on decentralized systems supports the intuition
that perceived trust tracks actual distribution rather than stated policy [160]. The pattern
does not replace the multisig; it composes with it, giving the quorum gate defense in depth
at the key layer as well as the approval layer.
 Timelocks are the temporal half of the same defense. A seven-day delay for standard
changes and fourteen for critical ones does not make unauthorized quorums impossible; it
makes them detectable, because the pending action sits in the evidence layer where
monitors, verifiers, and independent witnesses can observe and contest it before execution
[28, 29]. Detection latency and anchoring interval interact: an attacker who could both
satisfy a quorum and execute within a single anchoring gap would have a window, and the
constitution fixes the timelock to be comfortably longer than the anchoring interval for
governance events [28]. The kill-switch profile — five of seven with fourteen days —
applies the longest delay to the changes that would most reward an A4 adversary: changes
to the thresholds themselves.
The governance crate's quorum check compresses this section into a dozen lines, which is
the point: the control must be simple enough to verify by inspection and strict enough to
fail closed. The pseudocode below shows the decision path — eligibility, threshold,
revocation, timelock — in the order the checks are applied:
fn quorum_check(proposal, c: Constitution) :
eligible = c.signers_active(proposal.timestamp)
required = c.threshold_for(eligible) // 4-of-7 or 5-of-7; sub-two-thirds rejected
approvals = verify_all(proposal.signatures, c.trust_root)
approvals = approvals minus c.revoked_keys()
if count(approvals) is below required:
return DENY // fail-closed default
if not c.timelock_elapsed(proposal): // 7 days standard, 14 days critical
return PENDING
return APPROVE // evidence recorded in WormGraph
 Every branch but the last returns a non-approval, and the approval branch still emits
evidence rather than acting directly, because execution is the kernel's business, not
governance's. The check reads its parameters from the ConstitutionStore rather than from
configuration, so the code that enforces thresholds is inert without the rules that define
them [28, 29]. Readers will notice what is absent: overrides, emergency bypasses, and


=== PAGINA 84 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 84
break-glass paths. Their absence is ADR-011's quietest claim — that the fastest path
through the gate should be the honest one [29].
6.4 VetoGraph and the constitutional audit lineage
 Two internal artifacts connect the VTK's governance to a broader
constitutional-methodology program. The first is SASC v5.4α, the project's constitutional
audit methodology, applied to the 1988 Brazilian Federal Constitution: the corpus of
articles was parsed into a topological graph of 276 nodes and 261 edges — the VetoGraph
— encoding checks, limits, and veto relations among institutions [30, 32]. The second is
the PEC triage protocol, which scores constitutional-amendment proposals against that
graph. These artifacts are methodological demonstrations rather than deployed systems,
and the book presents them with that caveat [30]. Their relevance here is architectural: they
show that the constitution-as-code pattern scales from seven-signer wallets to
seven-hundred-article documents.
 The audit's central metric is d-Veto: for each article, the minimum length of a classified
veto path leading from it to the fundamental-rights core of the constitution — the shortest
institutional route by which another organ can block or reverse its effect. The distribution is
sobering: 151 of the 276 articles lack any classified veto path to the core, meaning that
most of the constitution's text is not structurally shielded by an explicit,
machine-recoverable chain of checks [30]. Chapter 20 presents the full analysis, including
the in-degree and centrality leaders that identify which articles function as the constitution's
load-bearing hubs. The number matters to VTK not as a claim about Brazilian law but as a
demonstration that veto topology can be computed, versioned, and audited at constitutional
scale [30, 32].
 A second statistic, the winding number, addresses cycles rather than paths: it counts
how a chain of competences loops through checking institutions before resolving,
distinguishing healthy mutual oversight from circular delegation that never terminates in an
accountable organ. The audit records winding numbers for the constitution's citation cycles
as part of its classified-path analysis, and the governance layer inherits the idea in a
restricted form — amendment chains must terminate in quorum-governed decisions, and
the machinery flags amendment graphs whose dependencies loop without grounding [28,
30]. The general lesson is that both paths and cycles carry governance meaning, and that a
rulebook without cycle discipline can be gamed by infinite regress as surely as by missing
vetoes. Chapter 20 develops the statistics; here they serve as evidence that the metaphor of
checks and balances can be made computable [30].
 The lineage also imposes a discipline that the governance layer inherits from the audit
tooling: every rule must cite its basis. In the CF/88 audit, a flagged tension cites the articles


=== PAGINA 85 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 85
in conflict; in the ConstitutionStore, an invariant cites the decision record, incident, or
external requirement that motivates it; in the mathematics program of Chapter 22, an
accepted claim cites its formalization artifacts. In all three domains the pattern is identical
— claims gain meaning from the explicit company they keep [28, 30]. The VetoGraph, in
this light, is not a curiosity of one audit but the largest existing stress test of the claim that
governance relations can be stated as data [30, 32].
 The forward pointer matters for the architecture's credibility. When Chapter 20 audits a
real constitution with 276 nodes and finds that most of them lack classified veto paths, it is
measuring the same quantity a deployer measures when asking which of an agent
platform's rules can actually be checked, by whom, and against what [30]. Machine
governance that cannot answer the veto question — who can stop this, and how fast — is a
policy document with a database behind it. The VetoGraph line of work is the project's
standing reminder that the answer must be computed, versioned, and anchored like
everything else in the architecture [28, 30].


=== PAGINA 86 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 86
PART III — VALIDATION, INCIDENTS, AND
COMPLIANCE
Four chapters test the design against the world. Chapter 7 replays three incidents as
counterfactual control experiments and assigns each failure to a missing verification gate.
Chapter 8 specifies the Multisig Inspector as the minimal instrument against blind signing.
Chapter 9 maps the architecture onto regulatory obligations from the EU AI Act to MiCA
and identifies Know-Your-Agent as the market signal. Chapter 10 defines the minimal
viable product — GGUF model verification — with success metrics and honest failure
modes.
7. Incident-Driven Validation: Bybit, StablR,
SUPERFORTUNE
 Part III turns from design to evidence, and this chapter is where the evidence begins.
Three documented incidents — the Bybit theft of February 2025, the StablR minting failure
of May 2026, and the SUPERFORTUNE airdrop diversion of May 2026 — are reduced,
case by case, to the question of which verification gate would have stopped them and what
risk would have survived. The three were chosen because each fails a different gate of the
architecture's ceremony-time set, so together they exercise the taxonomy rather than one
corner of it [2, 6, 34]. Sections 7.1 to 7.4 state the method and the cases; Section 7.5
synthesizes the gate taxonomy of failure; and Section 7.6 sets the incidents inside the
aggregate loss landscape that industry reporting measures annually [96, 97].
7.1 Method: counterfactual control analysis
 This chapter asks a disciplined counterfactual question of three documented incidents:
had the specific controls proposed by the VTK architecture been present at ceremony time,
at which step would the attack chain have been interrupted, and what residual risk would
have remained? The question is worth asking because the industry's incident literature is
rich in reconstruction and poor in counterfactual specification: post-mortems establish what
happened, but rarely state which enforceable check, placed where, would have changed the
outcome. We treat each incident, therefore, as a test that the architecture must be able to
explain, and we treat any failure to explain an incident as a design defect rather than as a
marketing inconvenience [28, 31]. The deliverable of the chapter is not certification — no
counterfactual can certify — but specification pressure: a list of gates, each of which is
either exercised by a real failure or justified by the threat model of Chapter 3.


=== PAGINA 87 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 87
 The method proceeds in five steps, applied identically to each incident so that the
results are comparable across cases and the analysis cannot quietly change rules between
them. The steps are stated once here and referenced by number thereafter. Each step
produces an artifact — a factual record, a chain, a gate set, a replay verdict, a residual-risk
statement — and those artifacts are what the case sections of this chapter present.
1.  Fix the factual record. The incident is reconstructed only from published forensic
sources, and reconstruction is kept separate from attribution, which is accepted only as
an institutional claim by the attributing authority [4, 93].
2.  Decompose the attack chain. The incident is expressed as an ordered chain of steps
— initial access, payload delivery, ceremony manipulation, value movement,
laundering — so that a control can be located at a specific step rather than waved at the
whole [5, 34].
3.  Define the gate set. The architecture's ceremony-time controls are stated as four
gates, G1 through G4, defined below; each gate is a check that either fires and blocks,
fires and records, or does not apply to the chain in question.
4.  Replay the chain. Holding the attacker's capability fixed, the chain is replayed
against the gates in order, and the first gate whose enforcement breaks the chain is
recorded as the decisive control for that incident.
5.  State residual risk. For every gate that fires, the analysis states what the attacker
retains, what new failure the gate itself introduces, and which assumptions the
containment depends on.
•  G1 — artifact identity. Every artifact that participates in a signing ceremony — an
interface build, a decoder, a contract — must present a hash with an anchored,
unrevoked attestation; an unattested artifact is fail-closed [9, 28].
•  G2 — independent decoding. The meaning of the transaction is re-derived from raw
material outside the presenting interface, and the displayed representation must agree
with the decoded semantics or the ceremony is refused [38].
•  G3 — governance arithmetic. Authority operations require a quorum threshold that
explicitly hypothesizes key compromise, per ADR-011's prohibition of sub-two-thirds
configurations [29].
•  G4 — anchored detectability. Evidence about the ceremony lands in an externally
anchored transparency log, so that silent replacement of any verified component is
detectable after the fact [9, 70].
 Four limitations bound every claim in this chapter, and stating them precisely is more
important than the conclusions they qualify. First, counterfactuals establish plausibility, not
causation: we can show that a gate would have had the opportunity to fire on the recorded
facts, not that it would have fired in a live organization with real operators. Second, the


=== PAGINA 88 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 88
replay holds attacker capability fixed; a determined adversary who discovers that gate G2
blocks interface tampering may shift effort to the verifier's own distribution chain, and the
replay does not model that second-order adaptation. Third, the factual record is
public-source: we had no access to victim telemetry, and details known only to the victims
and their investigators are outside our reach [4, 6, 34]. Fourth, attribution is institutional —
the Federal Bureau of Investigation's attribution of the Bybit incident is reported as the
FBI's claim, not as an independent finding of this book [93].
 A fifth limitation deserves its own paragraph because it is the one the project cannot
delegate. The control set being replayed is the project's own, so the analysis is a
self-assessment and inherits the optimism bias of every designer evaluating their own
design [28, 31]. We partially mitigate the bias by constraining the replay to gates whose
enforcement is mechanically checkable — a hash comparison, a decode-and-diff, a
threshold test, an inclusion proof — rather than to behavioral controls whose effectiveness
would be a matter of judgment. We also adopt the honest-status convention of Chapter 3:
each result in this chapter is reported in the form contained at gate Gk under assumptions
A1 through A4, so that a reader who rejects an assumption can recompute the claim for
themselves. Under these constraints the analysis supports weaker sentences than marketing
would prefer, and those weaker sentences are the ones the architecture can actually defend.
 Figure 7.2 previews the replay for the Bybit incident, and it is placed here rather than in
Section 7.2 because it is the only case in which all four gates participate, which makes it the
method's flagship exhibit. Table 7.1 assembles the verified timeline facts on which the
three case sections rely, so that dates, mechanisms, and responses can be checked against
the cited investigators before the counterfactual reading begins. Neither exhibit carries
counterfactual content; both are strictly factual, and the analysis starts only once they are
on the record.
 Figure 7.2 — Counterfactual replay of the Bybit incident under VTK mediation: the same attacker capability is

7.2 Bybit: interface trust as the root cause
 The factual record is consistent across the investigators who published independently.
On 21 February 2025, Bybit, one of the largest cryptocurrency exchanges, initiated what its
operators believed to be a routine transfer from a cold wallet secured by a Safe
multisignature contract; within minutes, roughly USD 1.5 billion in ether had moved to
attacker-controlled addresses [2, 3]. The transaction carried valid signatures from the
required signers; nothing about the ceremony failed at the cryptography layer. TRM Labs'
tracking of the outflow, Sygnia's forensic engagement, Wiz's analysis of the wallet supply
chain, and DFNS's technical post-mortem converge on the same mechanism despite
different vantage points [2, 4, 5, 7]. The incident immediately became the largest theft in
the industry's history, and its scale is what makes the mechanism worth anatomizing rather
than merely mourning [3, 96].
 The root cause lived in the interface, not the wallet. Sygnia's investigation traced the
intrusion to the developer environment and infrastructure of Safe{Wallet}, the interface
through which Bybit's multisignature transactions were assembled and displayed [4]. Wiz's
deep dive established the delivery mechanism: a developer machine was compromised, and
a malicious JavaScript payload was injected so that it executed only for the targeted
signers, at signing time, presenting one transaction to the screen while substituting different
semantics into the signed payload [5]. What the three signers saw was a legitimate-looking
transfer; what the contract executed was a change to the Safe's implementation pointer that
placed the wallet under attacker control and released its contents [5, 7]. DFNS's analysis
emphasizes the elegance of the construction: the signed message was crafted so that its
hash covered the malicious inner call, while the display layer — which the signers had no
independent way to audit — showed the benign intent [7].


=== PAGINA 90 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 90
 Attribution arrived days later and was institutional rather than academic. On 26
February 2025, the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a public service announcement
stating that North Korea was responsible for the theft and associating the operation with the
TraderTraitor alias used for DPRK cyber-enabled theft [93]. Reuters' coverage documented
the conversion pipeline through which the stolen assets were moved and laundered,
illustrating that the attack did not end at exfiltration [94]. TRM Labs followed the funds
across mixers and exchanges, and its reporting frames the operation as the largest exploit
attributed to North Korean actors to date [2]. The Wilson Center's policy reading drew the
supply-chain lesson outward: when the signing infrastructure of a single vendor mediates
institutional custody worldwide, the compromise of that vendor's build pipeline is a
systemic event rather than a private misfortune [98].
 Fireblocks' post-incident analysis named the structural flaw with unusual directness:
the ceremony operated on blind trust in the system that displayed the transaction [95].
Institutional key holders had verified, over years of operation, that the interface showed
them accurate representations; that verification was inductive, social, and invisible in the
protocol itself. The attacker did not defeat the multisignature scheme, the hardware devices,
or the signing quorum; the attacker defeated the assumption that the representation
justifying consent was produced by the component that appeared to produce it [95]. In the
vocabulary of this book, the display-semantics boundary was unpoliced, and every control
the organization had purchased policed a different boundary. The lesson generalizes
beyond one vendor: any signing ceremony whose consent-justifying representation is
rendered by an unaudited layer is a Bybit waiting for its attacker [3, 95].
 The counterfactual replay is the sharpest of the three cases because every gate
participates. At gate G1, the malicious interface build is an unattested artifact: a
deployment that required an anchored attestation for the code served to signers would have
refused or flagged the tampered bundle before any ceremony began [4, 28]. At gate G2, the
decisive control, an independent decoder re-derives the transaction's meaning from raw
calldata outside the presenting interface and diffs it against the displayed claim; the decode
shows an implementation-pointer change and an ownership transfer where the display
shows a routine transfer, and the mismatch fails the ceremony closed before a single
signature exists [5, 38]. At gate G3, the quorum is intact, but the governance layer of
Chapter 6 would have classified a transaction of anomalous size and anomalous destination
profile as requiring an explicit governance acknowledgement, converting a silent approval
into a deliberate one [29]. At gate G4, the verifier's own artifact is hash-anchored in a
transparency log, so the attacker's next move — replacing the verifier — is detectable
rather than silent [9].
 Residual risk survives the replay, and stating it is part of the method. A user who
ignores the verifier's verdict is unprotected by it; the control moves the failure from the


=== PAGINA 91 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 91
interface to the operator's discipline, which is where several of this book's later chapters
live [7]. A verifier that is itself compromised defeats the decode check, which is why the
verifier's distribution channel is anchored and its verdicts are signed evidence rather than
ephemeral advice [9, 70]. An attacker who adapts — poisoning the decoder's ABI
knowledge, targeting the governance acknowledgement flow, or compromising a signer's
device directly — is attacking controls the replay holds fixed. The honest conclusion, then,
is the one Fireblocks reached from the incident side: Bybit-class attacks are made
expensive, loud, and attributable, not impossible [95].
7.3 StablR: threshold failure at the authority
 In May 2026, the European stablecoin issuer StablR froze its EURR and USDR tokens
after an attacker minted approximately USD 13.5 million of unbacked stablecoins [6]. The
root cause, attributed by Blockaid's analysis and reported by KuCoin Research, was not an
exploit of contract logic but a governance configuration: the minting authority sat behind a
1-of-3 multisignature arrangement, and the attacker controlled one key [33]. One signature
was the entire quorum; possession of a single compromised key was therefore equivalent to
possession of the mint. CoinDesk's reporting recorded the issuer's response — freezing
both tokens — which contained the damage at the cost of halting the tokens' ordinary
function [6]. The case is young by the standards of the incident literature, but its
mechanism is clean, and it earns a place in this chapter for a reason the next paragraph
makes precise.
 StablR is uniquely instructive because the failure was not in an approval interface but
in the governance arithmetic itself. The Bybit signers approved a transaction whose
representation lied to them; StablR's key holder approved a mint that was, under the
configuration, entirely legitimate. No representation was subverted, no interface tampered
with, and no display deceived anyone; the vulnerability was the rule that made one key
sufficient. A threshold is a hypothesis about how many keys may be compromised
simultaneously, and a 1-of-3 threshold hypothesizes that no key is ever compromised — an
assumption the incident falsified in practice [33]. The freeze, meanwhile, demonstrated the
only lever the configuration left: post hoc central intervention by the same authority whose
delegation had failed.
A threshold is a hypothesis about simultaneous key compromise; a 1-of-3
threshold hypothesizes that no key is ever compromised. — ADR-011, internal
decision record [29]
 The decision record responds with arithmetic, not exhortation. ADR-011 fixes the
admissible thresholds at 4-of-7 or 5-of-7 and prohibits sub-two-thirds configurations
outright, because a threshold below two-thirds converts single-key or dual-key compromise


=== PAGINA 92 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 92
into full authority [29]. The record's deeper point is that thresholds are first-class, versioned
objects rather than deployment defaults: changing a threshold is itself a quorum-governed
event whose evidence is recorded, so the configuration that failed at StablR cannot be
quietly relaxed inside the architecture. Under the replay, gate G3 is decisive: a mint
presented under a 4-of-7 policy by a single compromised key is arithmetically impossible
to authorize, and the ceremony never reaches a signature.
 The remaining gates add depth rather than deciding the case. Under the separation of
authority from witness developed in Chapter 6, a mint is a constitution-governed action
whose evidence record carries the quorum proof, the issuing policy version, and the reserve
status it claims, rather than a configuration-controlled operation invisible to governance
[28, 70]. Anchoring contributes a detection property that the incident's actual timeline
lacked: a constitution that caps issuance against reserve attestations turns an unbacked mint
into an invariant violation visible to any auditor of the anchored graph, so the divergence
surfaces at the first mint rather than at redemption or freeze [9, 70]. The regulatory context
strengthens the property: MiCA's stablecoin regime obliges issuers to honor redemption at
par, at any time, and without fees, which makes an unbacked mint an insolvency event in
slow motion and the invariant check a solvency tripwire [92]. Chapter 9 returns to that
interlock in detail.
 Residual risk in this case is the cleanest to state. A 4-of-7 threshold still authorizes
collusion or compromise of up to three keys, and a patient attacker with a zero-day budget
may eventually reach any finite threshold; the gate converts a single-key catastrophe into a
multi-key campaign, which is a different and smaller attack surface but not an empty one.
Threshold governance also does not protect against compromise of the governance process
itself — the Chapter 6 machinery, including the ConstitutionStore's versioning, is what
bounds that risk, and its analysis belongs to later chapters [28, 29]. What the counterfactual
establishes, under assumptions A1 through A4, is contained at gate G3: the mint of USD
13.5 million in unbacked tokens under a single compromised key does not survive contact
with a 4-of-7 quorum [29, 33].
7.4 SUPERFORTUNE: look-alike addresses and automated
flows
 The third incident is smaller in dollars and larger in implication for automated flows. In
May 2026, approximately USD 15.18 million intended for an airdrop distribution was
redirected when a look-alike destination address was substituted into the transfer
preparation, in Halborn's reconstruction of the SUPERFORTUNE exploit [34]. The
attacker did not break a signature, compromise an interface, or touch a threshold; the
attacker relied on the fact that addresses are verified by human eyes through their first and
last characters, and manufactured a doppelgänger that matched where attention falls [34,


=== PAGINA 93 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 93
35]. Market data recorded the consequence for the platform itself: the GUA token drew
down more than 97 percent from its pre-incident peak within days, a measure of how
quickly trust exits a system that cannot distinguish its own counterparties [41].
 The incident belongs to the address-poisoning family, which has been analyzed at
campaign scale. Chainalysis' anatomy of the scam documents the standard mechanics:
attacker-controlled addresses are chosen or vanity-generated to visually mimic addresses a
victim has historically interacted with, dust transactions seed the victim's history with the
look-alikes, and the theft waits for a copying error inside a wallet or an automated flow
[35]. The scale is industrial — Chainalysis documented campaigns using tens of thousands
of attacker addresses, with attempted thefts approaching USD 68 million in a single case
[35] — and Blockaid's 2026 reporting records the family's continued evolution toward
wallet-drain automation [36]. An academic survey formalizes the attack class and its
detection surface, confirming that the mechanism is now part of the repertoire rather than a
novelty [37]. SUPERFORTUNE's contribution to the literature is to show the family
operating against an automated distribution pipeline rather than an end user [34].
 Automation is what converts the scam from opportunism into infrastructure. An
airdrop engine prepares thousands of transfers programmatically; if the destination it
prepares is validated only by string comparison against an expected address — or worse, by
visual similarity in a dashboard — then a single substituted entry propagates at machine
speed and no human ever examines the bytes [34, 36]. The platform in question marketed
itself as an AI-powered prediction engine [34], which makes the episode a preview of the
agentic era this book addresses: agents prepare transfers the way airdrop engines do, and
the representation they act on is whatever their tooling displays or parses. In that setting,
the attacked representation is not the human's glancing read of a hex string but the
machine's parse of a destination field, and the defense must operate at the same layer —
bytes against bytes [35, 37].
 The counterfactual replay places the decisive control at gate G2, joined to kernel
policy. The verifier computes the destination's semantic identity — the canonical address
derived from the transaction's raw material — and compares it against counterparties
pinned by hash in the agent's constitution; a doppelgänger differs in the bytes that matter,
so the mismatch fails the ceremony closed regardless of visual similarity [28, 35]. Gate G3
governs the exception path: amending an allow-list is a quorum event with recorded
evidence, so diverting an agent requires either compromising a quorum or persuading a
quorum on the record, both of which are visible fights [29]. Gate G4 records every refused
ceremony, which converts attempted poisoning into telemetry: the defender's graph
accumulates the attacker's infrastructure as evidence [70].


=== PAGINA 94 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 94
 Residual risk migrates to the allow-list and its governance, which is precisely where the
architecture wants the fight to happen. An allow-list can be captured at creation, by social
engineering the humans who approve amendments, or by compromising the identity
mapping that lives outside the append-only graph; each of these is a governance attack with
an evidence trail rather than a silent substitution [28, 29]. The analysis also inherits a
limitation of the method: the replay assumes the kernel's hash-pinning is correctly
configured for the flow in question, and a flow that legitimately varies its counterparties —
market-making, for instance — cannot be pinned this way and must rely on the decode
check plus post hoc governance review [31]. For distribution pipelines, airdrop machinery,
and any flow with a stable counterparty set, though, the containment claim is strong: the
SUPERFORTUNE mechanism does not survive a semantic destination check [34, 35].
7.5 Synthesis: the gate taxonomy of failure
 The three incidents, reduced to gates, form a taxonomy rather than a collection. Bybit
failed gate G1 — the interface build was an unattested artifact — and would then have met
its decisive refusal at gate G2, where display and decode diverge [4, 5]. StablR failed gate
G3 alone: every representation in its chain was honest, and the arithmetic that permitted
one key to mint was the vulnerability [33]. SUPERFORTUNE failed at gate G2 as well,
though with a different mechanism — not a hidden payload but a visible destination whose
visual identity masked its semantic identity [34, 35]. The taxonomy's usefulness is that it
converts anecdotes into coverage: an architecture can state which gates it enforces, and the
gate matrix then predicts, for any future incident in these families, whether the architecture
would have mattered [28, 31].
 Three patterns survive the reduction. First, all three incidents are attacks on
representations rather than on cryptography: no signature scheme was broken, no hash
collision exhibited, and no key derived; the losses flowed through layers whose job is to
make meaning visible, which is the book's thesis about the modern perimeter stated as three
data points [2, 6, 34]. Second, the decisive controls cluster in two layers — independent
verification and governance arithmetic — which is why the architecture places quorum and
decoding at its center rather than at its edge [29, 38]. Third, the real-world responses were
uniformly post hoc — freezes, disclosures, and fund tracking after value had moved —
whereas the gates act before signatures exist; the difference between freezing a token and
refusing a signature is the difference between mourning and enforcement [6, 95]. The
pattern matters for design economics: controls that act before value moves compete against
losses that have already accumulated, which changes the arithmetic of what a defender
should pay.
 The residual risks are themselves representational, and this symmetry is the chapter's
most uncomfortable finding. A verifier can be ignored by its user, replaced by an attacker,


=== PAGINA 95 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 95
or quietly degraded by its maintainer; an allow-list can be captured at creation or amended
under pressure; a threshold can be relaxed by the very process it governs. The architecture's
response, developed in Chapter 8, is to make the verifier's own identity part of the evidence
graph — the verifier's artifact hash is anchored, its verdicts are signed events, and the
question of which verifier said this is always answerable from the record [9, 70]. That
response does not eliminate the residual risks; it prices them, by forcing an attacker who
wishes to subvert verification to attack artifacts whose substitution is detectable and whose
replacement is an event in a log that outside parties read [9].
 Table 7.2 states the gate-level outcomes in matrix form, with each cell recording either
the decisive containment, a secondary containment, or an explicit non-implication. Reading
the matrix by row yields each incident's story as told in the case sections; reading it by
column yields the coverage profile of each gate across the three families of failure. Two
rows mark gates as not implicated not because those gates are unnecessary but because the
replayed chains never reached them — a fact the threat model of Chapter 3 must justify,
since a gate that no incident exercises is a gate defended only by argument [28]. The matrix
is therefore a specification artifact as much as a validation result: it tells the implementer
which gates the world has already tested on our behalf, and which ones we must test
ourselves.

7.6 The aggregate loss landscape, 2024–2026
 The three case studies sit inside an aggregate picture that industry reporting makes
concrete. TRM Labs' 2026 Crypto Crime Report estimates that USD 2.87 billion was stolen
across nearly 150 hacks in 2025, and observes that the Bybit breach dominates the total
[96]. Read as a base rate, the figure says something the case studies alone cannot: theft at
this scale is not a tail event but the ordinary weather of the industry, with roughly one
material hack every two and a half days in the report's accounting [96]. The three incidents


=== PAGINA 96 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 96
of this chapter are instances of that distribution, chosen for mechanistic clarity rather than
for rarity, and any control proposed against them must be judged against the whole
distribution rather than against its most famous member.
 The composition of the losses matters as much as their sum. Chainalysis' 2025 Crypto
Crime Report documents the professionalization of on-chain crime: industrial laundering
pipelines, specialized criminal services, and state-linked programs that treat stolen digital
assets as revenue at scale [97]. The Bybit case illustrates the trend at its apex — the FBI's
account and subsequent reporting describe a disciplined conversion pipeline moving USD
1.5 billion through mixing and over-the-counter channels within days of exfiltration [93,
94]. For the defender, professionalization changes the threat model in a specific way: the
adversary is competent, patient, funded, and repeatable, so controls that depend on attacker
error are structurally unsound [97, 98]. The gates of this chapter are designed for exactly
that adversary — they are mechanical checks whose enforcement does not require the
attacker to make a mistake.
 Figure 7.1 places the three incidents against the 2025 aggregate on a logarithmic scale,
because the magnitudes span more than two orders and a linear axis would flatten
everything below Bybit into noise. The log reading is the honest one for control economics:
a control that costs one unit and covers a failure mode whose annual loss is USD 2.87
billion justifies itself at very small coverage probabilities, while a control that defends only
against the single largest event must be priced differently [96]. The SUPERFORTUNE and
StablR entries sit orders of magnitude below Bybit, yet each represents a family — address
poisoning, authority compromise — whose aggregate losses across many incidents
approach the headline cases [35, 96]. The figure's context bar is therefore the number that
disciplines the whole chapter: controls are purchased against distributions, not against
anecdotes.


=== PAGINA 97 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 97
 Figure 7.1 — Loss magnitudes of the three archetypal incidents (log scale). The 2025 aggregate of USD 2.87
 billion across roughly 150 hacks is shown for context [96].
 The aggregate also has a composition, and the composition is where the chapter's
taxonomy meets the population. The interface-compromise family that Bybit exemplifies,
the authority-compromise family that StablR exemplifies, and the address-poisoning family
that SUPERFORTUNE exemplifies are all represented in the annual reporting as recurring
categories rather than as one-off curiosities [4, 33, 35]. Chainalysis' campaign-scale
documentation of address poisoning — tens of thousands of attacker addresses in ongoing
operations — indicates that the smallest of the three families is also the most industrially
organized [35, 36]. A gate taxonomy earns its keep exactly here: if the recurring categories
of loss map onto the gates an architecture enforces, then coverage can be reasoned about
category by category instead of incident by incident [28, 96].
 Two final cautions complete the landscape. First, aggregate loss figures are
investigators' estimates of an observable that is partly hidden — undetected compromises
and unreported thefts do not appear in any report — so the numbers should be read as
floors, not as censuses, and cited as such [96, 97]. Second, the trajectory matters more than
any single year: agentic automation multiplies the number of signing ceremonies, mint
operations, and destination selections per hour by factors that human-paced institutions
never planned for, and each ceremony is a potential surface of the kinds dissected in this
chapter [31, 36]. In that sense the loss landscape is not background to the architecture but
its demand curve: USD 2.87 billion in a single year is the market's own measurement of
what unverified representations cost, published annually by investigators with no stake in
the answer [96, 97].
