SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 98
8. The Multisig Inspector and Independent
Transaction Decoding
 Chapter 7 established that the decisive gate in two of the three incidents is independent
decoding, and that the gate is only as good as the independence of the decoder. This chapter
specifies the component that enforces it. We proceed from a precise statement of the
blind-signing problem (Section 8.1), through the design and behavior of the Multisig
Inspector (Section 8.2), to an explicit comparison with adjacent tooling and a statement of
what the inspector does not solve (Section 8.3). Throughout, the component is treated as a
verification gate in the sense of Chapter 12 rather than as a product feature: its verdicts are
evidence, and its own identity is part of the record [28, 70].
8.1 The blind-signing problem, precisely stated
 A digital signature is an act over a hash, but consent is an act over meaning, and the
gap between the two is where blind signing lives. The signer's device computes or receives
a digest; the justification for signing — the belief that this digest represents this intent — is
supplied by a representation rendered by some other component. Whenever that
component's integrity is not independently verified at ceremony time, the ceremony is blind
in the operational sense, regardless of how informative its screen appears. The definition is
deliberately broader than the wallet industry's usage: it covers a browser extension, a
transaction builder, a dashboard fed by an indexer, and any agent pipeline whose display
layer stands between raw bytes and human or machine consent [1, 38].
 The Safe smart account makes the problem concrete, because its semantics are well
documented and its usage is institutional. A Safe transaction is a typed structure hashed
under EIP-712, which gives signatures a structured framing over fields such as the target
contract, the value, the operation type, and a hash of the calldata [24]. A threshold of
owners signs the resulting struct hash off-chain, and the Safe contract executes the
transaction once the threshold is presented [25]. The typed hash is a genuine advance over
raw byte signing, and the reader should not mistake this section for a critique of EIP-712;
the point is narrower and harsher. The hash covers the data field only as a hash, so the
meaning of an inner call lives one derivation deeper than the signed structure, in a
pre-image the signature never committed to directly [24, 25].
 The delegatecall path is the canonical blind spot, and the practitioner literature is
unanimous about it. When the inner data is itself a call to another contract — or when the
operation field selects delegatecall, executing the inner call in the Safe's own storage
context — the outer transaction can look entirely routine while the inner call re-points an
implementation, rewrites ownership, or drains approvals [25, 38]. FreedomFactory's
analysis of device-level decoding states the consequence precisely: the fields that determine


=== PAGINA 99 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 99
what a Safe transaction actually does are exactly the fields a compressed interface does not
surface, and a device that receives only a struct hash cannot decode a pre-image it was
never given [38]. The Bybit incident is the existence proof: every signer's hardware device
faithfully signed the hash it was asked to sign, and the deception lived entirely in the layer
that chose which hash to request [4, 5, 95].
 Wallet-layer mitigations have improved materially, and they deserve credit before they
receive criticism. Clear-signing initiatives decode common transaction patterns at the
wallet layer so that users see human-readable intents rather than hex [1]; device-side
decoders now render Safe fields, including thresholds and owner sets, on the hardware
screen itself [38]. These mitigations shrink the blind window for the flows they cover, and
the architecture's own inspector uses the same decoding discipline. Their structural limits
are threefold. They operate inside the trust perimeter of the party that serves them — the
wallet vendor, the extension store, the firmware signer — which is exactly the perimeter
Bybit's attacker penetrated; they cannot decode what they are not given, so hashed inner
pre-images remain opaque; and they produce no evidence artifact, so the ceremony leaves
no record beyond the chain's own receipt [1, 38, 95].
•  R1 — independence. The decoder must run outside the presenting interface, with no
shared process, library, or trust root, so that subverting the display does not subvert the
decode [28].
•  R2 — completeness. The decode must descend through nested calls and delegatecall
indirections against known ABIs, and must surface the effective threshold and owner set
of the target Safe, because those fields are part of a transaction's meaning [25, 38].
•  R3 — verifiability of the verifier. The decoder's own artifact must carry an
anchored, checkable identity, so that the classic bootstrap attack — replace the checker
— is detectable [9].
•  R4 — evidence. The verdict must be emitted as a signed, anchored event, so that the
question of what was shown, decoded, and refused is answerable after the fact [70].
 Requirements R1 through R4 convert a slogan — verify before you sign — into a
contract that a component either meets or does not. They also explain why the inspector is a
gate rather than a feature: a gate, in the sense of Chapter 12, is a check whose failure blocks
the ceremony and whose success produces evidence, and R4 is what distinguishes the gate
from good advice [70]. The next section describes the component as specified against this
contract. Its design takes no credit for the decoding discipline, which it borrows from the
clear-signing movement; its contribution is the coupling of that discipline to independence
and evidence, which is where the existing tooling stops [1, 28].
8.2 The Multisig Inspector


=== PAGINA 100 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 100
 The Multisig Inspector is the application of the arkhe-verify-wasm verifier to Safe
transactions, packaged so that an operator can run it at ceremony time [28]. Its defining
property is architectural, not algorithmic: it runs outside the presenting interface, with no
shared runtime, no shared configuration, and no network path to the party whose
transaction it examines. The inspector consumes raw transaction material — the EIP-712
message, the inner calldata, and whatever claim the presenting interface makes about the
transaction — and produces a decode plus a diff plus a verdict. The verdict is fail-closed:
on any mismatch between display and decode, on any undecodable component, or on any
missing input, the inspector reports refusal rather than a best-effort interpretation [28, 38].
1.  Reconstruct the EIP-712 structure and validate the domain binding — chain
identifier, Safe address, and nonce — so that a transaction cannot be replayed across
contexts [24].
2.  Re-derive the Safe transaction hash and present it for comparison against the hash
the signer's device reports, closing the loop between what the device signs and what the
structure means [25].
3.  Decode the inner call, including delegatecall targets, against known ABIs,
descending until every meaningful field is resolved or explicitly reported as unresolved
[38].
4.  Display the effective threshold and current owner set of the target Safe, because a
transaction's meaning includes who can authorize it and whether that set has changed
[25].
5.  Diff the decode against the displayed claim and classify the ceremony as matching,
mismatching, or undecidable [28].
6.  Emit a signed verdict into the evidence layer, so that the inspection itself becomes an
event in the WormGraph with the same standing as the events it inspects [70].
 Implementation constraints follow the project's principle of verifiable distribution. The
decoding runs offline: no network access occurs during verification, which removes an
entire class of phoning-home failure and makes the tool admissible in air-gapped
ceremonies [28]. Output is deterministic for identical inputs, so that two independent
operators running the same artifact on the same transaction must produce byte-identical
verdicts, a property that makes the tool auditable by reproduction. The distributed artifact is
a static WASM build whose hash is anchored in a transparency log at release, so that any
operator can verify the verifier before relying on it [9, 28]. These constraints cost
engineering convenience and purchase the only property that matters in this niche: the
decoder must not become a second interface to subvert.
 A session transcript conveys the behavior more precisely than a specification, and the
listing below shows the tool refusing the canonical Bybit-class payload in a laboratory


=== PAGINA 101 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 101
replay. The replay uses the incident's published mechanism — a displayed transfer with an
inner delegatecall that swaps the Safe's implementation — against a test fixture rather than
live chain state; its purpose is to exhibit the output contract [5, 38]. The listing is
reproduced in the form documented for the project's fixture, and every line of it is designed
to be checked by the operator rather than trusted [28].
$ arkhe-inspector verify --tx tx-0x9f3a.json --claim display.json
[1/5] artifact .............. Multisig Inspector 0.4.1 (static wasm)
sha256 4b19...e2ac | rekor inclusion: OK (log seq 88,412)
[2/5] EIP-712 domain ........ chain 1 | Safe 0x1Cb3...37f | nonce 4,119
[3/5] safeTxHash re-derived . 0x6f1e...c42b equals device-reported hash
[4/5] inner call decoded .... delegatecall to 0x4675...Cde
effect: setImplementation(0x1c1e...d51), owner set rewritten
[5/5] diff against display .. MISMATCH
display claims: transfer 100,000 ETH to cold wallet
decode shows: implementation swap, no transfer
verdict: REFUSED (fail-closed) | evidence: whg://ev/01J8Q... | exit 2
 Reading the listing against the requirements is instructive. The first line pair discharges
R3: the operator sees the inspector's own version and anchored hash, with the
transparency-log inclusion already checked, before any transaction is examined [9]. The
middle lines discharge R2: the hash equality check closes the device loop, and the decode
descends into the delegatecall that the display layer omitted, surfacing the implementation
swap and the owner change that constitute the attack [25, 38]. The final lines discharge R4:
the verdict is fail-closed, carries an evidence pointer, and exits nonzero so that scripted
ceremonies abort on refusal rather than parsing prose [70]. The diff against the displayed
claim — a routine transfer — is the entire point of the tool: the operator is never asked to
compare the decode against the attacker's narrative, only the machine's decode against the
machine's display, and the two machines have no shared component to subvert [28].
 The verdict-into-evidence design has a governance consequence worth stating in its
own right. Because inspections are events, an organization accumulates a queryable history
of what was shown, decoded, and signed, ceremony by ceremony; the Bybit post-mortem's
hardest question — what did the signers see? — converts from a forensic reconstruction
into a lookup [4, 31]. The same history creates an accountability surface for the inspector
itself: a wrong decode is discoverable, attributable to a specific artifact version, and
correctable by supersession rather than by silent patching, in keeping with the append-only
doctrine of Chapter 3 [70]. Accountability cuts both ways, and that is the design intent: the
tool witnesses the ceremony, and the record witnesses the tool.
8.3 Comparison and boundary
 Positioned against existing tooling, the inspector occupies a narrow but load-bearing
niche, and the comparison is best drawn in three positions. The first position is hardware
clear-signing: device-side decoders that render transaction fields on the signing screen


=== PAGINA 102 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 102
itself, now shipped by several vendors and analyzed in the practitioner literature [1, 38].
The second is the inspector: an independent, offline, evidence-producing decoder that runs
beside the ceremony. The third is the full VTK pipeline, in which decoding is one gate
among four and its verdicts feed governance, anchoring, and the universal core of Part IV
[28]. The positions are complements rather than competitors, but their trust assumptions
differ in ways that matter operationally.
 Hardware clear-signing wins on display integrity at the key ceremony: the screen that
justifies consent is the device that holds the key, with no browser, extension, or vendor
service between them. Its structural limits are the mirror of its strengths. A device can
decode only what it is given, so a hashed inner pre-image — the delegatecall heart of the
Bybit mechanism — remains opaque to it no matter how good its renderer [38]; its trust
root is the firmware vendor, which relocates rather than removes the supply-chain question;
and it produces no organizational evidence, so an institution running ten thousand
ceremonies a year has no record of what was shown beyond the chain itself [1, 38]. The
inspector's decode runs on the full pre-image precisely because it is not the signing device
and can be handed the complete material.
 The full pipeline adds what a standalone tool cannot carry: quorum governance over
the ceremony itself, anchoring of every artifact including the inspector, and integration
with the constitution and witness machinery of Part II [28, 29]. The inspector is best
understood as the pipeline's minimal complete instance — one gate, runnable today, by an
organization that has adopted nothing else — and as an on-ramp in the adoption path of
Chapter 13. It shares the pipeline's evidence format, so an organization that begins with the
inspector and later adopts governance and anchoring inherits its inspection history rather
than migrating it [70]. This staging matters commercially as well as technically, because it
lets the heaviest control — governance — be adopted after the cheapest one has already
produced value [31].
 The boundary is equally explicit, and honesty about it is part of the design. The
inspector cannot make an operator read the verdict; a ceremony that ignores a refusal is
unprotected, and no client-side control can close that gap [7]. It cannot verify intent: a
decode that matches the display proves only that display and semantics agree, not that
either represents what the signer wants. It cannot recover funds, reverse an approved
transaction, or monitor execution after the ceremony; once a valid signature exists, the
chain's own rules take over. What it changes is the epistemic state of the ceremony: the
failure mode of Chapter 7 moves from the representation was subverted silently to the
subversion was detectable, the detection was recorded, and the record survives the attacker
[7, 95]. For an institution, that movement — from silence to evidence — is the difference
between a loss it cannot explain and a loss it can at least litigate, audit, and redesign against
[31].


=== PAGINA 103 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 103
9. Regulatory Alignment: Architecture as
Compliance Evidence
 Validation against incidents shows that the architecture's gates fire on real attacks; this
chapter asks a different question: what does the architecture give an organization that must
answer to a regulator? The claim, defended section by section, is that verifiable trust
infrastructure is not adjacent to compliance but constitutive of it — the records regulators
increasingly demand are exactly the records the architecture natively produces. Section 9.1
maps the architecture onto the obligations themselves; Section 9.2 works through data
protection in the European Union and Brazil; Section 9.3 treats crypto-asset regulation and
the management-system standards that audits actually run on; and Section 9.4 reads the
market's own signal, the Know-Your-Agent frameworks announced in 2026 [39, 40].
9.1 Mapping architecture to obligations
 Regulation increasingly demands what transparency logs natively produce: records that
are complete, tamper-evident, and reconstructable over the lifetime of a system. Article 12
of the EU AI Act requires that high-risk systems technically allow for the automatic
recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, and the Act's service-desk
materials make the intent explicit — logs sufficient to reconstruct what the system did and
under which conditions [17, 18]. The WormGraph is a direct implementation of that
requirement, and its contribution beyond compliance is structural: the causal edges of the
graph supply the traceability that flat logs lack, so the record supports questions about why
an event occurred, not only that it occurred [70]. An auditor who can walk the graph can
reconstruct the decision path of any action; an auditor holding a flat log can only enumerate
it [28].
 The Act's temporal staging converts this mapping from aspiration to calendar. The
regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024; prohibitions and AI-literacy duties applied
from February 2025; obligations for general-purpose AI models and the transparency tier
apply from 2 August 2026; and high-risk obligations follow on 2 December 2027 for
stand-alone systems listed in Annex III and on 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems
embedded in regulated products [17, 19, 117]. The project's planning read is that the
2026–2028 window is exactly when evidence infrastructure becomes a procurement
question rather than a research topic: providers and deployers confronting conformity
assessment will need machine-checkable logs, and vendors who can supply them will be in
the room where procurement happens [18, 31]. The architecture's evidence bundles are
designed to be ready before that window, not after it.
 The mapping extends beyond the Act to the frameworks organizations actually
operationalize. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes AI governance into


=== PAGINA 104 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 104
four functions — govern, map, measure, manage — and its measurement and management
functions are precisely where machine-checkable evidence earns its keep: invariants tested
continuously, telemetry anchored, and incident traces reconstructable [15]. ISO/IEC
42001:2023 defines certifiable requirements for AI management systems, and the
architecture is positioned as the technical substrate beneath such systems rather than as a
competing management system [16]. The distinction matters for audits: ISO 42001 certifies
that an organization's processes exist and are followed, while the architecture supplies the
machine-verifiable artifacts that make the certification's claims cheap to check [16, 28].
The same division of labor recurs with every instrument in this chapter, and Figure 9.1
sketches it across the full set.
 Figure 9.1 presents the authors' qualitative mapping between eight instruments and the
verification capabilities of the architecture; the mapping is deliberately coarse, since its
purpose is orientation rather than legal opinion. The method behind the figure, and behind
Table 9.1 at the end of this chapter, is a three-column discipline: the obligation as written,
the mechanism that produces the demanded evidence, and the honest boundary — what the
mechanism does not claim [28]. The discipline exists because the failure mode of
compliance technology is overclaim: a vendor who asserts that code satisfies a legal duty
invites both regulatory disappointment and moral hazard, and the boundary column is
where this book refuses to cross [31]. Each section that follows applies the discipline to one
family of instruments, and the table consolidates the results for reference. Readers should
treat the figure and the table as one artifact viewed at two resolutions.
 Figure 9.1 — Regulatory obligations versus verification capabilities (authors' qualitative mapping across eight
 instruments).


=== PAGINA 105 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 105
9.2 Data protection: GDPR and LGPD
 Immutability and data protection are in structural tension, and the architecture's answer
is honesty about scope rather than pretense. Under the GDPR, personal data benefit from
erasure rights under Article 17 and from the regulation's broader apparatus of principles
and accountability duties [22]; Article 30 in particular requires controllers and processors
to maintain records of processing activities, a duty that maps naturally onto the
WormGraph's export bundles [90]. Under Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, holders
of personal data hold rights consolidated in the statute's dedicated chapter, including
confirmation of processing, access, correction, anonymization, portability, and deletion,
together with a right to review of decisions taken solely by automated means [23]. An
evidence system that is append-only cannot delete, and a data-protection regime that grants
erasure cannot be ignored; the design has to give on one side or engineer around the
collision [28].
 The engineering answer is minimization at ingestion plus deletion outside the graph.
Evidence records reference subjects by hashes and keys rather than by identifiers, so that
the anchored store contains assertions about actions, not dossiers about persons; where a
mapping between hash and identity must exist, it lives outside the append-only store in a
service that can be deleted without corrupting the graph [28]. For the narrow cases where
personal data must enter the evidence layer itself, the design treats cryptographic deletion
— destroying the keys that make anchored ciphertext readable — as the pragmatic strategy,
with the honest caveat that the existence of the anchored ciphertext remains visible [28].
Data-protection impact assessment is likewise promoted from document to governance
invariant: a deployment that would ingest personal data beyond the minimization policy
must obtain a quorum-governed exception, which produces evidence either way [28, 29].
The result is a system in which the default is that the minimum necessary personal data
enters the evidence layer at all.
 Brazil's regulatory detail adds a transfer dimension that the European analysis alone
would miss. ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD nº 19/2024 consolidated the country's regime for
international transfers of personal data, organized around standard contractual clauses and
allied safeguards [91]. Anchoring is inherently cross-border — a transparency log is
credible precisely because it is replicated outside any single jurisdiction — so a deployment
that anchors evidence containing pseudonymized references must reason about whether
those references constitute personal data subject to the transfer regime [91]. The
architecture's minimization posture is the main mitigation: hashes that cannot be
re-identified without the out-of-graph map are, on the project's reading, outside the scope of
personal-data transfers, though the reading is hedged deliberately and flagged for counsel
rather than asserted as settled law [28, 91]. The honest boundary is recorded in Table 9.1 as
exactly that: a design position awaiting supervisory confirmation, not a legal opinion [31].


=== PAGINA 106 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 106
 The rights apparatus maps to architectural affordances with unusual cleanliness, and
the mapping is worth stating mechanism by mechanism. Access and portability correspond
to export: the graph's bundles are complete, signed, and reconstructable, which is what a
portability request demands [90]. Correction and deletion correspond to the out-of-graph
identity map plus supersession: the anchored record is corrected by appending an
authoritative correction, and the identity linkage that made a record personal is destroyable
[28]. The right to review of automated decisions corresponds to causal evidence: the graph
shows which policy version produced a given action, under which quorum, and with which
inputs, which is precisely the reconstruction a review requires [23, 70]. Each mapping is a
hypothesis until tested with a supervisory authority — a task scheduled in the
market-validation plan [31] — but it is the rare kind of hypothesis that can be tested by
walking an auditor through the graph rather than by arguing from principle.
9.3 Crypto-asset regulation and management systems
 For custody-adjacent deployments, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation
establishes the operative European regime. MiCA's authorization and conduct requirements
for crypto-asset service providers apply across the Union since 30 December 2024, and its
stablecoin chapter imposes reserve, custody, and redemption duties on issuers of
asset-referenced and e-money tokens [20, 21]. The redemption duty is the sharpest from
this book's perspective: issuers must honor redemption at par, at any time, and without fees,
which converts an unbacked mint from an accounting discrepancy into an immediate,
callable liability [92]. Chapter 7's StablR incident is therefore not merely a security case but
a preview of the supervisory question the regime now forces: what evidence does an issuer
hold that its minting authority is governed, its reserves are real, and its redemption promise
is exercisable [6, 92]? The architecture contributes the evidence dimension —
quorum-governed mint authority, reserve attestations as anchored invariants, and incident
traces that reconstruct exactly which keys authorized which issuance [28, 70].
 Operational resilience interlocks with the regime through the Digital Operational
Resilience Act, whose incident-reporting and ICT-risk machinery ESMA's overview
materials treat as complementary to MiCA's conduct framework [21, 72]. The architecture's
evidence layer serves that interlock directly: an ICT incident in a custody pipeline is, in the
WormGraph, a chain of events with causal edges, timestamps anchored externally, and the
specific artifacts involved identified by hash — the difference between filing a narrative
and filing a reconstruction [70, 72]. Supervisors gain a record they can check; the
institution gains a record it can defend. Neither gain requires the architecture to claim
anything about prudential adequacy, capital, or conduct, which remain outside its scope by
design [21].


=== PAGINA 107 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 107
 At the management-system layer, the standards that audits actually run on are ISO
27001 and SOC 2, and the architecture's contribution is to change their economics.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 defines the requirements for an information security management
system, and SOC 2 defines trust services criteria — security, availability, processing
integrity, confidentiality, privacy — against which service organizations report [170, 171].
Both regimes certify process and sample evidence: an auditor examines whether controls
exist and tests a selection of instances. The architecture replaces sampling with
reconstruction for the controls it enforces: instead of a sampled screenshot of an approval
flow, the auditor walks the anchored graph of every approval flow; instead of attestations
that logs exist, the auditor verifies inclusion proofs [9, 28]. The claim is not that the
architecture substitutes for either standard — it certifies no process — but that it makes the
evidence half of the audit continuous, machine-checkable, and cheap to examine [171].
 Table 9.1 consolidates the obligation-to-mechanism mapping developed across this
chapter, in the three-column discipline introduced at Figure 9.1: obligation, mechanism,
honest boundary. The table's rows are ordered by instrument family — AI regulation, data
protection, crypto-asset and management-system standards — and each row's boundary
column is the operative claim of this chapter: the architecture produces evidence, certifies
nothing, and adjudicates nothing [28, 31]. Where a row's boundary reads awaiting
supervisory confirmation, the mapping is a design position offered for testing, not a
representation of settled law [91]. Readers who need one sentence to carry out of this
chapter should take the table's last column, because the boundaries are where trustworthy
vendors and untrustworthy ones part company.

9.4 The market signal: Know-Your-Agent
 The regulatory analysis lands in a market that moved while this book was being
written. On 10 September 2026, Ant International announced a collaboration with Visa and
Mastercard on a Know-Your-Agent interoperability framework — an effort to give AI
agents verifiable identity and credentials in payments — unveiled in São Paulo [39]. The
announcement is notable less for its specifics than for its provenance: two global card
networks and a major payments infrastructure company treating agent identity as a problem
worth a framework [39, 40]. Trade coverage of the announcement framed KYA as the
agent-era successor to KYC, which is exactly the analogy the architecture's own vocabulary
would predict [40].
 The symmetry with this book's thesis is direct but incomplete, and the incompleteness
is the interesting part. KYA, read as attestation for agents, is the identity layer of the
verifiable trust stack: it answers who acted. The architecture's argument throughout Parts II
and III is that identity alone is insufficient without evidence governance — an agent that is
known must also be contained, its actions attested against a constitution, its authority
quorum-governed, and its failures recorded as evidence [28, 29]. A known agent that can
mint, transfer, or deploy without a gate is a known attacker with paperwork; the incidents
of Chapter 7 were all perpetrated by components that were, in the mundane sense, known.
The project therefore reads KYA as category validation rather than competition: it validates
the premise that agents need portable, verifiable credentials, and it leaves open exactly the
layer this book occupies [31, 39].
 The timing is itself a data point. KYA frameworks emerged in the same window in
which the EU AI Act's transparency obligations became applicable, 2 August 2026, and in
which agentic wallet infrastructure reached production announcements [17, 116, 117].
Regulatory pull and supplier push are converging on the same architectural slot —
machine-verifiable credentials and evidence for autonomous agents — from two directions,
which is the pattern that usually marks a category forming rather than a product being
marketed [31, 40]. For a small evidence vendor, the strategic reading is that identity
coalitions define the demand curve for evidence: once agents carry credentials, the question


=== PAGINA 109 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 109
of what those agents did, under which authority, becomes the natural follow-on purchase
[39].
 The boundary of the claim should be stated with the same discipline as the rest of this
chapter. The architecture does not implement KYA, does not participate in the announced
framework, and holds no position on its governance; the observation is that the market's
direction — verifiable agent credentials in payment rails — is congruent with the
architecture's evidence layer and would interoperate with it at the credential boundary [39,
40]. What KYA does not answer — behavioral containment, authority governance, and
anchored evidence of actions — is the subject of the rest of this book, and Chapter 23 treats
the coalitions forming around agent identity as integration surfaces rather than as rivals
[31]. The next chapter turns from the market's demand signal to the project's first
supply-side answer: an artifact small enough to ship, and honest enough to fail.
10. The Minimal Viable Product: GGUF Model
Verification
 Part III closes with the project's smallest shippable claim. The previous chapters
specified gates, built an inspector, and mapped obligations; none of that matters if the
architecture cannot put one verifiable artifact into a practitioner's hands. This chapter
defines the minimal viable product — verification of a single GGUF model file — and
states its success metrics, distribution strategy, and failure modes with the same
falsifiability the book demands of everything else [31]. The MVP is deliberately modest,
and its modesty is the argument: if the verifiable trust loop cannot close around one file, it
cannot close around anything.
10.1 Why the first artifact is a model file
 The project's executive analysis converged on a narrow first product: verify one GGUF
model, end to end, for one persona — the machine-learning engineer [31]. The choice was
made against broader alternatives, and the reasoning is worth reconstructing because it
generalizes. Transactions require governance context that does not exist yet; formal proofs
require the mathematical infrastructure that Chapter 22's program develops; but a model
file requires only that a publisher sign once and anchor once, and that a verifier hash and
compare [28, 31]. The MVP is therefore the smallest instance in which the architecture's
full loop — artifact, identity, anchored attestation, verdict, evidence — closes without any
organizational adoption, committee, or procurement.
 GGUF is the right container because it is where the persona already is. The format is
the dominant distribution container for open-weight models served by llama.cpp-derived
runtimes, and its documentation ecosystem makes it the de facto unit of exchange for


=== PAGINA 110 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 110
quantized weights [26, 27]. A single file carries the model's graph, weights, tokenizer, and
metadata, which means the hash of the file is a complete identity for the artifact the
practitioner actually runs. No sidecar, no manifest, no package graph: identity at the
granularity of the download, which is exactly where trust decisions are made today [26].
The attestation story consequently needs no infrastructure beyond Chapter 4's anchoring —
the publisher signs the hash, the hash is anchored, the verifier compares [9, 28].
 The runtime's own behavior sharpens the stakes. Ollama's documentation of local
model import states that importing a GGUF does not quantize or otherwise transform the
artifact; the model is used as provided [163]. The file is therefore not a source from which
behavior is derived but the behavior itself: whatever bytes arrive are the bytes that execute
on the user's machine, with no build step at which tampering might be caught or corrected.
This is the software supply chain with the packaging removed — the equivalent of running
a downloaded binary — and the ecosystem treats it with correspondingly little ceremony
[163]. The trust gap is visceral precisely because the artifact is self-contained: an engineer
who has downloaded a quantized model from an unknown mirror has performed exactly
the unverifiable-representation act this book is about, usually without noticing [31].
 The threat is not hypothetical, and the precedents deserve enumeration. Hugging Face
operates pickle-scanning infrastructure precisely because serialized model formats have
carried executable payloads [118]; ReversingLabs documented malicious models on the
platform whose payloads unpacked at load time [119]; JFrog's researchers reported a
family of models with silent malicious code embedded in trusted serialization formats
[120]; and the PickleBall line of work formalizes both the attack surface and secure
deserialization for pickle-based models [121]. GGUF's design avoids pickle's
arbitrary-code execution, and this section should not be read as claiming otherwise. The
supply-chain problem, however, is upstream of serialization: whatever the format's safety,
the question of who published these bytes, under what identity, and with what revocation
story remains open — and that question is exactly what model attestation answers [28,
118]. The pickle era is the right mental model not for its mechanism but for its lesson: an
ecosystem that ships executable artifacts without provenance will eventually ship someone
else's executable artifact.
 The product converts the act of downloading into an act of checking, and the flow is
deliberately boring. The user runs the arkhe-verify CLI or pastes the file into the static
browser verifier and receives one of three verdicts: verified, meaning the hash matches an
anchored attestation with no revocation along its dependency chain; unverified, meaning no
record exists; or revoked, meaning a superseding record invalidates the attestation [28].
Each verdict links to its evidence — the publisher's signature, the declared license and
training-data status, and the Rekor inclusion proof — so the verdict is a pointer into the
record rather than an oracle's pronouncement [9]. Nothing in the flow asks the user to trust


=== PAGINA 111 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 111
the project's servers; the verifier is a static artifact whose own hash is anchored, per the
same distribution principle as the inspector of Chapter 8 [9, 28].
10.2 Success metrics
 The analysis prescribes measurement before scaling, with four metrics defining success
for the MVP window, each stated with a target and a falsification condition [31].
Time-to-first-value targets under thirty minutes from discovery to a first successful
verification, because onboarding friction is where developer tools die. Verification latency
is targeted in seconds and is dominated by the hash operation for typical GGUF sizes,
because a verifier slower than the download is a verifier that will not be run. Verification
success rate — the fraction of attempted verifications that return a decisive verdict rather
than an error — is the honesty metric: errors are the system lying about its competence, and
a verifier that cannot decide should say so explicitly rather than fail opaquely [31]. The
fourth metric is a composite of activation, fourteen-day retention, and net promoter score
for the persona, which tests whether verification is a task or a toy.
 Figure 10.1 situates the metrics within the seven-phase, nine-month roadmap the plan
prescribes: the phases run from artifact and schema work through publisher onboarding to
an independent audit, and the metrics gate the transitions between them rather than
decorating the end state [31, 69]. The roadmap's discipline is that each phase ends with a
number, not a narrative; a phase that misses its metric is re-scoped or cut, in the same spirit
in which Chapter 22 treats a claim that cannot fail as not a claim [31]. The figure is the
authors' plan rather than a result, and it is presented as the commitment device against
which the MVP will be judged.
 Figure 10.1 — MVP roadmap for GGUF model verification: seven phases over nine months (authors' plan).


=== PAGINA 112 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 112
 Table 10.1 states the four metrics with their targets and the conditions under which the
project will declare them failed. The falsification conditions are as important as the targets,
because they are what makes the plan empirical rather than aspirational: a median
onboarding that exceeds thirty minutes across a cohort of twenty or more users falsifies the
first metric, a p95 latency beyond one minute on commodity hardware falsifies the second,
an error rate above five percent in field telemetry falsifies the third, and a cohort review
that finds retention or NPS below threshold falsifies the fourth [31]. The metrics are
deliberately few, because a scorecard nobody reads is a scorecard nobody obeys.

 Measurement infrastructure deserves a paragraph of its own, because metrics are only
as honest as the plumbing that produces them. Telemetry, where used, is consented and
minimized in the sense of Chapter 9: counters and durations leave the client, payloads do
not, and the deployment that wants more must argue for it through a governance exception
[28, 31]. The dashboards that display the metrics are themselves governance artifacts,
versioned alongside the constitution, so that a target cannot be quietly redefined after it is
missed [29]. Cohort reviews are conducted on a fixed calendar and their outcomes
recorded, which converts the scorecard from a slide into a record [31].
 Interpretation of the metrics deserves equal candor. Time-to-first-value dominates
adoption, and the thirty-minute target exists because the persona's alternative — doing
nothing — costs nothing and requires no trust; the MVP competes against inertia, not
against a rival product [31]. Latency and decision rate are engineering-honest metrics that
the team can move directly; the composite is the only metric that measures value rather
than function, and it is also the one most exposed to noise, which is why its threshold is set
at a cohort review rather than a live dashboard [31]. A plan that survives its own metrics
produces the credibility on which the next chapters' larger claims are financed.
10.3 Distribution and the wedge


=== PAGINA 113 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 113
 Distribution follows the persona's existing motion rather than inventing a new one, and
the plan names three channels [31]. The choice of channels is not a marketing question but
a trust question: each channel carries the verifier's anchored identity to a different audience,
and each preserves the property that the user can verify the verifier before using it [9, 28].
The three channels differ in what they can enforce, and the differences are the point.
•  Command-line first. The arkhe-verify CLI installs from the Rust ecosystem, meets the
persona in the terminal it already inhabits, and produces the same signed verdict artifact
as every other channel [28].
•  Continuous integration as policy. The GitHub Action verifies models at build time, so
an organization that adopts it converts verification from an individual virtue into an
enforceable institutional control, with failures that block builds rather than merely
disappoint [31].
•  Static web verification for the long tail. The browser verifier is a static,
hash-addressed artifact that requires no install and no account, serving the engineer who
needs one answer immediately; like every client-side control, it informs a decision it
cannot force [7].
 The strategic argument for the wedge is that model verification is the smallest complete
instance of the architecture's loop: one artifact, one identity, one verdict, full evidence
chain [31]. The MVP therefore doubles as the project's onboarding into its own ontology:
every user who verifies a model has, without necessarily knowing it, exercised the
WormGraph, a transparency anchor, and the constitution versioning of Chapter 6 [9, 28,
70]. Organizations that begin with model verification acquire the evidence format, the
verdict semantics, and the anchoring habit that later sectors reuse, which is the adoption
path of Chapter 13 taken from its cheapest step. The wedge metaphor is precise: it is thin,
and it opens a space.
 Demand signals for the wedge arrived before the supply did. Coinbase's AgentKit —
every AI agent deserves a wallet, as its repository's thesis reads — and the company's
subsequent agentic-wallet announcements put transacting agents into production
infrastructure, with authentication, telemetry, and security monitoring named as first-class
concerns [115, 116]. Ant International's KYA framework of Section 9.4 presumes the same
premise from the payments side: agents that act need identities, and identities that act need
evidence [39]. Both signals converge on a question the MVP answers at the smallest scale:
an agent that transacts runs on a model, and the provenance of that model is part of the
agent's trust story [31, 116]. The model file is where agent trust becomes personal for the
developer, because it is the component the developer themselves downloaded on faith.
 The honest caveats about distribution are three. CLI tools plateau at the size of their
evangelized audience, which is why the continuous-integration channel matters more than


=== PAGINA 114 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 114
its install count: one GitHub Action adopted by an organization verifies every model that
organization's pipeline touches, indefinitely [31]. The static verifier serves the long tail but
cannot enforce anything; it informs a decision the user is free to ignore, like every
client-side control in this book [7]. And publisher onboarding — the next section's central
problem — is the real bottleneck on all three channels, since a verifier without attestations
to check is a metal detector on an empty beach [31].
10.4 Failure modes of the MVP itself
 Intellectual honesty requires the MVP to be subjected to its own analysis, and the first
failure mode is the cold start. Until publishers sign and anchor their artifacts, every
verification returns unverified, which is correct and unhelpful — the metal detector rings
on nothing, and early users conclude the product does nothing [31]. The design mitigates
the mode in two ways. The negative verdict is made informative: an unverified result lists
exactly what a publisher must provide, converting every disappointed user into a potential
outreach channel. And the continuous-integration wedge targets the demand side rather
than the supply side: a build that fails on unverified models gives organizations a reason to
demand attestations from their suppliers, which is publisher onboarding by procurement
rather than by persuasion [31].
 The second failure mode is false assurance, and it is the most dangerous because it is a
failure of success. A user may read verified as safe, when the architecture attests identity
and provenance, not behavior: a verified model is the model its publisher published, signed
and anchored, and the publisher may have published something defective, biased, or
vulnerable [26, 27]. The design treats verdict wording and the evidence detail view as part
of the safety surface rather than as copy: the verified verdict is scoped to provenance in its
own text, and the evidence view leads with what the attestation does and does not cover
[28]. Chapter 24's risk map carries false assurance as a named limitation of the whole
program, and the MVP is where that limitation stands closest to the user [31].
 The third failure mode is verifier obsolescence through format drift. GGUF is an
evolving container; new key types, metadata conventions, and quantization encodings
appear with runtimes, and a decoder frozen at release will eventually fail on files it was
never built to read [26, 27]. The architecture absorbs the drift with the schema-versioning
discipline of Chapter 5: the verifier's version is part of the attested evidence, so a decode
performed by an older verifier is knowable as such, and revocations can target verifier
versions as well as models [70]. Decode-error telemetry is the detection signal: a rise in
undecidable verdicts after a runtime release is the observable that says the verifier, not the
ecosystem, needs updating [31].


=== PAGINA 115 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 115
 The fourth failure mode is attestation theater — adoption of the ritual without the
discipline. An organization may add the verification badge to its pipeline, pass the audit
checkbox, and continue shipping models nobody actually checked, because a control that
exists on paper satisfies procurement and satisfies no attacker [31, 97]. The design's
defense is the same evidence discipline as everywhere else in the architecture: verifications
are events with evidence pointers, so theater is distinguishable from practice by querying
the record — a pipeline whose verdicts are never read, never consulted in reviews, and
never correlated with incidents is visible as such [70]. Detection is the honest deliverable
here; prevention belongs to the governance layers of Part II.
 Each failure mode carries its own detection signal — onboarding conversion for the
cold start, verdict-read-through and wording comprehension for false assurance,
decode-error rates for obsolescence, and verdict-to-review correlation for attestation theater
— so the MVP can falsify itself on the same terms it imposes on everything else [31]. That
symmetry is the closing argument of Part III. The chapters of this part reduced three real
incidents to failed gates, specified the component that enforces the decisive gate, mapped
the gates' evidence onto regulatory obligations, and defined the smallest artifact through
which the gates reach a user's hands. Part IV takes the loop the MVP closes and generalizes
it: a universal verification core, the four-gate pipeline as a contract, and sector adaptation
without customization [28, 31].


=== PAGINA 116 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 116
PART IV — THE UNIVERSAL CONNECTION
LAYER
Three chapters generalize the thesis. Chapter 11 argues that VTK is verification
infrastructure in the manner of TCP/IP: an identical universal core, a strictly local
configuration tier, and sector adapters. Chapter 12 formalizes the four-gate pipeline as a
verification contract, specifying for each gate the question it answers, the counterexample it
catches, and the standard it descends from. Chapter 13 states the adaptation matrix for
seven sectors and the seven-step adoption path, and defends the distinction between
adaptation and customization.
11. The Universal Verification Core and Local
Configuration
11.1 The infrastructure thesis
 Every serious attempt to make autonomous AI agents trustworthy eventually confronts
a build-or-subscribe decision: does an organization adopt a trust product aimed at its
industry, or does it install a verification layer shared across industries? The VTK project's
answer, stated in the internal adaptability analysis dated 15 September 2026 that this
chapter expands, is that the system is not a product for any sector at all: it is verification
infrastructure, in the same relation to agentic workflows that TCP/IP holds for computer
networks and TLS holds for the web [28]. No company owns TCP/IP; every company that
wants to be on the network implements it, with its own addresses, routing policies, and
capacity plans. The analogy is not decorative. It fixes the economic category — horizontal
infrastructure rather than vertical application — and with that category the whole design
discipline governing what may vary between adopters and what may not.
 The category distinction has consequences that reach well beyond vocabulary. A
vertical product is sold to one industry, encodes one vendor's assumptions about its
customers' workflows, and survives commercially by rewriting itself for each new account;
its core, its governance, and even its trust anchors migrate between vendor and customer as
contracts demand. Horizontal infrastructure behaves in the opposite way: the core is
identical for everyone, governance is declared by each adopting organization, and the trust
root is chosen rather than received. The internet's protocol suite and the web's TLS layer
demonstrate the pattern at planetary scale; nearer the agentic domain, supply-chain
frameworks such as SLSA and in-toto show the same horizontal ambition for build
provenance [102, 103], and inter-agent protocols such as the Model Context Protocol and
the Agent2Agent protocol show it for communication [108, 110]. What the market has not


=== PAGINA 117 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 117
yet consolidated is a horizontal layer for verification — for answering, with re-derivable
evidence, whether an artifact or an action is what it claims to be.
 The gap is visible in the market's own recent construction. Agentic infrastructure is
arriving in force — protocol ecosystems, agent wallets with authentication and telemetry
[115, 116], and card-network collaboration with Ant International on a Know-Your-Agent
interoperability framework announced in September 2026 [39, 40] — yet these advances
address identity and transport, not the verification of what an agent's artifacts and actions
actually were. Meanwhile the incident record keeps pricing the omission: an estimated
USD 2.87 billion was stolen across roughly 150 hacks in 2025 alone [96], and retail
surveys find trust in agent tooling trailing adoption by an order of magnitude [161]. An
industry that is standardizing how agents connect has not yet standardized how agents are
believed. The thesis of this chapter is that the second standardization, if it is to happen at
all, will happen the way the first did — as infrastructure that no one owns and everyone
implements.
 The economics of the two categories differ sharply. A vendor that rewrites its core per
customer accumulates N codebases, N audit trails, and N sets of security guarantees, and an
audit that certifies one customer's deployment says nothing about the next; trust is
perpetually vendor-dependent and re-purchased in every engagement. An infrastructure
vendor that freezes a universal core and moves variance into configuration accumulates one
codebase, one evidence schema, and one set of verification semantics, so that an audit of
the core's behavior at one adopter is evidence about the core everywhere. Existing
assurance regimes illustrate the distance to be traveled: ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 certify
management systems and control descriptions at a point in time [170, 171], whereas the
layer proposed here re-derives verdicts from artifacts on demand. The contrast between the
postures is summarized in Table 11.1, which reproduces the six dimensions of the project's
comparison.
Table 11.1 — Vertical product versus horizontal infrastructure (after the
project's adaptability analysis [28]).

Scope and adaptation define the engineering posture: any sector, any artifact, configured


=== PAGINA 118 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 118
rather than rewritten. Core and governance define the political posture: the adopter, not the
vendor, owns the rules, which are declared in the ConstitutionStore described in Chapter 6.
Audit and trust root define the epistemic posture: verification is vendor-independent, and
the anchor of trust is chosen by the organization that bears the consequences of its failure.
Each row is instantiated concretely in Sections 11.2 and 11.3, and the whole set is
stress-tested against seven sectors in Chapter 13.
 The contrast also changes what procurement means. Organizations do not buy TCP/IP;
they buy implementations of TCP/IP, and their procurement questions concern
conformance, performance, and operational support rather than the protocol's existence.
The same shift awaits verification infrastructure: the purchased item becomes an
implementation of a verification contract, tested against the contract's semantics rather than
against a vendor's demonstrations. The reframing is quietly radical for assurance regimes
built around vendor questionnaires, because a conformance question can be answered by
re-derivation — load the artifact, replay the gates, compare verdicts — rather than by
correspondence. An assurance regime that can be answered mechanically is cheaper to
satisfy honestly and harder to satisfy dishonestly, which is the direction financial and
security regulators have been pushing for decades [71, 171].
 Two boundary conditions keep the thesis honest. First, the claim is architectural: the
universal core is specified, implemented in the project's crate ecosystem, and exercised in
the case studies of Parts II and III, but sector deployments at production scale remain future
work, as the executive analysis records [31]. Second, the TCP/IP analogy describes the
intended role, not an achieved network effect; TCP/IP became infrastructure through
adoption, and the same test applies here. What the architecture can control is readiness for
that test: a core small enough to verify, a configuration surface declarative enough to audit,
and an evidence trail external enough to survive the vendor's own failure. The remainder of
Part IV describes that readiness, and Part V applies it sector by sector.
11.2 What remains universal
 The universal core comprises six crates and five invariants. The crates — arkhe-core
(containment kernel), arkhe-verify (verification pipeline), arkhe-crypto
(post-quantum signatures and Merkle tooling), arkhe-wormgraph (immutable causal
graph), arkhe-mcp (JSON-RPC 2.0 interface), and arkhe-verify-wasm (client-side
verification) — are compiled once and shipped identically to every adopter, whether a
bank, a laboratory, or a ministry [28]. The invariants are the four-gate pipeline (hash, then
signature, then inclusion, then quorum), fail-closed semantics, honest status reporting,
layered verification, and non-custodial operation. Neither list is incidental: the crates define
where verification logic lives, and the invariants define what that logic may never do —
infer acceptance from silence, upgrade a pending state into a verified one, or concentrate


=== PAGINA 119 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 119
the power to declare a verdict in a single party.
 The reason these components can be frozen while everything around them varies is that
their correctness conditions are domain-independent. A hash function such as SHA-256 or
BLAKE3 does not know whether the bytes it digests are model weights, SWIFT messages,
or clinical documents; it returns the same fixed-size commitment with the same collision
resistance [106]. Ed25519 and the post-quantum scheme ML-DSA of FIPS 204 bind
signatures to keys, not to sectors [104]. Merkle inclusion proofs answer a question about
membership in a log, whatever the log records [8], and quorum arithmetic counts
independent witnesses without asking what business they are in [29]. The pipeline's
universality is therefore not a slogan about flexibility but a mathematical observation: each
gate's verification predicate is defined over bits and keys, and every sector's artifacts reduce
to bits and keys on entry.
 Figure 11.1 places the three tiers in relation: an identical core, a configuration layer that
every adopter fills differently, and seven sector adapters that translate regulatory worlds
without touching the core. The figure's direction of dependence is the architecture in
miniature: adapters depend on configuration, configuration depends on core, and nothing
depends upward. An adopter can replace its ConstitutionStore, re-issue its Capability
Manifest, or rotate its trust root without recompiling a line of the core; conversely, a core
upgrade propagates to every adopter through a hash-pinned release rather than through N
divergent patches [28]. The layer is a connection layer precisely because it sits between
universal mathematics and local law, and the figure names the sectors it will connect:
banks, pharmaceutical companies, governments, AI laboratories, defense, energy, and
health.
 Figure 11.1 — The universal connection layer: an identical core, a local configuration tier, and seven sector
 adapters.


=== PAGINA 120 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 120
 Three of the invariants deserve expansion because they are frequently misunderstood.
Fail-closed means that every error, timeout, or malformed input resolves to rejection, never
to a permissive default; availability may degrade, but acceptance may not silently widen.
Honest status means that every query about an artifact returns exactly one of VERIFIED,
PENDING, or [NONEXISTENT] — with [DECISION-PENDING] marking governance
actions awaiting quorum — and never a generic success that elides which of these held; the
discipline is the same one the earlier chapters applied to evidence records [28, 70]. Layered
verification means that checking is distributed across three moments — detection at
ingestion, post-selection re-check, and full client-side replay — so that no single failure of
attention, hardware, or honesty produces acceptance.
 The remaining invariants are structural. Non-custodial operation — the principle the
internal corpus labels §3.5 — forbids any component of the system from holding the assets,
the keys, or the authority whose actions it verifies; the layer witnesses, it does not own.
WormGraph supplies the immutable causal substrate: evidence records form a hash-linked
graph whose append-only structure Chapter 12 examines in detail [70]. The arkhe-mcp
crate exposes the whole surface as JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Model Context Protocol, so that
agents and human operators query verification state through one typed, session-oriented
interface [108] — an interface whose security posture matters, given documented
tool-poisoning attacks against MCP integrations [109]. Finally arkhe-verify-wasm
compiles the verifier itself to WebAssembly, so that any third party can re-derive any
verdict in a browser without trusting the vendor's binary. That last property is what makes
audit vendor-independent, and it is why client-side verification appears in Table 11.2 as a
universal component rather than as an optional extra.
 Table 11.2 collects the universal set and the reason each member resists sector-specific
variation. The pattern down the right-hand column is uniform: each component encodes
either mathematics (the pipeline), an epistemic discipline (fail-closed, honest status), an
economics of attention (layered verification), or a political commitment (non-custodial
operation, client-side auditability). None of these is a place where sector vocabulary could
attach without destroying the property that made the component worth standardizing. The
attestations the gates consume have their own standard lineage — remote attestation
procedures and hardware roots of trust such as TPM 2.0 supply the machine-level
analogues of the same discipline [100, 101] — and the pipeline treats them as inputs of the
same kind, whatever sector produced them.

 Universality is often misread as one-size-fits-all, and the misreading deserves an
explicit correction. What is universal is the verification semantics: which questions are
asked, in what order, with what verdict vocabulary, and with what default on failure. What
is emphatically not universal is the risk profile of the adopter — a defense ministry and an
AI startup do not face the same adversaries, regulators, or tempo, and the architecture does
not pretend otherwise. The variance between them is carried entirely by the configuration
tier: different invariants, different quorums, different timelocks, different roots. The claim,
stated carefully, is that every organization can express its own risk law within one shared
grammar, and that the grammar is small enough to verify; Section 11.3 describes that
grammar.
11.3 What is configured locally
 The configuration tier is where each organization's law lives, and its center is the
ConstitutionStore: a declarative store of falsifiable invariants, quorum thresholds, and
timelocks under which the organization's agents operate [28]. A bank may declare 5-of-7
quorum with a 14-day timelock on custody-critical actions; a startup estate may run 3-of-5
with a 24-hour timelock on its non-custodial internal operations; the core enforces
whichever declaration it is given, identically, in both cases. The distinction matters because
it separates policy authorship from policy enforcement: the organization authors, the core
enforces, and neither can silently do the other's job. Amendment of the constitution is itself
a quorum-governed event recorded in the WormGraph, so that the rules in force at any
moment are themselves evidence, and ADR-011 constrains the thresholds that critical
custody paths may declare [29, 70].
 Around the ConstitutionStore sit the remaining configurable surfaces. The Capability
Manifest declares, per agent, what that agent may do: permitted tools and data domains,
resource ceilings, and the human-in-the-loop checkpoints that must interrupt autonomy; a
pharmaceutical estate may grant read-only extraction to clinical-data agents, while a
trading estate caps its agents by exposure limits rather than by tool lists. The trust root
declares where the organization anchors identity: a Sigstore/Fulcio root as the default, a
national root where sovereignty rules demand it, or a self-hosted root — the project's


=== PAGINA 122 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 122
registered offline-first alternative, known internally as Crovia, is an example of the third
posture [9, 28]. Data domains declare which external sources feed the system and under
which integrity checks and rate limits. Sector adapters, finally, map verification outputs
into regulatory report formats and legacy integrations without altering the verification logic
that produced them.
 Trust-root choice deserves its own paragraph because it is where the architecture meets
sovereignty politics. The default anchor — Sigstore, with its Fulcio certificate authority
and Rekor transparency log — gives adopters a public, auditable identity layer without
capital expenditure [9]. Governments and regulated monopolies often cannot delegate this
function: the eIDAS 2.0 framework and the EU Digital Identity Wallet define national roots
precisely so that identity guarantees remain inside a jurisdiction [81, 82]. Defense estates
go further and demand air-gapped, self-hosted roots, as Chapter 13 details. The architecture
is deliberately indifferent among the three: the verification gates operate on whatever root
the configuration declares, and the choice itself is recorded as evidence, so an auditor can
always answer the question of whose word ultimately stands behind a verdict [28].
 Data domains translate the same discipline into each sector's native formats. A banking
estate declares SWIFT and FIX feeds with ISO 20022 message validation [89, 172]; an
energy estate declares SCADA historians and IEC 61850 substations [174]; a health estate
declares HL7 FHIR resources [88]; a laboratory estate declares model registries and
datasets with the integrity-scanning posture that Chapter 10 exercises against pickled model
formats [118]. Each domain entry carries its integrity check — hash pinning, schema
validation, or signed feeds — and its rate limits, so that the verification pipeline sees every
external input through the same lens of declared, checked provenance. The uniformity is
the point: sector formats differ arbitrarily, but the property demanded of them, declared
source with verifiable integrity under bounded rate, is constant.
 Configuration is also subject to governance, which is what keeps the local tier from
becoming a shadow codebase. Because every configurable artifact is declarative — the
corpus specifies YAML/JSON manifests — changes to it are diffable, reviewable, and
versionable like source code; because changes to the ConstitutionStore are
quorum-governed, no individual can quietly move a threshold or soften an invariant [28,
29]. Drift between declared and enforced configuration is detectable by the same client-side
re-verification that audits verdicts: an auditor loads the declared configuration and the
enforced evidence and checks that they agree. The local tier is thus local in authorship but
not in accountability, and Table 11.3 makes the division explicit.
Table 11.3 — Configurable components and example sector settings (after
