 Table 11.3 should be read against Table 11.2 as a division of labor. Every row on the
configurable side is a decision an organization must own and can be audited against; every
row on the universal side is a guarantee no organization is allowed to weaken. That division
is the practical content of the chapter's thesis — governance decisions stay local,
enforcement stays universal — and it is also the test by which the architecture asks to be
judged. If a sector requirement can be met in the left table, the universal claim holds; if
some requirement genuinely cannot, the claim's boundary has been found, and Chapter 13
argues that no such requirement has yet been identified.
 A worked example shows the grammar in motion. Suppose the bank of Table 11.3
decides, after a near-miss, that its drawdown invariant needs a tighter bound and that two
more witnesses must join the custody quorum. Under the architecture the decision is
drafted as a constitution amendment, reviewed like code, and put to the existing quorum;
the timelock holds it in [DECISION-PENDING] for the configured window; and on
passage the amendment enters the WormGraph as an event whose evidence includes the
amendment text, the votes, and the timestamp [28, 29, 70]. Nothing in that workflow
required the vendor's participation, and nothing in it could have been done quietly. The
organization changed its law; the core merely noticed, and the noticing is itself a permanent
record.
11.4 Adaptation versus customization
 The chapter's central distinction is three-way: customization, adaptation, and fork.
Customization rewrites the core for each client; the source analysis predicts, and software
history confirms, the result — a fork per client, with maintenance that becomes
unsustainable as the fleet diverges. Adaptation configures a single core per client; the core
remains one verifiable artifact while the configuration expresses each client's law. Fork,
finally, copies the code and lets it diverge; the copy loses upstream fixes, upstream audit
evidence, and eventually interoperability. The project adopts adaptation and treats the other
two outcomes as failure modes to be engineered against [28].
 The failure dynamic of customization is well understood in software engineering, and
the source analysis compresses it into one line: rewritten cores fork, and forks rot [28].
Each per-client rewrite moves verification logic out of the shared artifact, so the evidence


=== PAGINA 124 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 124
one deployment produces is no longer interpretable under another deployment's semantics,
and audits that certified customer A say nothing about customer B. Security fixes and
cryptographic upgrades must then be re-applied N times across divergent codebases, and
each application is an opportunity for silent divergence — the mechanism by which “we
use the same system” decays into “we run something descended from the same system”.
The rot is epistemic before it is economic: once verification semantics differ per customer,
no external party can re-derive a verdict without learning that customer's private dialect. A
trust layer that cannot be re-derived externally has, by the standard of this book, stopped
being a trust layer.
 A caveat keeps the argument precise: forking is not always pathological. Healthy
open-source forks exist and serve ecosystems — the Forgejo fork of Gitea, stewarded by
the nonprofit Codeberg, is a functioning example of divergence under public visibility
[144, 145]. The pathologies the architecture targets are the proprietary, per-customer forks
of trust logic, in which divergence is invisible to third parties and the fork's verification
claims cannot be independently checked against any upstream. Openness changes the
failure mode: a public fork at least leaves a visible lineage and can be audited on its own
terms. The project's commitment is therefore doubly served by open development — the
core should be forkable in principle, yet configured rather than forked in practice, because
configuration carries the variance that rewrites would otherwise carry.
 Configuration avoids the rot because it keeps verification semantics in one place. The
core's behavior is fixed and hash-pinned; configuration is declarative data, reviewable like
code, versioned like evidence, and interpreted by the same enforcement engine everywhere.
A change in governance is an amendment event with quorum and timelock, not a patch to
the verifier; a change in trust root is a declared parameter, not a rebuilt binary [28]. The
consequence is that the property an independent party can re-derive every verdict survives
every act of adoption, because the thing being re-derived — the core — never varied.
Adaptation is thus not a compromise between flexibility and integrity but the mechanism
by which both are obtained at once.
 There is a sense, indeed, in which the configuration is the product. The core, once
frozen, converges toward commodity — its releases become as uneventful as protocol-suite
releases — and the differentiating artifact an adopter accumulates is its constitution:
invariants tuned to its risk law, manifests tuned to its workforce, domains tuned to its data
estate. That accumulation is durable in a way that code customization never was, because it
survives core upgrades intact: a constitution written against the configuration grammar of
version k continues to express the organization's law under version k+1, exactly as a
routing table survives an operating system patch [28]. Vendors sell evolution; adopters own
their law. That division is why the source analysis calls the layer a connection layer rather
than a product [28].


=== PAGINA 125 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 125
 Vendor-independent audit operationalizes the claim. Because arkhe-verify-wasm
compiles the verifier to WebAssembly, an auditor — a regulator, a counterparty, a
customer — can load the evidence bundle in a browser, replay the four gates against the
organization's declared configuration, and watch the verdicts re-derive without contacting
the vendor or trusting its infrastructure [28]. This inverts the posture of conventional
assurance, in which the auditor relies on vendor attestation and on point-in-time
certifications such as SOC 2 reports [171]. In the VTK posture the auditor relies on
mathematics executed locally plus a configuration the organization has itself declared; the
vendor's honesty is not on the critical path. The property also disciplines the vendor,
because a core release that broke re-verification would be detected by every auditor at once
— the economics of maintaining trust fall on the code rather than on the relationship.
 The project marks the claim with a dated stamp:
ARKHE-OS-UNIVERSAL-LAYER-2026-09-15, the identifier under which the
adaptability analysis is filed in the internal corpus, with the status line “universal
connection layer — adaptable” [28]. Like the other stamps in this book — the Hodge
program plan of Chapter 22 among them — the stamp is a project artifact, not an external
certification; its function is to fix a claim and a date so that later evidence can confirm or
contradict it [28]. The chapters that follow are the confirmation work: Chapter 12 specifies
the verification contract that the universal core offers to every sector, and Chapter 13 shows
how seven very different sectors take delivery of that contract without forking it.
12. The Four-Gate Pipeline as a Verification
Contract
 Chapter 4 introduced the four-gate pipeline as the route from event to anchor; this
chapter restates it as a contract and examines each gate's primitive, question, and
counterexample. The contract language is deliberate. A contract is an offer that binds its
author identically for every counterparty, and the pipeline's offer is exactly that: to any
sector, for any artifact, the same four questions asked in the same order, with a verdict of
VERIFIED issued only when all four answers are yes [28]. Everything sector-specific —
which signers count as legitimate, which log anchors inclusion, which quorum authorizes a
state change — is supplied by the configuration layer of Chapter 11, never by the gates
themselves.
 Reading the gates as a contract also clarifies what they do not promise. They do not
promise that an artifact is good, useful, or safe — only that its bytes are the approved ones,
that the approval is attributed to the legitimate principal, that the event is part of the shared
history, and that policy authorized the state change. Each gate eliminates a class of failure
rather than conferring blanket approval, and the classes compose: an adversary must defeat


=== PAGINA 126 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 126
all four gates simultaneously to produce a false verification, while the system needs only
one gate to hold in order to produce an honest PENDING or a rejection. The StablR and
SUPERFORTUNE incidents of Chapter 7 are, in this vocabulary, environments in which
the gate ladder was absent and a single compromised surface answered every question at
once [6, 34].
12.1 Gate one: hash
 The first gate asks: are these the exact bytes that were approved? Its primitive is a
cryptographic hash — SHA-256 for interoperability, BLAKE3 where throughput matters
[106] — computed over the artifact and recorded before anything else happens. The hash's
properties are conventional but load-bearing: it is deterministic, so the same bytes always
yield the same digest; it is collision-resistant, so no practical procedure produces two
artifacts sharing one digest; and it is a one-way commitment, so the digest reveals nothing
about the content while binding it completely. From this moment the artifact is
content-addressed: every later reference — in a signature, in a log, in a WormGraph
evidence record — points to the digest rather than to a filename that could be silently
rebound [70].
 Byte-fixity rules out a specific and poorly appreciated class of failures: the silent
substitution. A model weight swap, a patched binary, a re-encoded dataset, or a
re-serialized configuration all change bytes, and therefore digests, and therefore fail the
gate if the digest was pinned at approval time. The machine-learning supply chain makes
the class concrete. Ollama's import path for GGUF models uses artifacts as provided,
without quantization or repair [163], which means that any transformation between
approval and execution would be invisible to a pipeline lacking hash pinning; and the
malicious pickled models found on public hubs — the JFrog and ReversingLabs findings
examined in Chapter 10 — would have been caught at this gate had consumers pinned the
digests they approved [119, 120, 121]. Byte-fixity also disciplines the producer: once an
approval is recorded against a digest, shipping different bytes is no longer an accident but a
detectable, attributable event.
 Content addressing has a lineage, and the gate inherits it consciously. Merkle's 1979
construction — certifying sets of documents by signing a tree of hashes — established that
large artifact collections can be verified digest by digest, and Certificate Transparency
industrialized the pattern for TLS certificates [8]; the same mathematics underlies IPFS
content identifiers, DNSLink publishing, and Arweave's permanent storage [136, 137], and
the hashtree system examined in Chapter 18 extends it to peer-to-peer model and code
distribution [147]. The WormGraph is the project's expression of the same lineage:
evidence records are addressed by digest and linked by reference, so the graph's history is
exactly as fixable as its members' bytes [70]. Gate one is thus not a novel invention but a


=== PAGINA 127 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 127
disciplined application of decades of content-addressing practice to agentic artifacts.
 Operationally, the gate is undemanding, which is why it can be universal. Hashes are
cheap to compute, cheap to store, and cheap to compare, so pinning a digest costs
effectively nothing at the moment of approval and pays for itself at the first suspicion; the
layered-verification economy of Chapter 11 exploits this by running hash checks at every
layer while reserving costlier checks for selected candidates [28]. The gate's edge cases are
administrative rather than mathematical: very large artifacts are handled by hashing chunks
into a Merkle structure whose root plays the digest's role, and artifact formats that embed
timestamps or nondeterministic serialization must be canonicalized before hashing so that
the same logical artifact always produces the same bytes [26, 106]. None of this changes
the contract; it changes only the care with which the bytes are defined.
 A subtlety deserves naming: a hash binds bytes, but the binding is only as meaningful
as the moment it was pinned. Trust-on-first-use applies — the first digest recorded for an
artifact is an act of declaration, not of proof — which is why gate one's output is always fed
forward into gates two and three, where the declaration acquires an author and a place in
history. Digests displayed to humans also inherit the look-alike and truncation problems of
any identifier; the pipeline's answer is that machines, not humans, are the hash comparator,
and the human sees structured intents rather than digests [1, 24]. The gate is thus
deliberately positioned as the pipeline's foundation rather than its judge.
 The gate's limits define the next gates. A matching digest proves identity, not approval:
the bytes could have been produced by anyone, including an attacker who simply published
a self-consistent artifact and invited the world to verify it. Nor does a digest prove intent: it
says nothing about what the approved bytes authorize, and a perfectly preserved artifact
may still be a perfectly preserved attack. Hash verification is therefore the cheapest gate
and the least sufficient — necessary for everything that follows, sufficient for nothing
alone. The contract's remaining three gates attach approval, history, and authorization to the
commitment that gate one fixed.
12.2 Gate two: signature
 The second gate asks: did the legitimate principal approve this intent? Its primitive is
the digital signature, and the core supports two families: Ed25519 for classical settings and
ML-DSA, the module-lattice scheme standardized in FIPS 204, for the post-quantum
transition [104, 105]. The two-family design reflects a sober reading of the quantum
timeline: classical signatures remain sound today, lattice signatures remain sound when
large quantum computers arrive, and the move between them is a configuration decision
rather than a rewrite, because both live in the same verification gate. The X-Wing hybrid
construction, which combines X25519 with ML-KEM-768 in a single component,


=== PAGINA 128 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 128
illustrates the project's general preference for hybrid primitives during the transition period
[107]: dual assurance now, single-algorithm simplicity once the lattice schemes have aged
in production.
 Authorship-binding rules out forgery and substitution. Without the private key, no
party can produce a signature the gate accepts as the publisher's; with the public key pinned
in configuration, no party can quietly substitute a different publisher for the expected one.
The gate thereby converts “an artifact exists” into “this artifact was approved by this
principal”, which is the minimal precondition for accountability anywhere downstream.
What it does not rule out is a legitimate principal approving the wrong thing — the signer
whose key signs under false pretenses, or whose signing device displays one transaction
while committing to another. That residual risk is where the next paragraphs, and much of
the incident record, live.
 The project therefore reads the signature gate as intent-binding rather than merely
authorship-binding, and the EIP-712 pattern is its closest analogy. EIP-712 introduced
typed, structured, human-readable signing for Ethereum: the signer sees and approves a
structured intent, and the signature commits to that structure rather than to an opaque byte
string [24]. The Bybit incident of February 2025 is the canonical counterexample in the
pattern's absence: signing devices displayed benign-looking transactions while the
underlying payload redirected a multisig contract's logic to the attacker, and roughly USD
1.5 billion left the treasury [2, 7, 95]. Clear-signing work such as Cyfrin's addresses the
display half of the problem [1]; the VTK answer is structural: the decoded intent that the
witnesses verify must be the decoded intent that was hashed at gate one, so that display,
approval, and commitment are one artifact rather than three.
 The gate presupposes a key-management lifecycle, and the configuration tier owns it.
Keys are generated in ceremonies the organization can describe, stored in vaults it controls,
rotated on schedules it declares, and revoked through events that themselves pass the
pipeline; a key whose compromise cannot be announced publicly and verifiably is a key
whose signatures cannot be trusted for long. Sigstore's short-lived certificate model offers
one posture — keys exist briefly, so theft windows shrink [9] — while air-gapped
long-lived keys offer the opposite posture, trading convenience against attack surface
[175]. The architecture does not arbitrate; it records. What the gate requires is only that, at
verification time, there exists a pinned and current mapping from principal to key, and that
changes to that mapping are events with evidence rather than silent database edits [70].
 The post-quantum half of the design deserves its rationale in the open. Signature
schemes face a different quantum horizon than encryption: a recorded signature can be
re-verified by a future adversary with a future computer, so arguments that work for
confidential data — migrate later — do not transfer to attestations whose validity is meant


=== PAGINA 129 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 129
to persist [104, 105]. FIPS 204's ML-DSA provides the lattice-based replacement whose
parameters the standard fixes, and hybrid constructions such as X-Wing let implementers
require agreement between classical and lattice primitives during the awkward decade in
which neither is beyond doubt [107]. The pipeline treats the pair as peers behind one gate,
so an adopter's transition plan is configuration — which schemes to require for which
artifact classes — rather than architecture.
 The gate's configuration surface — which keys count as legitimate publishers, which
certificate authority vouches for them, which rotation rules apply — is where sector law
enters, exactly as Chapter 11 promised. A laboratory pins Sigstore/Fulcio identities [9]; a
ministry pins its national root under eIDAS 2.0 [81, 82]; a defense estate pins keys minted
in an air-gapped facility [175]. The gate itself — the verification predicate over key and
signature — does not vary; the set of keys it will accept is the adopter's declaration. This is
the contract's division of labor in miniature: mathematics fixed, principals configured, and
the attestation machinery that vouches for machine-level provenance treated as one more
configured input [100, 101].
12.3 Gate three: inclusion
 The third gate asks: is this event part of the shared history? Its primitive is the
append-only Merkle log, standardized for certificate transparency in RFC 6962 and carried
forward in RFC 9162 [8, 99]. Signatures bind an event to a principal; the log binds events
to each other and to a public, ordered past. Each log entry is hashed into a Merkle tree, the
tree's root is published and pinned, and any entry can be proven present by a short inclusion
proof against that root. Because the log accepts only appends, an event once included
cannot be removed; because the root is pinned by parties beyond the operator, the operator
cannot present different histories to different observers without producing detectable
inconsistency.
 The property that matters for agents is retroactive-rewrite detection. An attacker who
compromises a system's present state has not necessarily compromised its past; but an
attacker who can rewrite the past can erase the evidence of how the present was reached,
and forensics loses its footing. Inclusion forecloses this: to rewrite history, the attacker
must produce a new tree root that diverges from the pinned root, and every auditor holding
the pinned root sees the divergence as proof of tampering. The project's WormGraph is the
property applied to evidence: records form a hash-linked, append-only structure whose
integrity is checked by re-walking the links [70], and the pipeline requires that
quorum-relevant events carry inclusion evidence, not merely a signature. The append-only
discipline is thus shared between the external log and the internal graph, each covering the
other's failure modes.


=== PAGINA 130 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 130
 The gate has production precedents and public infrastructure. Rekor, Sigstore's
transparency log, anchors software-artifact signatures and has been used to surface
malicious package releases by making release histories public and consistent [9, 10];
WhatsApp's key-transparency deployment brought the same auditability to the identity
keys of billions of users [11, 12]. The pipeline treats such logs as interchangeable anchors:
the configuration layer declares which log or logs anchor inclusion, the gate checks the
proofs, and no adopter is required to run the project's own log — the non-custodial
principle extends to infrastructure itself. A ministry may anchor to a national log; a
laboratory may anchor to Rekor and to content-addressed storage such as Arweave
simultaneously [9, 137]; the property demanded is only that the anchor's roots be pinnable
by parties other than their operator.
 Dual anchoring is the gate's resilience posture, and it costs little. An event's inclusion
can be proven against more than one log, and an adopter who pins the roots of two
independent logs has converted the compromise of either operator from a verification
failure into an observable inconsistency; auditors comparing anchors detect the split the
same way certificate-transparency monitors detect equivocation [8, 99]. The
gossip-and-monitor ecosystem that grew around certificate transparency — logs watching
logs, watchers watching logs — is the social technology that makes the mathematics bite,
and the pipeline assumes its analogue: somebody, somewhere, is holding the roots and
would notice. Non-custodial anchoring is thus not a single design choice but a small
ecology of independent witnesses to the history itself.
 Key transparency also previews what agent identity will need. The WhatsApp
deployment answered a question every agent fleet will face at scale: how does one let
millions of principals publish the keys that speak for them, and let anyone check that the
directory has not been quietly rewritten in their absence [11, 12]? The transparent-log
answer — publish key changes as log entries, prove consistency, let third parties audit — is
gate three applied to identity rather than to artifacts, and it composes with gate two to give
agents an attributable, tamper-evident identity history. For the sectors of Chapter 13 that
composition is not a luxury; European identity infrastructure is already being specified in
these terms [81, 82].
 Inclusion's limits, like gate one's, define what remains. A signed event in a public log is
part of history, but history is not authorization: an event can be perfectly attributed and
perfectly recorded and still violate policy. Nor does inclusion certify timeliness — an event
may be included long after the fact, and PENDING states exist precisely to name that
interval honestly rather than paper over it. Authorization is the fourth gate's question, and it
is the gate where the sector's own law speaks most directly.
12.4 Gate four: quorum


=== PAGINA 131 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 131
 The fourth gate asks: does policy authorize this state change? Its primitive is the
multisignature quorum: m-of-n independent witnesses must countersign the event for the
gate to pass. The project's decision record ADR-011 fixes the working band at 4-of-7 to
5-of-7 witnesses, prohibits thinner configurations — the 1-of-3 class in which one
compromised key suffices — and treats thresholds as hypotheses about simultaneous
compromise to be revised under incident data, as Appendix B records [29]. Sector
configuration sets the exact numbers within the architecture's constraints, from a
laboratory's 4-of-7 with a 7-day timelock to a defense estate's 6-of-9 with 30 days or more
[28]. The gate passes only when the declared threshold is met by distinct, independent
witnesses; collections of shares under one operator do not constitute independence, a
distinction that distributed-validator technology makes operational by splitting keys across
independent operators [138, 139].
 The gate's institutional logic is the separation of witness from authority, established in
Chapter 6. The ConstitutionStore — the authority — declares what counts as authorized;
the witnesses attest to what happened; the quorum gate evaluates the attestations against the
declaration [28, 29]. Neither party can do the other's job: witnesses cannot authorize by
attesting, and the authority cannot attest by declaring. This separation is the difference
between governance and its record, and the pipeline refuses to collapse it. An event that
meets quorum is evidence that policy authorized the change; an event that does not is
evidence of an attempt; both enter the WormGraph, and both remain auditable.
 Timelocks complete the gate's parameter set, and they are the temporal half of the same
hypothesis. A timelock holds a quorum-approved action in a [DECISION-PENDING]
state for the configured window — 24 hours in a fast-moving startup estate, 14 days in a
bank, 30 or more in defense — so that correction, objection, or recovery has time to operate
before the action takes effect [28, 29]. The Bybit post-mortems emphasized precisely the
absence of such a window: the transfer executed at the speed of the attacker [2, 5].
Timelock and quorum together encode the project's incident-derived lesson that capture is a
process, not an instant, and that giving honest defenders a scheduled interval is often the
difference between an incident and a loss.
 Independence is the gate's hardest requirement and the easiest to fake. Seven witnesses
who all take instructions from one operator are one witness with seven keys, and thresholds
count entities, not signatures; ADR-011's incident-derived stance assumes independence is
real, verified at ceremony time, and re-verified as the witness set evolves [29]. The
distributed-validator literature formalizes the point: key splitting across independent
operators, with consensus among the shards, changes the failure model from
compromise-the-operator to compromise-a-quorum-of-independent-organizations [138,
139]. The architecture accordingly treats witness-set composition — who the witnesses are,
whom they answer to, where they run — as configuration of consequence, and requires


=== PAGINA 132 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 132
changes to it to pass the same quorum discipline as the actions the set will witness [28].
 Fail-closed has a quorum-specific reading: an unavailable witness set does not lower
the threshold. Systems under operational stress are tempted to accept enough signatures,
and the gate refuses; if fewer than the declared number of independent attestations arrive,
the action remains [DECISION-PENDING] until the window closes, and the WormGraph
records the shortfall as evidence rather than as an inconvenience [28, 70]. This is the
correct trade for a verification layer, because availability lost to an honest wait is
recoverable, while authorization gained by an unverifiable shortcut is not. Adopters can
tune the pain — witness redundancy, timelock length, escalation invariants — but the
direction of the trade, safety over convenience, is not configurable.
 The counterexample class is unilateral capture, and the StablR incident of May 2026 is
its current textbook case. An attacker who obtained control of one key in a 1-of-3 multisig
minted USD 13.5 million of unsupported stablecoins before the issuers froze the contracts
[6, 33]; under ADR-011's arithmetic the configuration itself was the vulnerability, because
the quorum admitted a single point of failure. Bybit's loss shows the class from the other
side — a signing quorum whose members did not independently verify what they were
signing [2, 7, 95]. The gate's answer to both is structural: enough independent witnesses,
each verifying decoded intent, with timelocks that give correction windows time to work
[29]. Quorum is the only gate whose parameter is genuinely political — the mathematics is
fixed, but the choice of 4-of-7 versus 5-of-7, of 14 versus 30 days, is the adopter's own
judgment about its adversaries, regulators, and tempo, declared in the ConstitutionStore
and enforced identically everywhere [28].
12.5 Composition and honest status
 The contract's composition rule is that the gates chain. The digest that gate one fixes is
the input gate two signs; the signature gate two verifies becomes the event gate three
includes; the inclusion gate three proves is the event gate four authorizes. Because each
gate's output is the next gate's input, removing any gate re-admits a specific adversary class
— swap artifacts without hashes, forge publishers without signatures, rewrite history
without logs, capture outcomes without quorum — and the verifier's obligation is to ensure
that no verdict of VERIFIED is ever issued without all four answers being yes. The
composition is cheap at verification time and expensive to defeat at attack time, which is
precisely the asymmetry a verification contract wants.
 Honest status is the contract's reporting discipline and its anti-StablR principle. Every
query returns VERIFIED, PENDING, or [NONEXISTENT] — with
[DECISION-PENDING] for quorum-gated actions in flight — and the system never
renders an unverified state as if it were verified [28]. The naming is not cosmetic. The


=== PAGINA 133 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 133
StablR and SUPERFORTUNE losses were, in effect, pending states treated as verified:
markets and counterparties priced minted-but-unbacked supply and drained liquidity before
the truth surfaced, and the SUPERFORTUNE token fell 97.8 percent from its peak within
days [6, 33, 34, 41]. An honest-status regime makes that mislabeling structurally
impossible: unbacked supply is absent evidence until quorum says otherwise, and a
pending state is a warning, not a balance.
 Figure 12.1 summarizes the contract as the book will use it: four gates, the primitive
each applies, the question each answers, the counterexample each catches, and the
standards lineage each inherits. The figure's right-hand column is the chapter's bibliography
in miniature — Merkle-era content addressing [8], FIPS 204 lattice signatures [104], the
transparency-log lineage of RFC 6962 and RFC 9162 [8, 99], and the Safe and
distributed-validator patterns behind quorum design [25, 138] — a reminder that the
pipeline's novelty lies in its composition and its sector-neutral packaging rather than in its
primitives. Novelty in primitives would be a liability here; the contract borrows its
mathematics from the most scrutinized constructions available so that each adopter inherits
decades of review.
Figure 12.1 — The four-gate pipeline as a verification contract: primitives, questions answered, counterexamples
 caught, and standards lineage.
 Table 12.1 expands the figure into the reference form used throughout Part V: for each

rows together. Part V populates the final column sector by sector, beginning with banking.

 The contract also has a machine-readable surface, which is what makes it enforceable
rather than aspirational. Every verdict the pipeline produces is exposed through the
arkhe-mcp interface as JSON-RPC 2.0 responses whose fields name the status, the
artifact digest, the witness set, and the anchors consulted [108]; a caller cannot receive a
verdict without receiving its evidence lineage alongside. This is the practical meaning of
honest status — not a slogan but a schema, with [NONEXISTENT] as a literal return value
that clients must handle, and PENDING carrying the expected decision time under the
current timelock [28]. Integrators who have handled MCP tool responses know the failure
mode the schema forecloses: tool output that looks authoritative regardless of its
evidentiary state [109].
 One clarification closes the chapter. The contract's verdict semantics are deliberately
conservative: VERIFIED is a strong claim requiring four concurrences; PENDING is the
honest name for work in flight; [NONEXISTENT] is the honest name for absent evidence;
and rejection is the default on any anomaly. This ordering — verification earned, doubt
named, silence never promoted — is the epistemic content of the whole architecture, and it
is what makes the contract adoptable by sectors whose regulators would accept nothing
less. It also bounds the promise honestly: the contract attests to provenance and
authorization, not to an artifact's quality or an agent's future behavior, a boundary Chapter
24 examines further. Chapter 13 turns from the contract's terms to its delivery: how seven
very different sectors sign the same contract without changing a word of it.
13. Sector Adaptation Without Customization
 Part IV's first two chapters argued that the core is universal and specified the
verification contract it offers. This chapter demonstrates the argument's payoff across seven
sectors — banking, pharmaceuticals, government, AI laboratories, defense, energy, and
health — by reading each through the same three lenses: the parameters it declares in
configuration, the regulatory anchors that make those parameters non-optional, and the
adoption path by which it takes delivery of the core. The demonstration's claim is narrow
and checkable: in every sector, the same four-gate contract, the same fail-closed semantics,
and the same honest statuses suffice, provided the configuration layer is filled with the
sector's own law [28]. If that claim survives seven regulatory worlds, the universal
connection layer is more than a design aspiration.
13.1 The adaptation matrix


=== PAGINA 135 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology

quorum gradient runs from 4-of-7 (pharmaceuticals, AI laboratories, health) through 5-of-7
(banks, energy) and 5-of-7-or-higher across multiple agencies (government) to
6-of-9-or-higher (defense). The timelock gradient runs from 7 days to 30 or more, tracking
how long correction windows must stay open for the sector's regulators and remediation
cycles. The trust-root gradient runs from public anchors — Sigstore, supplemented for
laboratories by content-addressed storage in the style of Hashtree [9, 147] — through
national roots for government [81, 82], to air-gapped self-hosted roots for defense [175].
The data-domain gradient tracks each sector's native formats, from ISO 20022 and FIX in
banking [89, 172], through SCADA and IEC 61850 in energy [174], to HL7 FHIR in health
[88].

 Two readings of the matrix are worth making explicit. Read horizontally, each row is a
complete and coherent estate: the quorum, timelock, root, invariant, and domains in one
row are designed to fit one regulatory world, and an adopter departing from its row owes
itself an explanation, recorded as an amendment. Read vertically, each column is a
parameter the core varies identically for everyone — no column requires new code in the
core, because every value any cell holds is already within the ConstitutionStore's
declarative grammar [28]. The matrix thus demonstrates the adaptation thesis in a single
artifact: seven regulatory worlds, one verification engine, zero rewrites.
 The gradients also have an internal logic that the incident record of Chapter 7 supports.
Quorum and timelock scale together with the hypothesized capability of the adversary:
ADR-011's thresholds are stated as hypotheses about simultaneous compromise [29], and a
state-scale adversary — the class the defense row assumes — drives both the 6-of-9
threshold and the 30-day window, while a fraud-scale adversary in a laboratory context is
answered by 4-of-7 and 7 days. Trust roots scale with sovereignty: the further an estate sits
from public anchoring infrastructure, the more of that infrastructure it must operate itself.
The matrix is therefore not a set of arbitrary defaults but a readable map of threat models,
and the mapping is itself auditable evidence about each adopter's self-assessment [28].


=== PAGINA 136 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 136
 Quorum and timelock should also be read jointly, because they trade against each other
along a single axis: institutional decision latency. A 5-of-7 threshold with a 14-day window
is slow by construction — the design intends that custody-critical actions be interruptible
for two weeks — while a 4-of-7 threshold with 7 days accepts faster cycles for lower-stakes
classes [28, 29]. Regulators implicitly understand the axis: reconciliation and remediation
cycles in finance and health run on weekly and biweekly rhythms, and the timelock values
in the matrix mirror them. The configuration grammar could express arbitrary pairs, but the
matrix's pairs are the ones each sector's own clock can defend in an audit.
 The exemplary invariants in the fifth column repay attention because they are where
sector risk becomes falsifiable policy. A bank declares maximum exposure, drawdown, and
margin floors — the quantities whose breach defines its catastrophe; a defense estate
declares classification boundaries and need-to-know rules; an energy estate declares
availability floors and SCADA-integrity checks; a laboratory declares capability ceilings
and audit obligations over training runs. These invariants are each sector's own translation
of what must never silently happen, and the core's contribution is the enforcement
discipline: every invariant is falsifiable, every breach is an event with evidence, and every
amendment to an invariant is quorum-governed [28, 29]. The adapters, in short, do not
weaken the core; they aim it.
13.2 Regulatory anchors per sector
 The paragraphs that follow anchor each sector's configuration in the instruments that
make the anchors non-optional. The reading discipline is uniform: identify what each
instrument presumes about records, attribute the presumed property to the gate that supplies
it, and let the sector's own vocabulary fill the invariants and data domains. Nothing in the
mapping is exotic, and that is the point. The instruments were written for paper trails and
audit firms, and the pipeline's contribution is to make the same properties
machine-checkable at a scale their authors could not have imagined [28]. Part V returns to
each cluster with the full regulatory text in view.
 Banking is the sector whose regulators have most explicitly demanded the properties
the pipeline provides. Basel III's post-crisis reforms presume that institutions know their
own exposures with audit-grade confidence [83]; PSD2's strong-customer-authentication
regime requires payment approvals to be bound to authenticated intent, exactly the property
the signature gate operationalizes [84, 85]; DORA obliges financial entities to demonstrate
operational resilience with evidence of ICT risk management, incident recording, and
testing [71, 72]; and MiCA brings issuance and custody into a regime whose reserve and
redemption rules presume verifiable records [20, 92]. The banking adapter accordingly
declares 5-of-7 quorum with a 14-day timelock on custody-critical actions, pins trust in
Sigstore/Fulcio plus an on-chain Safe for custody events, and maps SWIFT, FIX, and ISO


=== PAGINA 137 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 137
20022 feeds into declared data domains [89, 172]. Chapter 14 develops this adapter in
depth.
 Pharmaceutical regulation is, at bottom, a provenance regime, which makes it the most
natural fit for the pipeline. ICH E6(R3), adopted in 2025 and implemented on both sides of
the Atlantic, reorganizes good clinical practice around risk-based, data-driven oversight
and presumes traceable, attributable records across the trial lifecycle [73, 74, 75]; FDA 21
CFR Part 11 has governed electronic records and electronic signatures since 1997 and
demands precisely the attribution, integrity, and audit-trail properties that gates one through
three supply [76]. The pharma adapter declares 4-of-7 quorum with a 7-day timelock, a
self-hosted root supplemented by Sigstore, batch-traceability and chain-of-custody
invariants, and data domains spanning Veeva Vault, the versioned terminology of
MedDRA [173], WHODrug, and HL7 FHIR. The invariant set is the sector's own: a batch's
custody chain must be reconstructable from evidence alone, without trusting any
participant's narrative.
 Government estates carry sovereignty obligations that the trust-root choice must honor.
LGPD in Brazil [23] and GDPR in Europe [22] impose lawful-basis, minimization, and
records-of-processing duties — GDPR Article 30 in particular — with ANPD's 2024
resolution adding rules for international transfers [90, 91]; the eIDAS 2.0 framework and
the EU Digital Identity Wallet define the national-root infrastructure through which identity
guarantees remain inside the jurisdiction [81, 82]. The government adapter accordingly
declares 5-of-7-or-higher quorum spread across multiple agencies, timelocks of 14 days or
more, a national trust root, invariants of transparency, auditability, and data sovereignty,
and data domains of public registries and census data. The constitutional audit of Chapter
20, performed on the Brazilian Federal Constitution with SASC v5.4α [30, 32], shows the
same estate's governance pattern applied to a normative corpus rather than to transactional
data.
 AI laboratories face the newest regime and the oldest evidence problem. The EU AI
Act's record-keeping obligations — Article 12's logging duties among them, with high-risk
obligations phasing in through 2026 and 2027 — presume that training and deployment
events are recorded in tamper-evident form [17, 18, 117]; ISO/IEC 42001 gives
management-system form to AI governance [16]; and the NIST AI Risk Management
Framework supplies the govern-map-measure-manage functions the invariants must
express [15], with MITRE ATLAS cataloguing the adversary side [112]. The laboratory
adapter declares 4-of-7 quorum with a 7-day timelock, anchors trust in Sigstore plus
content-addressed storage [9, 147], and declares model registries, arXiv, and open datasets
as data domains under hash-pinned integrity checks — the posture that Chapter 10's GGUF
attestation MVP exercises in detail [26, 27]. Its invariants are the field's own: declared
capabilities, behavioral verification, auditable training.


=== PAGINA 138 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 138
 Defense and national-security estates are the strictest configuration and the clearest
boundary case for the universality claim. ITAR controls the export of defense articles and
technical data under 22 CFR 120–130 [175]; NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 defines the
safeguarding of controlled unclassified information in nonfederal systems [77]; and NATO
STANAG agreements, named in the corpus, add interoperability requirements on top [28].
The defense adapter declares 6-of-9-or-higher quorum with timelocks of 30 days or more,
an air-gapped self-hosted trust root, classification and compartmentation invariants with
need-to-know enforcement, and data domains of classified holdings, SIGINT, and IMINT.
The estate demonstrates that the core's contract survives even an environment that cannot
touch public anchoring infrastructure at all — a result Chapter 16 examines together with
the energy sector.
 Energy and other critical infrastructure operate under availability-first regulation.
NERC CIP standards govern the security of the bulk electric system's critical assets [78];
the IEC 62443 series industrializes security for automation and control systems [79]; and
the EU's NIS 2 Directive extends comparable duties across member-state operators of
essential services [80]. The energy adapter declares 5-of-7 quorum with a 7-day timelock, a
self-hosted root, availability, SCADA-integrity, and fail-safe invariants, and data domains
spanning SCADA historians, IEC 61850 substations [174], and DNP3 links. The distinctive
pressure is temporal — control-loop latencies leave no room for heavyweight verification
on the loop itself — and the adapter's answer is the layered-verification economy of
Chapter 11: light checks on the loop, full gate evaluation on the records the loop produces.
 Health care completes the matrix with a sector whose data is both maximally sensitive
and maximally standardized. HIPAA's Security Rule, codified at 45 CFR Part 164, and the
HHS guidance that accompanies it define administrative, physical, and technical safeguards
for electronic protected health information [86, 87]; HL7 FHIR supplies the interoperability
standard through which records move between systems [88]. The health adapter declares
4-of-7 quorum with a 7-day timelock, a self-hosted root, custody-of-record and
consent-integrity invariants, and HL7 FHIR data domains. The pattern matches its
neighbors exactly: the same four gates, the same statuses, the sector's own law expressed in
configuration.
 One paragraph must honestly delimit this section: these are anchors, not audits. The
claim is that each sector's binding instruments presume exactly the properties the pipeline
provides — attribution, integrity, traceability, resilience evidence — so that compliance
mapping becomes a translation exercise rather than an architectural negotiation. Whether
each translation survives contact with a real regulator is Part V's question, developed in
depth for the finance, pharma-and-health, and government-defense-energy clusters in
Chapters 14 through 16. The matrix's role here is narrower: to show that no sector, so far,
requires a different core.
