 The chapter closes where it began, with the standard the book set for itself.
Counterarguments were stated in their proponents’ terms; limitations were bounded in
writing; open problems were listed with agendas rather than aspirations; and each objection
received a split verdict that leaves visible residue. What emerges is not an architecture
without weaknesses but an architecture whose weaknesses are enumerable, gated, and in
most cases scheduled — which is the property, rarer than strength, that a verifiable trust
product most needs to demonstrate about itself. The conclusion that follows in Chapter 25
claims correspondingly less than the chapters before it might license, and claims it with
evidence.
25. Conclusion: Sovereignty as a Property, Not a
Promise
 This book set out to examine one thesis: that trust in autonomous systems can be
converted from promise to proof, and that the conversion is an architectural act rather than
an act of governance, reputation, or faith. The examination is now complete enough to state
what it found. The architecture presented in Part II, validated against incidents in Part III
and generalized across sectors in Parts IV and V, rests on a vocabulary of exactly four
moves — hash, signature, inclusion, quorum — applied with a discipline that predates the
project: hash what matters, sign who stands behind it, anchor that the record exists outside
anyone’s discretion, and let no single party decide what the record means. Every
load-bearing element of the design is that vocabulary applied once more: the kernel of
containment, model attestation, the WormGraph, and the constitution that governs its own
change [28]. The incidents supplied the empirical pressure — Bybit’s subverted display,
StablR’s arithmetic of thresholds, SUPERFORTUNE’s forged identity [2, 6, 34] — and in
every reconstruction the same four gates stand between the attacker’s capability and the


=== PAGINA 240 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 240
loss.
25.1 The synthesis: one architecture, one vocabulary
 The synthesis the book reaches is that the architecture’s universality and its sovereignty
are the same property seen from two sides. Chapter 11 argued the universal case: the
verification pipeline — hash, signature, inclusion, quorum — the fail-closed posture, the
honest status contract, and layered verification are identical across every sector, while
everything that varies — invariants, capabilities, trust roots, quorums, timelocks, data
domains — is local configuration declared in the local ConstitutionStore. Chapters 14
through 16 demonstrated the claim in the sectors where adaptation costs are highest, and
the Hodge program of Chapter 22 pushed it to the limiting case: if the evidence layer
disciplines claims whose verification is as strong as mathematics can make it, the weaker
regimes of engineering practice lie within reach a fortiori [46, 69]. An infrastructure whose
core never changes and whose configuration is always local is, by construction, something
no vendor owns and every organization can verify — the same structural position TCP/IP
and TLS hold in their layers, which is why the sovereignty conclusion follows from the
universality conclusion rather than being appended to it.
 Sovereignty, in this book’s usage, is a property of systems, not a slogan about them: the
property that a party’s ability to act, verify, and remember does not depend on another
party’s continued goodwill. The architecture secures it in three moves that recur across
every chapter. Verification without permission: any third party can recompute hashes,
check signatures, and audit inclusion proofs without contacting the vendor [8, 9, 106].
Memory without rewriting: the WormGraph’s anchored history survives the compromise,
bankruptcy, or hostility of whoever once held the keys [28, 70]. Governance without
capture-by-default: quorums calibrated against incident data, veto topology measured
rather than assumed, and constitutions that version their own change [29, 30]. What these
moves compose into is stated plainly by the project’s wider program: firmware freedom on
the device — the LibrePhone line of work, in which the stack down to the
baseband-adjacent layers is rebuildable and attestable by its owner — and agent
verifiability on the services the device talks to are one architecture, not two; Figure 25.1,
discussed in Section 25.3, draws them as the single stack they are.
 The universality claim can be restated one final way, in the currency the whole book
has traded in: every sector chapter of Part V turned out to be the same four gates with
different numbers on the dials. The banking adapter is Basel-grade quorums and timelocks
over the same pipeline that carries the payment and reporting evidence [83, 84]; the
pharmaceutical and health adapter is batch lineage and record integrity over the same
pipeline that carries trial and clinical evidence [73, 76, 88]; the public-sector adapter is
national trust roots over the same pipeline that carries citizen-facing transparency; and the


=== PAGINA 241 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 241
mathematical frontier of Chapter 22 is zero-sorry proof artifacts over the same pipeline that
carries custody events [62, 69]. When one mechanism survives contact with that range of
obligations without growing sector-specific machinery, the infrastructure hypothesis —
that this layer resembles TCP/IP or TLS rather than a vertical product — stops being a
metaphor and becomes an engineering observation, and the sovereignty argument rests on
it.
 A closing word on what the synthesis does not claim. Universality of the core does not
mean the adapters are trivial, and nothing in Part V should be read as dismissing the
sector-specific engineering — regulatory interpretation, data integration, custodian
onboarding — that each deployment still requires; the claim is that this engineering
configures one mechanism rather than reinventing it [28]. Nor does sovereignty mean
isolation: a deployment whose trust root is local still consumes public anchors, public
algorithms, and public standards, and its independence is from vendor discretion, not from
infrastructure. Stating the boundaries here is what makes the affirmative claim in Section
25.3 checkable rather than promotional.
 The book’s honest summary of where this leaves the project is asymmetric, and it was
stated the same way in the senior analysis: on the side of assets, a coherent architecture
whose every layer answers a documented failure mode, an implemented crate ecosystem
with disciplined boundaries, a governance pattern with incident-calibrated defaults, and a
regulatory map unusually specific for a pre-product project; on the side of debts, no legal
entity, no external audit, no customers, no measured adoption, and a market that larger
players are now naming on their own schedules [31, 39]. The asymmetry is not a
contradiction of the thesis — it is what a design-science project looks like at the moment its
verification burden shifts from architecture to world. The chapters of Part X prescribed the
conversion: the MVP wedge with its phase gates, the audit that retires the largest credibility
debt, and the design partnership that turns evidence export into revenue [31]. What
remains, after the conversion is prescribed, is the part no architecture can supply: the
decision to build.
25.2 What would falsify the thesis
 A thesis held honestly is held with its falsifiers attached, and this book’s thesis has five.
The first is the incident dearth: if agent-mediated losses remain rare and small across the
coming years — no Bybit-scale failures, no cluster of attestation-relevant supply-chain
events [96, 119] — then the failure mode the architecture addresses is marginal, and the
book is a solution in search of a problem; the 2025 record of 2.87 billion dollars argues
against this, but records are not laws of nature [96]. The observation that would trigger the
falsifier is specific: two consecutive years in which no material incident turns on an
unverified representation — a substituted model, a subverted display, an unattested tool —


=== PAGINA 242 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 242
rather than on the familiar machinery of stolen keys and social engineering. The second is
the adoption recession: if the wedge metrics of Chapter 10 fail their gates through several
re-scoping cycles — publishers declining to attest, engineers declining to verify — then
verification economics are structurally absent, not premature, and the category-creation
claim of Chapter 23 fails [31]. The trigger is equally specific: gates missed not once, with
re-scoping, but repeatedly across distinct gate types, which would indicate demand failure
rather than execution failure. The third is the absorption scenario: if a proprietary managed
platform wins agent trust outright and the market demonstrably prefers convenience to
verifiability, the empty quadrant of Figure 23.1 stays empty because no one wants to live in
it [115, 116, 149]. The tell here is procurement behavior — buyers standardizing on
vendor-issued assurance despite the availability of independently verifiable alternatives at
comparable cost — and it would show up in contracts long before it showed up in
post-mortems.
 The fourth falsifier is the internal failure, and it is the one the architecture’s own logic
makes decisive: if the project’s evidence — its verifier, its transparency anchors, its
quorum — is ever subverted at scale without detection and without anchored aftermath,
then the central claim that capture leaves visible evidence is refuted by the one test case
that matters most, the architecture itself. The detection standard here is public: a subversion
counts as undetected only if it survives the audit path — third-party recomputation of
hashes, inclusion checks against the public logs, quorum inspection — that the evidence
layer exists to serve [8, 9, 28]. The fifth is the mathematical verdict: if the Hodge program
demonstrates that formal verification plus ordinary repositories subsumes everything the
evidence layer adds — provenance, anchoring, quorum acceptance rendered decorative by
Lean’s checker [62, 63, 125] — then the limiting-case argument collapses and the
architecture’s scope is narrower than claimed. The observation that would begin this
refutation is already visible in miniature: formalization campaigns whose repositories alone
carry attribution, acceptance, and dispute resolution, sustained over years without any
anchored evidence layer and without loss of trust [126]. Each falsifier is observable on a
timescale this book’s readers will live through, and each is stated precisely enough to be
checked against the record rather than argued away after the fact. It is equally worth stating
what does not falsify the thesis: criticism of the design, the arrival of competing
architectures, even the project’s commercial failure — a sound architecture can fail as a
venture, and the thesis concerns the property, not the company. Falsification requires the
world to demonstrate that verification is unnecessary, unverifiable in practice, or worthless
when delivered; anything less is market noise that the phase gates will absorb as data.
 Falsification also admits degrees, and honesty requires saying which parts of the thesis
survive partial refutation. If the identity layer standardizes — KYA credentials become
universal — while the evidence layer is absorbed into vendor platforms, then the thesis


=== PAGINA 243 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 243
survives as architecture but fails as infrastructure: agents would be known and still not
checkable, and the book’s central distinction between who an agent is and what it can prove
would have lost its institutional carrier [39, 100]. If the wedge succeeds while the
mathematical frontier stalls, the thesis survives with its scope narrowed to the supply-chain
register in which attestation demonstrably pays. The monitoring instruments are the ones
this book has already specified — phase gates, published metrics, anchored governance
history — so the degrees of falsification will be observable in public artifacts rather than
settled by interpretation [31]. A thesis that arrives with its own instrument panel is either
confirmed by the readings or retired by them; it does not get to argue.
25.3 Outlook 2027–2030
 The mathematics frontier will be the first place the thesis is tested at full strength,
because it is where verification is already the standard of truth. The 2026 demonstration
that an AI-generated solution to a Millennium Prize problem could ship with a
machine-checked Lean proof [65, 124] moved the question from whether machines can do
research mathematics to who did what in a machine-era proof — and attribution is a
provenance problem, which is to say an evidence problem. The program this book’s
Chapter 22 specified — conjecture statements, verified lemmas, and acceptance events as
anchored, quorum-counted artifacts [69, 70] — is one instance of a general pattern the
coming years will demand everywhere AI contributes to knowledge: AI-scale mathematics
with verifiable attribution, in which the contribution of a model, a formalizer, and a human
referee are separately attested and separately counted. The voices that matter most in that
field have said the same in public: machine verification is where mathematical trust is
actually expending effort, and the value of attacking hard problems with these tools is a
position argued by practitioners, not by vendors [67, 135].
 The institutional frontier will standardize what this book could only specify. The KYA
frameworks of 2026 [39, 40] and the RATS architecture [100] are converging on the same
relying-party question from opposite ends — identity and evidence — and the 2027–2030
window is when a credential profile joining them will either be written by a standards body
or fragmented across vendors; Chapter 24 stated the convergence agenda as an open
problem with a deliverable. The AI Act’s phase-in — 2 August 2026 and 2 December 2027
[17, 117] — supplies dated demand on the same schedule in the European market, with the
record-keeping duties of Article 12 as the anchor obligation [18]. On the infrastructure side,
the model commons — open-weight models as shared, attested capital — is the outcome
the GGUF wedge quietly serves: if the weights the world fine-tunes on carry verifiable
authorship and anchored history from the start [26, 27, 163], then the commons
accumulates evidence as it grows, and the alternative — an unattested commons in which
provenance is reconstructed forensically after each incident — accumulates incident reports


=== PAGINA 244 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 244
instead [118, 119]. The milestone structure is checkable in the same way as everything else
in this book: a credential profile joining KYA identity to RATS evidence roles, an ISO/IEC
42001 certification earned by a deployment that consumes anchored evidence, and a
cross-ecosystem adoption marker of the kind the Agent2Agent protocol already supplies at
the transport layer [16, 100, 111]. Each milestone carries a date range, an owning
institution, and a failure mode that the outlook can be scored against when 2030 arrives.
The scoring rule is the one this chapter has used throughout: predictions are written to be
checked, and a checked prediction that fails is information rather than embarrassment [31,
69].
 The complete stack, and the closing claim, are drawn in Figure 25.1. At the base,
firmware freedom: a device whose owner can rebuild and attest the software beneath their
own applications. Above it, agent verifiability: the four-gate pipeline, the evidence graph,
and the governed constitution, carrying every consequential action of the software the
device runs. The two halves are one architecture in the exact sense this book has used
throughout — the same hash, the same signatures, the same inclusion proofs, the same
quorums, configured locally at each layer [28, 100]. Sovereignty, so assembled, is not a
promise any component makes; it is a property the composition has, and it is checkable by
whoever cares to check it.
 Figure 25.1 — The complete digital sovereignty stack: firmware freedom (LibrePhone) and agent verifiability
 (VTK) as one architecture.


=== PAGINA 245 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 245
 The claim this book leaves standing is narrow, and it is engineered to be checkable.
There exists a coherent, implementable, and falsifiable architecture that converts agent trust
from promise to proof across every sector it was tested against, from billion-dollar custody
to the formal sciences; its every layer answers a documented failure mode; its every claim
about itself can itself be verified; and the distance between it and a deployed instance is no
longer architectural — it is organizational, financial, and, as trust has always finally been,
personal. The reader who wants to know whether that sentence is true is holding the wrong
artifact to decide it; the reader who wants to know how to decide it is holding the right one.
Prove, don’t promise.
Appendix A — Threat Model Reference
 This appendix consolidates the threat model developed in Chapter 3 into the reference
form incident responders and control auditors need: adversary classes, representative
incidents, capabilities, prerequisites, and the gates that detect each class. Table A.1 presents
the consolidated mapping with two cross-cutting patterns appended; the paragraphs that
follow state each class in full. The classes are labeled A1 through A4 and are ordered by
increasing sophistication of the adversary’s positioning rather than by severity of outcome;
as Chapter 7 demonstrated, a comparatively unsophisticated A1 artifact in a high-value
pipeline can out-earn a patient A4 campaign. Each class is stated so that its techniques
resolve to ATLAS-recognizable entries in the shared AI threat language [112], and the
detecting gates are the four-gate pipeline’s contract as specified in Chapter 12.
 A1 — the opportunistic supply-chain attacker. Capabilities: publishes artifacts,
models, or packages into public registries and hubs; no legitimate access to the target’s
infrastructure is required. Prerequisites: an unverified ingestion path on the victim side — a
download without attestation, a deserialization without sandboxing. Representative
evidence: malicious ML models discovered on public hubs and the scanning infrastructure
deployed in response [118, 119, 120]. Detected by: the hash and signature gates — an
unattested or misattested artifact fails closed before load; secure-deserialization research
defines the residual exposure inside accepted formats [121].
 A2 — the signing-infrastructure attacker. Capabilities: compromised development
or display infrastructure inside a trusted vendor, permitting payload injection at the moment
of signing or display while signatures remain cryptographically valid. Prerequisites:
supply-chain access to a vendor build or interface layer. Representative evidence: the Bybit
incident, in which a compromised wallet vendor machine subverted what signers were
shown while the transaction itself was well-formed [2, 4, 95]. Detected by: independent
decoding against anchored policy, the divergent-evidence event, and the quorum gate —
the architecture’s core answer to the incident [7, 28].


=== PAGINA 246 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 246
 A3 — the governance and key-custody attacker. Capabilities: theft, purchase, or
collusion of signing keys below or at quorum threshold; abuse of emergency or recovery
procedures. Prerequisites: access to key material or to the humans who hold it.
Representative evidence: the StablR failure, in which control of a single key in a 1-of-3
minting authority sufficed to mint unbacked value [6, 33]. Detected by: quorum thresholds
calibrated as hypotheses about simultaneous compromise (ADR-011, Appendix B),
timelocks on authority-affecting changes, and the constitution’s anchored version history
[29, 28].
 A4 — the state-scale and identity-visual attacker. Capabilities: sustained, patient
campaigns combining bespoke social engineering, infrastructure control, and visual
identity forgery; tolerance for long preparation. Prerequisites: targeted resourcing.
Representative evidence: the TraderTraitor campaign attributed by national authorities [5,
93] and the SUPERFORTUNE incident, in which a forged visual identity substituted an
attacker-controlled counterparty [34]. Detected by: anchored provenance of counterparties
(hash-pinned identities rather than displayed ones), the counterfactual replay discipline of
Chapter 7, and external audit of the verification path itself.

 Two reading rules make the table operational. First, the detected-by column names
gates, not products: the mapping is to the four-gate contract — hash, signature, inclusion,
quorum — plus the kernel’s capability bounds, so that any implementation of the contract
inherits the mapping and any gap in an implementation is locatable by gate. Second,
prerequisites are stated as victim-side conditions because that is where the defender’s
leverage lives: an attacker’s capability is a fact about the attacker, but a prerequisite is a
fact about the pipeline, and every prerequisite in the table is a condition the architecture is
designed to deny. Residual risk per class — what remains after all gates operate — is the
subject of Table 24.1 and is not restated here; the two tables are complements, and reading
them together is the intended audit path from adversary to residual.

Appendix B — ADR-011: Multisignature Quorum
Thresholds
 Architecture decision records are the constitution-as-code pattern applied to
engineering judgment: each decision is a versioned artifact with context, decision,
rationale, and consequences, anchored like any other evidence [28]. ADR-011, reproduced
below in its canonical form, records the project’s default policy for multisignature quorum
thresholds — arguably the single configuration value whose failure the incident record
documents most expensively. The context that forced the decision was twofold. StablR
demonstrated the bottom of the parameter space: a 1-of-3 minting authority converted one
stolen key into 13.5 million dollars of unbacked issuance within minutes [6, 33]. Bybit
demonstrated that thresholds do not defend against compromised display paths at any
threshold: three honest signers approved what a subverted interface chose to show them [2,
4]. A threshold policy must therefore be justified against theft-resistance on one axis and
availability on another, with the bybit-class failure handled by the decoding gate rather than
by the count of signers [95].
 The decision fixes two defaults and one invariant. The default quorum is 4-of-7 and the
critical quorum is 5-of-7 for treasury-scale and authority-affecting actions; and any quorum
below two-thirds of the signer set is prohibited outright — rejected at manifest parse time,
not discouraged by documentation. The rationale from incident data runs in three steps.
First, below two-thirds, a colluding minority within one signer of the threshold can carry an
authority-affecting vote unilaterally, which is precisely the StablR failure mode generalized
[33]; the two-thirds floor makes unilateral minority capture structurally impossible rather
than merely unlikely. Second, above 4-of-7 the marginal theft resistance of additional
signatures grows more slowly than the availability cost of additional unreachability: a
4-of-7 wallet tolerates the loss or incapacity of three signers before freezing, which incident
forensics suggest is the practical ceiling for small signer clubs managing operational keys
[29, 96]. Third, thresholds are hypotheses about simultaneous compromise, and hypotheses
must be per-organization: ADR-011 therefore fixes the floor and the prohibition, while
calibration within the permitted band is a declared, versioned parameter of each
deployment’s local constitution [28, 29].
 The consequences are recorded with equal candor. The availability trade-off is real:
four lost or unreachable keys freeze a default wallet, and recovery is itself a 5-of-7 event
with its own timelock, so the policy converts some categories of incident from loss to
outage — a trade the architecture makes deliberately and documents for insurers and
auditors to price. The prohibition has a cost in flexibility: sub-two-thirds configurations are
sometimes genuinely appropriate — low-value automation wallets, for instance — and
ADR-011 pushes those deployments to declare a separate, explicitly-labeled authority class


=== PAGINA 248 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 248
rather than to weaken the default. And the policy is auditable by construction: every
quorum value in force is a parsed, anchored, diffable parameter, so a violation of the
two-thirds floor is detectable in the evidence graph rather than discoverable in a
post-mortem [28, 70]. The canonical record follows.
ADR-011 — Multisignature quorum thresholds (constitution-as-code record)
status: Accepted | 2026-03-02 | supersedes ADR-007 (3-of-5 interim)
context:
- StablR 2026-05: 1-of-3 minting authority; one stolen key minted
13.5M of unbacked value within minutes [6, 33]
- Bybit 2025-02: signers honest; display path subverted [2, 4, 95]
- thresholds are hypotheses about simultaneous signer compromise [29]
decision:
default_quorum: 4 / 7 # theft floor; tolerates 3 unavailable signers
critical_quorum: 5 / 7 # treasury, key rotation, constitution amendment
invariant: m / n >= 2 / 3 for every authority-affecting action
prohibition: sub-two-thirds quorums are rejected at manifest parse time
calibration: per-organization, declared in the local ConstitutionStore;
values below the invariant are unparseable, not deprecated
rationale:
- below two thirds, a colluding minority can carry authority votes [33]
- above 4-of-7, availability loss outgrows marginal theft resistance [29]
- display-path compromise is handled by the decoding gate, not by m [95]
consequences:
- four lost keys freeze the wallet; recovery is a 5-of-7, timelocked event
- low-value automation requires a separate, labeled authority class
- every quorum value is parsed, anchored, and diffable in the evidence graph
Appendix C — GGUF Model Attestation Schema
 This appendix documents the model attestation schema that the MVP wedge ships,
with the rationale for each field group; the verification procedure follows. The schema’s
design principle is that every field must earn its hash: a field appears only if the four-gate
pipeline can check it and a relying party would act differently if it were false [26, 28]. The
artifact group carries the content identity — the byte-exact SHA-256 of the GGUF
container and the BLAKE3 Merkle root of its tensor tree — because the container is what
inference engines execute as provided and the tensor decomposition localizes any
byte-level difference to a named weight range [26, 27, 106, 163]. The author group binds
an Ed25519 identity to the artifact; the build group records toolchain and reproducibility
status with a link to SLSA-style provenance so that a skeptic can distinguish “signed by the
publisher” from “built reproducibly by the publisher” [102, 103]. The anchor group carries
the transparency-log inclusion data — log identity, index, and checkpoint — which
converts the attestation from a claim into a record no signer can quietly retract [8, 9]. The
signatures group admits a hybrid block precisely so that post-quantum migration (Section
24.3) can proceed per-attestation without schema change [104, 107].


=== PAGINA 249 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 249
{
"spec_version": "arkhe.model-attestation/1.1",
"model_id": "gguf:acme/qwen3-8b-instruct",
"artifact": {
"container": "GGUF v3",
"sha256": "9f1c4e2b7a8d...c31e",
"size_bytes": 8437234896,

],

"endorsements": { "required": 2, "received": 2,

 The verification procedure is five steps and is deliberately expressible in an afternoon
of engineering. Recompute the container hash and the tensor Merkle root from the bytes on
disk, failing closed on any mismatch — the hash gate. Verify the author signature and
every endorsement against the declared quorum — the signature and quorum gates. Verify
the Rekor inclusion proof and checkpoint against the public log — the inclusion gate,
which also establishes that the attestation existed at a time no signer can later deny [8, 9].
Evaluate the claims block against local policy — license class, reproducibility
requirements, toolchain allow-lists — which is where a deployment’s constitution connects
to a model’s attestation [28]. Emit honest status: verified, contested, or unattested, with the
failing gate named, and never a partial pass. The five steps are what the verifier CLI of
roadmap phase P3 automates, and they are intentionally few: the schema’s trustworthiness
comes from what each field commits to, not from how many fields it carries.
Appendix D — Infrastructure Workflows
 Two workflow specifications anchor the project’s day-to-day evidence discipline: the
continuous-integration gate that every proof-bearing repository runs, and the WormGraph
node schema that every evidence event conforms to. The CI workflow below is the
hodge-verify pipeline as configured for the Hodge program’s repositories (Chapter 22), and
it embodies two policies in code: the zero-sorry gate, which fails the build if any proof
relies on an unproved placeholder or a non-standard axiom, and the anchoring stage, which
hashes, signs, and submits every verified artifact to the transparency log before appending
the event to the WormGraph [62, 63, 69]. The same skeleton, with the Lean stages


=== PAGINA 250 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 250
exchanged for model-hash stages, is the gate the MVP wedge installs in machine-learning
pipelines — one workflow, two sectors, the universality claim running in CI.
name: hodge-verify
on:
push: { branches: [main] }
pull_request:
jobs:
lean-check:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: leanprover/lean-action@v1
- run: lake build
- name: zero-sorry gate
run: if grep -rn 'sorry' Proof/; then exit 1; fi
- run: lake env lean --run Check/Axioms.lean
wormgraph-anchor:
needs: lean-check
steps:
- run: hodge hash --canonicalize Proof/ > artifact.sha256
- run: hodge sign --key ed25519:$WITNESS_KEY --in artifact.sha256
- run: hodge anchor --rekor --attach attestation.json
- run: hodge witness commit --parents ${WORMGRAPH_PARENTS}
 The WormGraph node schema is the contract every evidence event satisfies,
reproduced here in the compact form the internal specification maintains [70]. The design
points worth reading for are three. Parents make the graph causal: every node cites the
evidence it was derived from, so the history is a DAG and a fork or rewrite is structurally
visible rather than merely disallowed. Inclusion makes the graph external: each node
carries the transparency-log data that places it in a log no project operator controls [8, 9].
And honest status makes the graph self-reporting: a node carries its current verification
verdict, so a contested or reverted node is a query, not an investigation.
node_id: blake3:e3f1... # content address of the record
event_type: proof-commit | lemma-accept | release-anchor
parents: [blake3:0a.., blake3:7b..] # causal DAG edges
artifact_hash: blake3:9c2d... # payload commitment
author: npub1q9...k4m (Ed25519)
signature: 5j8w...Qc # over canonicalized record
timestamp: 2026-09-14T11:02:31Z
inclusion:
log: rekor
log_index: 88412031
checkpoint: signed-tree-head:c0ff...ee
quorum: { required: 4, received: 5, status: accepted }
honest_status: verified | contested | reverted
 Deployment notes complete the workflow picture. The anchor stage is asynchronous
by design: verification blocks, anchoring does not, which is how the pipeline honors the
latency residual of Section 24.1 without sacrificing evidence. The witness key material
lives in the platform’s secret store and never in the repository, and the zero-sorry gate is
deliberately implemented as a plain text search plus an axiom check rather than a plugin, so


=== PAGINA 251 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 251
that auditors can verify the gate itself in one reading — the verifier of the verifier, kept
small enough to be read on a single screen [102, 103]. Repositories that adopt the workflow
inherit the evidence graph without adopting the project’s governance; the constitution that
interprets these events remains local, which is the universal-core discipline of Chapter 11
applied to build infrastructure.
Glossary
ADR — Architecture Decision Record: a versioned, anchored artifact that records a design
decision with its context, decision, rationale, and consequences. ADRs are first-class
evidence in the constitution-as-code pattern.
ADR-011 — The project’s decision record fixing default multisignature quorum thresholds
at 4-of-7 (standard) and 5-of-7 (critical), and prohibiting sub-two-thirds quorums outright
(Appendix B).
Agent — Software that plans and executes consequential actions — payments,
deployments, signatures — with partial autonomy on behalf of a principal, typically over
tool interfaces such as MCP or A2A.
Anchor — An external, append-only commitment to an artifact’s existence and content —
typically a transparency-log inclusion record — that no single project operator can retract
or rewrite.
Attestation — A signed claim binding an artifact or state to an author and time, structured
so that a third party can verify it without trusting the claimer; the model attestation of
Appendix C is the book’s worked instance.
BLAKE3 — A fast, parallel, tree-structured cryptographic hash function used for content
addressing of large artifacts such as model tensor trees [106].
Blossom — A Nostr media-storage standard (BUD specifications) for servers that store
files addressable by their SHA-256 sums, used in the decentralized stack as
content-addressed blob storage [142, 143].
Capability — An explicitly granted, bounded permission for an agent to perform a class of
actions; capabilities are declared in the Capability Manifest and enforced by the kernel of
containment.
Capability Manifest — The signed declaration of what an agent may do — tools,
counterparties, spending bounds, data domains — against which the kernel fails closed on
any out-of-manifest action [28].


=== PAGINA 252 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 252
CHK — Content Hash Key: a convergent-encryption scheme in which the key is derived
from the plaintext’s hash, permitting deduplicated, content-addressed encrypted storage as
used by hashtree-style stores [147].
Clear signing — Display-layer practice that renders the decoded, human-meaningful
content of a transaction at signing time, as distinct from blind signing over opaque bytes [1,
38].
Constitution-as-code — The practice of expressing governance rules as versioned, parsed,
anchored artifacts whose changes follow the same evidence pipeline as the actions they
govern.
ConstitutionStore — The authority component that stores the governing rule corpora as
versioned, hash-anchored documents, structurally separated from the witnesses that record
events [28].
Content addressing — Naming data by the hash of its bytes, so that a name provably
refers to exact content; the foundational identification move of the entire architecture.
Convergent encryption — Encrypting such that identical plaintexts yield identical
ciphertexts, enabling deduplication in content-addressed stores at the cost of confirmable
equality (as in CHK-style systems).
CT — Certificate Transparency: the append-only, publicly auditable log design for TLS
certificates (RFC 6962; updated by RFC 9162), the prototype for external anchoring of
signed claims [8, 99].
d-Veto — The veto-depth metric of the VetoGraph analysis: the graph distance of a node’s
classified veto path to the constitution’s core, used to measure capture topology rather than
assume it (Chapter 20) [30].
Ed25519 — The elliptic-curve signature scheme used for author and witness identities
throughout the architecture; classical, hence scheduled for hybrid post-quantum
companions (Section 24.3).
Evidence — In this book’s usage, a verifiable record — hash, signature, inclusion proof,
quorum verdict — that a stated event occurred, as distinct from testimony or assertion
about it.
Fail-closed — The design posture in which any unmet verification condition blocks the
action by default; the kernel denies rather than permits under uncertainty.
Four-gate pipeline — The architecture’s verification contract: hash, signature, inclusion,
quorum — the four checks every consequential artifact or event passes before honest status
is granted (Chapters 4 and 12).


=== PAGINA 253 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 253
GGUF — GPT-Generated Unified Format: the open-weight container format used by
llama.cpp-family inference engines, and the artifact type of the book’s MVP wedge [26,
27].
Governance — The rules and procedures by which a system’s own rules change; in this
architecture, always expressed as anchored, quorum-governed version history rather than
by convention.
Honest status — The verifier-output contract: a verdict of verified, contested, or unattested
with the failing check named, and never a partial or unexplained pass.
Inclusion proof — Cryptographic evidence that a specific entry exists in an append-only
log, verifiable against the log’s signed tree head without trusting the log operator’s word
(the third gate).
Invariant — A property declared to hold over all system states — exposure caps, custody
rules, zero-sorry — whose violation is a datable, witnessable event rather than a matter of
interpretation.
Kernel of containment — The fail-closed component that bounds agent capabilities
regardless of the agent’s claims or conduct; the architecture’s answer to the model-behavior
gap (Chapters 3 and 24).
KYA — Know Your Agent: emerging interoperability frameworks for verifiable agent
identity and credentials, notably the Ant International initiative with Visa and Mastercard
[39, 40].
Lefschetz (1,1) — The Lefschetz (1,1) theorem: the classical result that every integral
(1,1)-class on a smooth complex projective variety is a rational combination of divisor
classes; the principal known case of the Hodge conjecture (Chapter 22).
MCP — Model Context Protocol: the JSON-RPC-based protocol connecting LLM
applications to tools and context servers, and a documented carrier of tool-poisoning
attacks [108, 109].
Merkle tree — A hash tree in which a single root commits to an entire dataset, enabling
efficient, local proofs that any element is contained in the committed whole; used for tensor
trees and log structures.
ML-DSA — Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, standardized as NIST
FIPS 204; the post-quantum signature of the architecture’s hybrid migration path [104,
105].
Model attestation — The signed, anchored claim binding a model’s exact bytes and tensor
tree to an author identity (Appendix C); proves bytes and authorship, not behavior.


=== PAGINA 254 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 254
Model commons — The envisioned shared capital of open-weight models carrying
verifiable authorship and anchored history, so that commons growth accumulates evidence
rather than forensic debt.
Multisignature — A custody arrangement requiring m of n independent signers to
authorize an action; threshold choice is ADR-011’s subject [29].
NIP-34 — The Nostr Implementation Possibility specifying git events — repositories,
patches, issues — over Nostr relays, used by the decentralized development stack [140,
141].
Nostr — Notes and Other Stuff Transmitted by Relays: a simple, relay-based signed-event
protocol providing identity and transport for the decentralized stack of Chapter 18.
npub — A Nostr public-key identifier (bech32-encoded), used in this architecture as a
portable author and witness identity in attestations and evidence nodes.
PQC — Post-quantum cryptography: cryptographic algorithms designed for security
against quantum adversaries, standardized in the approved FIPS 203/204/205 suite [104,
105].
Provenance — The verifiable account of where an artifact came from and how it was
produced — in supply-chain terms, the SLSA/in-toto evidence class the architecture
extends to models and agents [102, 103].
Quorum — The required count of independent signatures for an action or verdict;
calibrated as a hypothesis about simultaneous compromise, never as ceremony (the fourth
gate).
Quorum acceptance — The evidence-layer operation by which a claim or artifact
becomes accepted when the required number of witnesses have signed; the mechanism that
makes acceptance datable and attributable.
RATS — Remote ATtestation procedureS (IETF RFC 9334): the reference architecture of
attester, verifier, and relying-party roles for conveying evidence about system state; the
convergence target for agent-evidence profiles [100].
Redox signaling — Cellular communication through reactive oxygen species, the
biological homeostasis model that Chapter 21 maps onto verification invariants [155].
Rekor — The Sigstore transparency log for software artifacts: an append-only, publicly
verifiable record of signatures and attestations, and the project’s default external anchor [9,
10].
Relying party — In RATS terms, the actor that consumes evidence about a system and
acts on it; in this book, anyone who accepts an agent’s action based on its anchored


=== PAGINA 255 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 255
evidence [100].
Reproducible build — A build process that independent parties can repeat byte-for-byte
from source, converting build claims into checkable ones; the evidence posture behind
SLSA provenance levels [102].
SCC — Strongly connected component: a maximal subgraph in which every node reaches
every other; the graph-theoretic lens used in the CF/88 audit to locate circular citation
structure in the constitutional graph (Chapter 20) [30].
Sector adapter — The local configuration tier — regulation mappings, data domains,
quorums, timelocks — through which a sector or organization adopts the universal core
without customizing it (Chapter 13).
SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a graded framework for build
integrity and provenance, used here as the evidence standard for the verifier’s own supply
chain [102].
Sovereignty stack — The complete composition, from rebuildable firmware on the device
(LibrePhone) to agent verifiability on services (VTK), in which each layer’s trust root is the
user’s rather than a vendor’s (Figure 25.1).
Stigmergy — Coordination through traces left in a shared environment rather than direct
signaling; the bioinspired coordination model of Chapter 19’s swarm discussion [158].
Threshold signature — A scheme in which any subset of at least t shareholders produces
one signature, distinguished in this book from multisig quorums by its single composite
signature and distinct key-management profile.
Timelock — A declared delay before an authority-affecting change takes effect, giving
relying parties time to observe, object, or exit; configured per sector (Chapters 13 and 14).
TPM 2.0 — Trusted Platform Module 2.0: the vendor-neutral hardware root of trust whose
measured-boot and key machinery anchors device-side attestation [101].
Transparency log — An append-only, publicly auditable log with cryptographic inclusion
proofs (CT, Rekor), providing evidence that a signed claim exists and when, independent of
the signer’s later cooperation [8, 9].
Trust root — The ultimate verification anchor a deployment chooses — its own keys, its
own logs, its own auditors; the architecture’s stance is that the trust root belongs to the
relying organization, not the vendor.
Universal core — The sector-invariant portion of the architecture — the four-gate
pipeline, fail-closed posture, honest status, layered verification — identical across every
deployment (Chapter 11).

SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 256
VetoGraph — The veto-topology analysis framework applied to constitutional corpora,
measuring d-Veto depth and citation structure over a governance graph (Chapter 20) [30].
WASM — WebAssembly: the sandboxed, portable binary instruction format in which the
project’s verification tooling is distributed for in-browser and embedded verification
surfaces.
Winding number — The integer counting how many times a closed curve wraps around a
point; the prototype of the integer-valued topological invariants that cohomology classes
generalize in the Hodge setting (Chapter 22).
Witness — The component or signer that records and signs events without authority to
define them; the structural counterpart to the ConstitutionStore’s authority in the separation
of powers (Chapter 6).
WormGraph — The project’s append-only causal evidence graph: hash-addressed nodes,
signed by witnesses, anchored externally, with quorum verdicts and honest status (Chapters
4 and 22) [70].
X-Wing — The hybrid key-encapsulation construction combining X25519 and
ML-KEM-768, cited as the pattern for hybrid classical/post-quantum migration [107].
Zero-sorry — The Lean discipline that no accepted proof may rely on an unproved
placeholder or non-standard axiom; enforced mechanically by the hodge-verify CI gate
(Appendix D).

PART XI — INTEGRATED CORPUS
SYNTHESIS
This part consolidates the three corpora of the research program — the verification-first
framework (VFG), the Verifiable Trust Kernel (VTK), and the Orchestration Layer — into a
single architecture of evidence. It formalizes the falsifier definition, the four-gate pipeline,
and the epistemic state machine; maps the corpus mechanisms to NIST AI RMF, the EU AI
Act, and ISO/IEC 42001; and reports the aggregate conjecture ledger across corpora (26
conjectures: 7 Measured, 3 Reduced, 13 Unproven, 3 Falsified), including the program's
recorded self-corrections.
1. Introduction
 In his personal observations appended to the Rogers Commission report on the
Challenger accident, Richard Feynman distilled the failure of a great engineering
institution into a single sentence: reality must take precedence over public relations, for
nature cannot be fooled [1]. The commission found that the decision to launch had been
reached by managers who assessed risk qualitatively, while the engineers who owned the
numbers had objected without being able to force those numbers into the decision loop.
The accident was not, at its core, a failure of computation or of goodwill; it was a failure of
epistemic infrastructure. The number existed, the instrument existed, but no governance
mechanism connected the two to the decision.
 Four decades later, the same failure mode has re-emerged at industrial scale in
artificial-intelligence governance. Modern assurance documents — model cards,
compliance self-assessments, vendor questionnaires, and procurement question banks —
are overwhelmingly assertive: they state that systems are safe, accurate, fair, or compliant,
and they attach signatures to those assertions. Empirical work on hallucinating language
models documents how fluently plausible but false claims can be generated and propagated
[2]; work on benchmark generalization shows that measured headline numbers can silently
fail to transfer to the underlying population of interest [3]. In this environment, an audit that
samples assertions is an audit of prose, not of evidence. The gap between what governance
documents claim and what can be mechanically demonstrated has become the central
liability of AI assurance.
 This monograph presents the architecture of a research program built specifically to
close that gap, and whose working slogan — a disciplina VFG não é dizer 'sim' ou 'não', é
dizer 'mostre o número' — encodes the position that a governance claim is not a verdict but
a number with provenance. The program comprises three mutually dependent artifacts.


=== PAGINA 267 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 267
VFG (Provisional Axioms, Contradictions, Instruments, Refutations) is an epistemic
discipline that assigns every claim one of five machine-readable statuses and requires each
claim to carry an instrument and an executable falsifier [4][5]. VTK is a formal kernel — a
Rust workspace with Python bindings — in which those falsifiers are compiled, composed
categorically, and executed under model checking and property-based testing [6]. the
Orchestration Layer is the governance layer: a provenance-preserving architecture with
post-quantum identity infrastructure, a formal governance model (CGF) with impossibility
results, and an adversarial evaluation harness [7][8].
 The central thesis of this monograph is that trustworthy governance of engineered and
AI systems requires exactly three properties at once — a machine-readable epistemic status
for every claim, an executable refutation path for every claim, and an immutable
provenance chain for every number — and that these three properties are best realized by
three cooperating layers rather than by a single monolithic framework. We argue this thesis
constructively: by specifying the integration semantics of the three layers (Section 6), and
by reporting the aggregate empirical ledger the integrated stack has produced across three
independent domains (Section 7), including three documented falsification events in which
the framework's own previously recorded claims were refuted and downgraded.
 The contributions are fivefold. C1. A unified formal account of the VFG epistemic
discipline: five states, falsifier soundness, declared coverage, the measured-evidence
condition, interval reduction with error propagation, and an information-theoretic
admissibility gate (Section 3). C2. A description of the VTK kernel as the execution
substrate for falsifiers: categorical composition of verification stages, information-theoretic
invariants, and content-addressed evidence storage (Section 4). C3. A synthesis of the
Orchestration Layer governance layer: layers L1–L5, the CGF mixture model with its
alpha-dynamics fixed point and impossibility results, the RLM decision rule, and
post-quantum identity infrastructure (Section 5). C4. The integration semantics binding the
three layers into one stack, with an explicit mapping to NIST AI RMF 1.0, the EU AI Act,
and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Section 6). C5. A consolidated, cross-domain empirical ledger
— 19 aerospace conjectures, 7 Phantom Twist conjectures, 19 audited market-research
improvements, and 9 externally executed components — with honest status counts and
three falsification case analyses (Section 7). Sections 8 and 9 discuss limitations,
counterarguments, and future work.
 A note on method and posture is warranted at the outset. The case-study corpora
consolidated here were produced within a single research program with a single principal
author; they are presented as objects of study, with their claims re-verified against external
primary sources where such verification was possible, and with internal inconsistencies that
were discovered during integration reported candidly (Sections 7 and 8). Where a number
originates in the corpus rather than in an independent instrument, the text says so. This


=== PAGINA 268 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 268
monograph applies its own discipline to itself: the reader should expect statuses, not
adjectives.
2. Background and Related Work
2.1 Falsifiability and Strong Inference
 The epistemic position underlying VFG is Popper's falsificationism: a claim that
forbids no observation is not empirical, and scientific rationality proceeds by subjecting
bold conjectures to severe attempted refutation [9]. Platt codified the practice as strong
inference — the systematic formulation of multiple alternative hypotheses, the design of
crucial experiments capable of excluding each, and the prompt execution of those
experiments — and documented how fields that institutionalized this loop advanced
dramatically faster than fields that did not [10]. VFG can be read as a mechanization of
strong inference for engineering governance: the multiple hypotheses are the corpus's
conjectures, the crucial experiments are compiled falsifiers, and the prompt execution is
continuous integration. The decisive difference is institutional rather than philosophical:
where Platt's scientists designed experiments by hand, VFG requires the refutation path to
exist as code before the claim may circulate, which converts falsifiability from a virtue of
the author into a property the artifact either has or lacks.
2.2 Formal Verification in Industrial Practice
 The engineering half of the stack stands on a mature industrial record. Hoare's
axiomatic basis established that programs can carry machine-checkable correctness
obligations as part of their very semantics [11]; Rice's theorem bounds that ambition by
showing that any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable in general [12],
so all practical verification is bounded, partial, and explicit about its limits. Within those
bounds, formal specification and model checking have repeatedly paid for themselves in
production: Amazon Web Services applied TLA+ to critical distributed systems and found
that the specification exercise surfaced defects and ambiguities that neither testing nor
review had caught [13][14]. Rust occupies a strategic niche in this landscape because its
type system enforces a large class of memory-safety invariants by construction, a property
formalized and proved at scale by the RustBelt semantic model [15]; on top of that
substrate, bounded model checkers such as Kani verify assertions over all bounded
executions rather than sampled ones [16]. The VFG's falsifiers are ordinary Rust predicates
compiled into exactly these verification and testing harnesses, which is what makes
'refutation path exists' a build-time, tool-checked property.
2.3 Property-Based Testing as Executable Falsification


=== PAGINA 269 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 269
 Property-based testing, inaugurated by QuickCheck, reframes testing as falsification of
universally quantified properties: the tester states an invariant, the framework generates
inputs until a counterexample is found, and shrinking reduces the counterexample to a
minimal refutation [17]. The Rust proptest library carries this pattern into the language of
the VTK kernel, with persistent regression files that record each counterexample for
posterity [18]. VFG adopts this machinery directly, and the correspondence is exact: a
corpus conjecture is a universally quantified property; its falsifier is the property's negation
instrumented for execution; a recorded counterexample is a refutation event; and the
shrinking artifact is the minimal evidence object that the ledger archives. This equivalence
is what allows governance claims to inherit sixty years of tooling maturity — from
QuickCheck's generators to Kani's bounded model checking — without translation effort.
2.4 Governance Standards and Their Measurement Gap
 Three instruments dominate the contemporary governance landscape. The NIST AI
Risk Management Framework 1.0 organizes AI risk into four functions — Govern, Map,
Measure, Manage — with 19 categories and 72 subcategories, and is explicit that its
mechanisms are voluntary and non-certifiable [19]. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU)
2024/1689) attaches binding obligations to high-risk systems, including a documented,
continuously maintained risk-management system (Article 9), logging (Article 12), human
oversight (Article 14), and accuracy and robustness requirements (Article 15) [20].
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 defines a certifiable AI management system in the ISO
management-system tradition [21]. All three instruments prescribe that organizations
measure; none of them prescribes in what machine-checkable form a measurement must
exist, which states a claim may occupy, or how refutation must be recorded. The gap is not
rhetorical: a compliance regime in which 'measured' is a self-description rather than a
machine-verifiable state cannot distinguish evidence from assertion, and VFG is designed
precisely as a candidate substrate for that distinction (Section 6.3).
2.5 Adversarial Measurement: Goodhart, Reward Hacking,
and Hallucination
 Any framework that elevates numbers into governance objects must confront the
adversarial dynamics of measurement. Manheim and Garrabrant's taxonomy decomposes
Goodhart's law into four mechanisms — regressional, extremal, causal, and adversarial —
each of which degrades the correlation between a proxy metric and its target under
optimization pressure [22]. Skalse et al. formalize reward hacking as the untriviality of the
divergence between a reward proxy and the true objective, proving that the hackable set is
essentially never empty [23]. In the language-model era, hallucination adds a third channel:
generated text manufactures plausible numbers without instruments at all [2]. These results
do not merely motivate VFG; they constrain its design. Falsifiers must be robust against


=== PAGINA 270 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 270
gaming (their inputs must be tied to instruments, not to self-reports), coverage must be
declared rather than implied (Section 3.2), and refutation events must be recorded
immutably, because a governance system that can silently lower its own numbers is
indistinguishable from the failure mode it exists to prevent.
2.6 Identity and Provenance Infrastructure
 The third pillar draws on deployed standards for verifiable identity and cryptography.
W3C Decentralized Identifiers provide globally resolvable, registry-independent identifiers
for actors and artifacts [24]; NIST FIPS 204 standardizes ML-DSA, the module-lattice
digital signature scheme selected for post-quantum security [25]; and the Trusted Platform
Module 2.0 specification provides hardware-rooted key protection and remote attestation
[26]. For protocol-level guarantees, ProVerif supplies automatic symbolic verification of
secrecy and authentication properties [27], TLA+ covers system-level temporal behavior
[14], and the Coq proof assistant supports machine-checked proofs of higher-level
properties [28]. the Orchestration Layer composes these instruments so that every evidence
artifact in the governance layer is signed, identity-bound, and anchored (Section 5), and
external white-box audits — the class of engagement Cure53 conducts as a matter of
practice [29] — remain the designated adversarial check on the composition itself.
2.7 Design-Science Framing
 Finally, the program is best understood in Simon's terms as the sciences of the
artificial: the proper concern is not how governance is, but how it could be, given artifacts
designed to transform existing situations into preferred ones [30]. The Orchestration Layer
metaphor is repurposed deliberately from Raymond's contrast between centralized and
bazaar-style development [31]: here the cathedral names the load-bearing quality of slowly
accumulated, verified structure, in which each claim is a stone that has survived inspection,
and the enemy is the 'castle in the air' — plausible structure resting on nothing. Category
theory supplies the composition language [32][33], monads the disciplined sequencing of
computations that carry evidence [34], and information theory the quantitative semantics of
what it means for evidence to reduce uncertainty about a claim [35][36]. These choices are
not ornamental; each is load-bearing in the sections that follow.
3. VFG: The Epistemic Discipline
3.1 Design Principles
 VFG (Provisional Axioms, Contradictions, Instruments, Refutations) was developed
and exercised in two domain corpora — world space-development programs [4] and an
advanced unmanned-aerial-vehicle research program [5] — before being generalized here.


=== PAGINA 271 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 271
Its four design principles can be stated compactly. P1 (show the number): every
governance-relevant claim must expose a quantitative expression — a threshold, an
interval, a rate, a bound; a claim that cannot say what would count as evidence for or
against it is inadmissible. P2 (instrument): every number must name the instrument or
authoritative source that produced it, with retrieval metadata sufficient for independent
re-verification. P3 (falsifier): every claim must ship with an executable predicate that,
when presented with a world-state, refutes the claim if its negation is observed; the falsifier
is code, versioned and compiled, not prose. P4 (statuses are data): epistemic qualification
is a five-valued typed field, not an adjective; it is set only by admissible transitions (Section
3.4) and is auditable in the evidence ledger.
 Two clarifications prevent common misreadings. First, VFG does not decide truth; it
decides what may be asserted, by whom, in which document class — a distinction that
matters because governance failures almost always involve assertion inflation rather than
measurement error per se. Second, the discipline is symmetric in an important sense: it
treats the corpus's own claims with exactly the machinery it applies to external claims, and
Sections 7 and 8 report the resulting self-corrections without editorial softening.
3.2 Claims, Invariants, and Falsifiers
 Let C be the set of claims under governance and W a space of world-states. A claim is a
typed proposition c ∈ C together with a declared quantitative expression (the 'number'). An
invariant is a property I(c) over states that must hold for c to remain unrefuted. The central
object is the falsifier:
 Definition 1 (falsifier). A falsifier of c is a total, computable predicate φc : X → {0,1}
 such that, for every world-state x:
 (D1)
 φc(x) = 1  ⇒  ¬ c(x),
 (1)
 that is, the falsifier fires only on genuine violations of the claim — a soundness
requirement whose violation would let the framework manufacture false refutations.
Soundness is enforced by construction, since falsifiers are compiled from the invariant they
negate, and by review, since every falsifier ships with the invariant it encodes. Because
Rice's theorem forbids total verification of non-trivial semantic properties [12], the
framework requires an honest, declared coverage bound:
 Definition 2 (declared coverage). ρ(c) = |Dom(φc) ∩ Fail(c)| / |Fail(c)| ≥ ρmin, with
 ρ(c) stated in the ledger.
 (2)
 In practice ρ(c) is realized as the fraction of the claim's failure surface that the
compiled falsifier can reach under its verification regime — for instance, the bounded
unrolling depth of a Kani harness or the generator space of a property test [16][17].


=== PAGINA 272 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 272
Declared coverage converts an uncomfortable theoretical limit into an auditable
engineering quantity; a claim is never allowed to borrow confidence from a falsifier that
examines only part of its failure surface.
3.3 The Five Epistemic States
 Every claim carries exactly one status from the set Σ = {Proven, Measured, Reduced,
Unproven, Falsified}. Table 1 defines the states, their admissible evidence, and their
transition rules; Figure 1 depicts the state machine. Two of the five states deserve emphasis
because they are systematically abused in ordinary governance practice. Reduced marks
claims that are derived — not measured — from measured premises through a verified
derivation, with the propagated error bound made explicit by interval arithmetic:
 Reduction (interval). If c = g(x1, …, xk) with measured intervals □xi, then □c =
g(□x1, …, □xk) (the interval extension of g), and the ledger reports □c, not a point
 estimate.
 (3)
 Unproven is the default state of every scheduled or announced future capability: a
launch date, a roadmap milestone, a promised benchmark. The corpus's empirical finding,
developed in Section 7, is that Unproven dominates governance corpora (10 of 19 space
conjectures), and that the single most valuable service the framework performs is
preventing Unproven claims from acquiring the rhetorical force of Measured ones. A claim
is Measured only when two independent instruments agree within tolerance:
Measured condition. Measured(c) ⟺ ∃ s, r ∈ I, s ≠ r: |x̂s − x̂r| ≤ ε, each with stated
 confidence 1−δ.
 (4)
 and Falsified when a recorded event fires the falsifier. The fifth state, Proven, is
deliberately rare: it requires a proof object (a machine-checked certificate) or survival of a
pre-registered adversarial evaluation, and the consolidated corpora of Section 7 contain no
Proven aerospace claim — an absence that is itself informative about the epistemic texture
of the domain.

3.4 Evidence Monotonicity and the Ledger
 The state machine of Figure 1 is monotone: evidence may promote a claim (U → M →
P) or refute it (any state → F), but a Falsified claim cannot be silently rehabilitated;
successor conjectures must be registered as new records citing the refutation. The formal
rationale is that statuses index subsets of an evidence poset, and refutation events are
immutable entries in an append-only ledger. Transitions themselves are gated by an
information-theoretic admissibility condition: a promotion requires that the presented
evidence actually reduce uncertainty about the claim by a stated margin κ:
 Information gate. U → M admissible only if ΔH = H(c) − H(c | E) ≥ κ > 0, with H
 the entropy of the claim's truth distribution under the ledger's model.
 (5)
 Equation (5) operationalizes the slogan 'mostre o número': evidence that does not move
the number does not move the status, and the ledger records ΔH per transition so that
auditors can challenge the model, not merely the conclusion. This gate, borrowed from
Shannon's formulation of information as uncertainty reduction [35] and from
minimum-description-length practice in model selection [36], is what prevents the ledger
from accumulating ceremonial evidence — the governance analogue of the cargo-cult


=== PAGINA 274 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 274
rituals Feynman criticized in the Challenger era [1].
3.5 Falsifiers as Code
 Listing 1 reproduces the falsifier pattern exactly as the space corpus compiles it [4]:
docstring carries the conjecture; the function body is the negated invariant; the return value
true means 'refutation observed'. The conservative falsifier for the Artemis schedule claim
fires only on an official crewed landing before the GAO-assessed window, and the
DRACO and Mars Sample Return falsifiers are event-triggered — both, as Section 7.1
reports, have in fact fired, which is precisely how the corpus acquired its two Falsified
entries.
/// ART-01: Artemis III performs its crewed lunar landing no earlier than 2027
/// (GAO-24-107249 schedule assessment). Fires iff an official crewed lunar
/// landing is recorded before 2027-01-01.
pub fn falsify_art_01(official_landing: Option<Date>) -> bool {
matches!(official_landing, Some(d) if d < date(2027, 1, 1))
}
/// NG-01: a recovered New Glenn booster is reflown in 2026. Fires iff no
/// reflown-booster event is recorded by the end of 2026.
pub fn falsify_ng_01(booster_reflown_in_2026: bool) -> bool {
!booster_reflown_in_2026
}
/// NTP-01: the DRACO nuclear-thermal demonstration proceeds to flight.
/// Fires iff the programme is cancelled.
pub fn falsify_ntp_01(programme_cancelled: bool) -> bool { programme_cancelled }
/// MSR-01: Mars Sample Return proceeds on its 2031 baseline. Fires iff the
/// approved architecture is cancelled or re-planned beyond ~2040.
pub fn falsify_msr_01(approved_architecture_dropped: bool) -> bool {
approved_architecture_dropped
}
/// ACC-01: Artemis Accords reaches 71 signatories by September 2026.
pub fn falsify_acc_01(signatories: u64, now: Date) -> bool {
now > date(2026, 9, 30) && signatories < 71
}
 Three implementation patterns recur across the corpora and deserve naming, because
they are the practical content of soundness. The conjunctive pattern composes primitive
invariants conjunctively (a claim survives only if all conjuncts hold), mirroring the
categorical product (Section 4.2). The relative-tolerance pattern expresses thresholds as
relative rather than absolute deviations, so that unit changes do not silently break refutation
semantics. The envelope-conditioned pattern fires only within a declared operating
envelope, preventing out-of- regime observations from producing spurious refutations.
These patterns were extracted from the Phantom Twist corpus's Kani harness family and
are reused verbatim by the space corpus [5][4].
4. VTK: The Formal Kernel


=== PAGINA 275 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 275
4.1 Architecture Overview
 VTK is the execution substrate of the stack: a Rust workspace, with Python exposure
through the PyO3 bridge [37], in which every falsifier, invariant, and ledger operation is
compiled and run. The kernel exists for a simple reason of epistemic hygiene: if
governance logic is allowed to live in documents, spreadsheets, and ad-hoc scripts, it
inherits exactly the unverified provenance it is supposed to police. Routing it through one
kernel gives the entire stack a uniform trust base — memory safety by construction under
Rust's ownership discipline [15], bounded model checking through Kani [16], and
property-based refutation through proptest [18] — all under one build system, one
dependency audit surface, and one evidence schema. The 252-page architecture volume
documents the crate inventory, the verification posture, and the deployment profiles in full
[6]; this section summarizes only what the integration requires.
4.2 Categorical Composition
 Verification stages in VTK compose categorically [32][33]. Requirement
transformations, invariant conjunctions, and falsifier disjunctions are morphisms; a
verification pipeline is their composition; and the ledger is the codomain functor into which
every pipeline deposits evidence. Conjunction of invariants is realized as a categorical
product (a claim survives when every component survives), and disjunction of falsifiers as
a coproduct (a claim is refuted when any component refutation fires), which is precisely the
algebra governance logic wants and which keeps pipeline semantics independent of any
particular tool. Evidence accumulation itself is sequenced monadically [34]: each stage
returns a value paired with the evidence it generated, the writer monad appends to the
ledger, and the bind operation enforces that no stage can bypass recording. The practical
consequence is that a governance pipeline is auditable end-to-end by construction — the
composition operator itself cannot drop evidence, because dropping evidence is not
expressible in the monad.
4.3 Information-Theoretic Invariants
 The kernel enforces the information gate of Eq. (5) natively: promotions are computed
from entropy deltas, and every recorded transition stores its ΔH alongside the evidence
object. The same machinery supports minimum-description-length arbitration when
competing explanations of a refutation event exist — the ledger selects the explanation
minimizing L(H) + L(E | H), in Rissanen's formulation [36] — and supports the provenance
economics of the evidence store, since content-addressed artifacts deduplicate exactly
when their information content coincides [35]. These are not exotic additions; they are the
bookkeeping that makes Eq. (5) computable rather than metaphorical.


=== PAGINA 276 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 276
4.4 Content-Addressed Evidence: Hashtree and Verifiable
Model Artifacts
 Two kernel services matter directly to the integration. Hashtree is the
content-addressed storage layer: evidence objects are Merkle-addressed, CHK-encrypted at
rest, and exposed through mutable references anchored to decentralized infrastructure, so
that an archived measurement cannot be edited without changing its address [6]. Verifiable
model artifacts extend the same discipline to learned models packaged as GGUF files:
each artifact carries a signed manifest binding tensor checksums, provenance metadata, and
evaluation records, and the kernel's fail-closed loader refuses any artifact whose manifest
does not verify [6]. Together these services give the ledger of Section 3.4 its immutability
guarantees at the byte level rather than by policy, and they are the mechanism by which the
'castle in the air' failure mode — plausible structure resting on nothing — is made
structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. Table 2 maps the kernel's
verification concerns to their tools and to the artifacts each produces.

4.5 A Kani Harness for an Invariant
 Listing 2 shows the harness pattern by which invariants graduate to bounded
exhaustive verification in the kernel: the harness asserts the invariant over nondeterministic
inputs, Kani checks all executions within its unrolling bound, and the resulting proof
artifact is archived with its bound declared — an operational instance of the
declared-coverage discipline of Eq. (2). The example is drawn from the Phantom corpus's
synchronization-invariant family [5], where the order-parameter invariant governs
propeller-phase coherence (Section 7.2).

#[kani::proof]
#[kani::unwind(32)] // declared bound: r(c) coverage reported in the ledger
fn check_phase_order_invariant() {
let th1: f64 = kani::any();
let th2: f64 = kani::any();
kani::assume(th1.is_finite() && th2.is_finite());
// Order-parameter magnitude must never exceed 1 (Kuramoto coherence [S]);
// |S| > 1 would mean the synchronization state is unphysical.
let s_re = (th1.cos() + th2.cos()) / 2.0;
let s_im = (th1.sin() + th2.sin()) / 2.0;
let s2 = s_re * s_re + s_im * s_im;
assert!(s2 <= 1.0 + 1e-9, "coherence bound violated");
}
5. the Orchestration Layer: Governance, Identity,
and Provenance
5.1 Layers L1–L5
 the Orchestration Layer is the governance layer of the stack, documented in a 222-page
monograph [7] and, in a two-audience exposition, in the VTK–the Orchestration Layer
documentation corpus [8]. Its architecture is layered. L1 (identity) establishes who may
act: actors and artifacts carry W3C Decentralized Identifiers [24], attested through
threshold ML-DSA signatures standardized in FIPS 204 [25] and hardware-rooted TPM
keys [26], subject to the corpus's BEACONS binding criteria. L2 (provenance) records
what happened: the evidence pipeline of Figure 2, from raw event to content-hash,
signature, DID binding, anchoring, and immutable audit trail. L3 (policy) encodes gates —
machine-executable rules that refuse actions whose required evidence statuses are not
present. L4 (enforcement) executes those gates at run time on the VTK kernel. L5
(deliberation) exposes the human-readable surface — dashboards, monographs, and audit
reports — in which numbers, not adjectives, are the unit of communication. The
two-audience corpus additionally catalogues the system's concepts (Z1–Z9) and its
invariant catalogue (I15 through I420), each invariant carrying a falsifier and an honest
status [8].
 The name is programmatic. Raymond's cathedral figure contrasts slow, centralized
construction with bazaar-style accretion [31]; the corpus repurposes the metaphor to name
what verified structure is: load-bearing, assembled from inspected stones, and permanently
contrasted with the 'castle in the air' — assertive structure resting on nothing. The design
posture follows the sciences of the artificial [30]: governance is treated as a designed
artifact whose fitness is evaluated by adversarial experiment (Section 5.4), not asserted.
