 The philosophical foundation of the approach is Popperian fallibilism: a claim only has
empirical content if it can be refuted by an objective test [1]. Transposed to product
management, this means that every promise of the ecosystem must come with a falsifier —
a measurable condition whose failure demands public retraction or correction. This
discipline protects the company against its own confirmation bias while simultaneously
creating a commercial asset that is hard to copy: verifiable transparency in a research
market where inflated claims are the norm.
 The purpose of this document is threefold. First, to ground each improvement in
reliable external sources, so that investment decisions do not rest on internal opinion.
Second, to make each proposal's falsifier explicit, with numeric targets and cost, so that the
executive committee can approve a portfolio — not a wish list. Third, to organize the
nineteen improvements into a prioritization matrix and a three-phase roadmap, with exit
gates based on verified falsifiers. The target audience includes the executive board, product
and engineering leaders, and the legal and data-protection functions.
2. Method and Source Criteria
 The evidence base was built through document research in September 2026, with
explicit prioritization of five classes of sources, in decreasing order of authority: (i)
international quality standards, such as ISO 20252:2019, which establishes service
requirements for organizations conducting market, opinion and social research [2]; (ii)
sectoral and due-diligence standards, such as the ESOMAR questionnaire for buyers of
online samples [3]; (iii) Brazilian legislation and official data, such as the LGPD and the


=== PAGINA 317 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 317
open-data catalogs of the Receita Federal, the IBGE and the Central Bank; (iv)
peer-reviewed literature in psychometrics and machine learning; and (v) official platform
documentation — Meta/WhatsApp, LinkedIn, Tableau, Looker and Power BI — cited in
the exact format in which it was published.
 Two principles of epistemic honesty govern the use of these sources. First, internal
numbers — estimated costs, targets, the count of 19 million respondents and the current
8/19 falsifiers — are claims of the company's own VFG analysis, not external facts;
external sources serve to validate methodological feasibility and calibrate targets, never to
confirm unmeasured numbers. Second, when external evidence is partial or belongs to
another domain, the limitation is declared in the body of the text — as in the application of
the RCAEval benchmark, created for root-cause analysis in microservices, which here
serves as a methodological reference, not as direct evidence [1].
 Each improvement is presented in four components: the problem identified by the VFG
analysis; the grounding in external sources; the concrete implementation, summarized at
the level of an executive decision; and the falsifier, with the objective failure condition and
the estimated cost in reais. The costs are internal engineering estimates at the
order-of-magnitude level — not vendor quotations — and therefore Section 10
recommends a risk buffer of 20% to 30% on the consolidated budget. Prioritization uses the
impact × effort product, with impact assessed by credibility gain and potential revenue, and
effort assessed by technical complexity and development time.
 The method has limitations that should be read ahead of the results. This is a
documentary synthesis, not a controlled primary study; the proposed targets depend on
self-measurement, which only becomes evidence once the protocols are pre-registered and
published; and the Brazilian competitive and regulatory landscape may change within the
18-month horizon, requiring semiannual revision of this document. None of these
limitations weakens the central thesis — they reinforce the need for falsifiers: if the targets
fail, the very mechanism proposed here will reveal it publicly and auditably.
3. Tap Panel — Improvements in the Respondent
Layer
 The panel is the foundation of the ecosystem: if the sample is not verifiable, nothing
built on top of it withstands scrutiny. The four improvements in this layer attack,
respectively, the unaudited count, the absence of a quality metric, the impossibility of
matching against client databases, and the potential inflation of job titles in the B2B
segment. The common logic is to convert internal claims into third-party-auditable
evidence, following the ruler the research market itself uses for self-regulation.


=== PAGINA 318 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 318
1.1 Public panel audit
 The claim of 19 million respondents is in the Measured status: there is internal
measurement, but no third party has validated the number, and the market standard
demands more than that. ISO 20252:2019 — the international standard specific to market,
opinion and social research — establishes quality-management, documentation and
process-transparency requirements precisely so that buyers can trust research providers [2].
In the same direction, ESOMAR maintains the due-diligence questionnaire for buyers of
online samples — today in a 28-question version, successor to the classic “26 Questions”
— which asks panel providers, among other points, how members are recruited, verified
and deduplicated [3]. Publishing the answers to these questions, with counts by region, age,
gender and social class, is the equivalent of opening the panel's accounting books.
 The institutional precedent exists in Brazil: audience and media metrics only gained
commercial value once they came to be measured and audited by dedicated organizations
— and the Brazilian operation of this industry, historically known as Kantar IBOPE Media,
began in 2026 to present itself as IBOPE, a company of the Fifty5Blue group, reaffirming
the role of independent auditing of numbers [5]. Integrating the Tap Panel into independent
audit — via sectoral bodies such as ABEP [4] or specialized firms — and publishing a
public dashboard with updated quarterly data at paineltap.com.br/auditoria is the shortest
route to turning the number into an asset rather than a reputational liability.
Implementation. Quarterly report with counts by region, age, gender and social class; integration
with independent audit (ABEP [4], media firms such as IBOPE/Fifty5Blue [5]); public dashboard
at paineltap.com.br/auditoria.
Falsifier. TAP-01 — audited count < 90% of the declared figure.
Cost. Low — ~R$ 50 thousand/year.
1.2 Per-respondent quality score
 The low friction rate is a Reduced claim: it sounds good in a pitch, but says nothing
about the quality of what enters the database. The psychometric literature offers a mature
ruler for this: Meade and Craig (2012), in Psychological Methods, systematized the
detection of careless responses in surveys through indicators such as inter-item consistency,
the length and informativeness of open-ended answers and attention patterns, with an
explicit statistical cutoff [6]. This is the direct embryo of a per-respondent score. The
proposal materializes the concept as a composite index from 0 to 100 with transparent
weights: 40% completion rate, 30% open-ended answer quality, 20% consistency on
control questions and 10% recency.


=== PAGINA 319 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 319
 Two methodological safeguards are needed so that the score does not become a black
box. First, the weights must be calibrated empirically and the correlation between score and
actual answer quality must be published — falsifier TAP-04 sets the floor at 0.5. Second,
the score must be monitored against systematic bias: penalizing legitimate short answers or
lower-education profiles would degrade the representativeness of the sample, contrary to
ISO 20252 itself [2]. With the safeguards in place, the score becomes a commercial
argument in sample selection and a statistical weighting input for the client.
Implementation. Score 0–100 per respondent (completion 40%, open-ended answers 30%,
consistency 20%, recency 10%), visible to the client at sample selection; an ML pipeline
recomputes the score every cycle.
Falsifier. TAP-04 — correlation between score and answer quality < 0.5.
Cost. Medium — ML pipeline, ~3 months of development.
1.3 Client-CRM integration API
 B2B clients cannot match panel responses against their internal databases, which limits
adoption in larger accounts. The correct technical design for this matching without
exposing personal data is hash-based matching — a pattern consolidated by the platform
industry itself: Meta requires that identifiers such as e-mail and phone be hashed with
SHA-256 before any custom-audience matching [8]. The proposed endpoint — POST
/panel/respondents/match — receives SHA-256 hashes of e-mail/phone and returns only
anonymized attributes, with SDKs in Python, Node.js and Java.
 Legal precision is essential here: under the LGPD, anonymization only removes the
personal character of data when the data subject can no longer be identified by reasonable
means (art. 12) [7]. A SHA-256 hash of an e-mail is, strictly speaking, pseudonymization
— the data remains protected by the law, because the e-mail is reversible through
dictionary attacks. Therefore the API requires the respondent's explicit opt-in, a declared
purpose, the right to be forgotten (art. 18 and following) and a review of the company's
DPIA. With those controls, the falsifier is operational: a matching rate below 30% on a test
base disqualifies the feature.
Implementation. REST endpoint POST /panel/respondents/match with SHA-256 hashing (the
Meta pattern [8]); explicit opt-in and right to be forgotten per LGPD art. 12 and 18 [7]; Python,
Node.js and Java SDKs.
Falsifier. Matching rate < 30% on a controlled test base.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 200 thousand of development.


=== PAGINA 320 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 320
1.4 B2B panel with job-title verification
 Self-declared C-level job titles may be inflated — and the enterprise client knows it.
Verification can be split into two tracks of distinct risk. The documentary track is national
and robust: the Receita Federal publishes open CNPJ data for download [10] and exposes
the official Consulta CNPJ API in the government API catalog [9], allowing validation of
the company's existence and, with the state trade registries, the corporate ownership links
of partners and directors. The professional track is verification via LinkedIn, which in
practice requires joining the Sales Navigator API partner program — a program with
known restrictive rules, such as the prohibition on charging third parties for access and the
ban on reusing data outside the contracted integration [11].
 The recommended design is a two-layer badge: “verified role (CNPJ)”, based on
official sources and respondent consent, and “verified profile (LinkedIn)”, subject to the
partnership and the platform's restrictions. Falsifier TAP-05 — the share of verified C-level
contacts below 60% of the declared figure — is deliberately aggressive: it forces
verification to produce a published number, not merely an internal process. The
dependency risk of the LinkedIn track is treated in Section 10; the CNPJ track is sovereign
and should be prioritized.
Implementation. Verification via the RFB's Consulta CNPJ API [9] and open CNPJ data [10] for
partners/directors; verification via LinkedIn Sales Navigator API with consent [11]; “verified” vs.
“self-declared” badges.
Falsifier. TAP-05 — % of verified C-level < 60% of the declared figure.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 150 thousand.
4. Tap Analysis — Improvements in the Analysis
Layer
 The analysis layer concentrates the ecosystem's riskiest claims: the AI capabilities are
Unproven, and the agility promise is Reduced. The correction requires the same ritual
computational science imposed on itself in recent decades — public benchmarks,
comparative baselines, explainability and reproducibility — applied to the market-research
context. The five improvements that follow turn the platform from a convincing black box
into a system whose performance any client can check.
2.1 Public AI benchmarks
 Smart Discovery, sentiment analysis and root cause have no public performance
evidence. For sentiment, the classic reference is SemEval-2017 Task 4 (Sentiment Analysis


=== PAGINA 321 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 321
in Twitter), whose organizers documented that the best systems for English — BB twtr and
DataStories — achieved a macro recall of 0.681 on subtask A [12]; the internal target of F1
≥ 0.75 is therefore demanding and plausibly verifiable, but not trivial, and must be treated
as a heavy commitment. For Smart Discovery, OpenML offers curated, comparable
benchmark suites, with public baselines such as random forests over hundreds of datasets
[13][14], allowing the platform's accuracy to be situated against a community standard
instead of a homemade baseline.
 For root cause, the emerging reference is RCAEval — an open-source benchmark
presented at ASE’24, with datasets RE1–RE3 and a standardized evaluation environment
for RCA in microservices [15]. Honesty requires declaring the limitation: RCAEval
measures failure diagnosis in distributed systems, not root cause of customer satisfaction;
the transfer is methodological (evaluation protocol, holdout, precision metrics), not direct.
The recommended plan is to publish a GitHub repository with code, seeds and results on
the three benchmarks, updated per release — falsifier TAP-10/11 sets the floor at F1 ≥
0.70 and precision ≥ 0.70.
Implementation. Technical paper + GitHub repository with reproduction: sentiment
(SemEval-2017 Task 4 [12]); Smart Discovery (OpenML suites vs. a Random Forest baseline
[13][14]); root cause (protocol inspired by RCAEval [15], with a domain caveat).
Falsifier. TAP-10/11 — F1 < 0.70 or precision < 0.70.
Cost. Low — ~1 month of research.
2.2 Published time baseline
 The “70% more agility” claim is Reduced: the direction is credible, but there is no
baseline. The correction is a controlled comparative study with a pre-registered protocol:
one group of analysts executes the same task portfolio with manual tools (SPSS/R/Python)
and another with Tap Analysis, measuring two primary variables — time to first insight
and time to final report — on the same dataset with standardized tasks. Publishing the
methodology, sample size and raw results, aligned with the transparency ISO 20252
requires for client relations [2], turns the number into Measured.
 The 20-analyst design is sufficient for an order-of-magnitude study, not for
fine-grained inference — and this must be stated in the publication, because underreporting
limitations is the kind of practice the VFG discipline exists to eliminate. Falsifier TAP-07
defines the failure ruler: a gain below 50% invalidates the commercial claim of 70%. If the
measured gain falls between 50% and 70%, the claim must be rewritten to the actual
number — which, paradoxically, strengthens the brand, because it becomes an auditable
number.


=== PAGINA 322 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 322
Implementation. Controlled study: Group A (manual analysis in SPSS/R/Python) vs. Group B
(Tap Analysis); metrics of time to first insight and to final report; pre-registered, published protocol
with methodology and N.
Falsifier. TAP-07 — gain < 50% (does not reach 70% × 0.71).
Cost. Low — ~R$ 30 thousand with 20 analysts.
2.3 The AI “explainability” mode
 Users do not trust opaque AI — and the hesitation is rational. The interpretability
research agenda formalized by Doshi-Velez and Kim (2017) proposes evaluating
explanations at three levels: functional, in the application; human, with real users; and
social, with broad audit [16]. The proposed explainability mode translates this into the
product: every AI insight comes with its source (which variable, question and subgroup),
confidence (score 0–100%), statistical method (χ², t-test, Pearson) and rival hypotheses not
ruled out, accessible through the “Why?” button.
 The critical concern is calibration: displaying poorly calibrated confidence can reduce
user trust instead of increasing it — an effect documented in the interpretability literature
when explanations display uncertainty that does not correspond to actual performance [16].
The falsifier is therefore a user-trust survey with a 60% floor, measured after real usage —
not an internal technical criterion. The estimated cost (~R$ 300 thousand) reflects the
cross-cutting integration into every insight module of the platform.
Implementation. Insights with source, confidence, statistical method and non-ruled-out
alternatives; a “Why?” button with a detailed explanation; confidence calibration by holdout
validation.
Falsifier. User trust rate (post-usage survey) < 60%.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 300 thousand.
2.4 Integration with external data
 Analysis in isolation loses market context — and Brazil offers high-quality public
sources to contextualize any survey. On the demographic and social side, the IBGE exposes
the API de Agregados (the engine behind SIDRA), with all survey and census series in
programmatic form [17]. On the economic side, the Banco Central (Central Bank of Brazil)
provides the Sistema Gerenciador de Séries Temporais (SGS) through the public endpoint
api.bcb.gov.br/dados/serie/bcdata.sgs.{codigo}/dados?formato=json, covering thousands
of financial series [18]. On the search-interest side, Google Trends is accessible via
PyTrends — an unofficial API maintained by General Mills, with the instability risk that


=== PAGINA 323 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 323
this condition implies [19].
 For social sentiment, the 2026 reality demands sobriety: social-media APIs such as X
now operate in paid tiers with significant costs and restrictive terms, and Reddit charges for
enterprise-level access — the design must therefore provide for formal licensing or
alternative sources, and never assume stable free access. Automatically crossing these
sources with the client's survey — normalized by period, geography and category —
creates immediate comparative context and justifies the falsifier: a perceived-value gain
below 20% in an A/B test disqualifies the integration.
Implementation. Native connectors: IBGE/SIDRA [17], Banco Central SGS [18], Google Trends
via PyTrends [19], social sentiment under formal licensing; automatic crossing with the client's
survey.
Falsifier. Perceived-value gain < 20% in an A/B test.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 250 thousand.
2.5 Export to R, Python and Stata
 Advanced clients want to continue the analysis outside the platform — and trying to
keep them inside it is a short-term strategy. The implementation exports native formats
(.RData for R, .dta for Stata, .sav for SPSS) and goes further: it automatically generates
R/Python code that reproduces the analyses performed on the platform, plus a pre-filled
Jupyter notebook. This is the same open-science spirit that guides OpenML — experiments
documented in enough detail to be reproduced by third parties [13] — applied to the
analyst's workflow.
 The commercial value is twofold. First, it reduces the technical objection in purchasing
processes run by analytics teams, which today discard closed platforms. Second, it creates
indirect evidence of quality: if the generated code faithfully reproduces the platform's
analyses, the client audits the product at no cost to the company. Falsifier TAP-06 is binary
and zero-tolerance — a percentage of failed formats above 0% — reflecting the
infrastructure role export plays.
Implementation. Export to .RData, .dta and .sav; automatic generation of R/Python code that
reproduces the analyses; pre-filled Jupyter notebook (reproducibility in the OpenML spirit [13]).
Falsifier. TAP-06 — % of failed formats > 0%.
Cost. Low — ~R$ 80 thousand.


=== PAGINA 324 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 324
5. VisionCX — Improvements in the
Customer-Experience Layer
 VisionCX measures well — NPS and CSAT with consolidated instruments — but it
does not yet close the loop with operational discipline and does not anticipate
abandonment. The five improvements in this layer give the product what the Net Promoter
System has always required to work: fast response to detractors, correction of causes with
learning from error, churn anticipation and interoperability with the enterprise client's BI
ecosystem.
3.1 Closed Loop with SLA and escalation
 The current Closed Loop has no defined SLA — which makes the feature a log, not a
process. NPS was conceived as a management system, not as a showcase metric:
Reichheld's original article in the Harvard Business Review (2003) already emphasized that
the value lies in the action following the score [20], and the operational architecture of the
Net Promoter System formalizes the “inner loop” — the individual contact with the
respondent who signaled dissatisfaction [21]. Market practice has converged on fast
detractor contact windows, typically 24 to 48 hours, associated with a measurable retention
effect [22]. The proposal materializes this as an SLA per segment: detractors (NPS 0–6)
answered within 24h, passives (7–8) within 72h and promoters (9–10) through an
informational flow.
 An SLA without consequence is decorative; the proposal therefore includes automatic
escalation at three milestones — manager notification at 50% of the SLA consumed,
escalation to the director at 100% and an alert on the executive dashboard at 150% — a
consolidated service-governance practice on service-management platforms [23]. Falsifier
CX-03 combines two conditions: resolution rate ≥ 70% and SLA attainment ≥ 80%. The
cost is low (~R$ 100 thousand) because the ticketing infrastructure already exists; what is
missing is a commitment regime and escalation — exactly the kind of change that alters
organizational behavior without a product rewrite.
Implementation. SLA per segment (detractor ≤ 24h; passive ≤ 72h; promoter informational);
automatic escalation at 50%, 100% and 150% of the SLA; executive dashboard of breaches.
Falsifier. CX-03 — resolution rate < 70% or SLA attainment < 80%.
Cost. Low — ~R$ 100 thousand.
3.2 Root-cause analysis with human feedback
 The root cause pointed out by the AI is Reduced: it appears in the product, but no one
validates whether it is right. The most economical correction is not a new model — it is


=== PAGINA 325 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 325
learning from human corrections. The active-learning literature, systematized by Settles
(2009), shows that a model reaches higher accuracy with fewer labels when the human
supervises the right examples [24]. The proposed design: after the AI classifies the root
cause, the manager confirms it, corrects it with a new label or adds an unforeseen cause; the
corrections feed the model in retraining cycles, and the label scheme is versioned so that F1
remains comparable over time.
 Evaluation follows the root-cause benchmark protocol — holdout, precision metrics
and comparison against a baseline — with the domain caveat already discussed in Section
2.1 [15]. Publishing the F1 after six months of real usage is part of the deliverable: a
number that only exists after real clients have corrected the AI carries more credibility than
any synthetic demonstration. Falsifier CX-04 sets the floor: precision after the correction
cycle below 70% invalidates the learning-from-feedback claim.
Implementation. Manager flow for confirming/correcting/adding causes; active learning with
retraining in cycles [24]; versioned label scheme; F1 published after 6 months.
Falsifier. CX-04 — precision after correction < 70%.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 200 thousand.
3.3 Predictive churn detection
 VisionCX reacts to the detractor but does not anticipate abandonment — and
anticipation is where the retention budget lives. The technical feasibility is well
documented: in telecommunications churn — the reference domain of the literature —
gradient-boosting models such as XGBoost report AUC on the order of 0.869 on public
benchmarks [25], and comparative reviews cite AUC above 0.85 on industry datasets. The
proposed design uses what VisionCX already has: NPS/CSAT response history, ticket
frequency, time since last interaction and sentiment of open-ended answers, producing a
0–100 churn score per client with an alert above 70.
 The falsifier — AUC-ROC ≥ 0.75 on holdout — is deliberately more conservative
than the 0.85+ of the telecom literature, because the signal here is behavioral-subjective
and the labeled base of real churn tends to be short in the first cycles. This slack is honest,
not loose: it acknowledges that the model will be retrained quarterly as the abandonment
label matures. The cost is the highest in the layer (~R$ 500 thousand, six months) and the
main operational risk is class imbalance, treated in Section 10.
Implementation. Predictive model with NPS/CSAT history, ticket frequency, interaction recency
and open-ended sentiment; 0–100 score per client; automatic alert > 70.
Falsifier. AUC-ROC < 0.75 on holdout.


=== PAGINA 326 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 326
Cost. High — ~R$ 500 thousand, 6 months.
3.4 WhatsApp with Meta-approved templates
 Delivery via WhatsApp depends on approved templates — an external, non-negotiable
condition of the platform. Meta's official documentation is explicit: template messages
generally require approval before sending, with automatic review at creation and
APPROVED status as a precondition for dispatch [26]; the ecosystem organizes templates
into categories (utility, marketing, authentication) and, since April 2025, recategorizes
utility templates as marketing without 24 hours' prior notice in misuse cases [27]. The
proposal turns this reality into an asset: a library of 20+ pre-approved templates covering
survey invitation, reminder, thank-you and loop closure, with a visual editor that validates
in real time and submits automatically to Meta.
 Falsifier CX-02 — an approval rate below 80% on first submission — measures the
operational quality of the template pipeline, and the target is justified because repeated
rejections degrade account quality standing with the platform. The structural risk is
dependence on external policy: Meta rule changes affect the business without notice, which
reinforces the need for alternative channels (SMS, e-mail) in the campaign design — not as
an improvised plan B.
Implementation. Library of 20+ pre-approved templates (invitation, reminder, thank-you, loop
closure); visual editor with real-time validation; automatic submission to Meta following the
official review flow [26][27].
Falsifier. CX-02 — approval rate < 80% on first submission.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 150 thousand.
3.5 Export to enterprise BI
 Enterprise clients do not accept data locked in a silo — they expect to consume
VisionCX within the BI stack they already govern. The three targets have official
integration paths: Tableau exposes the Connector SDK for building native connectors with
SQL dialects and their own connection dialogs [28]; Looker offers the Looker–Tableau BI
Connector, which exposes Explores as a data source in Tableau Desktop, Cloud and Server
[29]; and Power BI consumes custom connectors built with the Power Query SDK [30].
The proposed design delivers a native connector for all three, a documented GraphQL API
and normalized data (responses, tickets, NPS/CSAT metrics) with a versioned dictionary.
 The falsifier — adoption below 20% of Professional-plan clients within 12 months —
is a demand test, not an engineering test: if quality connectors do not generate adoption, the


=== PAGINA 327 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 327
feature's priority was wrong. This is the function of falsifiers in product: to protect the
roadmap against the team's own conviction. The estimated cost (~R$ 250 thousand) covers
the three connectors and the documentation.
Implementation. Native connector for Power BI, Tableau and Looker (via the Connector SDK
[28], the Looker–Tableau BI Connector [29] and the Power Query SDK [30]); documented
GraphQL API; normalized data with a versioned dictionary.
Falsifier. Adoption rate < 20% of Professional-plan clients.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 250 thousand.
6. Cross-Cutting Layer — Ecosystem Integration
 The fourth layer is where the ecosystem stops being three products under the same
brand and becomes one product with three surfaces. The five improvements attack identity
friction (three accounts), data friction (manual flow), content friction (surveys reinvented),
competence friction (underused potential) and trust friction (no public evidence). It is also
the layer with the highest risk of effort underestimation — and therefore concentrates two
of the three P2 items.
4.1 Unified Single Sign-On (SSO)
 Requiring three accounts from a single client is inflicting the cost of internal
architecture on whoever pays the bill. The standard market solution is to federate identity
with the two protocols that dominate the segment: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) for delegated
authorization in API and modern-web scenarios [31], and SAML 2.0 — the OASIS
standard for federated web single sign-on — where the enterprise sector demands it, since
corporate identity providers speak SAML natively [32]. The implementation covers single
login with access to the three products, unified role and permission mapping, and account
provisioning at first access.
 The falsifier is adoption: fewer than 40% of clients with accounts in more than one
product migrating to the unified SSO within two quarters invalidates the priority. It is
worth recording the positive side effect — SSO reduces the credential attack surface and
simplifies access compliance, an argument that typically anticipates approvals in the
clients' own security committees.
Implementation. SSO via OAuth 2.0 [31] and SAML 2.0 [32]; single login for Tap Panel, Tap
Analysis and VisionCX; unified roles and permissions.
Falsifier. Adoption < 40% of multi-product clients.


=== PAGINA 328 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 328
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 200 thousand.
4.2 Unified data pipeline
 Today data moves manually between the three products — the weakest link of any
ecosystem promise. The proposal replaces the manual movement with an automated ETL
pipeline with three legs: Tap Panel → Tap Analysis (raw responses), Tap Analysis →
VisionCX (actionable insights) and VisionCX → Tap Panel (client feedback for
recruitment and segmentation), orchestrated by events and webhooks with a versioned data
contract. This is internal engineering with no external benchmark — and for that very
reason the falsifier is technical and public: end-to-end latency above 5 minutes in 95% of
cases invalidates the integration claim.
 The cost is high (~R$ 500 thousand) because the Tap Analysis → VisionCX leg
requires reconciling data semantics that evolved separately — the hard part is not moving
bytes, it is versioning meaning. The execution recommendation is to defer this
improvement to Phase 3 (as the roadmap indeed does), after SSO and explainability have
stabilized the interface contracts the pipeline will carry.
Implementation. Automated ETL with three legs (Panel → Analysis → VisionCX → Panel),
webhooks and events, versioned data contract, end-to-end observability.
Falsifier. End-to-end latency > 5 min in 95% of cases.
Cost. High — ~R$ 500 thousand.
4.3 Template marketplace
 Clients reinvent surveys from scratch — wasting knowledge the company has already
accumulated. The proposed marketplace organizes 100+ ready-made templates by industry
(retail: NPS, CSAT, Mystery Shopper; SaaS: Product-Market Fit, Churn Survey;
healthcare: Patient Satisfaction), validated by specialists, with two-tier monetization: free
on the Essential plan and premium on the Professional plan. The mechanism replicates in
content what the AI layer replicates in analysis: turning the company's tacit assets into
packaged products.
 The falsifier — usage below 20% of active clients — protects against the common fate
of content libraries: becoming a dead archive. A usage target, not a publication target, is the
detail that matters; a marketplace measured by the number of templates published would be
the very negation of the VFG discipline. The estimated cost is ~R$ 300 thousand including
specialist curation and platform.


=== PAGINA 329 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 329
Implementation. Library of 100+ templates by industry, validated by specialists; free (Essential)
and premium (Professional) tiers; per-template usage telemetry.
Falsifier. Usage rate < 20% of active clients.
Cost. Medium — ~R$ 300 thousand.
4.4 Analyst certification program
 Clients underuse the platforms because competence in using them is unevenly
distributed — and certification is the industry's standard mechanism for solving this. The
research market already works this way: the Insights Association maintains a code of
standards and professional certification programs [33], and the British Market Research
Society combines formal qualifications with the promotion of the ISO 20252 standard
among its members [34]. The proposal defines three levels — Essential Tap Analyst (basic
research and analysis), Advanced Tap Analyst (ANOVA, cluster, driver analysis) and
VisionCX Specialist (CX, closed loop, predictive churn) — with an online exam plus a
practical project and a public directory of certificates.
 The expected commercial effect is threefold: it accelerates adoption, creates a
community of practice that advocates the platform and generates a hiring channel (clients
seek certified analysts; certified analysts push the product). The falsifier measures program
health along two vectors — program NPS ≥ 50 and completion rate ≥ 40% — because a
program with high NPS and low completion is a showcase, and a program with high
completion and low NPS is bureaucracy. The cost is low (~R$ 100 thousand) for the
potential reach.
Implementation. Certification in 3 levels (Essential, Advanced, VisionCX Specialist); online exam
+ practical project; public directory of certificates, in the pattern of sectoral programs [33][34].
Falsifier. Program NPS < 50 or completion rate < 40%.
Cost. Low — ~R$ 100 thousand.
4.5 The VFG Transparency Program
 None of the three products publishes falsifiers or benchmarks — and this gap is the
natural destination of this entire undertaking. The proposed program creates the public page
paineltap.com.br/pacir with the 19 falsifiers (TAP-01 through CX-05), the current status of
each (OK / FALSIFIED / PENDING), links to independent audits and a changelog of
changes, updated quarterly. The choice is deliberately aligned with the due-diligence
practices ESOMAR recommends between research buyers and providers [3] and with the
experimental-transparency principle that platforms such as OpenML institutionalized in


=== PAGINA 330 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 330
machine learning [13].
 It is the highest return-on-cost improvement in the entire portfolio: ~R$ 30
thousand/year to convert the VFG philosophy into visible evidence. The reputational risk
— publishing that a falsifier failed — is the value mechanism itself: commercial credibility
is born from the demonstration that the company exposes itself to refutation. The program's
falsifier is symmetric to what it measures: a transparency NPS below 60% in a client
survey invalidates the claim that transparency is perceived, not merely published.
Implementation. Public page paineltap.com.br/pacir with 19 falsifiers, status
(OK/FALSIFIED/PENDING), links to independent audits and a changelog; quarterly updates.
Falsifier. Transparency NPS (survey) < 60%.
Cost. Low — ~R$ 30 thousand/year.
7. Prioritization Matrix
 The prioritization crosses two variables — impact on client and business, and
technical-organizational effort — and produces three execution classes. The P0 class (six
items, all low effort) concentrates the credibility measures: they are cheap, fast and remove
the most frequent objections in purchasing processes. The P1 class (eight items, medium
effort) builds defensible differentials that competitors cannot replicate without investing in
equivalent data and processes. The P2 class (two items, high effort) attacks enterprise scale
and should only start after the interface contracts of the previous classes are stable. Table 2

8. Three-Phase Execution Roadmap
 The sequencing follows a simple rule: first credibility, then differentiation, finally
scale. Each phase ends with an exit gate based on falsifiers — the next phase only opens if
the previous gate is verified. This design protects cash against the classic roadmap mistake,
which is investing in scale on top of a credibility foundation that does not yet exist.

 Phase 1 has the explicit objective of establishing scientific and operational credibility
— it is the cheapest and the most transformative phase, because it unlocks the commercial
conversations that today stall for lack of public evidence. Phase 2 builds defensible
competitive advantages: each item creates a proprietary asset (calibrated score, base of
human corrections, certificates, API partnerships) that a competitor does not copy with
rhetoric, only with equivalent investment. Phase 3 scales to enterprise clients, when the
credibility foundation and the differentials already sustain the higher prices and longer
sales cycles of that segment.

10. Risks, Limitations and Counterarguments


=== PAGINA 333 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 333
 A program whose principle is public refutation must begin by refuting itself. This
section gathers the main counterarguments to the program, with their respective mitigations
— none invalidates the central thesis, but all condition the execution.
 Goodhart risk in benchmarks. When a metric becomes a target, it stops measuring what
it used to measure: models can be tuned to the benchmark dataset (SemEval, OpenML)
rather than to the clients' real task [12][13]. Mitigation: publish results on multiple datasets
and maintain an internal holdout labeled by clients, evaluated quarterly; always state which
official metric each benchmark uses — in SemEval-2017, for example, the official metric
of subtask A was macro recall, not F1 [12].
 Partial benchmark transfer. RCAEval was designed for root cause in microservices, not
in satisfaction surveys; using it as direct proof would be imprecise [15]. This document
treats it as a methodological reference (protocol, holdout, metrics), and the platform's paper
must state the domain difference explicitly. The legitimate counterpoint — “if the
benchmark is not from your domain, publish your own” — is accepted: Phase 1 provides
for exactly that, with a proprietary dataset and a public protocol.
 Platform dependencies. Three improvements depend on third parties with unilateral
change power: LinkedIn verification requires a partnership with restrictive usage and
billing rules [11]; WhatsApp templates are subject to Meta's review and recategorization
policy, with recent precedents of changes without prior notice [27]; and Google Trends is
only accessible via an unofficial API [19]. Mitigation: the sovereign CNPJ track as the
basis of B2B verification [9][10], alternative channels (SMS/e-mail) in campaign design
and formal monitoring of platform changelogs.
 Legal risk in hash-based matching. SHA-256 pseudonymization does not strip personal
data of legal protection under the LGPD; CRM matching requires opt-in, a specific purpose
and data-subject rights in full force [7]. Mitigation: DPIA review, an operator contract with
the client and a matching test on a synthetic base before real traffic. The cost risk is
symmetric: internal estimates tend to underestimate effort — the recommended buffer of
20% to 30% on the consolidated budget and the reconciliation note of Section 7 exist to
make that underestimation visible before it becomes an overrun.
 Adoption and reputation risk. Marketplace, certification and transparency fail if no one
uses, completes or trusts — which is why their falsifiers measure adoption and perception,
not publication volume. The reputational risk of the transparency program, in turn, is real
and desired: publishing a FALSIFIED falsifier costs image in the short term and builds an
asset in the long term. The mitigation is to formalize the retraction policy: every correction
published with changelog and deadline. Finally, the underlying methodological limitation:
this is a documentary study without a controlled primary study; the targets proposed here
only become evidence when the Phase 1 and Phase 2 protocols are executed and published


=== PAGINA 334 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 334
— which, again, is the expected functioning of the VFG discipline.
11. Conclusion and Recommendations
 The nineteen improvements grounded here follow a single logic: to move the
ecosystem's epistemic status from Measured to Proven in panel quality, from Reduced to
Measured in analysis performance and from Unproven to Reduced in AI capabilities —
always with public evidence and a verifiable falsifier. The portfolio is executable with ~R$
3.5 million over 18 months, with the first credibility turnaround available in 90 days for
less than R$ 340 thousand.
 The immediate recommendation is threefold. First: approve the six P0 improvements
of Phase 1 within the current quarter — the transparency program, the time baseline, AI
benchmarks, the panel audit, the Closed Loop with SLA and statistical export — and install
the measurement of the six indicators of Table 4 before any other investment. Second:
reconcile the declared budget with the recalculated sum (Section 7) and set the risk buffer
at 20%. Third: institute the quarterly review of falsifiers as a standing agenda item of the
executive committee, with the right of formal retraction — because a falsifier that cannot
fail publicly is just marketing with a scientific name.
 The final thesis is the one that opened this document, now with external support: in a
market where panels claim millions of respondents, platforms claim agility and AIs claim
understanding, sustainable competitive advantage belongs to those who show the number
— audited by third parties, compared against public benchmarks and exposed to refutation
itself. The VFG discipline does not say “yes” or “no”. It says “show the number” — and,
from this report on, the Tap ecosystem will be able to show its own.

PART XIV — ADVANCED R&D; DOSSIER:
THE PHANTOM TWIST PROGRAM
This part formalizes the advanced R&D program of the Phantom Twist — a 30 g
micro-UAV whose fuselage counter-rotates at up to 25 revolutions per second, exploiting
motion blur to cut visual perceptibility by roughly an order of magnitude versus a
conventional quadcopter. The contribution is methodological: the verification-first
governance (VFG) discipline converts seven R&D directions into numbered conjectures
(PT-01 to PT-07), each carrying measurable sub-goals — acoustic noise below 40 dB(A) at
1 m, visual invisibility quantified by LPIPS ≤ 0.02, and comparable thresholds across
materials, swarm, control, and energy — with formulas and executable Rust falsifiers,
verified with the Kani model checker and property-based tests. Cross-validation with 2026
data reclassified PT-06 from UNPROVEN to FALSIFIED — measured maximum power
(0.086 W at 12,000 RPM) falls below the initial 0.5 W target — and raised the viability of
PT-01 and PT-05. The consolidated status is 1 MEASURED, 2 REDUCED, 3 UNPROVEN,
and 1 FALSIFIED conjecture, over which an 18-month roadmap ordered by probability of
refutation is proposed.
1. Introduction
 At the Robotics: Science and Systems 2026 conference, in Sydney, engineers from
Northwestern University presented a drone that disappears from view: the Phantom Twist
is a 30 g micro-UAV with a single motor and a single propeller in which the
motor-propeller assembly spins in one direction while the entire fuselage counter-rotates in
the opposite direction, at up to 25 revolutions per second [1]. At that speed, the human
visual system cannot fix stable references, and the aircraft dissolves into a semitransparent
haze against the sky [2]. The effect exploited is the same motion blur that renders the
blades of a fast-spinning fan invisible — except that in the Phantom Twist it is the entire
body of the vehicle that spins, not merely the propeller [3]. A two-stage computational
pipeline evaluated roughly 20,000 configurations capable of stable flight and selected the
one with the lowest visibility under the LPIPS perceptual metric: the final prototype
registered 0.0104, approximately ten times less perceptible than a quadcopter of equivalent
size [4].
 The success of the prototype, however, creates a research-management problem that
this part confronts head-on. With the initial demonstration completed, a broad space of
future directions opens up — silencing the propeller, making the structure transparent,
coordinating swarms, stabilizing flight under wind, harvesting energy on board — and each
of these directions would compete for resources on the basis of equally plausible narratives.


=== PAGINA 338 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 338
The verification-first governance (VFG) framework proposes that this competition be
decided not by rhetoric but by programmed refutation: in the spirit of Popper's
falsificationism [5], every R&D direction must be expressed as a quantitative conjecture
accompanied by an executable falsifier — a program that, fed with measurement data,
returns true when the conjecture has been refuted. The maxim that guides the method is
direct: the VFG discipline does not say "yes" or "no" — it says "show the number" [6].
 This part extracts and organizes the research contribution embedded in the technical
dossier of the Phantom Twist Program [6], converting seven advanced R&D directions for
the Phantom Twist into formalized conjectures (PT-01 to PT-07), each with three artifacts:
(i) a quantitative statement with explicit thresholds; (ii) formulas that specify the quantities
involved — from the blade passing frequency to the Kuramoto order parameter; and (iii)
pure Rust functions that implement the refutation, verified with the Kani model checker
and exercised by property-based tests. In addition, the complete epistemic cycle is
demonstrated in a concrete case: the conjecture PT-06 (piezoelectric harvesting) started as
UNPROVEN with a 0.5 W target and was refuted by measurement — 0.086 W maximum
at 12,000 RPM — illustrating, in miniature, the mechanism that the framework seeks to
institutionalize.
 The contributions are four. C1: a set of seven falsifiable conjectures that covers the
advanced R&D space of the Phantom Twist, with explicit epistemic classes (MEASURED,
REDUCED, UNPROVEN, FALSIFIED) and an auditable count (Sections 3 and 4). C2: the
mathematical formalization of the critical quantities — LPIPS, blade passing frequency,
sound pressure level, Kuramoto synchronization, Euler dynamics, and the power budget —
with the corresponding design thresholds (Section 3.2). C3: the engineering architecture of
the executable falsifiers — a multi-crate Rust workspace, Kani harnesses, property-based
tests, and continuous integration — including the pattern of the falsifier conditioned on an
operational envelope (Section 3.3). C4: a critical analysis of the limitations of the approach,
from the reach of the LPIPS metric to the model-reality gap in formal verification (Section
5), followed by an 18-month roadmap ordered by probability of refutation (Section 6).
 The remainder of the part is organized as follows. Section 2 contextualizes the
Phantom Twist, the LPIPS metric, and the VFG discipline, and reviews related work on
swarm synchronization, propeller acoustics, predictive control, and energy harvesting.
Section 3 presents the complete methodology — conjectures, formulas, and code. Section 4
reports the measured numbers and the epistemic life cycle of the conjectures. Section 5
discusses counterarguments and limitations. Section 6 unfolds the roadmap and the
implications, and Section 7 concludes.
2. Context and Related Work


=== PAGINA 339 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 339
2.1 The Phantom Twist and the LPIPS metric
 The Phantom Twist belongs to a barely explored class of single-propeller UAVs in
which the aerodynamic reaction of the propeller is deliberately harnessed: instead of
compensating the torque with counter-rotating rotors or control surfaces, the design lets the
fuselage spin. The automated design pipeline described in [1] operates in two stages — it
first samples physically viable configurations (batteries, control board, motor-propeller
assembly, and counterweights), then optimizes the placement of these components to
minimize visibility under the constraint of stable flight. The objective function is LPIPS
(Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity), a metric proposed by Zhang et al. [7] that
compares deep representations of two images and proved remarkably aligned with human
perceptual judgment — hence the designation "human-aligned perceptual metric" used by
the authors. The relevant comparison is made between a background frame (the sky, for
instance) and the same frame with the UAV present: the lower the LPIPS, the less the
vehicle stands out from the background.
 The reported numbers are precise and auditable: the pipeline evaluated 20,000
candidate configurations, the optimized prototype reached an LPIPS of 0.0104, and the
comparative analysis indicates visibility about ten times lower than that of a quadcopter of
the same size; an equivalent layout arranged manually registered roughly twice the
visibility of the optimized one [4]. The physical demonstration included the fabrication and
flight of multiple prototypes, confirming that the optimized design remains stable and
controllable [1]. The team itself notes the limitations: the propeller produces audible noise,
and the wires and support booms remain partially visible — with declared plans for future
iterations in more transparent materials or quieter propulsion [2]. It is precisely on these
and other gaps that the present part operates.
 The scope of the invisibility in question must be delimited. Independent
countermeasure analyses observe that the Phantom Twist does not reduce the radar
cross-section or the infrared emission: the target of the technique is exclusively the visual
detection layer — the human eye, optical sensors, and many tracking cameras [8]. This
delimitation is not a defect of the method but a characteristic of the problem treated; it does,
however, condition any generalization regarding safety and regulation, a theme revisited in
Section 5.1.
2.2 The VFG discipline: from demand to falsifier
 The VFG discipline is an epistemic governance protocol for engineering that
transforms demands into refutable artifacts. The conceptual pipeline has five stages:
proposal (the statement of the R&D direction in natural language), analysis (identification
of the physical quantities and constraints involved), conjecture (a quantitative statement
with an explicit threshold), invariant (a condition that must remain true over the entire


=== PAGINA 340 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 340
declared domain of operation) and refutation (an executable falsifier that operates over
measurements) [6]. The philosophical inspiration is Popperian: the scientific value of a
statement resides in its exposure to refutation, not in its rhetorical confirmability [5]. The
practical difference from philosophical falsificationism is that here the falsifier is a
versioned software artifact — subject to tests, code review, and continuous integration —
and not an informal argument.
 Each conjecture receives an epistemic status class with fixed semantics. MEASURED
designates quantities actually measured on the prototype, with documented
instrumentation. REDUCED indicates that the conjecture has been reduced to a model or
to a particular case already demonstrated — for example, stability demonstrated on a subset
of the wind envelope. UNPROVEN marks plausible conjectures still without
demonstration; it is the natural initial state of an R&D direction. FALSIFIED registers
conjectures refuted by measurement — and it remains in the ledger as acquired knowledge,
not as a failure to be erased. The final count of the set is always declared and auditable; in
the case of the Phantom Twist Program after cross-validation, 1 MEASURED, 2
REDUCED, 3 UNPROVEN, and 1 FALSIFIED [6]. This explicit accounting contrasts
with common practice in R&D proposals, in which promises and results coexist without a
shared status vocabulary.
Guiding principle of the VFG discipline: it does not say "yes" or "no" — it says "show the number".
Every conjecture carries a threshold; every threshold carries a falsifier; every falsifier is a program
that runs in CI.
2.3 Related work
 Swarm synchronization. The Kuramoto model — a mean-field population of coupled
phase oscillators — is the canonical paradigm for spontaneous synchronization transitions,
with rigorous mathematical treatment established in the statistical physics literature [9].
Recent applications in robotics demonstrate that coupled oscillators can coordinate drone
swarms in a decentralized and fault-tolerant way, without reliance on dense communication
[10]. What does not exist, as far as our review reaches, is a demonstration of Kuramoto
synchronization with counter-rotating UAVs of the Phantom Twist type — a gap that
conjecture PT-04 makes explicit and that Figure 2 quantifies in simulation. Propeller
acoustics. The reduction of tonal noise through synchrophasing — phase control between
propellers — is established for distributed propulsion, with recent studies of adaptive
extremum-seeking control reporting substantial reductions in the BPF (blade passing
frequency) tone [11] and systematic analyses of tonal noise reductions in propeller sets
[12]. Bioinspired structures produced by 3D printing, emulating the flexible trailing edge of
owl feathers, reduce the noise of UAV propellers by up to 5 dB without thrust loss [13].


=== PAGINA 341 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 341
Conjecture PT-02 inherits this evidence as context, but demands demonstration on the
specific object.
 Acoustic measurement. The dB(A) thresholds adopted here refer to the A-weighting
standardized by IEC 61672-1 for sound level meters [14] — with a low-frequency
particularity discussed in Section 4.3. Acoustic and optical materials. Triply periodic
minimal surface (TPMS) structures fabricated by additive manufacturing exhibit broadband
sound absorption configurable through porosity gradients [15], motivating their
consideration as a porous material for the Phantom Twist enclosure (PT-01). Control.
Model predictive control (MPC) with wind preview has already demonstrated effective
rejection of atmospheric disturbances in multirotors [16], and the MPC formulation with
moving horizon estimation (MHE) provides the standard theoretical scaffolding for
conjecture PT-05 [17]. Energy harvesting. Systematic reviews of piezoelectric harvesting
in multirotor structures document powers in the milliwatt range and address the integration
challenges of flight-ready systems [18] — direct context for the refutation of PT-06.
Formal verification in Rust. The Kani Rust Verifier is a bit-precise model checker for
Rust programs, suited to proving properties over pure functions [19], and proptest extends
unit testing with property-driven random generation and automatic shrinking of
counterexamples [20]. The combination of the two instruments the third layer of the VFG
pipeline — the verifiable refutation.
3. Methodology: Conjectures, Formulas, and
Falsifiers
3.1 The conjecture set PT-01 to PT-07
 Table 1 presents the complete conjecture set of the Phantom Twist Program, with the
initial epistemic class and the associated executable falsifier. The set covers five
subsystems of the vehicle — acoustics (PT-01, PT-02), materials (PT-03), collective
behavior (PT-04), control (PT-05), energy (PT-06) — and one meta-epistemic item: the
validation of the visibility metric itself as a predictor of human detection (PT-07). This
self-application is deliberate: if LPIPS fails to correlate with detection by human observers
(r > 0.85), the entire design optimization loses its empirical anchor, and the conjecture that
guarantees this correlation must be as falsifiable as the others.

 Three design decisions deserve justification. First: PT-01 is a conjunctive conjecture —
it requires simultaneously low noise and low visibility, preventing the trivial solution of
"silencing" the vehicle at the cost of compromising the visual concealment function (for
instance, with opaque acoustic shrouds). Second: PT-02 fixes the gain at 6 dB because it
lies above what the bioinspired literature reports in isolation (up to 5 dB [13]) and below
what synchrophasing among distributed propellers promises (~10 dB [11, 12]) — the value
forces an engineering advance without being unattainable. Third: PT-05 is conditioned on
an envelope — the falsifier only operates for winds up to 5 m/s, and measurements outside
the envelope do not refute the conjecture; this scope clause prevents spurious refutations
from conditions outside the contract of operation (Section 3.3).
3.2 Mathematical formalization
 Perceptual visibility. The objective function of the design pipeline is LPIPS, which
compares the background frame Ibg with the frame containing the drone Idrone through
differences in the deep layers of a pre-trained convolutional network (VGG or AlexNet),
weighted by learned weights [7]:
 LPIPS(Ibg, Idrone) = Σl wl · ‖φl(Ibg) − φl(Idrone)‖22
 (1)
 where φl denotes the activations of layer l and wl the weights calibrated against human
judgments. The optimized prototype reaches 0.0104, against a design threshold of 0.02 and
a quadcopter baseline of 0.104 (visibility ratio ≈ 0.1; Figure 1). Conjecture PT-07 requires
that this quantity correlate with human detection at r > 0.85 — the falsifier receives the
coefficient measured under a protocol with observers and returns refutation below the
threshold.
 Propeller acoustics. The dominant tonal noise of a propeller occurs at the blade
passing frequency:
 fBPF = (Nb · Ω) / 60 [Hz]
 (2)
 with Nb blades and Ω in RPM. For the current configuration (Nb = 2, Ω = 1,500 RPM),
fBPF = 50 Hz — inside the audible band, which explains the reported hum [2]. The sound


=== PAGINA 343 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 343
pressure level scales according to the simplified model:
 SPL ∝ 10 · log10(Ω3 · D4 / σ) + C
 (3)
 where D is the propeller diameter and σ the solidity. The cubic term in Ω implies that
rotation is the most influential factor on noise — a structural tension with the concealment
mechanism, which requires high rotation. It is this tension that makes PT-01 and PT-02 the
conjectures of highest technical risk and, precisely for that reason, of highest informational
value if confirmed.
 Swarm synchronization. For N coupled units, conjecture PT-04 adopts the Kuramoto
model [9], in which each vehicle i carries a phase θi and a natural frequency ωi:
 dθi/dt = ωi + (K/N) · Σj=1..N sin(θj − θi)
 (4)
 r = |(1/N) · Σj=1..N eiθj|
 (5)
 The order parameter r ∈ [0, 1] measures collective coherence: r → 1 indicates aligned
phases; r ≈ 0, complete dispersion. The synchronization transition depends on the coupling
K relative to the dispersion of the natural frequencies; Figure 2 (Section 4.2) shows the
simulated evolution of r(t) for N = 10 and different K, with the design threshold r ≥ 0.95
marked. The conjecture combines dynamic coherence (r ≥ 0.95) and the visual objective
(swarm LPIPS ≤ 0.03), preventing synchronization from being achieved through
formations that make the ensemble more visible.
 Attitude dynamics. The counter-rotating fuselage is a rigid body in continuous
rotation, whose behavior follows the Euler equations [21]; for the principal axis x:
 Ix·ω̇x = (Iy − Iz)·ωy·ωz + τx
 (6)
 and cyclic permutations in y and z, with I the principal inertias and τ the applied
torques. The asymmetry of inertia — a consequence of the optimized placement of batteries
and counterweights — is the main control challenge, and actuation takes place through
periodic rotational torque:
 τ(t) = τ0 · square(2π·fctrl·t + φ)
 (7)
 Conjecture PT-05 requires that an MPC controller with allocation of this torque keep
the lateral deviation below 0.5 m under 5 m/s crosswind. The power budget that constrains
the entire system closes with the cruise electrical power, a function of the thrust T, the
induced velocity vinduced, and the efficiencies of motor and propeller:
 Pelectric = (T · vinduced) / (ηmotor · ηprop)
 (8)
 This equation delimits the energy surplus available to conjecture PT-06: any
piezoelectric harvesting competes directly with endurance, because the harvested vibration


=== PAGINA 344 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 344
is not free — it is energy that the motor injects into the structure.
3.3 Engineering the executable falsifiers
 Each falsifier is a pure Rust function, deterministic and total over its declared domain,
that receives measurements and returns a refutation boolean. Purity is a design requirement,
not an aesthetic one: pure functions are amenable to exhaustive verification by model
checking and to composition in proof harnesses. The Rust workspace of the program
organizes the falsifiers by subsystem (Listing 1), with a crate dedicated to Kani harnesses
and a unified CLI; the thresholds of the conjectures live in configuration files
(conjectures.json), separated from the refutation logic — which allows targets to be
recalibrated without changing the semantics of the refutation.
Listing 1 — Acoustic and visibility falsifiers (pt-acoustics).
// pt-acoustics/src/falsifiers.rs — refutation of conjectures PT-01 and PT-02
pub const LPIPS_THRESHOLD: f64 = 0.02; // ~10x less visible than the baseline
/// Visibility falsifier (PT-03/PT-07): LPIPS exceeds the threshold.
pub fn falsify_lpips(lpips: f64) -> bool {
lpips > LPIPS_THRESHOLD
}
/// PT-01 (conjunctive): noise < 40 dB(A) at 1 m with LPIPS <= 0.02.
pub fn falsify_pt_01(spl_db: f64, lpips: f64) -> bool {
spl_db > 40.0 || lpips > 0.02
}
/// PT-02: 3-blade swept propeller reduces >= 6 dB without increasing LPIPS.
pub fn falsify_pt_02(reducao_db: f64, lpips_antes: f64, lpips_depois: f64) -> bool {
if reducao_db < 6.0 {
return true; // insufficient acoustic gain -> refuted
}
lpips_depois > lpips_antes * 1.05 // LPIPS may not grow by more than 5%
}
 Listing 1 illustrates the two central patterns of refutation engineering. The first is the
conjunction of thresholds in PT-01: the conjecture is refuted if either of the two conditions
is violated, encoding the requirement that acoustic gain and visual gain coexist. The second
is the relative tolerance in PT-02: the post-change LPIPS may grow by up to 5% — a
statistical dead band that prevents refutation by irrelevant measurement noise, without
opening room for visible regressions. The swarm falsifier (Listing 2) shows the third
pattern: composition of metrics of distinct natures — dynamic (r) and perceptual (LPIPS)
— into a single refutable contract.
Listing 2 — Order parameter, Kuramoto step, and swarm falsifier (pt-swarm).


=== PAGINA 345 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 345
// pt-swarm/src/kuramoto.rs — swarm coherence (PT-04)
/// Order parameter r = |1/N * sum of e^{i theta_j}|.
pub fn order_parameter(phases: &[f64]) -> Result<f64, String> {
if phases.is_empty() { return Err("Lista de fases vazia".into()); }
let sum_cos: f64 = phases.iter().map(|t| t.cos()).sum();
let sum_sin: f64 = phases.iter().map(|t| t.sin()).sum();
let n = phases.len() as f64;
Ok(((sum_cos / n).powi(2) + (sum_sin / n).powi(2)).sqrt())
}
/// Discrete step of the Kuramoto model.
pub fn kuramoto_step(
phases: &mut [f64], omegas: &[f64], coupling: f64, dt: f64,
) -> Result<(), String> {
let n = phases.len();
if omegas.len() != n { return Err("Tamanhos inconsistentes".into()); }
let mut new_phases = vec![0.0; n];
for i in 0..n {
let mut sum = 0.0;
for j in 0..n { sum += (phases[j] - phases[i]).sin(); }
new_phases[i] = phases[i] + (omegas[i] + (coupling / n as f64) * sum) * dt;
}
phases.copy_from_slice(&new_phases);
Ok(())
}
/// PT-04 (conjunctive): coherence >= 0.95 AND swarm LPIPS <= 0.03.
pub fn falsify_pt_04(r: f64, lpips_enxame: f64) -> bool {
r < 0.95 || lpips_enxame > 0.03
}
 The formal verification layer complements the property-based tests. proptest exercises
the falsifiers with random inputs and shrinks counterexamples automatically [20]; Kani
proves properties over all the values allowed in the assumed domain, by bit-precise model
checking [19]. Listing 3 presents two representative harnesses: the proof that the order
parameter always lies in [0, 1] — a mathematical property of Equation (5) — and the proof
of the monotonicity of the LPIPS falsifier, which guarantees that no value accepted by the
threshold can coexist with the refutation of a smaller value. These proofs do not verify that
the drone is silent or invisible; they verify that the refutation machine is internally
consistent — a necessary condition for future refutations to be attributable to the world and
not to bugs.
Listing 3 — Kani harnesses for falsifier properties (pt-kani).


=== PAGINA 346 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 346
// pt-kani/src/lib.rs — formal verification harnesses
#[cfg(kani)]
mod harnesses {
use pt_swarm::kuramoto::order_parameter;
use pt_visibility::falsify_lpips;
/// Proof: the order parameter is always in [0, 1] (Eq. 5).
#[kani::proof]
fn proof_order_parameter_bounded() {
let p1: f64 = kani::any();
let p2: f64 = kani::any();
kani::assume(p1.is_finite() && p2.is_finite());
let r = order_parameter(&[p1, p2]).unwrap();
assert!(r >= 0.0 && r <= 1.0);
}
/// Proof: the LPIPS falsifier is monotonic at the threshold.
#[kani::proof]
fn proof_lpips_monotonic() {
let lpips1: f64 = kani::any();
let lpips2: f64 = kani::any();
kani::assume(lpips1 > 0.0 && lpips1 < 1.0);
kani::assume(lpips2 > lpips1 && lpips2 < 1.0);
if !falsify_lpips(lpips2) { assert!(!falsify_lpips(lpips1)); }
}
}

 Two design details merit record. The falsifier of PT-05 is envelope-conditioned: for
winds above 5 m/s it returns true (refuted) by construction — an explicit encoding that
measurements outside the envelope are not evidence against the conjecture, but against its
application out of scope. And the vector algebra of the pt-control crate uses nalgebra [22],
keeping the Euler dynamics calculations (Equation 6) in sized types and without implicit
allocations, which simplifies the model checker's reasoning over the execution paths. The
script count_falsifiers.sh closes the audit loop: the count of falsifiers in the repository must
match the count of declared conjectures — if PT-06 is in the table, falsify_pt_06 must exist
with CI green.

4. Empirical Results and Epistemic Status
4.1 Measured prototype numbers
 Table 2 consolidates the quantities actually measured on the Phantom Twist, with their
VFG class. This is the empirical substrate over which the conjectures operate: nominal
rotation of 25 revolutions per second (1,500 RPM, with an operational envelope of 15–25
rev/s), mass of 30 g, LPIPS of 0.0104, and a visibility reduction of approximately one order
of magnitude relative to the reference quadcopter [1, 2, 4]. Two negative results are also
measured and integrate the ledger: the acoustic noise exceeds 40 dB(A) at 1 m — which, in
the VFG reading, constitutes a refutation of the current state of the system with respect to
the PT-01 target — and the wires and support booms remain partially visible, anchoring
PT-03 [2]. Figure 1 situates the LPIPS score of the prototype between the baseline and the
design threshold: the margin from 0.0104 to 0.02 is the budget space that PT-01 and PT-02
cannot consume while improving the acoustics.

 It is instructive to note what Table 2 does not contain: a synchronized swarm,
piezoelectric harvesting, and extended endurance — all R&D directions that remain
without physical demonstration on the object. The differentiation between what has been
measured and what is conjectured is precisely the service that VFG accounting provides;
without it, R&D announcements tend to fuse the two categories.
4.2 The 2026 cross-validation and the epistemic life cycle
 A cross-validation campaign, conducted over the 2026 literature and public data,
updated the status of the seven conjectures [6]. The most significant result is the refutation
of PT-06: the maximum power reported for piezoelectric harvesting in relevant rotational
regimes is 0.086 W at 12,000 RPM — almost six times below the initial 0.5 W target. The
supporting literature corroborates this order of magnitude: systematic reviews of
piezoelectric harvesting in multirotors describe powers in the milliwatt range and point to
structural integration as the dominant bottleneck [18]. Consequently, PT-06 was
reclassified as FALSIFIED in its original formulation, and a successor conjecture —
PT-06′, with a revised target of ≥ 0.1 W — takes over as the open direction, still
UNPROVEN. Refutation does not end the research line; it repositions it with an honest
number.
 The same exercise raised the estimated viability of PT-01 and PT-05. In acoustics,
synchrophasing among distributed propellers reports relevant tonal reductions at the BPF
— with adaptive extremum-seeking control demonstrated on a test bench [11] and
systematic analyses of phased propulsors [12] — while bioinspired structures already
deliver up to 5 dB on the directly comparable object [13]; the dossier also records a


=== PAGINA 349 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 349
reference of 3.69 dB for the bioinspired propeller [6]. In control, results with MPC and
moving horizon estimation report lateral deviations of 0.05 m under 1 m/s wind and 0.31 m
under crosswind, against 0.85 m and −1.13 m for an equivalent PID — evidence that the
0.5 m threshold of PT-05 is demanding, yet plausible within the 5 m/s envelope [6, 16, 17].

 The simulated dynamics of conjecture PT-04 illustrate how conjectural thresholds are
calibrated before physical demonstration. Figure 2 shows the evolution of the order
parameter r(t) for a swarm of N = 10 Kuramoto oscillators with natural frequencies uniform
in [−1, 1] and integration at Δt = 0.01 s, averaged over 40 trials: with K = 2.0 the swarm
crosses the coherence threshold r ≥ 0.95 within a few seconds; with K = 1.0 the coherence
saturates around 0.6 — below the design threshold; with K = 4.0 the synchronization is
practically immediate. The simulation does not demonstrate the conjecture — it
demonstrates that the threshold is attainable in model and defines the minimum coupling
that the communication layer of the physical swarm will have to sustain.
