4.3 The A-weighting trap at low frequency
 The threshold of PT-01 is expressed in dB(A) — and this choice has a numerical
consequence that the design must assume explicitly. A-weighting, standardized for sound
level meters by IEC 61672-1 [14], approximates the sensitivity of the human ear; at low
frequencies it attenuates strongly: at 50 Hz the correction is −30.3 dB, and at 75 Hz (the
BPF of a 3-blade propeller at the same rotation), −23.4 dB (Figure 3). In other words, a
pure 70 dB sound-pressure tone at 50 Hz reads only ~40 dB(A) on a standard sound level
meter. The 40 dB(A) threshold of PT-01 is therefore more permissive in raw sound
pressure than the intuition of "40 decibels" suggests — and precisely for that reason it is a
defensible choice: it aligns the conjecture with the metric by which human disturbance is
actually measured, without demanding absolute physical silence. The counterpart is
methodological: the measurement protocol must report simultaneously dB(A) and the
spectrum in one-third-octave bands, so that refutation does not depend on a single number
sensitive to microphone placement and to the harmonic content of the signal.


=== PAGINA 351 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 351
 Figure 3 — A-weighting curve per IEC 61672-1 [14], with the Phantom Twist BPF marked: 50 Hz for the
current 2-blade propeller at 1,500 RPM (−30.3 dB) and 75 Hz for the 3-blade propeller of PT-02 (−23.4 dB).
 The shaded band indicates the operating region of the vehicle's BPF.
 This point generalizes a principle of conjecture design: every threshold incorporates a
theory of what counts as failure. Expressing PT-01 in dB(A) encodes the theory that what
matters are the perceptual effects on humans, not raw acoustic energy; expressing it in
dB(Z) or in peak pressure would encode a different theory — for instance, one relevant to
acoustic detection sensors, which do not have the auditory attenuation. The VFG discipline
does not resolve this choice, but forces its explicit statement: the conjecture is the place
where the decision is recorded and made refutable.
5. Counterarguments and Limitations
5.1 Scope and validity of the LPIPS metric
 The first structural counterargument targets the metric that grounds the entire
framework. LPIPS is a full-reference metric: it compares the frame with the drone against
the background frame under controlled capture conditions — and real detection occurs
under variable backgrounds, adverse illumination, video compression, camera motion, and
observers with distinct visual priorities. Conjecture PT-07 (correlation with human
detection, r > 0.85) is, for that reason, the most important conjecture of the set — and also
the most vulnerable: its MEASURED status derives from the general alignment of LPIPS
with human perceptual judgment documented in the literature [7], not from a specific
protocol of detection of counter-rotating targets with naive observers. If such a protocol
were to produce a lower correlation, the entire design optimization loses its anchor — the
measured numbers are not invalidated, but their meaning changes. Moreover, as


=== PAGINA 352 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 352
countermeasure analyses observe, the concealment is restricted to the visual layer: radar
and infrared remain unchanged [8], and any use in a regulated context must take this limit
into account, not only the optical performance.
5.2 Simplifications of the physical models
 The formulas of Section 3.2 are deliberately minimalist, and each simplification opens
a model-reality gap. The SPL model of Equation (3) captures the scaling with rotation,
diameter, and solidity, but omits mechanisms relevant in the Phantom Twist regime:
blade-wake aerodynamic interaction, trailing-edge thickness, blade-tip effects, and the
amplitude modulation induced by the rotation of the fuselage itself — which can produce
periodic Doppler shifts and sidebands around the BPF. The Kuramoto model assumes
homogeneous mean-field coupling; physical swarms have communication topologies,
latencies, and asymmetric failures, and the synchronization transition under local coupling
may differ substantially from the field mean [9, 10]. The lateral deviation model under
wind treats the vehicle as a point mass with aggregate drag, ignoring the gyroscopic
dynamics of the counter-rotating fuselage — precisely the phenomenon that makes the
control of this vehicle non-trivial (Equations 6 and 7). None of these simplifications
invalidates the conjectures — the falsifiers operate over measurements, not over the models
— but they restrict the explanatory and predictive power of the intermediate artifacts, and
must be treated as working hypotheses, not as descriptions of the system.
5.3 Limits of formal verification
 The Kani proofs of Listing 3 verify properties of the falsifiers — not of the drone.
Three limits deserve explicit statement. First, the proofs operate over IEEE 754
floating-point values [23] with assumed domains (for instance, finite phases);
floating-point arithmetic in model checking is subject to precision and scalability
limitations, and properties involving long sums may require bounded unrolling — Kani is a
model checker with depth limits, and the coverage is that of the declared bound, not that of
the infinite [19]. Second, the proved properties are local and conservative — interval
bounding (r ∈ [0, 1]) and monotonicity of thresholds; no proof establishes that the swarm
reaches r ≥ 0.95, only that the coherence-measuring machine does not lie about individual
values. Third, there is the classic gap between the verified code and the physical system:
the falsifiers consume measurements whose instrumentation chain (microphones, cameras,
protocols) is not verified. The framework treats this gap by supervision: the count of
falsifiers in CI guarantees the presence and sanity of the refutation functions, but the
validity of the inputs remains the responsibility of the measurement protocol.
5.4 Methodological limitations of the study


=== PAGINA 353 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 353
 Finally, four methodological limitations of the study itself. First: part of the reference
numbers (the 3.69 dB of the bioinspired propeller, the 0.05–0.31 m of MPC, the 0.086 W of
harvesting, the RF-piezoelectric hybrid at 1–3.4 V) comes from the program's internal
dossier [6] and not from independently auditable publications — we mark these values as
such in all tables, and replication by third parties remains open. Second: the epistemic
count (1/2/3/1) is sensitive to the cut — if PT-06′ (revised target of 0.1 W) is counted in
place of PT-06, the count changes to 1 MEASURED, 2 REDUCED, 4 UNPROVEN; the
discipline requires declaring which cut is used, and this part reports both. Third: the single
authorship and the absence, to date, of independent replication of the falsifiers reduce the
strength of the REDUCED and MEASURED classifications — the framework is designed
precisely to invite such replication, because the artifacts (conjectures in JSON, falsifiers in
Rust, Kani harnesses) are self-contained and executable. Fourth: the roadmap of Section 6
reflects technical priorities, not a funding commitment; the ordering by probability of
refutation is a heuristic of informational value, not a guarantee of outcome.
6. The 18-Month Roadmap and Implications
 The roadmap operationalizes the conjectures into six sequential phases with falsifiable
deliverables (Table 4). The ordering follows the reading of Table 3: the phases F1
(acoustics) and F2 (control) come first because they have the highest probabilities of
success in light of the available evidence — synchrophasing and the bioinspired propeller
for the former [11, 12, 13], MPC with MHE already demonstrated at compatible deviations
for the latter [6, 17]. Phase F3 (materials) depends on the supply of substrates with
transmittance > 95%; phase F4 (swarm) is the longest and concentrates the integration risk
— ten counter-rotating units flying with communication sufficient for a K that sustains r ≥
0.95 (Figure 2); phase F5 closes the cycle by testing the revised 0.1 W target of PT-06′ with
RF-piezoelectric hybrid harvesting [6]. Each phase delivers, besides the physical artifact,
the execution of the corresponding falsifier over measurement data — the phase exit
criterion is a number, not an opinion.

 The target value of F3 deserves a derivation note: 0.0073 LPIPS corresponds to a 30%
reduction over the measured 0.0104 — the exact content of conjecture PT-03. This
traceability of numbers (a target derived publicly from the conjecture, without ad hoc
adjustments) is the property that the framework wants to preserve under schedule pressure.
Beyond the Phantom Twist, the case suggests a broader implication for the management of
R&D in robotics: when every research direction is registered as a conjecture with an
executable falsifier in CI, the portfolio gains three observable properties — the count of
epistemic statuses is auditable by third parties; refutation ceases to be narrative and
becomes software execution; and the reallocation of resources can anchor on estimated
probabilities of refutation, rather than on the eloquence of the proponents. The cost is the
rigor that Section 5 describes: poorly cut conjectures or poorly chosen metrics produce
empty refutations — the framework is not a substitute for engineering judgment; it is an
instrument for making it contestable.
7. Conclusion
 This part extracted from the dossier of the Phantom Twist Program a complete research
contribution: the conversion of the advanced R&D program of the Phantom Twist UAV
into seven falsifiable conjectures (PT-01 to PT-07), accompanied by explicit formulas —
LPIPS, blade passing frequency, sound pressure level, Kuramoto dynamics, the Euler
equations, and the power budget — and by executable falsifiers in Rust, verified with Kani
and exercised with proptest. The consolidated epistemic status after the 2026
cross-validation is auditable: 1 MEASURED conjecture (PT-07), 2 REDUCED (PT-03,
PT-05), 3 UNPROVEN (PT-01, PT-02, PT-04), and 1 FALSIFIED (PT-06, refuted by the
measurement of 0.086 W against the 0.5 W target, with successor PT-06′ recalibrated to 0.1
W). The numbers that remain from the prototype are 25 revolutions per second, 30 grams,
an LPIPS of 0.0104, and roughly ten times less visual perceptibility than an equivalent
quadcopter.
 Two conclusions exceed the case studied. First, the "conjecture–formula–falsifier"
architecture proved sufficient to cover heterogeneous subsystems — acoustics, materials,
swarm, control, and energy — under a single epistemic contract, with the count of statuses
as the public interface of the portfolio; the falsification of PT-06 at design time, before any
manufacturing investment, is the demonstration of the expected value of this contract.
Second, the mapped limitations — the full-reference scope of LPIPS, the simplifications of
the physical models, the limits of model checking over floating point, and the dependence
on an internal dossier for part of the evidence — delineate the immediate work agenda: a


=== PAGINA 355 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 355
human validation protocol for PT-07, independent replication of the falsifiers, and spectral
measurements in one-third-octave bands for PT-01. Immediate future work prioritizes
phases F1 and F2 of the roadmap, whose supporting evidence suggests the highest
probabilities of moving the portfolio count — and, with it, the number that the VFG
discipline will always demand to see: show the number.

PART XV — VERIFIABLE MODEL
ARTIFACTS: FAIL-CLOSED GGUF
VERIFICATION
Open-weight machine-learning artifacts circulate through distribution chains characterized
by opaque provenance, executable metadata, and trust delegated to promises. A four-gate,
fail-closed verification pipeline for open-weight GGUF model artifacts: metadata
sanitization, digest and signature verification, witness quorum, and transparency-log
inclusion — specify, don't simulate.
1. Introduction
 On February 21, 2025, the exchange Bybit lost approximately US$1.5 billion to North
Korean actors whom the FBI attributes to TraderTraitor [28], [29] — the largest
cryptocurrency theft recorded to date. The detail that matters here is not the magnitude but
the mechanism: the cryptography worked flawlessly, and what was compromised was the
signing interface, which led operators to approve transactions whose real semantics
differed from what they believed they were approving. The distance between what one
believes one is signing and what one actually verifies is the same epistemic void that
currently crosses the machine-learning model supply chain, in which billions of bytes of
weights change hands daily with no requirement of cryptographic evidence attached to the
artifact itself.
 In the open-model ecosystem, that void has already produced concrete incidents. JFrog
documented models hosted on Hugging Face that silently execute arbitrary code during
deserialization via crafted pickle payloads [5]; a subsequent scan concentrated roughly one
hundred malicious models on the platform [6], [7]. In February 2025, the nullifAI
campaign used malformed pickle files to bypass automated scanners [8], and the scanning
tool itself was later shown to be bypassable (CVE-2025-1716) [9]. The technical root is
documented in the Python standard library itself: pickle data can execute arbitrary code
during deserialization and must never be unpickled from untrusted sources [3]. The
safetensors format [4] eliminated the code-execution attack class — but a safe format is not
provenance: intact bytes do not answer who produced the model, when, with what identity,
under which capability declarations, and with what distribution history.
 Meanwhile the parser layer — the code that reads model containers — accumulated its
own vulnerability record. Between 2024 and 2026, llama.cpp and Ollama, the two most
widely deployed local inference runtimes, disclosed heap overflows, integer overflows, and
uncontrolled memory allocations in GGUF metadata parsing (CVE-2024-23496,


=== PAGINA 358 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 358
CVE-2024-23605, CVE-2024-37032, CVE-2024-39719 through CVE-2024-39721,
CVE-2025-53630, and CVE-2026-65315) [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. A model file is
thus not merely data: it is a parser input with a demonstrated history of memory-corruption
consequences, and its metadata block is an attack surface long before the first token is
generated.
 This article takes as its object of study the arkhe.gguf framework — the model-
verification component of the VTK trust layer [36] — across its two most recent source
documents: the consolidated delegation package (seal
ARKHE-GGUF-DELEGATION-CONSOLIDATED-2026-09-15) and the complete
project structure (seal ARKHE-GGUF-COMPLETE-STRUCTURE-2026-09-15), both
dated September 15, 2026. The package is an engineering document with an explicit
methodological thesis, summarized in its golden rule: when evidence does not exist, it is
not simulated; what cannot be generated is specified. Hashes that have not been computed
appear as placeholders; capabilities that have not been verified are declared as an empty
list; weights, base models, trust roots, and signatures that require external execution
resources are enumerated as non-generable items rather than fabricated.
 Our contribution is fourfold. First, we dissect the framework's two-layer construction: a
delegation methodology that separates the generable from the executable and the declarable
(Section 3), and an attestation schema that reached version 1.3 with five blocks and an
expanded rule set (Section 4). Second, we formalize the fail-closed four-gate verification
pipeline now implemented as a Rust workspace — sanitization, hash, signature, and
transparency-log verification with witness quorum — together with the negative tests that
make rejection behavior an executable specification (Section 5). Third, we trace the
thirteen-step provenance pipeline and its hash-ordering discipline, including an erratum we
identified between the specified and the actual rekor-cli interface (Section 6). Fourth, we
position the pipeline within its governance (Safenet/FROST), distribution (Hashtree/Nostr
with npub pinning), and execution (WebGPU/WASM local inference) layers, and we
confront the whole construction with its limitations (Sections 7–10). Throughout, the
distinctions that organize the argument are the ones the source package itself insists upon:
PROMISE is not VERIFIED, signed is not safe, and identity is not behavior.
2. Background and Threat Model
2.1 The GGUF format
 GGUF (GGML Universal File) is the container format used by llama.cpp, Ollama, and
the broade local-inference ecosystem to distribute quantized language models [1]. Its v3
header is deliberately compact: a four-byte magic (the ASCII bytes GGUF), a little- endian


=== PAGINA 359 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 359
uint32 version, a uint64 tensor count, and a uint64 metadata key-value count, followed by
the metadata block and tensor data [1], [2]. The metadata block is an ordered map whose
values are typed (uints, floats, booleans, strings, arrays); the format prescribes a default
alignment of 32 bytes unless the general.alignment key states otherwise [1]. Hugging Face
Hub treats GGUF as a first-class distribution format [2], which makes the header and its
metadata the first code path every local runtime executes when loading a model from
public infrastructure. This is precisely the surface that arkhe.gguf targets: the framework
treats the header as a verification object, injects its own attestation keys into the metadata
namespace, and insists that any consumer parse it only after sanitization.
 Figure 1. The byte-exact minimal GGUF v3 header fixture (fixtures/arkhe.gguf). The 24 bytes are deterministic;
 the SHA-256 digest shown was computed by local deterministic execution in this study, honoring the package
 rule that digests are calculated, never invented.
2.2 Deserialization and parser attacks, 2024–2026
 The empirical record justifies the framing of a model file as a hostile input. Table 1
consolidates the vulnerability record that Gate 0 of the pipeline is designed against. Two
classes dominate. The first is deserialization: pickle-based loading executes
attacker-controlled constructors [3], exploited in the wild by malicious Hugging Face
uploads [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. The second is memory safety in container parsers: Talos
disclosed two heap overflows in llama.cpp's GGUF reader in February 2024 [10], [11];
Wiz's Probllama research turned an Ollama path-handling flaw into remote code execution
[12]; Oligo disclosed a family of Ollama flaws including malformed- GGUF denial of
service [13]; and in 2025–2026 both ecosystems disclosed integer- overflow and
uncontrolled-allocation conditions reachable from GGUF metadata [14], [15]. The two
identifiers embedded in the arkhe.gguf schema — CVE-2026-65315 (Ollama, uncontrolled
memory allocation in the GGUF metadata parser) and CVE-2025-53630 (llama.cpp,
integer overflow in gguf_init_from_file_impl) — were independently confirmed against
public CVE databases during the preparation of this article, which matters because the
framework's own honesty rule makes every claim auditable.
Table 1. Verified vulnerability record motivating Gate 0 (metadata
sanitization).

2.3 The provenance gap and related infrastructure
 Format safety and parser hygiene address integrity of execution, not authenticity of
origin. The provenance gap has a mature institutional response in the software supply
chain, and arkhe.gguf deliberately reuses it rather than inventing new cryptography.
Sigstore provides keyless signing in which an OIDC identity (for CI, the GitHub Actions
issuer token.actions.githubusercontent.com) is bound into a short-lived Fulcio certificate,
with signature objects recorded in the Rekor transparency log [16], [19], [20], [40].
Certificate Transparency contributed the underlying append-only machinery: RFC 6962
defines Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs [17], later consolidated in RFC 9162 [18],
and the structure descends from Merkle's original signature scheme [25]. SLSA contributes
build-level provenance vocabulary [23], and in-toto contributes the Statement v1 envelope
whose subject digests enumerate exactly which files a signature covers [22]. On the model
side, the OpenSSF Model Signing tool (model-transparency; PyPI package model-signing)
wraps these primitives for ML artifacts [21], and the Model Cards literature supplies the
declaration vocabulary that the schema's capability fields operationalize [24]. Hash agility
is provided by dual SHA-256/BLAKE3 digests [26], [27]. What was missing, and what
arkhe.gguf specifies, is the binding of this machinery to the specific container format,
metadata namespace, and parser threat model of GGUF — plus the honesty discipline that
keeps declaration separate from verification.
2.4 The VTK context
 VTK is a verifiable trust layer for autonomous AI agents, of which arkhe.gguf is the
minimum viable product: model verification is the first concrete object to which the
architecture's invariants apply [36]. The surrounding architecture contributes three concepts
that recur in this article. WormGraph provides evidence records in a SHA-256/Ed25519


=== PAGINA 361 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 361
hash chain anchored to transparency infrastructure — the same shape as the provenance
chain in Section 6.4. ConstitutionStore provides governance thresholds under which
quorum policies (such as the witness quorum of Section 5.3 or the FROST attestation
quorum of Section 7) are configuration, not hard-coding. And the incident narratives
consolidated after the Bybit, StablR, and SUPERFORTURE losses motivate the
architectural insistence that enforcement must move from the warning path to the execution
path — the requirement that Section 7 implements on-chain [28], [31].
3. Methodology: Specify, Don't Simulate
3.1 The delegation-package pattern
 The arkhe.gguf documents practice a methodology that deserves explicit treatment
because it is unusual in AI engineering writing. A delegation package is neither a
specification frozen in intent nor a fabricated demonstration; it is a three-way ledger. The
generable is generated: twelve artifacts in the consolidated package, growing to more than
twenty-five in the complete project structure — fixture, schemas, scripts, Rust crates,
configuration, documentation, and negative tests. The executable is delegated: thirteen
steps that require real resources (model downloads, OIDC identities, log submissions) are
written as a checklist with acceptance criteria, expected exit codes, and prohibitions. The
non-generable is declared: training weights, the base model, a real trust root, a real Rekor
inclusion proof, a real Sigstore signature, and the resulting production arkhe.gguf itself are
listed in a what-was-not-generated table [36]. Every hash that could not be computed
appears as the literal placeholder .
 The pattern's value is epistemic. A reader can distinguish, at every point in the
document, between claims that are specifications (auditable against external references),
claims that are artifacts (auditable by re-execution), and claims that are future obligations
(auditable against the acceptance criteria). We note one internal inconsistency that the
methodology itself surfaces: the opening ledger of the consolidated package counts five
non-generable items while its closing README table counts six (the production
arkhe.gguf appears only in the latter) — exactly the kind of discrepancy that consistency
checks in Section 4.3 are designed to catch, and exactly the kind that a simulated package
would have hidden.
3.2 The byte-exact fixture and the computed digest
 The framework's minimal verifiable artifact is a 24-byte GGUF v3 header with zero
tensors and zero metadata pairs (Figure 1, Listing 1). Its bytes are fully determined by the
format specification: magic GGUF, version 3, and two zero counts in little- endian
encoding [1]. Because the bytes are deterministic, the fixture functions as a


=== PAGINA 362 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 362
cross-implementation test vector: the Python generator, the Rust parser tests, and any
third-party reimplementation must agree on both the bytes and their digests. In preparing
this article we executed the digest computation locally and obtained SHA-256
a4e5e156ddec27e286f75328784d7106b60a4eb1d246e950a001a3f944fbda99 over the hex
string 474755460300000000000000000000000000000000000000 — the same value
reported in the source package, which had itself computed it by execution rather than
asserting it. BLAKE3, by contrast, remained a placeholder in our environment because the
reference implementation was not installable offline; the package's discipline is that the
placeholder stays visibly unfilled, marking an obligation, rather than being invented [27].
Listing 1. Deterministic fixture generation (scripts/fixture.py, excerpt).
def generate_fixture() -> bytes:
return (
b"GGUF" # magic
+ struct.pack("<I", 3) # version 3 (little-endian)
+ struct.pack("<Q", 0) # tensor_count = 0
+ struct.pack("<Q", 0) # metadata_kv_count = 0
)
# invariant enforced at generation time:
assert len(fixture) == 24
3.3 Fail-closed as a design axiom
 Across all four gates, the package specifies a single failure semantics: fail-closed. Any
gate that cannot complete its verification rejects the artifact; there is no degraded mode, no
warning-only path, and no default-allow branch. The choice is deliberately conservative
and is justified by the incident record of Section 2: warning-path security is precisely the
failure mode that turned interface approval into a US$1.5 billion loss at Bybit [28], [31].
What makes the axiom more than rhetoric is Section 5.4: the package ships negative tests
whose success condition is that malformed inputs are rejected, so the fail-closed property is
itself executable and regressable, not merely asserted.
4. The Attestation Schema v1.3
4.1 Five blocks
 Schema version 1.3 organizes an attestation into five top-level blocks under the
arkhe.attestation.* namespace (Figure 2). The source block (new in v1.3) records the
SHA-256 and BLAKE3 digests and the size of the base artifact before metadata extension.
The verifiable block records signing time, the Ed25519 signature algorithm, the signing
identity (OIDC subject, identity provider, Fulcio issuer), the sanitization flag, the CVE list
checked, and the model-signing manifest summary. The anchored block carries the
transparency-log evidence: anchor type rekor, log identifier and index, UUID, tree size,


=== PAGINA 363 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 363
root hash, inclusion proof, and — new in v1.3 — a consistency proof and witness quorum
with cosignatures. The attested block carries the declaration: type PROMISE, an explicitly
empty declared-capabilities list, an explicit not-capabilities list (code-execution,
network-access, file-write, shell-execution), an SLSA level of 0 flagged as undefined, the
signer trust root, and the disclaimer that capabilities are signer claims, not verifications
[24], [36]. The revocation block points to a revocation document and names the revocation
strategies, which v1.3 extends from short_lived alone to short_lived plus safenet_enforced.
Figure 2. The arkhe.attestation.* schema v1.3: five blocks with the v1.2 to v1.3 delta highlighted. Red lines mark
 fields introduced or made mandatory in v1.3, including the source block, the external-manifest hash location,
 CVE attestation, consistency proofs, and the witness quorum.
4.2 What changed from v1.2 to v1.3
 The delta from v1.2 to v1.3 is not decorative; each addition closes a specific
verification gap (Table 2). Three changes deserve emphasis. First, the final-hash location
moves into an external manifest: because metadata injection changes the file that was
signed, v1.2 contained an inherent tension between in-file attestation keys and the hash of
the file that contains them; v1.3 resolves it by letting the signed in-toto manifest (which
covers the whole bundle, external to the file) be the final digest's home [22], [21]. Second,
sanitization becomes attested: the fields metadata_sanitized and cve_checked record that
Gate 0 ran against the identified parser vulnerabilities, converting a private engineering
step into a claim a third party can require and audit [14], [15]. Third, the anchored block
stops treating the log as a single trusted party: consistency proofs and a witness quorum of
at least two cosignatures are required, which is the minimal configuration under which a


=== PAGINA 364 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 364
malicious or compromised log cannot equivocate without detection [17], [35].

4.3 Consistency rules
 The schema is accompanied by consistency rules that make malformed attestations
detectable before any cryptography runs. The five v1.2 rules carry over: every entry in
declared_capabilities must carry an explicit status; slsa_level is valid only when
slsa_level_defined is true; an ANCHORED_IN_REKOR status requires non-empty log
identifier, index, UUID, and tree size; the short_lived strategy requires bounded certificate
validity; and the default trust root is Sigstore/Fulcio [36]. We flag one tension inside rule
four that verification ought to enforce more strictly than the source does: the schema retains
a certificate_validity_hours bound of 72 from v1.2, while the public Fulcio instance issues
certificates with approximately ten-minute lifetimes [20]; we interpret 72 hours as an upper
bound for private deployments and recommend that verifiers require the public-good
default unless the trust root explicitly declares otherwise. To the carried-over rules, the v1.3
artifacts add three: metadata_sanitized must be true (not merely present) for artifacts
produced by the reference pipeline; cve_checked must name the concrete CVE identifiers
the sanitizer defends against; and an attestation claiming witness quorum must carry at least
that many distinct, valid cosignatures.
4.4 JSON as canonical source, GGUF as flat projection
 GGUF metadata is a flat, typed key-value map: the format has no nested objects [1].
The framework therefore designates the JSON document as the canonical schema source
and projects it into the container as a dotted, flat namespace —
arkhe.attestation.verifiable.signed_at and so on — via the gguf Python library's


=== PAGINA 365 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 365
reader/writer interface [39] (Listing 3). The projection rule has a non-obvious verification
consequence that the package makes explicit: because the metadata lives inside the file, any
change to it changes the file's digest. Attestation keys therefore can never claim to contain
the hash of the file they inhabit; the digests they do carry refer to the pre-extension base
(source block) and to external bundles (manifest). This is the same self-reference paradox
that Listing 5 encodes as a negative test, and it is the engineering reason the schema's
honesty is structural rather than declared.
5. The Four-Gate Verification Architecture
 Verification in arkhe-verify, the Rust crate at the center of the complete project
structure, is a four-gate pipeline (Figure 3). The gates are ordered by dependence:
sanitization before parsing, parsing before hashing, hashing before signature checks, and
everything before transparency-log checks. The crate is deliberately small — it composes
the ggus parser [32], the ct-merkle implementation of RFC 6962 proofs [33], SHA-2 and
BLAKE3 digest implementations [26], [27], and Ed25519 verification [26] — so that the
security-relevant logic remains auditable in a few hundred lines.
Schematic figure described in the original artifact: Figure 3. The arkhe-verify four-gate pipeline. Gates
are ordered by dependence and the semantics is fail-closed: any failed gate rejects the artifact, with no
warning-only or default-allow path.
5.1 Gate 0: metadata sanitization
 Gate 0 exists because the first code to touch a model file is a parser, and Section 2
records what parsers have done with hostile inputs [10], [11], [13], [14], [15]. The sanitizer
enforces fixed limits before any allocation: strings at most 1 MiB, arrays at most one
million elements, at most ten thousand metadata pairs, at most eight tensor dimensions, and
a cumulative allocation ceiling of one gibibyte (Table 3). Each limit maps to a known
vulnerability class — uncontrolled allocation (the CVE-2026-65315 pattern), integer
overflow (CVE-2025-53630), and count-field overflow (CVE-2024-23605) — and each
violation is a hard rejection, not a clamp. The gate ships twice: as a standalone Python
script that can run before signing in the pipeline, and as the Rust sanitize module that runs
at verification time; both implement the same limits so that the producer-side and
consumer-side checks cannot drift apart silently.

5.2 Gates 1 and 2: digest and signature
 Gate 1 recomputes the artifact's SHA-256 and BLAKE3 digests and compares them
against the values recorded in the signed manifest; the source block preserves the pre-
extension digest so that both stages of the artifact's life are independently auditable [26],
[27]. Gate 2 verifies the OpenSSF Model Signing envelope: an in-toto Statement v1 whose
subject list enumerates the bundle's files with their digests, signed keylessly — a GitHub
Actions OIDC token bound into a short-lived Fulcio certificate, recorded in Rekor, and
verifiable against the Sigstore trust root [21], [22], [16], [40]. Two properties of this
envelope matter for the model use case. The subject list covers every file in the bundle, so a
signature cannot be reused across a partially swapped set of artifacts; and the certificate's
short lifetime bounds the window in which a stolen signing session remains usable,
complementing the schema's revocation block.
5.3 Gate 3: transparency log with witness quorum
 Gate 3 is where v1.3 most materially departs from v1.2. The verifier now requires three
properties, not one: an inclusion proof that the artifact's entry is in the log's Merkle tree at a
stated size; a consistency proof that the tree at that size is a prefix of the current tree,
establishing append-only behavior [17]; and a witness quorum — at least two valid
checkpoint cosignatures from independently configured witnesses, matching the
ecosystem's direction of travel in which Rekor v2 treats witness cosigning as a first-class
deployment component [35], [18]. The quorum is configured, not hard-coded, so an
operator can raise it; the tauri-side updater configuration of Section 8.2 mirrors the same
field. Figure 4 depicts the full structure, and Listing 2 shows the resulting obligations as
implemented in the crate's verify_full routine. The design assumption is explicit: the log
operator is not automatically trusted, and a single-log compromise must not suffice to
produce an artifact that passes Gate 3.
Listing 2. Gate 3 verification obligations (crates/arkhe-verify/src/rekor.rs, excerpt).


=== PAGINA 367 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 367
pub fn verify_full(&self) -> Result<(), RekorError> {
self.inclusion_proof.verify(&self.root_hash)?; // 1. leaf in tree
let consistency = self.consistency_proof.as_ref()
.ok_or(RekorError::ConsistencyProofMissing)?;
consistency.verify(self.trusted_checkpoint.root_hash(),
&self.root_hash)?; // 2. append-only
let quorum = self.witness_signatures.iter()
.filter(|ws| self.trusted_checkpoint.witnesses()
.contains(&ws.identity)).count();
if quorum < self.trusted_checkpoint.min_witnesses() { // 3. quorum >= 2
return Err(RekorError::InsufficientWitnesses { quorum,
required: self.trusted_checkpoint.min_witnesses() });
}
// 4. each witness signature verified against the trusted checkpoint
...
}
Schematic figure described in the original artifact: Figure 4. Transparency log verification in Gate 3:
artifact bytes become leaves of an RFC 6962 Merkle tree; inclusion and consistency proofs establish
membership and append-only behavior, and an independent witness quorum of at least two
cosignatures prevents a malicious log from equivocating.
5.4 Negative tests as executable specification
 The crate's test suite encodes the fail-closed axiom as executable expectations (Table
4). Oversized strings, oversized arrays, invalid magic numbers, missing consistency proofs,
and insufficient witness quorums must all be rejected; the tests assert that they are [36].
One test deserves singling out for its epistemic neatness:
final_artifact_does_not_contain_its_own_hash asserts that the artifact's bytes do not
contain the hex encoding of the artifact's own SHA-256 digest — a fixed-point
impossibility that any implementation claiming in-file final hashes would fail. The negative
tests are the mechanism that keeps the pipeline's failure semantics honest over time: they
regress whenever a code change accidentally introduces a default-allow path.
Table 4. Negative test matrix (tests/negative_test.rs) — each test must pass by
rejecting.

5.5 The Rust workspace in context


=== PAGINA 368 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 368
 The complete project structure organizes the implementation as a five-crate workspace:
arkhe-core (session and principal types), arkhe-crypto (digest and signature facades),
arkhe-verify (the gates), arkhe-governance (Safenet integration), and arkhe-storage
(Hashtree integration) [36]. Two third-party dependencies deserve mention because they
are small-community rather than industrial crates: ggus, the Rust GGUF parser (version
0.5.x), and ct-merkle, the RFC 6962 proof library (version 0.3.x) [32], [33]. Their selection
is consistent with the framework's minimalism, but it concentrates supply-chain risk in
single-maintainer code, a trade-off we return to in Section 10.6. The nostr crate (version
0.38) supplies event verification and NIP-19 bech32 encoding for the distribution layer
[34].
6. Provenance Pipeline and Hash-Ordering
Discipline
6.1 Thirteen steps
 The production pipeline is a thirteen-step checklist (Figure 5, Table 5). It begins with
conversion of a third-party base model to GGUF and ends with full verification; between
those endpoints it interleaves the two disciplines the package treats as inviolable —
hash-ordering and fail-closed gating. Four steps are new relative to the twelve-step v1.2
checklist: sanitization (step 3), consistency-proof verification (step 9), witness-quorum
verification (step 10), and Nostr identity verification (step 12). The delegation brief
specifies mandatory ordering for implementers, prioritizing the three critical items — Gate
0 sanitization, consistency plus witness verification, and npub pinning — before any
convenience features [36].

boxes mark steps added in v1.3 (sanitization, consistency proof, witness quorum, Nostr identity
verification); the gold box marks the hash-ordering invariant whose violation breaks verification
detectably.

6.2 Hash-ordering invariants
 The pipeline's central discipline is that digests have a direction. The base digest is
computed before extension; the final digest is computed after extension and never inside
the artifact; the manifest enumerates the bundle only after both exist; and the log entry
anchors the signed manifest rather than an ad-hoc structure. Inverting any two adjacent
steps breaks verification in a detectable way: the served bytes will not reproduce the
anchored digest, which is exactly the failure the negative tests and the checklist's
acceptance criteria encode. The v1.3 move to an external manifest simplifies this discipline
at one point — the signed statement covers the whole bundle, so no in-file field needs to
claim the final digest — while preserving it everywhere else. The package's prohibitions
state the corollaries operationally: do not invent hashes; do not sign before sanitizing; do
not publish before verification; and do not trust the user interface — verify the payload
independently [36], [28].
6.3 A tooling erratum, and what it demonstrates
 During bibliographic verification for this article we identified an erratum in the
checklist as written: steps 9 and 10 cite rekor-cli verify --consistency and rekor-cli verify
--witness-quorum 2, flags that do not exist in the rekor v1 command- line interface. The
actual interface performs inclusion, checkpoint, and signed- entry-timestamp verification
inside rekor-cli verify, and computes consistency evidence through the separate rekor-cli
logproof command [19]; witness-quorum verification is the province of the witness
ecosystem and Rekor v2 rather than a flag [35]. We flag this not as a defect of the
methodology but as its demonstration: the checklist specifies verification obligations, and
the delegated executor must map obligations to the tooling that actually exists — the same
specify-don't-simulate rule applied to tooling. The erratum also illustrates why every
delegated step carries an acceptance criterion: an executor that ran a nonexistent flag would
fail step 9's exit-0 criterion immediately, rather than silently skipping a verification.


=== PAGINA 370 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 370
6.4 The provenance chain
 The pipeline emits docs/provenance.json, a four-record hash chain in which each
record carries a BLAKE3 record hash and the previous record's hash as prev_hash, with a
genesis prev_hash of sixty-four zeros [27], [36]. The records correspond to the pipeline's
state transitions — header plus attestation metadata, signature, Rekor anchoring, and
Hashtree publication — making the chain isomorphic to the WormGraph evidence
structure of the surrounding VTK architecture [36]. The chain's value is auditability across
processes: an auditor can confirm that the artifact's publication claim descends from the
signing claim that descends from the metadata claim, with each link independently
recomputable.
Listing 3. Metadata injection with dotted keys (scripts/extend_metadata.py,
excerpt).
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.schema_version", "1.3")
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.source.file_hashes.sha256",
base_sha256) # digest of the BASE artifact
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.verifiable.final_hash_location",
"external_manifest")
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.verifiable.signed_at",
datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat())
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.anchored.anchor_type", "rekor")
writer.add_string("arkhe.attestation.attested.attestation_type",
"PROMISE")
# after writing, the FINAL digest is computed over the output file —
# never embedded in it.
7. Governance Enforcement: Safenet and FROST
 Verification is epistemics; enforcement is politics of the execution path. The
arkhe-governance crate integrates Safenet, the Safe Ecosystem Foundation's on-chain
security network, whose SafenetGuard contract sits in front of every execTransaction call
of a guarded Safe wallet and blocks transactions that lack a valid attestation [31]. The
integration's logic is a four-step fail-closed sequence: confirm the guard is installed on the
target Safe; request attestation for the transaction; validate the attestation's FROST
threshold signature over known oracle data; and only then submit. FROST — the Flexible
Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold protocol, specified in RFC 9591 as an IRTF Crypto
Forum Research Group informational document [30] — provides the threshold property:
the attestation is produced by a quorum of independent signers and verifies as a single
signature, so on-chain enforcement does not require trusting any single operator.
 The architectural claim, inherited from the VTK incident analyses, is that this moves
security from the warning path to the execution path [31], [28]: instead of showing an
operator a warning that human attention may or may not catch, the execution environment
itself refuses to run the unsafe action. For model artifacts the analogy is direct — a model


=== PAGINA 371 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 371
whose attestation fails is not displayed with a warning but is not loaded — and the
revocation block's safenet_enforced strategy gives the schema a concrete revocation
mechanism: attestation validity is checked against network state at enforcement time, not
against a static certificate lifetime alone. The framework maps its quorum policies onto
ConstitutionStore thresholds, keeping the ratio strict (no quorum below two-thirds) and
consistent with the witness quorum of Section 5.3 [36].
8. Decentralized Distribution: Hashtree and
Identity Pinning
8.1 Content-addressed publication
 After verification, the artifact is published through Hashtree, the content-addressed
storage layer that distributes files over Nostr relays and serves them by content identifier
[36]. Publication uses the htree add and htree publish workflow; the CID binds the served
bytes to the digests that Gate 1 verified, so the decentralized distribution layer inherits
rather than redefines integrity. The storage crate's client verifies the Schnorr signature of
the Nostr event that carries the mutable reference and checks that its author key matches the
configured trusted set, using NIP-19 bech32 npub encoding as the identity presentation
format [34].
8.2 npub pinning and verified updates
 The distribution layer's critical control is npub pinning: the updater accepts release
references only from explicitly configured public keys. The tauri-side configuration in the
package makes the parameters explicit — relay endpoints, trustedNpubs, signature
verification enabled, minimum two witnesses, and a required consistency proof — so the
desktop application's update path is governed by the same quorum discipline as the model
path [37]. This closes a loop that the framework considers essential: a verified model
distributed through an unverified channel would reinstate exactly the gap the pipeline
eliminates, and an update channel is the classic supply-chain pivot from a compromised
dependency to compromised hosts. The implementation priority list in the delegation brief
marks npub pinning as critical for precisely this reason: without it, updates from untrusted
sources are accepted by default [36].
9. Local Inference: The Flare Engine
 The pipeline's endpoint is execution, and execution is kept local. The frontend engine
wraps the Flare LLM runtime — a WASM-first browser inference engine with WebGPU
acceleration [38] — in a loader that attempts GPU initialization and falls back to WASM


=== PAGINA 372 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 372
SIMD128 unconditionally, so the artifact runs without any server component. The choice is
attestation-relevant rather than merely ergonomic. First, it keeps the verified artifact and
the executing runtime in the same trust domain: no upload, no opaque remote execution, no
re-introduction of the trust-the-provider gap between verification and use. Second, it makes
the verifier's obligations symmetric with the runner's: the same metadata the verifier
checked is available to the runtime that loads the model. Third, it completes the sovereignty
narrative that runs through the surrounding VTK work — free firmware at the hardware
layer, content-addressed distribution at the network layer, on-chain governance at the
coordination layer, and now attested local inference at the model layer [36]. The fallback
structure also models the framework's broader approach to capability negotiation: degrade
deterministically rather than fail open. Figure 6 summarizes the resulting stack.
Schematic figure described in the original artifact: Figure 6. The arkhe.gguf stack: from the 24-byte
minimal verifiable artifact through the attestation schema, the four-gate verification core, on-chain
governance enforcement, and content-addressed distribution, to sovereign local inference.
10. Counterarguments and Limitations
10.1 Attestation is not behavior
 The strongest objection to the whole construction is that it verifies containers, not
conduct. A model whose weights encode harmful behavior passes every gate if the
container is intact, properly signed, and honestly anchored; the schema's empty capabilities
list and PROMISE type exist precisely to prevent the pipeline from being read as a
behavioral guarantee. The disclaimer field states it in the artifact itself, and the framework's
roadmap (behavioral probes that would justify a VERIFIED type) remains future work
[36]. We regard this as the correct epistemic posture — an attestation that claimed behavior
would be unfalsifiable — but users must understand that Gate 1 through Gate 3 answer
who produced and who anchors an artifact, never what it will do.
10.2 Signed is not safe
 Gate 0 defends against the parser vulnerabilities that are known and identified; it
cannot defend against zero-day memory-safety flaws in the underlying runtimes, and its
numeric limits are engineering judgments rather than derived optima. The 2024– 2026
record of Section 2 cuts both ways: it justifies sanitization as necessary, and it implies that
sanitization is not sufficient [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. The pipeline's own honesty
about this — signed is not safe is one of its stated mottos — is worth preserving against the
temptation to market the four gates as a security boundary in the strong sense.
10.3 Trust anchors remain


=== PAGINA 373 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 373
 The pipeline relocates trust; it does not eliminate it. Verifiers trust the Sigstore root and
the Fulcio PKI [16], [20]; OIDC identities authenticate a workflow, not the good faith of its
author; the witness quorum is only as independent as its configuration, and an operator who
configures two colluding witnesses has recreated single-party trust with extra steps. The
framework's answer — quorums as explicit, auditable configuration via ConstitutionStore,
with strict ratios [36] — is the right kind of answer, but the residual is real and belongs in
any deployment's threat model.
10.4 Certificate validity and the 72-hour question
 The schema's carried-over certificate_validity_hours bound of 72 sits in tension with
the public Fulcio instance's approximately ten-minute certificates [20]. We read 72 hours as
an upper bound appropriate to private deployments and recommend that verifiers treat the
public-good default as normative unless a deployment's trust root declares otherwise. The
discrepancy is documented here because the package's own consistency rules demand that
declared bounds be enforced; a rule that permits what the ecosystem never issues is a rule
that should be tightened, and we say so in Section 11.
10.5 Delegation residuals
 The methodology's honesty has a boundary: a delegation package cannot verify its own
delegated execution. The acceptance criteria map obligations to observable exit codes and
artifacts, but the AI coder (or human executor) who runs the thirteen steps is outside the
package's epistemic control; the checklist's prohibitions are norms, not mechanics. Two
mitigations exist in the structure — the negative tests re-run at verification time on the
consumer side, and every claim the executor makes is re-checkable by a third party from
the published evidence — but the residual trust in the executor is real and should be
recorded as such.
10.6 Engineering and ecosystem risks
 Three practical risks round out the picture. The small-community dependencies (ggus,
ct-merkle) concentrate review burden [32], [33]. Quorum and relay liveness are operational
dependencies: a distribution layer that requires two witness cosignatures and healthy Nostr
relays has an availability profile that single- operator infrastructure does not. And the
GGUF projection of a five-block schema adds metadata weight to every artifact; the dotted
namespace is compact, but the inclusion proofs and manifest references it points to must
remain retrievable for the attestation to be checkable years later, which is an archival
commitment as much as a cryptographic one.
10.7 What the threat model excludes


=== PAGINA 374 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 374
 Finally, the boundary of the model: training-data poisoning, weight-level backdoors
that trigger on distributed inputs, and all behavioral attacks leave no trace in container
metadata. The pipeline is supply-chain infrastructure; it is not, and does not claim to be, an
alignment or auditing technique. The scanner-evasion record of Section 2.2 — where even
dedicated behavioral scanners were bypassed [8], [9] — suggests that behavioral
verification is a hard open problem, which reinforces rather than undermines the decision to
build the verifiable floor first.
11. Conclusions and Future Work
 The arkhe.gguf framework demonstrates that a verifiable floor for open-weight model
distribution is achievable with existing, institutionally maintained primitives — Sigstore,
RFC 6962 transparency, in-toto envelopes, SLSA vocabulary — provided two things are
added: a binding to the specific container format and parser threat model of GGUF, and an
honesty discipline that keeps specification, execution, and declaration separately auditable.
The four-gate pipeline implements the first; the delegation methodology and the empty
capabilities list implement the second. Schema v1.3's additions — the source block, the
external manifest hash location, sanitization attestation, consistency proofs, and witness
quorum — each close a gap that v1.2 left open, and the negative tests make the pipeline's
failure semantics executable rather than aspirational.
 Future work follows from the limitations, and the framework states most of it itself.
First, fill the remaining placeholders by execution: a base model, a real trust root, real log
entries, and the resulting production artifact, each adding a column of verified evidence to
the ledger. Second, tighten the consistency rules that this review found loose — the
certificate-validity bound of Section 10.4 and the rekor-cli command mapping of Section
6.3 are the two concrete errata. Third, move from PROMISE toward VERIFIED:
behavioral probes whose results would be recorded in the attested block, with the same
honesty rule that a probe not run leaves the field empty. Fourth, publish the public catalog
of verified GGUF artifacts — the blob-database pattern the surrounding LibrePhone work
models — so that verification becomes a property of a shared infrastructure rather than a
per-consumer chore [36]. Fifth, propose the arkhe.attestation.* metadata convention
upstream to the llama.cpp and Hugging Face communities, where a shared namespace
would let independent verifiers interoperate. Sixth, formalize the gate implementations —
the Rust crates are small enough that machine-checked proofs of the fail-closed property
are plausible. The broader claim the framework stakes out survives every caveat we have
raised: in a distribution ecosystem that today operates on promises, the verifiable floor is
not the ceiling — but without it, there is nothing to build on.
