SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 378
PART XVI — CONTENT-ADDRESSED
STORAGE AND CAUSAL EVIDENCE
An audit-grade analysis of the Hashtree content-addressed storage design:
convergent-encryption attack surface, availability tail risks, incentive vacuums, and the
coordination plane, each claim paired with a falsifier and an explicit epistemic status.
1. Introduction
 On three occasions in the last fifty-three months, the operational fragility of
concentrated web infrastructure became visible to non-specialists. On 8 June 2021, a single
software defect propagated through the configuration service of the content delivery
network (CDN) Fastly and removed approximately 85% of its traffic, including major news
sites, e-commerce platforms, and public-sector portals, for much of an hour (Fastly, 2021;
ThousandEyes, 2021). On 19 October 2025, an empty DNS record for the DynamoDB API
endpoint in the AWS US-EAST-1 region cascaded across dependent services and
temporarily disabled large parts of the consumer internet (Amazon Web Services, 2025;
Pragmatic Engineer, 2025). On 18 November 2025, Cloudflare disclosed a global outage
that again disrupted dashboards, gateways, and downstream applications (Cloudflare, 2025;
ThousandEyes, 2025). These incidents did not involve data loss, and in each case recovery
was measured in minutes to hours; what they exposed instead is a structural property: when
publication, authentication, and delivery are leased from one vendor, that vendor's worst
hour becomes everyone's worst hour.
 The academic and free-software communities have proposed structural alternatives for
decades: Merkle trees for verifiable content addressing (Merkle, 1987), archival write-once
stores such as Venti (Quinlan & Dorward, 2002), anonymous storage networks such as
Freenet, now maintained as Hyphanet (Clarke et al., 2001; Clarke et al., 2002), distributed
hash tables such as Kademlia (Maymounkov & Mazières, 2002), and generalized
content-addressed hypermedia systems such as IPFS (Benet, 2014). Nevertheless, the
deployment center of gravity for code hosting, media distribution, and web publication
remains centralized. The reasons are well understood and are not purely technical:
incumbent platforms bundle naming, discovery, payments, moderation, and reliable
availability into one contract, and decentralized substitutes have historically asked users to
sacrifice one or more of those functions.
 Hashtree is a recent open-source attempt to reassemble that bundle without a central
operator. The project, published under the MIT license and under active development
(1,880 commits and 72 tags at the time of access, with release 0.2.148 dated 10 September


=== PAGINA 379 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 379
2026), describes itself as content-addressed storage, git transport, and an application
runtime on Nostr, in which data is chunked, CHK-encrypted by default, and fetchable from
Blossom-compatible storage, FIPS peers, or a local daemon (Hashtree, 2026b). Merkle
roots can be published to Nostr relays to obtain mutable npub/tree/path addresses, and a git
remote helper allows push and clone over the same fabric (Hashtree, 2026a, 2026e).
Production usage is reported for video streaming at video.iris.to, which the project
documents as serving content over Hashtree rather than a conventional CDN (Hashtree,
2026a).
 This paper asks three questions. First, does the architecture cohere: do the merkle data
model, the CHK encryption layer, the Nostr resolution layer, and the
FIPS/Blossom/WebRTC transport layer compose into a system whose guarantees are
stronger than its parts? Second, what does the design cost: which security, privacy,
availability, and governance trade-offs are intrinsic to the approach, and which are
incidental? Third, how does Hashtree compare with the systems from which it borrows —
and with the centralized fabric it aims to replace? The central thesis is that Hashtree
demonstrates a plausible post-CDN design point in which verification is pushed to the
edges and coordination is pushed to a public-key event protocol, but that its availability
story remains structurally weaker than its integrity story, and that several claims about
encryption and gatekeeper-free operation deserve sharper qualification than the project's
own documentation provides.
 The contributions are fourfold. C1 is a reconstructed architecture, assembled from the
reference implementation, the crates.io and npm package documentation, and the project
website, covering the write path, the read-path cascade, and the authorization model
(Section 3). C2 is a security and availability analysis that maps the design onto the
peer-reviewed literature on convergent encryption, deduplication side channels, DHT
security, and peer-to-peer performance modeling (Section 4). C3 is a structured comparison
against IPFS, Hyphanet, BitTorrent v2, Radicle, and conventional CDNs (Section 4.4). C4
is a limitations section that takes the project's own claims seriously and identifies where
they hold and where they do not (Section 5), followed by a research agenda (Section 6).
The intended audience includes distributed-systems researchers, reviewers of
decentralized-infrastructure claims, and practitioners evaluating alternatives to
CDN-dependent delivery.
2. Background and Related Systems
2.1 Content-Addressed Storage and Merkle Trees


=== PAGINA 380 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 380
 A content-addressed store identifies data by the cryptographic hash of its contents
rather than by a mutable name, so that any reader can verify integrity by recomputing the
identifier and any two identical objects collapse to the same address. Merkle introduced the
tree-shaped generalization in the context of digital signatures: leaves carry hashes of data
blocks, interior nodes carry hashes of their children, and a single root commits to the entire
dataset, enabling membership proofs of logarithmic size (Merkle, 1987). Content-addressed
storage (CAS) matured in archival systems: Venti used the hash of block contents as its
write-once identifier across a network storage service, demonstrating that deduplication
and immutable provenance follow naturally (Quinlan & Dorward, 2002). The same
discipline underlies modern version control: Git names every object — blob, tree, commit
— by its cryptographic hash, which makes repository history a Merkle DAG and enables
safe peer-to-peer exchange of objects (Chacon & Straub, 2014).
 Two refinements matter for what follows. Content-defined chunking, introduced by
LBFS, cuts files at content-dependent offsets so that insertions and deletions only reshuffle
chunks locally rather than invalidating the remainder of a file; Muthitacharoen, Chen, and
Mazières (2001) showed that Rabin-fingerprint breakpoints reduce transferred bandwidth
by an order of magnitude on typical edits. Second, BitTorrent v2 replaced flat piece hashes
with per-file Merkle trees over SHA-256 so that a torrent's integrity metadata scales
gracefully with file size and hybrid swarms remain verifiable (BEP 52; Bittorrent.org,
2021). IPFS generalized both ideas into a transport-independent Merkle DAG with content
identifiers (CIDs), positioning CAS as a substrate for the web itself (Benet, 2014).
Hashtree's data model — chunking, hashing, and tree construction — sits squarely in this
lineage, and Section 3.1 makes its specific choices explicit.
2.2 Encrypting for Deduplication: Convergent Encryption
and CHK
 Encryption and deduplication pull in opposite directions: encryption randomizes
plaintexts, while deduplication requires identical ciphertexts for identical contents.
Convergent encryption resolves the tension by deriving the data-encryption key from the
plaintext itself, typically as its hash, so identical plaintexts yield identical ciphertexts that a
server can deduplicate without reading them (Douceur, Adya, Bolosky, Simon, & Theimer,
2002). The Freenet storage network independently operationalized the same idea as the
content hash key (CHK): the key under which a chunk is stored is derived from hashing the
content, so fetches verify themselves and no naming authority is needed (Clarke et al.,
2001; Clarke et al., 2002; Hyphanet contributors, 2026). Storer, Greenan, Long, and Miller
(2008) later systematized secure-deduplication designs for storage systems, including the
hash-as-key variant.


=== PAGINA 381 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 381
 The cost of convergent-style schemes is a well-mapped attack surface. Because the key
is a deterministic function of content, an adversary who guesses a file's contents can test the
guess offline; a malicious storage server can additionally run confirmation-of-file attacks,
learning whether a client owns a target file by observing the deduplication response
(Harnik, Pinkas, & Shulman-Peleg, 2010). Halevi, Harnik, Pinkas, and Shulman-Peleg
(2011) proposed proofs of ownership to blunt the client-side-deduplication variant of the
attack, and Bellare, Keelveedhi, and Ristenpart (2013) formalized message-locked
encryption and its limits, including interactive constructions that require an online server.
These results define the honest threat model for any system whose encryption key is the
hash of the plaintext, and Section 4.2 applies them to Hashtree's CHK layer.
2.3 Nostr, NIP-34, and Blossom
 Nostr is a public-key event protocol in which each user holds a keypair, publishes
signed events of typed kinds, and delegates relay servers for distribution; relays forward but
cannot forge, since signatures bind events to their authors (NIP-01; Nostr NIPs, 2026). The
protocol has become a coordination layer for applications that want publisher-held identity
without DNS or certificate authorities. Two NIPs matter here. NIP-34 defines git
collaboration events — repository announcements, repository state, patches, pull requests,
and issues — so that hosting and review can be conducted over relays rather than through a
single forge (Nostr NIPs, 2024). Blossom is a companion standard: a set of BUD
specifications for servers that store and serve blobs addressable by their SHA-256 digests,
giving Nostr applications a conventional HTTP storage tier without conventional account
systems (Blossom contributors, 2025). Hashtree's design places Nostr relays and Blossom
servers at exactly these two coordination points, as Section 3.4 details.
2.4 The FIPS Peer Transport
 Beneath Hashtree's storage semantics runs a mesh transport called FIPS. Project design
documentation expands the name as the Federated Interoperable Peering System and
describes a self-organizing encrypted mesh that requires no registrars, central authorities, or
administratively assignable names (FIPS Design Documents, 2026; Sovereign Engineering,
2026). Nodes authenticate with Nostr keypairs, discover and relay through neighbors
without a privileged coordinator, and are transport-agnostic in the sense that the design
contemplates UDP overlays, Bluetooth, Tor, or serial links as carriers (Sovereign
Engineering, 2026). An independently evolved fork powers a mesh-VPN data plane with
byte-metered exit nodes, which corroborates the transport's existence and maturity for
byte-carrying workloads (mmalmi, 2026). Two cautions apply. First, the abbreviation
collides with the United States Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS 140-3),
which certify cryptographic modules — a naming accident that will confuse indexing and


=== PAGINA 382 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 382
search but has no technical relationship to the mesh (NIST, 2019). Second, specification
maturity claims for the mesh rest largely on project documentation; this study treats them
as claims, not as verified properties.
2.5 Scope, Sources, and Method
 The study is a documentary architectural analysis conducted on 15 September 2026.
Primary sources comprise the project website and its documentation, including the package
descriptions and data-flow specifications (Hashtree, 2026a), the reference implementation
repository with its release history (Hashtree, 2026b), the crates.io package page for the CLI
and daemon, including its configuration and command reference (Hashtree, 2026c), the
scoped npm packages (Hashtree, 2026d), and the FIPS design documentation (FIPS Design
Documents, 2026). Secondary sources comprise protocol specifications (Nostr NIPs, 2024,
2026; Blossom contributors, 2025) and the peer-reviewed literature cited throughout. No
source code was executed, no network measurements were performed, and no interviews
were conducted; claims about runtime behavior are therefore as strong as the
documentation behind them, and this limitation is revisited in Section 5.6. Where the
documentation is silent — the hash construction behind the project's nhash primitive and
the chunking strategy are the clearest examples — the silence itself is reported as a finding
rather than papered over with assumptions.
3. The Hashtree Architecture
3.1 Data Model: Chunked Merkle Trees and Content
Identifiers
 Hashtree organizes all stored content as chunked Merkle trees. Files and directories are
read and written in a streaming fashion, chunk by chunk, without whole-file buffering; each
chunk is encrypted and hashed, and hashes are combined into interior nodes up to a tree
root that commits to the entire object (Hashtree, 2026a). The project's JavaScript core
package, @hashtree/core, exposes the content-hash and nhash primitives together with
shared types for content-addressed storage, which places the identifier algebra at the center
of the design rather than in an auxiliary library (Hashtree, 2026a, 2026d). The root hash
plays the role that Git assigns to commit objects and IPFS assigns to CIDs: a
self-authenticating name from which the full object can be retrieved and verified from any
cooperative replica (Chacon & Straub, 2014; Benet, 2014). Figure 1 summarizes the
resulting layering.
 Two properties follow directly from the data model and are worth stating before any
implementation detail. First, verification is local and end-to-end: once a reader holds the
root identifier, every block received from any peer, server, or cache can be checked against


=== PAGINA 383 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 383
the tree, so no transport is trusted for integrity. Second, addressing is self-certifying and
deduplication is global: identical chunks found in different repositories, uploaded by
different users at different times, produce identical identifiers and can collapse to a single
stored copy wherever the storage tier permits. Both properties are inherited from the CAS
lineage rather than invented here; the architectural question is how Hashtree combines
them with encryption and mutable naming, which the next two subsections address.
3.2 CHK Encryption and Deduplication-Compatible
Confidentiality
 By default, chunks are encrypted with what the project calls CHK encryption: the key
is the hash of the plaintext, so the same content always produces the same ciphertext and
deduplication remains possible even on encrypted data (Hashtree, 2026a). This is
convergent encryption by another name, and the lineage matters: the technique was
introduced for encrypted network storage (Douceur et al., 2002), shipped at scale in
Freenet's CHK keys (Clarke et al., 2002), and has been analyzed formally as
message-locked encryption (Bellare et al., 2013). The direct benefit is that a Blossom
server or FIPS peer can store and serve ciphertext blocks, participate in global
deduplication, and never need to understand either the user's identity or the plaintext. The
documented visibility modes build on this primitive and are summarized in Table 1: public
content is readable by anyone with the URL; link-visible content is encrypted and readable
only by link holders; private content is encrypted to the owner's key only (Hashtree,
2026a).
 The costs of the primitive are inherited rather than eliminated. A deterministic
key-derivation function leaks equality: any party who holds a chunk identifier can test
whether any other party holds the same chunk, and an adversary who can guess plaintext
content can derive keys and verify guesses offline. Section 4.2 develops the consequences,
including the confirmation attacks characterized by Harnik et al. (2010) and the mitigations
proposed by Halevi et al. (2011) and Bellare et al. (2013). For the present analysis it
suffices to note that Hashtree's documentation presents CHK as confidentiality by default
without engaging the known side-channel literature, and that the gap between those two
framings is where an evaluator's attention belongs.
3.3 Mutable References: npub/path Addresses and
Nostr-Published Roots
 Immutable trees need a mutable naming layer, and Hashtree obtains it from Nostr
rather than from a naming service. A stable permalink takes the form npub/tree/path, where
npub is the bech32 encoding of a Nostr public key; the latest Merkle root for a tree is
published to relays as a signed event, and resolution means querying relays for the current


=== PAGINA 384 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 384
root of a given npub and path (Hashtree, 2026a). Because roots are signed events, the
mutable layer inherits Nostr's trust model: relays can lose, delay, or refuse events, but
cannot forge a root, and clients can consult multiple relays and verify signatures locally
(Nostr NIPs, 2026). The project's nostr package provides root resolution and signed
tree-snapshot helpers, indicating that snapshot freshness and authenticity are handled as
first-class concerns in the client library (Hashtree, 2026a, 2026d).
 The design choice is best understood against the alternatives. IPFS uses IPNS records
or DNSLink for mutable names, both of which reintroduce infrastructure whose failure
modes differ from the data plane (Benet, 2014); conventional web publishing leans on DNS
registrars and certificate authorities, the exact dependency set that Hashtree eliminates
(FIPS Design Documents, 2026; Sovereign Engineering, 2026). Nostr-published roots have
their own failure mode — relay liveness becomes a freshness dependency — but the
dependency is plural (many relays), verifiable (signatures), and separable from data
availability, since a stale root yields old-but-valid content rather than no content. A further
affordance is portability of administration: the FUSE mount interface exposes any
npub/tree as a local filesystem path, so the mutable-reference layer doubles as a sync fabric
for ordinary applications (Hashtree, 2026c).
3.4 Transports and Placement: FIPS, WebRTC, Blossom, and
the Local Daemon
 Distribution is multi-transport by design. The Rust daemon and CLI (hashtree-cli)
maintain an LMDB-backed local store, optional FUSE mounts, pins, and an adaptive blob
router; peers can be declared statically in configuration as FIPS origin/cache peers with
npub identities and UDP addresses; Nostr relays are likewise configurable (Hashtree,
2026c). Blob transfer over the mesh uses verified request/response frames over FIPS, and
the documentation is explicit about two boundaries: a share link names the remote provider
with a hops-to-live parameter of ten, in the manner of Hyphanet's request routing, and
merely connecting a WebRTC peer never makes it a blob source — FIPS owns path
discovery and authentication (Hashtree, 2026a). Blossom servers form the conventional
HTTP tier of the same fabric; the default configuration ships with cdn.iris.to as a read
server and upload.iris.to as a write server, with optional write-behind replication targets and
a bounded replication queue (Hashtree, 2026c).
 The authorization model is unusual and merits attention. The daemon maintains a local
social-graph store, crawls follow lists (kind-3 events) from relays at startup, and uses
follow distance to control write access to the operator's Blossom server, replacing manual
allow-lists with a social distance threshold; a companion API exposes the computed
distance per public key (Hashtree, 2026c). New identities also seed a bootstrap follow of
the project's release-signing identity so that the graph begins with a usable entrypoint


=== PAGINA 385 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 385
(Hashtree, 2026c). The design is elegant in that admission control follows the same keypair
identity that already secures the data plane, but it converts a governance problem into a
graph-shape problem, and Section 4.2 examines the Sybil exposure that follows. Payment
rails appear at the edges: a Cashu wallet helper ships alongside the CLI, and the companion
mesh-VPN project demonstrates byte-metered exit nodes paid in Bitcoin through Cashu,
suggesting an emerging micro-payment economy for transport services in this ecosystem
(Hashtree, 2026c; mmalmi, 2026).
3.5 The Client Data Plane: Write Path, Read-Path Cascade,
and Media Streaming
 The browser data plane is documented as a strict cascade. On the write path, uploads
are stream-read and stream-written chunk by chunk; encrypted chunks are persisted to local
IndexedDB first, the nhash is returned immediately, and upload to configured Blossom
write servers proceeds in the background. On the read path, each needed block is looked up
first in the IndexedDB cache; on a miss, from Blossom read servers; and only then from the
provider named by the share link, with remote hits cached back to IndexedDB (Hashtree,
2026a). Media streaming is handled by a service worker that intercepts /htree// requests and
forwards them to the worker, which serves HEAD and byte-range requests so that video
elements can seek using partial responses under the HTTP range mechanism (Hashtree,
2026a; IETF, 2022). The cascade is a deliberate availability hierarchy: local persistence
absorbs latency and offline use, serverless peering absorbs popularity, and the named
provider backstop guarantees liveness for cold blocks. Figure 2 renders the cascade; Table
2 inventories the component surface across registries.
 The CLI mirrors the same structure for non-browser use. htree add ingests a file or
directory (CHK-encrypted by default, with an explicit unencrypted escape hatch), htree
push places content on configured Blossom servers, htree get and htree cat retrieve by hash,
pin management controls local retention, htree start --daemon joins the peer network, and
htree mount exposes a tree through FUSE; publishing binds a tree to an npub/path address
via htree publish (Hashtree, 2026c). Identity is local and self-generated: an auto-created
Nostr keypair lives in the configuration directory, and the htree user command reports the
resulting npub (Hashtree, 2026b, 2026c). No account, DNS name, or certificate appears
anywhere in the lifecycle, which is the concrete meaning of the project's no-gatekeepers
claim at the client level (Hashtree, 2026a).
3.6 Git Without GitHub
 The most tangible application of the fabric is code hosting. A remote helper
(git-remote-htree) implements the gitremote-helpers interface so that standard git push and
git clone operate against htree:// URLs: htree://self/name resolves the local identity, while


=== PAGINA 386 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 386
htree://npub.../name resolves any third party's published tree, making a repository cloneable
from its author's key alone (Hashtree, 2026a, 2026e; Git contributors, 2026). Pull requests
and review ride on NIP-34, which encodes repositories, patches, pull requests, and issues as
signed Nostr events, and the project operates a web application at git.iris.to for that
workflow (Nostr NIPs, 2024; Hashtree, 2026a). The release channel is self-hosted on the
same fabric: the installer for the CLI is distributed through an npub-addressed release path,
an instance of the system bootstrapping itself (Hashtree, 2026a).
 Radicle is the closest prior art and the comparison is instructive. Radicle replicates git
repositories across peer nodes with gossip and seed nodes, using decentralized identities for
nodes and repositories, and deliberately leaves review to clients (Radicle contributors,
2026; LWN.net, 2024). Hashtree instead grafts hosting onto a general-purpose storage
fabric whose mutable-reference and blob-transfer layers it shares with media delivery and
application runtime; git support is one consumer of the CAS rather than the system's reason
to exist. The architectural bet differs accordingly: Radicle optimizes for code-collaboration
semantics, while Hashtree optimizes for a uniform verified-storage substrate, and the web
of trust used for write authorization in Hashtree has no direct counterpart in Radicle's node
model. Whether the bet pays off is an empirical question that Section 4.3 frames in terms of
availability economics.

4. System Analysis


=== PAGINA 389 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 389
4.1 Trust and Verification Model
 Hashtree's security argument begins from the CAS property: content is named by
hashes, so every byte received over any transport — local daemon, FIPS peer, WebRTC
peer, Blossom server, or browser cache — can be verified against the tree root before use
(Hashtree, 2026a). Integrity therefore does not depend on the honesty of any intermediary,
only on the preimage resistance of the hash construction and on the correctness of the
client's verification logic. Authenticated naming likewise reduces to key custody: an
npub/tree/path address resolves through signed Nostr events, so the authority to update a
name is exactly the authority of the corresponding private key, and relay misbehavior can
affect freshness but not authenticity (Nostr NIPs, 2026; Hashtree, 2026a). In the vocabulary
of self-certifying identifiers, Hashtree sits with Git, Venti, and IPFS on one side of the
ledger, and with DNS- and CA-mediated publishing on the other (Benet, 2014; Chacon &
Straub, 2014).
 The trust reduction is real but bounded, and three residuals deserve explicit statement.
First, verification presposes possession of the correct root, which typically arrives through
a link, a relay query, or out-of-band communication; an attacker who controls the channel
through which the root is first communicated can mount a substitution attack until the user
cross-checks the root fingerprint. Second, verification logic is implemented in clients
across at least two runtimes (Rust daemon and browser worker), and implementation
divergence is a classic source of verification gaps, as the web-PKI literature has repeatedly
shown. Third, hash-function agility is unstated in the documentation reviewed; a system
whose addresses are hashes must plan for hash-break and upgrade events the way
BitTorrent v2 fixed SHA-256 at the outset (Bittorrent.org, 2021). None of these residuals is
unique to Hashtree, but all three belong in any deployment threat model.
4.2 Security Analysis
 The CHK layer inherits the convergent-encryption attack surface. Deterministic key
derivation means chunk equality is public: any observer of an identifier can confirm
possession of the corresponding content elsewhere, and any party who can guess
high-entropy-deficient content — a well-known installer image, a popular license file, a
leaked document — can derive the key offline and test the guess directly (Douceur et al.,
2002). Against storage operators, the confirmation attacks of Harnik et al. (2010) apply
nearly verbatim: a curious Blossom server can time deduplication responses to learn
whether a client already holds a target file, and the read-path cascade's cache-first design
adds a browser-side timing oracle for link-holders probing visitor state. The published
mitigations — proofs of ownership (Halevi et al., 2011), interactive message-locked
encryption (Bellare et al., 2013), or simply disabling cross-user deduplication for sensitive
classes (Harnik et al., 2010) — are absent from the documentation reviewed, which treats


=== PAGINA 390 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 390
CHK as a confidentiality feature. A charitable reading is that Hashtree targets the Freenet
threat model, in which CHK protects availability and naming rather than per-file privacy
against global adversaries; the documentation should say so.
 Capability URLs are the second exposure. Link-visible content is readable by anyone
who holds the link, a bearer-capacity model that is convenient and matches the casual
sharing behavior of the web, but which converts every referrer header, server log, chat
archive, and browser history entry into a potential access-control failure (Hashtree, 2026a).
The fragment-based visibility distinction mitigates accidental indexing — content behind a
fragment is not fetchable without the fragment — yet links leak in practice, and there is no
documented revocation mechanism short of re-uploading content to new keys. Third, relay
dependence reappears as a liveness and freshness attack surface: relays can selectively
withhold root announcements to serve stale trees, and although signatures prevent forgery,
nothing in the model obliges relays to serve the latest root. The documented mitigations —
multiple relays, signed snapshots, client-side signature verification — reduce the attack to
partitioning, which is the best any relay-based design can do without a stronger gossip
substrate (Nostr NIPs, 2026).
 The social-graph write authorization introduces a Sybil dimension. Follow distance is
computed from kind-3 contact lists, which any key can fabricate at will: an adversary who
creates a cluster of mutually-following keys can insert itself at an arbitrary graph distance
from a target operator, because trust here is attested by edges rather than by scarce
resources or verified identity (Hashtree, 2026c). The classic DHT security literature makes
the general point — id-based admission without a sybil-resistant resource invites identity
inflation (Sit & Morris, 2002) — and the bootstrap follow shipped by default slightly
concentrates initial trust in the project's own identity, a soft centralization worth flagging
(Hashtree, 2026c). Finally, operational maturity signals are encouraging but early: the
0.2.148 release notes describe mesh retry and rekey corrections (Hashtree, 2026b), which
suggests active hardening of exactly the key-rotation and recovery paths that matter most
when accounts are keypairs and there is no customer support desk to reset them.
4.3 Availability and the Economics of Demand-Scaled
Distribution
 The project's distribution thesis is that a decentralized CDN gets stronger with demand:
delivery continues over peers and alternate routes during centralized outages, costs do not
grow linearly with popularity, and each successful fetch can add another source for
subsequent viewers (Hashtree, 2026a). The mechanisms reviewed in Section 3 support a
qualified version of each claim. Peer-to-peer swarms do convert popularity into replica
count, and fluid models of BitTorrent-like systems established long ago that service
capacity grows with the seeding population under reciprocity (Qiu & Srikant, 2004), with


=== PAGINA 391 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 391
measurement studies confirming both the availability benefits and the flash-crowd
dynamics (Guo, Chen, Xiao, & Zhang, 2005). Figure 3 renders the underlying analytical
intuition: availability rises steeply with the number of reachable seeders, while publisher
cost under seeded distribution grows sub-linearly with demand, in contrast with the linear
egress economics of a conventional CDN.
 Figure 3. Illustrative availability and cost models (analytical, not measurement). (a) Probability that at least one
 of k seeders is reachable, for per-seeder uptime p in {0.25, 0.35, 0.50}. (b) Normalized publisher cost versus
 demand: linear egress for a conventional CDN versus a saturating seeded-distribution model.
 The qualification is the long tail. The availability function in Figure 3a is a statement
about populations: for content with a handful of seeders, the probability that at least one is
online is low, and churn makes it lower at night and across time zones — precisely the
regime in which most content lives (Qiu & Srikant, 2004; Guo et al., 2005). Hashtree's
cascade mitigates the cold-tail problem with the named-provider backstop and Blossom
servers, but that backstop is, in the common case, a small set of project-operated servers
(cdn.iris.to, upload.iris.to), which reintroduces a partial centralization at the availability
layer even while the integrity layer remains decentralized (Hashtree, 2026c). The IPFS
ecosystem displays the same equilibrium: gateway operators and pinning services exist
because pure peer-to-peer retrieval is uneven, and operational guidance recommends
pinning to multiple nodes for reliability (IPFS Docs, 2026). The honest summary is that
Hashtree buys outage-independence and cost decoupling for popular content while
re-assuming cold-tail risk that a paid CDN does not have.
 Incentives are the missing institution. BitTorrent's tit-for-tat made reciprocity local and
self-enforcing (Cohen, 2003); Hashtree's seeding is documented as voluntary — the
daemon participates when started, pins retain content, and the social graph gates who may
upload, but no economic mechanism rewards byte-serving (Hashtree, 2026c). The
ecosystem's own experiments point in the direction the literature predicts: the companion
VPN ships byte-metered exits paid in Bitcoin over Cashu, and the CLI includes a Cashu
wallet helper, suggesting that micropayment-denominated transport is anticipated if not yet


=== PAGINA 392 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 392
wired into storage placement (mmalmi, 2026; Hashtree, 2026c). Production evidence is
correspondingly early: the cited deployment is a video application within the same
ecosystem (Hashtree, 2026a), and the repository's engagement metrics — eleven stars and
two forks at the time of access — place the project in a pre-network-effect stage where its
availability claims are prospective rather than demonstrated at scale (Hashtree, 2026b).
4.4 Comparative Evaluation
 Table 3 positions Hashtree against the systems it descends from and the incumbent it
challenges. Three observations follow from the table. First, Hashtree is the only entry that
combines default encryption with cross-user deduplication and gatekeeper-free naming in a
single fabric; IPFS achieves the CAS and naming properties but leaves encryption to
applications, Hyphanet achieves encryption and anonymity but has never been positioned
as an application runtime, and BitTorrent v2 remains a distribution protocol rather than a
storage system (Benet, 2014; Clarke et al., 2002; Bittorrent.org, 2021). Second, every
decentralized entry pays for coordination somewhere: IPNS records, Hyphanet's routing
overhead, Radicle's seed nodes, Hashtree's relays and project-operated Blossom defaults —
the differences are about which dependency is cheapest to tolerate, not about whether one
exists. Third, the conventional CDN remains unmatched on worst-case latency and on
contractual availability guarantees; the 2021–2025 incidents argue for complementarity
rather than replacement, which is exactly the hybrid posture Hashtree's cascade
implements.

5. Counterarguments and Limitations
5.1 Privacy Limits of Hash-Keyed Encryption
 A defender of the design might argue that convergent encryption's weaknesses are
theoretical for this threat model, since link-visible and private content is not advertised and
the mesh has no global view. The counterargument is that equality leakage is not an exotic
capability but a property of the public identifiers themselves: chunk hashes appear in share
links, relay events, and any network observation, so possession correlation is available to
anyone with passive visibility of the fabric (Douceur et al., 2002; Harnik et al., 2010). For
high-entropy content the practical risk is negligible; for low-entropy content — contact
lists, configuration files, short documents — offline guessing is straightforward. The
literature's mitigations exist but cost either server interaction or deduplication (Halevi et al.,
2011; Bellare et al., 2013), and adopting them is a design decision Hashtree has not
documented; until then, the correct guidance is that CHK protects against passive storage
parties, not against adversaries who can guess or observe.
5.2 No Gatekeepers, Examined
 The no-gatekeepers claim is accurate at the level of accounts, DNS, and certificates:
the lifecycle from keypair generation to publication requires none of them (Hashtree,
2026a). It weakens at three other levels. Relay operators are gatekeepers of freshness, since
they choose which roots to serve; Blossom operators are gatekeepers of admission and
jurisdiction, since they decide whose bytes their servers accept and under which legal
regime they operate; and the bootstrap follow plus default read/write servers concentrate
initial trust in project-operated infrastructure (Hashtree, 2026c; Blossom contributors,
2025). None of this restores the credential gatekeeping of the incumbent web, and
pluralism — many relays, many servers — is a structural mitigation the protocol permits.
The fair conclusion is narrower than the slogan: Hashtree replaces identifiable, accountable
gatekeepers with unaccountable, plural, and mostly voluntary ones, which is a different and
not obviously worse failure surface, but not an empty one.
5.3 Availability Caveats and the Incentive Vacuum


=== PAGINA 394 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 394
 The demand-scaled CDN claim, as Section 4.3 argued, holds for content with active
seeding populations and fails asymptotically for cold content; the named-provider backstop
resolves liveness but reintroduces exactly the single-operator risk profile the project
criticizes, at smaller scale (Hashtree, 2026a, 2026c). A sympathetic reader might respond
that early deployments are seed-funded by enthusiasm, as BitTorrent's were, and that
economic layers can be added later (Cohen, 2003; mmalmi, 2026). The counterargument is
asymmetry of expectations: a CDN advertises worst-case performance under contract,
while a swarm's worst case is unbounded in the tail, and applications that assume
swarm-average behavior will observe it as flakiness precisely on the rare-but-critical
requests that define user trust. Measurement is the deciding instrument, and none is yet
public; until swarm-level retrieval distributions for Hashtree content are published, its
availability thesis should be treated as a hypothesis with a plausible mechanism rather than
a demonstrated property.
5.4 Client-Side and Platform Constraints
 The browser data plane inherits the platform's storage semantics. IndexedDB
persistence is subject to storage pressure and eviction policies, service workers are
terminated under memory pressure and lifecycle rules, and neither mechanism offers the
durable guarantees of the daemon's LMDB store; the documented cache-first design is
therefore strongest on the desktop and weakest on mobile browsers, where eviction is
aggressive and background networking is throttled (Hashtree, 2026a). The FUSE mount
and daemon path avoid these constraints but require installation, which re-raises
distribution questions that the browser path was designed to avoid (Hashtree, 2026c). These
are constraints of the environment rather than defects of the design, and the project's
dual-plane architecture is a reasonable response; the residual risk is behavioral divergence
between the two planes, which multiplies the verification-implementation surface noted in
Section 4.1.
5.5 Governance, Content Policy, and Regulation
 Removing gatekeepers does not remove liability. Blossom server operators, relay
operators, and application publishers each occupy positions that domestic law already
regulates for hosting and intermediary services; the European Union's Digital Services Act,
for instance, imposes notice-and-action and transparency obligations on hosting services
irrespective of their storage architecture (European Union, 2022). CHK encryption
complicates, but does not dissolve, these duties: operators of ciphertext stores hold less
knowledge than conventional hosts, which may reduce certain liabilities while attracting
the attention that encryption-by-default storage always attracts. The project's social-graph
admission control is also a governance choice with political consequences — web-of-trust


=== PAGINA 395 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 395
admission historically reproduces the biases of the seed community, and the default
bootstrap follow hard-codes one community's entry point (Hashtree, 2026c). None of these
observations is disqualifying; all of them belong in an honest roadmap.
5.6 Methodological Limitations of This Study
 The analysis has boundaries that readers should weigh. It is documentary: the project
website's data-flow descriptions were reviewed as published, the repository and registry
pages as indexed on 15 September 2026, and no binary was executed, no protocol exchange
observed, and no performance measurement attempted; runtime claims — including
streaming behavior, daemon routing, and mesh transport properties — are therefore
documentation-conditional. The documentation itself is incomplete on security-relevant
specifics: the nhash construction, chunking parameters, chunk sizes, and cipher details are
not stated in the materials reviewed, which limits both this analysis and third-party audit
generally. Production evidence for CDN independence is a single in-ecosystem deployment
(Hashtree, 2026a). Finally, the project is young and moving quickly — 1,880 commits with
release 0.2.148 in September 2026 — so specific implementation details cited here may age
faster than the architectural analysis, which is anchored in properties that the CAS, CHK,
and Nostr substrates guarantee independently of release numbers.
6. Conclusion and Implications
 Hashtree is best read as a synthesis experiment: take the verification discipline of
content-addressed storage, the deduplication-compatible confidentiality of CHK
encryption, the publisher-held identity of Nostr, and the transport pluralism of FIPS,
WebRTC, and Blossom, and ask whether the composition holds together as a general
storage and delivery fabric. On the evidence reviewed, the composition holds. The data
model guarantees end-to-end verification that no intermediary can subvert; the naming
layer inherits authentication from signatures and freshness pluralism from relays; the
cascade gives applications a graceful degradation path from local cache to swarm to named
provider; and the git surface demonstrates that the fabric can carry one of the web's most
demanding workloads without a forge. The costs are equally clear: convergent encryption's
side channels are inherited and unmitigated as documented; availability for cold content
depends on backstops that partially recentralize; seeding is unpaid; and governance
questions are displaced into graph shape and operator jurisdiction rather than resolved.
 Four research directions follow. First, measurement: public retrieval-latency and
availability distributions for real workloads, particularly the long tail, would convert the
demand-scaled-CDN hypothesis into an evidence-based claim; the IPFS experience shows
both the feasibility and the value of such studies (IPFS Docs, 2026). Second, privacy


=== PAGINA 396 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 396
engineering: integrating proofs of ownership or message-locked encryption with explicit
deduplication policy would let the system make differentiated promises for public,
link-visible, and private content (Halevi et al., 2011; Bellare et al., 2013). Third, formal
transport verification: the FIPS mesh is the least-specified layer with the largest trust
surface, and machine-checked session-type or symbolic models of its authenticated frames
would be a disproportionate contribution for their cost. Fourth, incentive design: the
ecosystem's Cashu experiments suggest a path from voluntary seeding to metered
reciprocity, and the open question is whether such a layer can be added without recreating
the concentrated markets that peer-to-peer systems exist to avoid (mmalmi, 2026).
 The broader implication concerns autonomous agents. Systems that verify content by
hash, name resources by public key, and pay for transport at the margin are precisely the
infrastructure that machine-scale traffic requires, because agents cannot hold accounts
everywhere but can hold keypairs, and cannot read terms of service at every hop but can
verify every byte (Hashtree, 2026a; Nostr NIPs, 2026). If the measurement and incentive
questions are answered well, fabrics of this kind are plausible default substrates for agentic
publication and exchange; if they are answered poorly, Hashtree will remain what it is
today — a technically coherent, honestly licensed, early-stage demonstration that the
post-CDN design space is larger than the incidents of 2021–2025 made it look. Either
outcome is informative, and the project has already earned the second-order contribution of
making the trade-offs explicit enough to argue about.

PART XVII — THE GOVERNANCE OF
AUTONOMOUS TRADING AGENTS
This part applies the verification-first governance (VFG) framework to autonomous trading
agents: a nine-layer, multi-market, multi-domain quantitative trading architecture in which
every layer — agent attestation; economic, geopolitical, scientific-technological, and
sociocultural data; verification and oraclization; markets; governance and execution;
institutional reporting — is covered by a dedicated verifier. The design is incident-driven:
the Bybit blind-signing loss attributed to North Korea (DPRK), the StablR quorum failure,
and the Mango Markets oracle manipulation motivate per-layer falsifiers and fail-closed
containment. The part examines LLM multi-agent trading stacks, regulated prediction
markets, and TOAD-ML anomaly detection for oracle price feeds — incorporating its
declared latency limitation explicitly — within the regulatory perimeter of the EU AI Act
and MiCA. Decentralized distribution, bioinspired invariants with falsifiers, and honest
limitation accounting complete the picture: end-to-end verifiability is necessary, not
sufficient, for institutional admissibility of AI-agent trading.
1. Introduction
 On 21 February 2025, the exchange Bybit lost approximately US$1.5 billion in the
largest cryptoasset theft in history, attributed by the official investigation to North Korea
(FBI, 2025). The decisive point of the attack was not a cryptographic failure: the signers
approved transactions whose content, as displayed by the interface, did not correspond to
the payload actually signed — a canonical case of blind signing, in which the presentation
layer becomes, in practice, the system's source of trust (Fireblocks, 2025). Months later, in
May 2026, the European stablecoin issuer StablR froze USDR and EURR after an attacker
minted about US$13.5 million in unbacked tokens, exploiting an administrative control
protected by a 1-of-3 multisig (CoinDesk, 2026; Crowdfund Insider, 2026). In October
2022, the Mango Markets protocol had lost US$112 million to price oracle manipulation,
an episode that led the CFTC to file an action charging a manipulative and deceptive
scheme against token prices (CFTC, 2023; Blockworks, 2022). Three incidents, one
common lesson: at every link of the chain — interface, custody, price data — trust was
deposited where there was no verification.
 This deficit tends to deepen as AI agents enter the execution of financial strategies.
LLM-based multi-agent trading frameworks, such as TradingAgents — which organizes
the roles of fundamental, technical, and sentiment analysts around a simulated trading desk
— have already accumulated more than 100,000 stars in a public repository, indicating
broad adoption in research settings (Tauric Research, n.d.). Yet when such agents begin to


=== PAGINA 401 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 401
move real capital, questions arise that the multi-agent systems literature does not answer:
who the agent is, where its data come from, which model produced them, who authorizes
critical decisions, and how an institutional allocator can independently audit all of this. The
conventional answer — internal policies, spot audits, and reputational trust — reproduces
exactly the pattern that failed at Bybit, StablR, and Mango.
 This article develops and consolidates the response proposed by the Verifiable Trust
Kernel (VTK) project: a transversal layer of verifiable trust that connects multiple data
domains (economic, geopolitical, scientific, technological, social, and cultural) and
multiple asset classes (crypto, equities, forex, commodities, and prediction markets) to
cryptographic verification components, forming an auditable market-intelligence stack.
Documented in four internal project documents dated 15 September 2026 (Oliveira, 2026a,
2026b, 2026c, 2026d), the architecture is organized into nine layers, each with a dedicated
verification component, and is complemented by a fully decentralized implementation plan
that eliminates single points of failure in the distribution of the system itself (Oliveira,
2026b).
 The thesis defended is the following: end-to-end verifiability — from the data
source to the signed payload — is a necessary, albeit not sufficient, condition for
quantitative trading conducted by AI agents to be institutionally admissible. To
examine it, the article offers four contributions: (i) the systematization of the nine-layer
architecture, with its verification components and risk invariants (Section 3); (ii) the
analysis of the plan for decentralizing software distribution, confronted with existing and
verifiable tools (Section 4); (iii) the explicit statement of the bioinspired grounding of the
invariants — neuroscience, nanonetworks, and redox biology — which converts biological
metaphors into operational falsifiers (Section 5); and (iv) a critical assessment of gaps,
schedule, risks, and counterarguments, including the methodological limitations of the
study itself (Sections 6 and 7). Section 8 synthesizes conclusions and implications for
research, industry, and public policy.
2. Context and Related Work
2.1 The trust deficit in trading infrastructure
 In recent years, the literature on the security of decentralized financial infrastructure
has converged on the diagnosis that most catastrophic losses stem from failures of
misallocated trust, not from cryptographic breaks. The Bybit case illustrated the fragility of
the interface as a source of truth: the multi-signature signing infrastructure operated
correctly, but what was displayed to the signers diverged from what was signed
(Fireblocks, 2025; FBI, 2025). The StablR case demonstrated that an insufficient quorum


=== PAGINA 402 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 402
threshold — an administrative key in a 1-of-3 scheme — reduces the multisig to a
disguised single point of failure (CoinDesk, 2026). The Mango Markets case showed that
price data, when originating from a single manipulable oracle, turn any liquidation logic
into an attack vector (Blockworks, 2022; CFTC, 2023).
 The regulatory response follows the same diagnosis. In the European Union, the MiCA
regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114), fully applicable since 30 December 2024 for
cryptoasset service providers, requires robust governance and segregation of duties from
issuers and service providers (EUR-Lex, 2023). The European AI Act entered into force on
1 August 2024 and became applicable on 2 August 2026, with Article 50 imposing
transparency obligations on providers and deployers of certain AI systems — obligations
that reach conversational systems and synthetic content and that tend, in practice, to extend
to agents operating on behalf of users in financial markets (European Commission, n.d.;
Cooley, 2026). A trading framework that produces verifiable attestation of each decision
finds in this regulatory design not an obstacle but a point of alignment.
2.2 AI agents in finance and the identity gap
 The emergence of autonomous LLM agents in finance has, in parallel, created an
identity and provenance gap. Platforms have begun to remunerate agents but can rarely
verify who — or what — the agent is; track records can be forged in copy-trading
operations; and humans can impersonate agents to extract incentives. The technical
ecosystem has responded with two families of mechanisms. The first is hardware
attestation: trust extensions such as Intel TDX, with DCAP remote attestation primitives
and evidence profiles standardized at the IETF (Intel, n.d.; IETF, 2023), make it possible to
prove that an agent executes inside a trusted execution environment measured against
manufacturer roots of trust. The second is financial agent infrastructure: in May 2026,
Circle launched the Agent Stack, a toolset that allows AI agents to maintain and move
value programmatically, with the Arc blockchain as the ecosystem's settlement layer
(Circle, 2026). The component proposed in the VTK plan — ArcID, a registry of agent
identity anchored in DCAP attestation receipts — belongs to this second family and is
described in Section 3.1 (Oliveira, 2026a).
 There is, moreover, an instructive analogy with the evolution of the software supply
chain. The SLSA framework (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) popularized the
idea of graduated levels of provenance assurance; the proposal for Warrant Certificate
Authorities (WCA) for agent tool-call chains — certifying the source of a datum, not its
content, at levels WAL-0 through WAL-3 — transposes that logic to data consumption by
agents (Oliveira, 2026a). The distinction is subtle and important: a warrant attests that the
datum came from a given source with a given assurance, transferring the evaluation of
content to the consumer, who can then record the complete chain in an auditable


=== PAGINA 403 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 403
provenance graph.
2.3 Provenance, transparency, and verifiable price data
 On this ground, three lines of work establish the primitives that the architecture
combines. The first is cryptographic transparency: Merkle trees (Merkle, 1979) allow a
complete set of records to be committed to a single root, and Certificate Transparency
(RFC 6962) formalized inclusion and consistency proofs with domain separation between
leaves and inner nodes — primitives adopted by the VTK in the WormGraph and in the
Rekor anchors (Laurie, Langley, and Kasper, 2013). The second is verifiable public
statistics: recent proposals to anchor official statistical datasets to their sources via
blockchain indicate that the verifiability of macroeconomic data is a recognized problem
beyond the crypto domain (Rusev, n.d.). The third is oracle manipulation detection: the
TOAD-ML framework, published in September 2026 in Frontiers in Blockchain, validates
decentralized price feeds by fusing five independent sources — labels from DeFiHackLabs,
Chainlink, Uniswap V3 TWAP, CoinGecko, and DeFiLlama — achieving 96.72%
accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.97 in identifying price anomalies, with a 5.27%
performance drop when multi-source fusion is removed (Venkatraman and Kuppusamy,
2026). This result quantifies, for the first time in the reviewed literature, the marginal value
of the multi-source validation that Layer 5 of the VTK adopts as its component.
2.4 Multi-domain data: from geopolitical risk to generational
sentiment
 The hypothesis that non-price data domains carry tradable information underlies
Layers 1 through 4. In the geopolitical domain, the GPR index of Caldara and Iacoviello
(2022), built by counting newspaper articles on geopolitical threats and acts, has been
robustly associated with declines in investment and employment and with higher tail risks,
and has become the reference for quantifying risk regimes (Caldara and Iacoviello, 2022).
Recent studies of logistical friction episodes in the Strait of Hormuz document
heterogeneous repricing of cryptoassets in event windows — with elevated pre-event
turnover predicting larger abnormal returns — and the adoption, in 2026, of cryptoasset
tolls by Iranian maritime passages, illustrating the channeling of geopolitical tension into
crypto rails (ScienceDirect, 2026; Chainalysis, 2026). In the social domain, explicit crowd
signals on social media have demonstrated short-term predictive power over cryptoasset
prices (Haase et al., 2025); sociocultural factors — peer influence, financial literacy,
religious conformity, and environmental awareness — explain adoption patterns in
emerging economies (Khan, 2026); and exchange-sponsored surveys indicate a
generational trust gap: 40% of Gen Z and 41% of US millennials assign high trust scores to
crypto platforms, against 9% of boomers (Forbes, 2026b). In the implied-probability
domain, prediction markets regulated by the CFTC — Kalshi and Polymarket — have


=== PAGINA 404 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 404
jumped to combined monthly volumes in the tens of billions of dollars, with US$51 billion
traded in 2025 and a federal rulemaking process under way in 2026 (Pew Research Center,
2026; DLA Piper, 2026; Forbes, 2026a). The methodological implication is direct: if each
of these domains informs decisions, then each must enter the verification perimeter —
which is exactly what the nine-layer architecture formalizes.
3. The Nine-Layer Architecture of the VTK
 The structural principle of the framework is simple to state and demanding to execute:
each layer integrates one data domain or one execution function, and each layer is
verified by a dedicated component of the VTK (Oliveira, 2026a). Figure 1 presents the
nine layers and their components; Table 1 summarizes the verification function of each.
The following subsections detail each layer, systematically distinguishing three classes of
statements: components already implemented and verified in the cited sources;
external-ecosystem components cited by the project documentation and not independently
verified as of the access date; and parameters proposed by the project, which remain
specifications subject to ratification.

principle stated above.

3.1 Layer 0 — Agent attestation and identity
 Layer 0 answers the question “who is operating?” before any datum or order is
processed. ArcID — described in the project documentation as a universal identity registry
for agents, anchored in the Arc blockchain of the Circle ecosystem — proposes that agents
executing inside an Intel TDX register by submitting hardware-signed DCAP attestation
receipts, receiving a permanent canonical identifier (Oliveira, 2026a). The underlying
attestation architecture is mature and verifiable: DCAP provides evidence that the agent's
virtual machine was booted from a measured image, and the IETF profile for TDX
evidence standardizes the format of that evidence (Intel, n.d.; IETF, 2023). The ArcID
component itself, however, was not located in independent sources as of the access date
and must be treated as a project specification built on real external infrastructure.
Complementarily, the Warrant Certificate Authorities proposal certifies data sources at
graduated levels WAL-0 through WAL-3, analogous to SLSA, and the WormGraph — the
VTK's immutable provenance graph, with chained SHA-256 hashes and Ed25519
signatures — records every warrant, creating an auditable provenance trail for all
consumed data (Oliveira, 2026a). The target problem has a proper name in the
documentation: semantic laundering, the apparent gain in trust that a datum acquires when
it crosses interface boundaries without the institutional position of its real source being
preserved.
3.2 Layers 1 through 4 — Verified data domains
 The four data layers follow the same pattern: one data API per domain, an MCP
(Model Context Protocol) component that exposes the signal to the agent, and multi-source
verification before consumption. In Layer 1 (economic), macro signals — policy rates,
inflation, and divergence among central banks — from aggregators such as FXMacroData
feed a regime classifier (arkhe_macro_regime), whose evolution is recorded in the
WormGraph; the GPR of Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) supplies the geopolitical risk
quantifier, with regime thresholds (for example, GPR above 150 as a high-risk regime)
adopted as project conventions rather than as empirical results of the original article. In
Layer 2 (geopolitical), three transmission chains organize the reading: energy → inflation
→ interest rates; the dollar as safe haven → liquidity drainage; and market structure →
amplification through liquidations. The empirical evidence on cryptoasset repricing in
Hormuz episodes (ScienceDirect, 2026) and the emergence of crypto tolls on maritime


=== PAGINA 406 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 406
routes (Chainalysis, 2026) support the relevance of the domain; operational sanctions
verification proposes cross-checking against multiple lists (OFAC, European Union) before
any interaction. In Layer 3 (scientific and technological), on-chain metrics from public
providers, literature monitoring, and AI model attestation — SHA-256 digests of GGUF
artifacts with Ed25519 or ML-DSA signatures and training provenance — compose the
perimeter; the GGUF format, standardized by the llama.cpp ecosystem and documented by
Hugging Face, encodes tensors and metadata in a single file, which makes it a natural
artifact for attestation (GGML, n.d.). In Layer 4 (social and cultural), sentiment signals are
handled with the hierarchy suggested by the evidence — explicit crowd signals with
documented predictive power (Haase et al., 2025), news as a source subject to semantic
noise — and structural adoption factors by region and generation are indexed as context,
not as trigger (Khan, 2026; Forbes, 2026b).
3.3 Layer 5 — Verification and oraclization
 Layer 5 is the architecture's differentiating technical core and combines three
mechanisms. The first is multi-source oracle validation, for which TOAD-ML provides the
reviewed state of the art: trained on labels from documented attacks, the framework reaches
96.72% accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.97, outperforms SVM (88.42%), Random Forest
(91.76%), and standalone XGBoost (93.85%) baselines, and flagged suspicious oracle
behavior before price collapses in case studies (Venkatraman and Kuppusamy, 2026). The
VTK documentation adopts this design as its validation layer (arkhe-verify) and proposes
an additional operational invariant: below a trust score of 0.5, trading is paused
(INV-RISK-05, Section 3.5). The second mechanism is zero-knowledge verification of
off-chain data: DIA ZK, a product documented by the DIA Association, uses zkTLS and
selective disclosure to prove that a value — reserve, NAV, collateral — comes from a
named source without revealing the values, with constant-time on-chain verification (DIA,
2026). The third is PoSoF (Proof of Source of Funds), proposed in the project
documentation as a cryptographic framework that transfers to the user the local,
zero-knowledge proof that their funds come from compatible sources — UTXO and
account-based histories formalized in a unified temporal DAG, with incremental
verification (IVC) and a declared cost of approximately 1.5k gas per EVM verification
(Oliveira, 2026a). PoSoF was not located in the independent literature, and its cost
parameters therefore remain project claims; the underlying IVC architecture, however, is
well established in contemporary cryptography.
3.4 Layer 6 — Markets and instruments
 Layer 6 unifies access to five classes of instruments through a venue connector
(arkhe-venue-connector): crypto (spot, perpetuals, options, and stablecoins, with


=== PAGINA 407 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 407
monitoring of funding, margin, and ADL mechanisms); equities and ETFs (price, volume,
composition, and NAV); forex (majors and emerging markets, with policy rates and
inflation as verification variables); commodities (metals, energy, and agricultural, with
COT, inventories, WASDE, and weather); and prediction markets (implied probabilities of
political, macroeconomic, and sports events on regulated platforms such as Kalshi and on
crypto venues such as Polymarket) (Oliveira, 2026a). The structural growth of the last
domain is documented by independent sources: combined monthly volume in the tens of
billions of dollars since mid-2025, US$51 billion in 2025, projections of up to US$240
billion, and the first CFTC-specific rulemaking process in 2026 (Pew Research Center,
2026; DLA Piper, 2026; Forbes, 2026a). The relevant architectural point is that the
connector introduces no new source of trust: every feed from every venue traverses Layers
0 and 5 — attested identity and multi-source validation — before feeding any signal, and
the risk model applies invariants specific to each asset class (Section 3.5).
3.5 Layer 7 — Governance and execution
 Layer 7 materializes the principle that limits must be executable, not merely
documented. The ConstitutionStore — the source of truth for the system's invariants, with a
quorum of 4/7 or 5/7 and a timelock of 7 or 14 days for amendments — houses, among
others, six proposed risk invariants (Oliveira, 2026a): maximum exposure per venue
(INV-RISK-01); maximum drawdown (INV-RISK-02); minimum margin (INV-RISK-03);
exposure restriction under a high geopolitical-risk regime, for example GPR above 150
(INV-RISK-04); automatic pause when the oracle validation trust score falls below 0.5
(INV-RISK-05); and a cross-venue aggregate exposure limit (INV-RISK-06). Each
invariant is accompanied by a falsifier — the observable condition that would characterize
it as violated — and by a fail-closed mechanism: in doubt, the action is denied. For critical
decisions, the HITL (human-in-the-loop) flow adopts a deny-on-timeout policy: a decision
that requires a human signature and does not receive it within the deadline is denied by
default, with the complete record of the decision — action, requester, justification, impact
analysis — anchored in the WormGraph (Oliveira, 2026a). The combined Safe + SSV
custody reproduces the institutional lesson of the incidents of Section 2.1: Safe provides
on-chain multisig with thresholds compatible with the constitutional parameters (Safe,
n.d.), and the SSV Network applies Shamir Secret Sharing to distribute validation keys
across independent operators, with Byzantine fault tolerance via QBFT consensus and
infrastructure that already secures the equivalent of billions of dollars in staking (SSV
Network, n.d.; Ethereum Foundation, n.d.). The project documentation makes explicit the
rule derived from Bybit: the interface cannot be the source of trust — independent
verification of the payload before signing is mandatory (Oliveira, 2026a).
3.6 Layer 8 — Verifiable institutional reporting


=== PAGINA 408 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 408
 Layer 8 closes the trust loop with the institutional allocator. Every performance report
— NAV, exposure per venue and per asset, risk metrics such as VaR, drawdown, and
Sharpe — is attested with hash and signature and anchored as an inclusion proof in the
Rekor transparency log, following the cryptographic transparency model of RFC 6962
(Laurie, Langley, and Kasper, 2013; Oliveira, 2026a). The differential requirement lies on
the consumer side: the allocator can independently verify the conformity of the report in the
browser itself, via arkhe-verify-wasm — a WebAssembly module that redoes the hash,
signature, and Merkle proof verification against a fixed root of trust, without trusting any
intermediate server (Oliveira, 2026a). In a market where track records of automated
strategies are notoriously easy to fabricate — the attribution problem that motivates Layer
0 — the ability to audit the complete decision chain without depending on the manager's
word reconfigures the very mechanics of institutional due diligence.
4. Fully Decentralized Implementation
 Verifiable trust does not survive a distribution process that depends on a single actor:
an attestation pipeline is of no avail if the verified binaries are served by a server that can
be compromised, censored, or discontinued. The VTK decentralized implementation plan
(Oliveira, 2026b) maps each single point of failure of conventional distribution — domain,
frontend, code, binaries, updates, governance, identity — and proposes a verifiable
substitute for each, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 2. Unlike the remaining layers, one of
them is already implemented: the publication of the VTK binaries in content-addressed
storage with Merkle roots published on Nostr (Hashtree), verified by the project itself with
a public manifest and version 0.1.0 on the stable channel (Oliveira, 2026b).

4.1 Domain and frontend: DNSLink, IPFS, and Arweave
 Resolution of the arkhe.computer domain migrates from a conventional registrar to
DNSLink — a specification of TXT records that associates a DNS name with an IPFS
content path, following the RFC 1464 format (IPFS, n.d.; dnslink.dev, n.d.). At each
content update, a new CID is generated and the record is updated; gateways can then
resolve the name to the current content. The plan explicitly acknowledges the limitation:
DNS remains a residual centralized point — updating the record requires the registrar —
which is why Hashtree is kept as a sovereign alternative, resolving content directly from
npub/tree/path addresses without DNS or gateway (Oliveira, 2026b). The static frontend, in
turn, is served from IPFS or Arweave by deploy services that distribute content across
networks — 4EVERLAND, for example, provides simultaneous hosting on IPFS,
Arweave, Internet Computer, and BNB Greenfield (4EVERLAND, n.d.). Arweave adds the
property of permanence: content, once paid for, is replicated by storage incentives,
reducing the risk of silent discontinuity of pages.
4.2 Code, binaries, and identity: Codeberg, Hashtree, and
Nostr
 At the code layer, the plan calls for migrating the repository from GitHub to Codeberg
— non-profit hosting maintained by the German Codeberg e.V. on top of Forgejo, a
community fork of Gitea — with a decentralized Git transport alternative via Hashtree (the
htree:// remote), which dispenses with any forge as an intermediary for push and clone
(Codeberg, n.d.; Forgejo, n.d.; mmalmi, n.d.). At the binaries layer, Hashtree — described
in its public repository as content-addressed storage, Git transport, and an application
runtime over Nostr, with Merkle roots published to obtain mutable npub/tree/path
addresses (mmalmi, n.d.) — is the already operational component: the published manifest
(schema hashtree.update.v1, application org.arkhe-os.arkhe, version 0.1.0, stable channel)
declares the available assets, and integrity is guaranteed by construction — the bytes served
from inside the published tree are identical to the bytes swept during build sanitization


=== PAGINA 410 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 410
(Oliveira, 2026b). The project's identity is itself a Nostr public key: the npub that signs the
mutable release roots serves as the official identity, communication channel, and,
potentially, a lightweight governance mechanism through protocol groups (Oliveira,
2026b). The design eliminates the dependence on DNS, TLS certificates, and platform
accounts: whoever trusts the public key trusts the channel; whoever does not trust it verifies
the Merkle tree directly.
4.3 Self-hosted updates
 The updates layer proposes the tauri-plugin-hashtree-updater plugin for Tauri v2
applications: a Hashtree mutable root, signed by the project's Nostr key, is treated as the
update authority — the plugin resolves the root on Nostr relays, reads the release manifest,
selects the platform asset, and installs binaries authenticated by the tree itself, dispensing
with additional signing infrastructure (Oliveira, 2026b). The specification acknowledges
honest limits: installer formats such as NSIS and MSI are recognized but not
self-installable, with a fallback to a human release page foreseen. The design inverts the
conventional update architecture: instead of an update server that the client queries and
trusts, there is a cryptographic root that the client resolves and verifies — the equivalent,
for software distribution, of what Certificate Transparency did for certificates: inclusion in
a verifiable log replaces trust in the server endpoint (Laurie, Langley, and Kasper, 2013).
4.4 Governance and client-side verification
 The last two layers of the plan connect decentralized distribution to constitutional
governance. The governance layer operates through Safe multisig with a quorum of 4/7
(default) or 5/7 (critical), timelocks of 7 or 14 days, and signers on hardware wallets, with
the SSV Network as distributed custody infrastructure via Shamir Secret Sharing (Safe,
n.d.; SSV Network, n.d.). The web verification layer proposes model inference in the
browser itself — WebGPU with WASM — so that the verification experience does not
depend on servers: the project documentation cites the Flare LLM engine, WASM-first in
Rust with native GGUF support, as an integration candidate (Oliveira, 2026b). The Flare
engine was not located in independent sources as of the access date; the viability of the
solution class, however, is corroborated by verifiable implementations of in-browser LLM
inference via WebGPU/WebAssembly, such as WebLLM (MLC, n.d.), and by the widely
documented GGUF quantization formats (GGML, n.d.). Table 2 consolidates the complete
mapping, with the declared status of each layer on 15 September 2026; the joint reading of
Figures 1 and 2 makes the project's symmetry evident: just as each data layer has its
verifier, each distribution layer has its decentralized substitute.
5. Bioinspired Grounding of the Invariants


=== PAGINA 411 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 411
 The invariants of the VTK are not arbitrary engineering choices: the project
documentation derives them from three reference biological and physical systems — neural
networks, molecular-communication nanonetworks, and redox homeostasis — and
converts them into operational falsifiers (Oliveira, 2026c, 2026d). This methodological
program follows the logic that an invariant is only useful if the observable condition that
would invalidate it can be specified; the bioinspired grounding supplies the vocabulary for
that specification. Table 3 consolidates the eleven proposed invariants with their falsifiers
and groundings.
