4.2 Prioritization, governance and waves
 Prioritization combines two measured dimensions — usage (normalized traffic, search
presence, support references) and change (release touches and deployment frequency of the
owning subsystem) — with three expert-assigned modifiers: criticality, risk exposure and
maintenance debt, at illustrative weights of 0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15 and 0.10 respectively.
The usage-by-change quadrant carries the policy: high-usage, high-change articles are
regeneration candidates under an effort ceiling; high-usage, low-change articles justify a
single well-resourced human rewrite; low-usage, high-change articles get deliberately
minimal investment; and low-usage, low-change articles are archive candidates subject to a
criticality override, because a rarely visited but safety-critical page in a patient-facing
product is retained and reviewed on cadence regardless of traffic. Governance is frugal by
design: a weekly thirty-minute triage reviews the highest-scoring pending articles; an
append-only decision log records identifier, signals, disposition, owner, target wave and
date; and the team manager signs off at wave boundaries — attaching formal agreement to
the plan rather than to each micro-decision. The work is sequenced in five waves: Wave 0
instruments the inventory and telemetry (one to two sprints); Wave 1 takes the highest
exposure first — regenerating code-carried reference material and migrating or rewriting
top-usage task topics; Wave 2 builds the acquisition pipelines before scaling prose, because
rewrites of UI-dependent pages performed before the pipelines exist must be repeated when
bindings arrive; Wave 3 works the long tail under effort ceilings; and Wave 4 executes
archives with tombstones and redirects. No wave begins without the previous wave's
sign-off, and any change event touching a not-yet-processed article forces a triage-row


=== PAGINA 479 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 479
update so the plan never silently diverges from reality (internal corpus, on file).
4.3 Knowledge the code does not contain
 The paper's second loop addresses four classes of knowledge that no repository holds:
market and plan differences (which features in which countries and tiers, under which
regulatory caveats), on-screen wording, what the patient sees, and screenshots. Each class
receives a repeatable acquisition protocol with a named owner, a structured capture
mechanism, a machine-readable artifact, build-time integration and an expert review gate:
the plan-availability matrix is authored by the product manager in a quarterly workshop,
stored as versioned YAML/CSV, rendered into pages at build time with a CI rule that fails
any hand-written mention of plan availability that does not match it; string-catalog binding
ties documentation to tokens that resolve against the localization catalog per release, so an
automated diff at string freeze produces the documentation backlog; scripted staging
walkthroughs with synthetic patient data across representative plans capture what the
patient actually sees, passing a plain-language review scored against health-literacy
guidance and a clinical sign-off for any claim about care — obligations grounded in
systematic evidence that portal usability and comprehension mediate outcomes (Carini et
al., 2021); and the screenshot suite runs in continuous integration with visual comparisons
on a fixed device matrix over synthetic accounts, so visual change is detected by tooling
rather than by a reader's confusion (Playwright, n.d.). The counterarguments are candid:
telemetry is biased, regeneration is not a quality theory, audits decay, governance adds
friction, localization multiplies everything, and the method is a synthesis rather than a
controlled study — its staleness and maintenance claims are design predictions to be
evaluated with instrumented metrics across a full portfolio cycle.
4.4 A closing note: the commercialization narrative
 The same research program also produced a commercialization deck (artifact seal
ARKHE-PITCH-DECK-2026-09-17) translating the smartphone program into investment
language across ten sections, seven tables and 37 references (internal corpus, on file). The
revenue model combines four sources — premium hardware margin under the
bill-of-materials ceiling of US$ 450 (marked as an internal premise to be validated with
real quotations in Phase 0), a recurring corporate attestation subscription on the kernel's
fail-closed server and verification console, licensing of the VTK layer to other device
makers, and government contracts pairing devices with sectoral invariants. The capital
thesis rests on verifiable 2026 facts: Decree 13,065/2026 authorizing BNDES and Finep
instruments for the semiconductor chain, the USP PocketFab with its R$ 89 million
investment and reported 60 million chips per year (Jornal USP, 2026), and Brazil's Premier
membership in RISC-V International. Market dimensioning is flagged as the authors' own


=== PAGINA 480 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 480
estimate — a Brazilian secure-mobility market in the hundreds of millions of reais
annually, derived from the 36.8 million units sold in 2025 and a three-year capture target of
about 1% of the institutional base — with recalibration promised in Phase 0, and the deck's
first milestone is deliberately cheap and revealing: ratify INV-FLAG-01 through 06 and
produce the PRD by week 8, demonstrating the governance machine end-to-end before any
capital-intensive commitment, with the Anatel dossier submitted by week 42 (internal
corpus, on file).
5. Topological Triage of Constitutional
Amendment Proposals
 The fifth adjacent document moves the verification standard into constitutional law.
Brazil's 1988 Constitution has absorbed 137 amendments in 36 years — an average of 3.7
per year — with no objective, verifiable, a priori filter of the structural constitutional risk of
a proposal (internal corpus, on file). The paper extends a prior topological audit of the
permanent body, conducted in the SASC v5.4α framework with its VetoGraph module and
HOPM analyzer, in two directions: it integrates the Act of Transitional Constitutional
Provisions (ADCT) into the normative graph, and it executes the triage protocol in batch
over nine cases — six real amendment proposals and three controls with known judicial
outcomes. The normative graph is built from the official compiled text up to Amendment
137/2025; nodes are constitutional provisions, directed edges are normative
cross-references, and four petrine veto nodes anchor the unamendable core of article 60, §
4.
5.1 The 2025 bridge and the integrated graph
 The integration produces a structural discovery. The permanent body and the
transitional act lived, from 1988 to 2025, in one-directional coupling: 200 cross-references
ran from the ADCT to the permanent body and not one ran the other way. The sweep of the
permanent body for referrals to the act returned exactly one normative edge: article 165, §§
19 and 22 — inserted by Amendment 136/2025 — refer to article 107-A of the ADCT for
the computation of the 2026 primary-expenditure limit. That single bridge has an effect
disproportionate to its unit weight: it welds the anchor of the fiscal transition to the heart of
the administrative-financial axis, expanding the main strongly connected component from
31 to 37 norms and global circularity from 462 to 2,209 simple cycles — a 4.8× increase
produced by one edge — while raising the share of permanent-body norms reachable to the
petrine core from 47.5% to 52.1% (internal corpus, on file). The winding-number analysis
makes the discovery concrete: the operational winding number counts the simple cycles in
which a norm participates, and while the top of the ranking remains the
administrative-financial axis (article 167 with 2,129 cycles, followed by articles 84, 62, 5


=== PAGINA 481 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 481
and 37), the ninth place overall belongs to ADCT article 107-A with 1,745 cycles — 79%
of all cycles in the integrated network pass through a transitional norm created in 2025. The
most circular norm of the last decade of reforms is not in the permanent body; it is in the
transitional act, installed by the same amendment that built the bridge.

5.2 The triage protocol and the batch of nine
 The triage protocol classifies a proposal by the minimum veto distance of its target set
— class I, blocking, if any target reaches a petrine node within one hop (scale 0.0–0.1);
class II, mandatory doctrinal review, at two to five hops (0.2–0.5); class III, ordinary
examination, at six or more hops or never (≥ 0.6) — and then simulates the proposal as a
perturbation of the graph (suppression, reconfiguration or insertion), recomputing
PageRank, betweenness, components, cycles and winding numbers; PageRank uses a
damping factor of 0.85 and the class thresholds were fixed in the preceding audit, before
the batch (internal corpus, on file). Target sets for enacted proposals are extracted
mechanically from the canonical amendment markers of the official compilation, while the
un-enacted PEC 110/2019 is modeled by object and flagged as modeled. The batch
validates the protocol at three levels. Level 1: the abolitionist control — suppression of the
separation of powers — is the only class I case, triggering the blocking vetoes
NR-2026-010 and NR-2026-011 with a zero-length protection path. Level 2: the two
historical controls — Amendment 3/1993, struck down in part in ADI 939 (Supremo
Tribunal Federal, 1993), and Amendment 62/2009, struck down in part in ADIs 4357 and
4425 — fall exactly in class II, the zone the protocol designates for doctrinal review, which
is where the Court in fact operated. Level 3: all six real proposals are class II, and none had
been condemned for violation of a petrine clause as of the paper's closing — no false block


=== PAGINA 482 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 482
and no false relief in the observable outcomes. The batch also quantifies impact spread
across two orders of magnitude: PEC 45/2019 (enacted as Amendment 132/2023; BRASIL,
2023) with 39 targets yields a PageRank L1 distance of 0.248, drops the main SCC from 37
to 15 norms and cycles from 2,209 to 30; PEC 6/2019 shears the axis at its core — SCC 37
to 4, cycles to 13; PEC 241/2016, by reconfiguring ADCT article 107, cuts 72% of all
circularity (cycles to 618); while PEC 66/2023, whose transitional targets are cyclically
passive, leaves the network intact at 2,209 cycles.
5.3 The ADCT buffer and second-layer alerts
 The batch's most robust finding is the characterization of the transitional act as a
topological buffer: amendments confined to the ADCT produce PageRank perturbations of
0.010 to 0.014, against 0.065 to 0.248 for permanent-body reforms — 17 to 24 times
smaller — because their targets are either cyclically passive or drain circularity without
redistributing normative authority. The buffer has an expiry written into it: since the 2025
bridge chained article 107-A to the administrative-financial axis, transitional amendments
on the expenditure limit are no longer locally contained, as the PEC 241/2016 simulation
shows. The paper registers three second-layer alerts in the framework's executable veto
registry — severity Caution: NR-2026-012 anchored on article 37 (the hub with 19
incoming referrals, crossed by PEC 6/2019 and PEC 32/2020), NR-2026-013 on article 167
(maximum torsion, 2,129 cycles), and NR-2026-014 on ADCT article 107-A (1,745 cycles;
the 2025 bridge), each requiring a propagation memorandum for any amendment rewriting
the fiscal transition (internal corpus, on file). The implications are calibrated: for legislative
advisory bodies the filter is executable in seconds over any proposal with an identifiable
target set; for constitutional theory, rigidity is a distributed property of the graph,
reconfigured between 2016 and 2025 more by transitional additions than by
permanent-body reform; and for judicial review the distance map supplies the
structural-proximity parameter that decisions such as ADI 939 must motivate — informing,
never replacing, the proportionality judgment.
6. A Falsificationist Audit of Parapsychology
Meta-Analyses
 The final adjacent document applies the book's standard to the most contested literature
it touches: the experimental parapsychology of telepathy, examined through the proposal to
reinterpret the phenomenon as low-amplitude oscillatory phase coherence between brains
— measurable by electroencephalography, dependent on psychological bond, and
concentrated in the alpha (8–12 Hz) and low-beta (13–20 Hz) bands (internal corpus, on
file). The review's tone is deliberately respectful and strictly methodological: the oscillatory
hypothesis is credited with what the classical construct never had — a positive definition, a


=== PAGINA 483 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 483
measurable observable (phase-locking value, coherence), pre-specified moderators and a
spectral signature — and the audit asks only whether the evidence base can carry it. Its
answer is that the hypothesis remains promising but not established, and the interest of
the document for this book lies in the precision with which that verdict is earned.
6.1 The Ganzfeld evidence base
 The behavioral core is the Ganzfeld protocol: a percipient under homogeneous sensory
stimulation must identify a target mentally transmitted by a sender in a separate room, with
chance at 25% over four-target matrices. The most comprehensive synthesis is a registered
report consolidating studies published between 1974 and 2020 — 113 studies in the
authors' compilation — which estimated the effect simultaneously under frequentist and
Bayesian random-effects models and reported an effect size of the order of 0.08 with a 95%
confidence interval of 0.04 to 0.12 (Tressoldi and Storm, 2021). Three properties matter for
the audit: the aggregate is statistically significant but very small; heterogeneity between
studies is high, so the aggregate masks subpopulations with distinct results; and inclusion
decisions move the estimate, as the critical exchange around the earlier 1992–2008
synthesis demonstrated — that synthesis reported 0.142 for the Ganzfeld bank, 0.110 for
non-Ganzfeld noise-reduction studies, and −0.029 for standard free-response (Storm,
Tressoldi and Di Risio, 2010), a pattern consistent with the noise-reduction model but
equally consistent with methodological differences between banks, as the accompanying
critique argued (Hyman, 2010). The power arithmetic is unforgiving: detecting a
population effect of 0.08 with 80% power at alpha 0.05 requires on the order of 1,200
observations, which is why the review anchors its power argument in the Physicians'
Health Study, where more than 22,000 physicians were needed to establish a 44% relative
reduction in myocardial infarction — and concludes that small individual psi studies have
almost no probative value either way (internal corpus, on file).
6.2 Publication bias, QRPs and the decline effect
 The metascientific layer is where the audit's verdict is decided. On one side, the 0.08
estimate survives four formal publication-bias tests and shows no decline with publication
year, and the authors contend publication bias in parapsychology does not differ from
mainstream psychology (Tressoldi and Storm, 2021). On the other side, formal tests for
questionable research practices applied to the psi meta-analytic corpus found patterns
consistent with effect inflation, even though the adjusted aggregate remained significant;
and the most pointed result is the decline effect: effect size falling systematically as a
function of the statistical power of the studies, with a Spearman rho of −0.397 across N =
873 study-level observations and p below 10-30 — the signature of early effects inflated by
analytical flexibility and publication bias (Bierman and Spottiswoode, 2026). The


=== PAGINA 484 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 484
moderators reported in the registered report cut both ways: previously selected participants
showed an effect almost three times larger than unselected ones, and tasks simulating
telepathic communication about twice that of guessing tasks — patterns predicted by the
oscillatory hypothesis's bond moderator, but equally predicted by expectancy effects and
demand characteristics, which is why the review insists moderators must be pre-registered
with multiplicity correction rather than fished post hoc (Tressoldi and Storm, 2021).
6.3 Adjacent lines of evidence and the preregistered failure
 The review's systematic sweep covers the adjacent lines honestly. A
telecommunication meta-analysis across 15 publications and 26 experiments (2003–2024)
reported hit rates above chance at p = 1 × 10-7 with bonded pairs outperforming strangers,
but with modest statistical power and residual concern for selection and information
leakage (internal corpus, on file). Distant EEG studies — rhythmic visual stimulation of a
sender with modulation at 9–10 Hz in an isolated receiver at a maximum p of 0.003 across
25 pairs, and partial coherence at 13 Hz between sensorily isolated monozygotic twins —
are suggestive but compromised by uncorrected multiple comparisons and small samples.
The human–dog coupling study — frontal correlation rising from 0.09 to 0.37 and parietal
from 0.06 to 0.40 over five days, disorganized in Shank3 mutant dogs and rescued by LSD
— is the strongest bond-dependence evidence available, yet proximity permits ordinary
sensory pathways, and the review classifies it as interaction-dependent synchrony, not
remote coupling. The decisive case study is the Bem episode and its metascientific closure:
Feeling the Future reported nine experiments of precognitive influence in a selective
journal in 2011; Bayesian reanalysis and preregistered direct replications failed to confirm
it; and the Transparent Psi Project — a full preregistered, blinded, transparent replication
with researchers of divergent expectations — found the erotic trials, where Bem had
reported his maximum effect, below chance at 49.48% (p = 0.042) and 49.65% (p = 0.013),
with neutral trials at chance (Walleczek et al., 2025).
6.4 What VFG-style thresholds would demand
 The review closes by translating the controversy into the VFG idiom this book has
applied throughout: a claim earns empirical content only against explicit, pre-registered
falsification conditions. Table 6 condenses the audit's claim-by-claim verdicts. The
constructive program is specified with equal precision — five cumulative conditions for the
oscillatory hypothesis to count as established: registered-report format with the analytical
pipeline fixed in advance; multi-laboratory collaborations with hundreds to thousands of
pairs, since plausible effects sit near 0.08–0.15 and single laboratories are underpowered;
neurophysiological rigor including source localization, artifact control, electromagnetic
shielding, synchronized clocks and non-bonded control pairs; discriminant tests separating


=== PAGINA 485 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 485
phase coupling from information transfer — for coupling without decodable content is a
physiological phenomenon, not telepathy in the strong sense; and explicit falsification
criteria, the proposed threshold being that absence of above-chance phase coupling in the
pre-specified band and region, in a multi-laboratory pre-registered test with power of at
least 0.95, would refute the strong version. Until such tests run, the burden of proof remains
with the proponents — and the review's closing judgment is that psi research, including its
failures, functioned as a metascientific mirror that accelerated reforms benefiting all of
psychology (internal corpus, on file).

1.1 Reconciliation arithmetic
 The reconciliation is exact. The aggregate ledger of 26 conjectures equals the space
program's 19 plus the Phantom Twist dossier's 7; the class counts add likewise (6 + 1 = 7
Measured; 1 + 2 = 3 Reduced; 10 + 3 = 13 Unproven; 2 + 1 = 3 Falsified). No conjecture is

 Two presentation rules deserve emphasis because they discipline the counts
themselves. First, no corpus uses the Proven class for empirical claims: Measured is the
terminal empirical status, and reserving Proven for proof-amenable statements prevents the
slow inflation of measured results into unconditional truths. Second, partial
measurements split rather than blend: when the verification sweep found that
TOUR-01's ticket-sales claim was realized while its flight schedule was not, the conjecture
was recorded as partially Measured with the two components named, instead of being
averaged into a misleading single status. Both rules are applications of the framework's
core refusal: a status that cannot be computed from the evidence log is not a status.
1.2 What the ledger does not contain
 Several programs in this book generate invariants or gates but not registered
conjectures, and therefore do not appear in Table 1. The GGUF verification pipeline (Part
XV) specifies four fail-closed gates that were executed against deterministic fixtures; these
are verification obligations, not forecasts, so they admit no Unproven class. The trust
kernel's threat model (Part III and Appendix A) enumerates adversary capabilities T1–T12
rather than empirical claims. The trading framework (Parts VI and XVII) registers decision
rules whose epistemic status is carried by their backtest evidence rather than by the
conjecture register. Keeping these objects out of the ledger is itself a discipline: a ledger
that absorbs non-conjectures becomes unfalsifiable, and an unfalsifiable ledger is exactly
what this book was written to prevent.

PART XXII — EPISTEMIC AUDIT OF THE
INTERNAL REFERENCE CORPUS
This part reports a formal epistemic audit of six internal “on file” references — the
monographs, dossiers, and reports of the program itself, archived without a public address.
Five criteria are operationalized (C1 public recoverability, C2 independence, C3 external
vetting, C4 verifiability of content, C5 functional role) and applied reference by reference,
supported by a weakest-link model in which k self-citations sum to zero external
verification. The verdict is conditional and twofold: as evidence for empirical claims, the
list attests nothing — every item fails C1 and C2 and lacks C3; as artifact and process
documentation, internal self-citations attest traceability and precedence. A five-level
credibility ladder (L0–L4) and eight recommendations (R1–R8) operationalize the remedy:
a citation taxonomy, APA labeling, DOI/Zenodo minting, SHA-256/PROV manifests, citable
replication packages, an external audit of ADR-018, mandatory external anchors, and a
declared citation policy. Credibility is not attested by citing one’s own archive; it is attested
by making the archive verifiable by third parties.
1. Introduction: The Paradox of the Number on
File
 Every research program that declares itself verifiable inherits a rhetorical obligation:
the numbers that support its claims must have an address. The corpus produced by the
verification-first governance (VFG) framework, the Verifiable Trust Kernel (VTK), and the
Orchestration Layer adopts as its motto the demand to “show the number” [1] — and,
indeed, it has built an unusual apparatus of epistemic discipline, with numbered
conjectures, executable falsifiers, and registers of epistemic state. It happens, however, that
when the program is presented to an external audience, a substantial part of its
documentary base is cited by means of six internal references — monographs, dossiers, and
reports of the program itself, archived with the indication “on file” [1][2][3][4][5][6]. The
present part takes that list as its object of analysis and asks, with academic rigor: does
maintaining such references attest scientific credibility?
 The answer, developed throughout the text, is conditional and twofold. As evidence for
empirical claims, the list does not attest credibility: no item is publicly retrievable, all are
self-referential (with a single internal co-authorship as the only variation), none has
undergone external review, and, by formal construction (Equation 2), k self-citations sum
to zero independent verification — no matter how voluminous they are. As documentation
of process and artifact, however, the list is legitimate and even valuable: it records the chain
of knowledge production, sustains claims of precedence, and incorporates, in several items,


=== PAGINA 490 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 490
elements that are verifiable in themselves — executable falsifiers, lists of primary sources,
verification-by-execution protocols. The thesis defended here is that the correct question is
not “keep or remove” but “in which role to keep them, and at what verification cost”: the
recommendation is to reclassify the six references as artifact/process citations, to label
them according to editorial norms, and to elevate them on the L0–L4 credibility ladder
proposed in Section 5.
1.1 Material and Research Question
 The material under evaluation is the list of six references reproduced verbatim in
Appendix A: (i) the Space-Sector Falsification Program corpus — an internal monograph
of 24 pp. with 19 conjectures and executable falsifiers [1]; (ii) the Phantom Twist Program
— a technical dossier of 1,117 lines with conjectures, formulas, and code [2]; (iii) the
VTK–Orchestration Layer explanatory documentation, 2nd ed., 43 pp., incorporating the
ADR-018 external verification corpus (9 components verified by execution; threat model
T1–T12) [3]; (iv) the Verifiable Trust Kernel (VTK) architecture monograph — an internal
monograph of 252 pp. in 25 chapters [4]; (v) the Tap ecosystem report — a business report
of 26 pp. with 34 independently verified sources [5]; and (vi) the Orchestration Layer
(Context-Completion Governance Framework, CGF) technical monograph — v2.0, 222
pp. [6]. The research question is the one stated above, operationalized in five criteria
(Section 3) and answered item by item (Section 4), in aggregate (Section 4.4), and by way
of operational recommendations (Section 5).
1.2 Epistemic Position, Conflict of Interest, and Limits of the
Method
 Two declarations precede the analysis. First: the author of this evaluation is also the
author of five of the six references under evaluation and co-author of the sixth in the
context of the program; this is, therefore, a self-assessment assisted by external norms, not
an independent review. The conflict is mitigated — without being eliminated — by three
methodological choices: all criteria derive from citable external norms and literature; the
text explicitly distinguishes fact (what the documents declare), inference (what may be
concluded), and recommendation (what to do next); and the list is treated as an object of
study, never as a source of evidence. Second: the analysis rests on the declared attributes of
the documents (extent, authorship, incorporated elements), not on content review;
conclusions about the internal quality of the documents are out of scope. Credibility is,
moreover, a judgment relative to an audience — what satisfies an internal reviewer may not
satisfy a program committee or a security audit; the verdicts issued here hold for the
external academic audience, the most demanding among the relevant ones.


=== PAGINA 491 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 491
2. Background: Citation, Verifiability, and Grey
Literature
2.1 The Functions of Citation and the Scientific Ethos
 In the four institutional norms described by Merton — universalism, communism
(communal ownership of knowledge), disinterestedness, and organized skepticism —
scientific knowledge is a public good subjected to scrutiny [7]. Citation is the instrument
that materializes two of these norms: communism, by pointing to where the good is
deposited, and organized skepticism, by allowing the reader to exercise independent
verification. Popper formalizes the underlying requirement: scientific statements must be
potentially refutable by observations accessible to any competent observer [8]; Platt shows
that accelerated progress comes from strong inference — multiple alternatives and tests
that discriminate among them [9]. From these principles follows a criterion of function: a
citation may (i) register intellectual precedence, (ii) offer evidence for a factual claim, or
(iii) document an artifact or process. All three functions are legitimate; credibility is
affected only when function (i) or (iii) is presented as if it were (ii). The core of this part’s
question is precisely this framing: do the evaluated references function as evidence or as
artifact?
2.2 Grey Literature: Definition, Value, and Limits
 The Luxembourg definition — material produced by governments, academia, business,
and industry, outside the control of commercial publishers — describes documents such as
those under evaluation with precision: technical reports without a formal editorial channel
[10]. Grey literature is not, in itself, disqualified: in evidence syntheses its inclusion is
decisive — McAuley et al. showed that meta-analyses that exclude it overestimate effects
by about 15% (odds ratio of odds ratios 1.15; 95% CI: 1.04–1.28) and that 33% of the
included meta-analyses contained grey literature [11]; Mahood et al. document gains in
completeness and scope [12]. But the case of institutional grey literature reveals the
condition that matters: agencies and laboratories publish technical reports with institutional
reputational accountability and, increasingly, with a public identifier — NIST assigns
PubIDs and Crossref-registered DOIs to its entire technical series, creating an “official
version of record” [13]. The effect of availability is measurable: freely accessible articles
receive substantially higher impact [14]. The historical problem of grey literature is
precisely acquisition — the difficulty of locating and obtaining the document [15]; “on
file” is the extreme form of that problem: the document exists, but its address is private.
2.3 The Normative Treatment of Non-Retrievable Sources


=== PAGINA 492 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 492
 Editorial norms converge on two points. First, non-retrievable material does not belong
in the reference list as evidence: APA requires that personal communications be cited only
in the text, because readers cannot access or retrieve them [16][17]; ICMJE adopts an
analogous rule [18]. Second, APA admits — and normalizes — citations of unpublished
manuscripts, with the explicit label [Unpublished manuscript] and indication of the
institution [16][17]. That is: the norms do not forbid maintaining internal references such as
those under evaluation; they require that they be labeled as what they are, and that they not
substitute for retrievable evidence. The ethics of citation adds the third point: COPE
classifies excessive self-citation with inflationary intent as citation manipulation and, at the
same time, recognizes legitimate reasons for self-citation — among them, citing one’s own
previous work as an artifact and giving continuity to a research program [19][20]. The
distinguishing criterion, in all the norms, is the same: function and label, not the existence
of the reference.
2.4 Self-Citation and Credibility: What the Evidence Shows
 The empirical evidence on self-citation reinforces the functional criterion. Ioannidis et
al., in standardizing citation metrics for a broad base of authors, observe that extreme
self-citation rates should discourage the use of any citation-based metric, because they
anticipate incentive distortions [21]. The mechanism is structural: inflationary self-citation
converts the system of attestation — citation as verification by peers — into
self-evaluation. The corollary for this part is precise: it is not the volume of self-citations
that corrupts, it is the role they play in the support of claims. A 252 pp. monograph cited as
evidence of its own validity is inflationary self-citation even if cited only once; the same
document cited as documentary artifact is ordinary practice in the technical literature
[13][19].
2.5 Transparency, Data, Software, and Registration
 The open science movement offers the instruments that convert “on file” into
verifiable. The TOP guidelines operationalize transparency in eight standards, including
citation policies for data and code [22]; the FAIR principles require that data and metadata
be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, with persistent identifiers [23]; the
software citation principles determine that citable code have version, persistent identifier,
and metadata that allow reuse [24]. General repositories with DOI (Zenodo, operated by
OpenAIRE/CERN) accept unpublished artifacts — reports, dossiers, code — and make
them citable and preserved [25]. The integrity of the bond between the cited version and the
content can be guaranteed by standardized hash functions (SHA-256, FIPS 180-4) [26], and
the provenance metadata by the W3C PROV model [27]. For vetting, the spectrum runs
from preprints — early availability with a public identifier [28] — to Registered Reports, in


=== PAGINA 493 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 493
which peer review occurs before the results [29], up to independent adversarial audit. The
reproducibility crisis is the common backdrop: replication rates between 36% and 39% in
psychology [30] and the diagnosis that much of the published literature may be false when
incentives and verification fail [31] — with formal recommendations for the entire
ecosystem [32]. The VFG program, with executable falsifiers and formal verification in the
Hoare tradition [33], already operates in this verification economy; the gap is, essentially,
one of public address.
3. Method: Five Criteria and a Minimal Model
 The evaluation follows a three-step documentary protocol: (i) inventory of the declared
attributes of each reference; (ii) application of five criteria (Table 1) with an ordinal
judgment — yes, partial, no — justified by the corresponding attribute; (iii) aggregate
verdict by two minimal models, formalized below. The criteria derive directly from the
background of Section 2: retrievability and labeling come from the citation norms;
independence and vetting come from publication ethics and the practice of peer review;
verifiability of content comes from the FAIR principles, software citation, and falsifiability;
and the functional role comes from citation theory. The protocol is deliberately replicable:
any reader can reapply the five criteria to the list of Appendix A and reach the same
classifications, because each judgment is anchored in a declared attribute, not in
impressions of quality.
Table 1 — Evaluation criteria (C1–C5) applied to each reference.
Criterion
Diagnostic question
Evidence required for “yes”

 Let r be a reference and Ci(r) ∈ [0, 1] the degree of satisfaction of criterion i. The
weakest-link model is adopted:
 C(r) = min { C1(r), C2(r), C3(r), C4(r), C5(r) }
 (1)
 Let E be an empirical claim supported by the set of references R(E), and let ind(r) be
the indicator of editorial independence: ind(r) = 1 if r is editorially independent of the


=== PAGINA 494 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 494
author of E (external authorship and vetting), and ind(r) = 0 otherwise. The maximum
external verification of E is:
 Vext(E) = 1 − Π ( 1 − ind(r) · C(r) ), r ∈ R(E)
 (2)
 Equation (2) captures the central result of this evaluation: if all the references in R(E)
are self-referential (ind(r) = 0 for every r), then Vext(E) = 0, regardless of the number k of
references, of their extents (24 pp., 252 pp., 222 pp.), or of the internal quality of each one.
In words: k self-citations sum to zero external verification. The model is purposefully
minimalist — it does not weight quality or relevance — because the relevant point is
structural, not quantitative; models that add weights for quality or relevance would refine,
but not reverse, the result.
4. Results

Second, three items carry elements that are verifiable in themselves: executable falsifiers
and state registers ([1], [2]), a verification-by-execution corpus with a threat model ([3]),
and a list of 34 externally verified sources ([5]); this matters because such elements can be
extracted and checked without access to the full document. Third, the unit of extent of [2]
— “lines” — is a unit of software artifact, not of published text; the very format of the
reference signals its nature as code.

4.3 Item-by-Item Analysis
 [1] The Space-Sector Falsification Program. This is the most ambiguous case in the
list, because it is the item whose content comes closest to complete scientific practice:
numbered conjectures with executable falsifiers, explicit epistemic states, and an honest
balance of refutations (the corpus declares 6 Measured, 1 Reduced, 10 Unproven, and 2
Falsified) [1]. Under Equation (1), however, the weakest link dominates: the document is
retrievable only in the private archive (C1 = no) and is authorially self-referent (C2 = no),
so that citing it as evidence for the space-sector facts it discusses is an invalid structure —
the facts themselves require their external anchors (audit agencies, launch registries, public
reports), which the corpus records but which must be cited directly. The correct role of [1]
is twofold: artifact of method, because the falsification protocol is reusable, and register of
precedence for the conjectures. Both roles survive reclassification; neither requires that the
document attest its own numbers.


=== PAGINA 496 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 496
 [2] The Phantom Twist Program. Here the problem is taxonomic before it is
epistemic: the extent declared in lines (1,117) indicates that the reference is, in practice, a
software artifact — conjectures, formulas, and code — and should be cited as software,
with version, hash, and persistent identifier, according to the software citation principles
[24]. The FAIR principles and the TOP guidelines apply in full: a deposit with DOI (for
example, Zenodo) would convert the dossier into a citable, versioned item in a low-cost
operation [23][22][25]. In that format, what is today “on file” becomes “on record”, and the
embedded falsifiers become executable by third parties — transforming C4 from “partial”
to “yes” without any change of content.
 [3] The VTK–Orchestration Layer explanatory documentation. This is the only
item with variation in authorship (Bednarski, J. as co-author), which introduces partial
independence — though internal to the program, insufficient to alter the structural
judgment (C2 = partial) [3]. The item is also the most sophisticated in verification
mechanisms: the ADR-018 corpus declares 9 components verified by execution and a
threat model T1–T12. “Verified by execution” is internal reproducibility — the maximum
value a closed system can offer — and the threat model is, by design, an invitation to
external adversaries. The priority action follows from that very design: turn the invitation
into a process — an independent external audit, whose report would become a new
reference, editorially independent, elevating the entire VTK–Orchestration Layer block in
Equation (2).
 [4] The Verifiable Trust Kernel (VTK) monograph. This is the most voluminous
monograph (252 pp., 25 chapters) and the most exposed to the diagnosis of the
“unreviewed book” [4]. Its declared value is architectural — the description of a verifiable
trust architecture — a genre that, in computing practice, is normally conveyed through
channels with vetting: books from university or technical publishers, theses in institutional
repositories, or technical series with DOIs [13]. Among the six items, [4] has the greatest
expected gain per unit of effort from an institutional or general deposit with DOI (L2),
followed by editorial submission (L4): the same text, today labelable as [Unpublished
manuscript] [16], becomes a citable artifact tomorrow.
 [5] The Tap ecosystem improvement report. This is the structurally strongest item,
and the reason is instructive: its content was built on 34 externally verified sources, with
access links [5] — that is, the report already practiced the solution this evaluation
recommends for the rest of the list. The implication is direct: for any empirical claim
contained in [5], the correct citation is the corresponding primary source (which is
retrievable), not the report; [5] remains as a methodological artifact — the demonstration
that the program knows how to produce auditable documentation. It is the existence of [5]
that allows recommendation R7 (Section 5) to be formulated as a consolidated standard of
the program, and not as an aspiration.


=== PAGINA 497 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 497
 [6] The Orchestration Layer (CGF). It concentrates the most demanding quantitative
results of the corpus (formal verification and experiments declared in the v2.0 monograph)
[6]. Numbers of this kind have a peculiar status: they are claims that invite replication —
and replication requires the artifacts of execution (models, configurations, logs, code).
Equation (2) imposes the limit: as long as the artifacts reside in the private archive, the
claims of [6] are not externally verifiable, however rigorous they may be internally. The
path is level L3 of the ladder: a citable replication package (code, models, logs), referenced
by a persistent identifier [24][25], with the monograph kept as a program document.
4.4 Aggregate Assessment: What the List Attests and What
It Does Not
 Applying Equation (2) to the list as a whole: for any empirical claim E supported
exclusively by the evaluated references, Vext(E) = 0. This is the structural verdict, and it is
not sensitive to arguments of volume (567 pp. plus 1,117 lines), of effort, or of internal
quality — none of these attributes alters ind(r). Maintaining the list, in the role of evidence,
does not attest scientific credibility; it merely transfers the demand for verification to the
reader, who will not be able to exercise it. This result is not a criticism of the documents
themselves, but of the addressing structure: the same text changes epistemic status when it
changes address.
 In the role of artifact/process, the verdict reverses. The list attests three things that the
scientific community recognizes as procedural virtues: (i) traceability — the chain of
knowledge production is documented from end to end; (ii) precedence — numbered and
dated conjectures sustain claims of anteriority; (iii) a discipline of self-verification —
executable falsifiers, verification by execution (ADR-018), and a report with external
anchors ([5]) evidence internal practice above the average. There is, however, a specific
rhetorical cost: the program’s motto — “show the number” [1] — becomes, under a closed
archive, an ironic tribute to its own violation. The internal consistency of the VFG program
is not a matter of style here: it is an evaluation criterion. A program whose epistemology
demands showable numbers must apply to itself the demand it applies to others — and this
is exactly what the ladder of Section 5 operationalizes.
“The VFG discipline is not saying ‘yes’ or ‘no’ — it is saying ‘show the number’.” — motto
recorded in the corpus [1]. Where does the number live, and who can go and see it? As long as the
answer is “in the program’s private archive”, the motto describes an aspiration; after L2–L3, it
describes a fact.
5. From “On File” to “On Record”: Ladder and
Recommendations


=== PAGINA 498 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 498
5.1 The Credibility Ladder for Documentary Evidence
 This section presents the credibility ladder for documentary evidence, and Table 4
details the requirements of each level. The design has three important properties. First, the
levels are cumulative: L3 does not waive the DOI of L2, and L4 does not waive the
replication package of L3. Second, the levels are monotonic in decreasing cost of return —
L1 and L2 are operations of hours or days, not months, and produce most of the gain in
verifiability. Third, the ladder does not require full disclosure: L1 admits escrow (custody
of hashes with access under agreement), and deposits may be redacted when confidentiality
imposes limits. The evaluated corpus currently sits entirely at level L0; the program’s own
history shows that the transition is feasible, since one of its reports ([5]) already operates
with public external anchors.
Editorial note. In the source article, Figure 1 depicted the L0–L4 credibility ladder for documentary
evidence as a vector diagram — a staircase whose steps carry each level’s minimum requirements, with
the evaluated corpus marked at level L0. The diagram is not reproduced in this book part; Table 4
details the level-by-level requirements.
Table 4 — Levels of the credibility ladder: requirements, what they attest, and

5.2 Operational Recommendations
 Eight recommendations operationalize the transition. Each identifies the criterion it
attacks and the approximate cost of execution; none requires any change to the content of
the documents.
R1. Citation taxonomy. Classify every citation of the corpus into one of two classes,
declared in the text: evidence citation (exclusive to independent external sources) and


=== PAGINA 499 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 499
artifact citation (for [1]–[6] and their kind). The rule eliminates, by construction, the use of
self-citations in the role of evidence and attacks criteria C2 and C5.
R2. Labeling according to editorial norms. Label the six references in the appropriate
editorial format — [Unpublished manuscript] / [Unpublished internal report], with the
institution of origin — and never present them as personal communication, which does not
enter reference lists [16][17][18]. Attacks C1 and C5; zero cost.
R3. Deposit with DOI. Deposit [1]–[6] in a repository that assigns DOIs (Zenodo or an
institutional repository), with explicit versions — the v2.0 of [6] is the internal precedent
— and declared licenses [25][23]. Attacks C1 directly; cost of days.
R4. Cryptographic manifest. Publish a SHA-256 manifest per document with provenance
metadata (who produced it, when, from what) [26][27] — the level L1, attainable in a
single afternoon, which converts “on file” into “on record” even under escrow. Attacks C1
partially, and C4; cost of hours.
R5. Citable replication packages. Package and cite the executable falsifiers and the
artifacts of [2] and [6] as software — version, hash, persistent identifier, and execution
instructions [24]; replication by third parties becomes possible without access to the full
document. Attacks C4; cost of days.
R6. Independent adversarial audit. Commission an independent external audit of the
ADR-018 corpus of [3] — the threat model T1–T12 is the adversary’s natural roadmap —
and publish the report as a reference in its own right, editorially independent [19][29].
Attacks C2 and C3 of the entire block; medium cost.
R7. Mandatory external anchor. Adopt, as a program standard, that every empirical
claim cite the independent primary source — the model is [5], with 34 verified sources.
The internal monographs may accompany the primary citation as context, never as a
substitute. Attacks C4 and C5; zero cost for new documents.
R8. Declared citation policy. Declare, in the body of the public documents, the program’s
citation policy — the percentage and function of self-citations, the class of each citation —
anticipating the scrutiny that excessive self-citation rates already provoke in external
evaluations [21][22]. Attacks C5; zero cost.
6. Counterarguments and Limitations
 Self-citation of artifacts is normal practice. A first counterargument holds that citing
one’s own work is legitimate — and it is correct. COPE recognizes legitimate reasons for
self-citation, including the continuity of a research program [19]; computing routinely cites
its own technical reports, code bases, and specifications. This part does not propose


=== PAGINA 500 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 500
removing the evaluated references; it proposes only that they not play the role of evidence
and that they gain a public address. Correctly understood, the counterargument supports the
thesis: what makes self-citation legitimate is precisely the functional criterion adopted here
— function and label, not the existence of the reference.
 Grey literature has proven scientific value. Second counterargument: grey literature
has value, and excluding it distorts evidence syntheses — meta-analyses that omit it
overestimate effects [11] and lose completeness [12]. This is also correct — and it does not
rescue the list in its current form, for a reason that the grey literature itself teaches: the
cases of value combine institutional production, reputational accountability, and public
identification [13]. The historical problem of grey literature has always been retrieval, not
quality [15]; “on file” is retrieval taken to its minimal limit. The correct lesson from the
value of grey literature is to deposit and identify — not to keep documents in a drawer.
 Confidentiality and intellectual property may justify not publishing. Third
counterargument: contractual or intellectual-property restrictions may prevent full
disclosure. The argument is legitimate and has intermediate paths: redacted deposits,
escrow of hashes with trusted dating [26][27], and access under agreement for accredited
auditors. Note, however, that none of these paths preserves the evidential role of the
reference — they preserve integrity and precedence, which are exactly the roles this part
recommends for the list. Confidentiality, therefore, explains L1; it does not justify
remaining at L0.
 Internal verification is better than nothing. Fourth counterargument: verification by
execution (ADR-018) and the internal falsifiers constitute above-average practice. True —
internal reproducibility is a necessary condition of any subsequent verification [32]. But
credibility is a judgment by third parties: the transition from “it works on my machine” to
“it works under scrutiny” requires independence, and independence is an attribute of the
process, not of the content. The ladder formalizes this transition without disqualifying the
starting point; on the contrary, the value of the internal work is only fully realized when
third parties can check it.
 Limitations of the evaluation itself. Five limitations must be declared. First, the
analysis is by declared attributes — without content review of the six documents — so that
the verdicts bear on the citation practice, not on the internal quality of the texts. Second,
this is an assisted self-assessment: the author evaluates his own references, and the
mitigation adopted (external criteria, separation of fact/inference/recommendation)
reduces, but does not eliminate, the bias. Third, credibility is relative to an audience; the
judgments adopt the external academic audience as reference — for internal or contractual
audiences, the same artifacts may have a different probative value, moderated by access
agreements. Fourth, the model of Equations (1)–(2) is minimalist by choice; models that


=== PAGINA 501 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 501
weight quality, relevance, and partial independence would refine, but not reverse, the
structural result. Fifth, the cited norms are mostly Anglophone and editorial; national
bibliographic traditions may differ in detail, without altering the normative core of
recoverability and function.
7. Conclusion and Implications
 The question that titles this part now admits a complete answer. Maintaining the
evaluated references does not, by itself, attest scientific credibility: in their current state
(L0, private archive), all items fail public recoverability and independence, lack external
vetting and, used as evidence, produce null external verification by construction (Equation
2). But removing them would be worse than keeping them: the list documents the chain of
production, sustains precedence, and contains elements that are verifiable in themselves —
executable falsifiers, verification by execution, listed primary sources. The correct course is
to keep with reclassification — artifact/process citations, labeled according to editorial
norms, never in the role of evidence — and with upgrading: public DOI, cryptographic
manifest, replication packages, external audit, and primary anchors for every empirical
claim. In synthesis: keep, yes; as evidence, no; as verifiable artifact, yes — and the sooner,
the better.
 The practical implications are immediate. For submissions to conferences and journals
— the concrete case of the corpus — the internal list should migrate to an appendix of
artifacts or an availability note, with the body of the text anchored in external sources, in
the pattern that [5] already demonstrates to be feasible. For the public documents of the
program, the declared citation policy (R1–R8) converts the current fragility into a
differentiator: few programs document, with executable falsifiers, what others merely
assert. The final reading is optimistic and demanding at the same time: the corpus has
already built the hard part — the discipline of verification; the missing part is cheap and
mechanical. Credibility is not attested by citing one’s own archive; it is attested by making
the archive verifiable by third parties. Or, in the vocabulary of the program itself: the
number needs a public address — show the number, and show where it lives.

APPENDIX K — THE MONOREPO
VERIFICATION CORPUS (CODE)
This appendix reproduces the verification corpus of the monorepo that implements the
Verifiable Trust Kernel: 39 named blocks and 3,963 lines, extracted deterministically from
the project specification and reproduced verbatim — including original artifact identifiers,
comments, and file paths — so that every listing can be matched against the referenced
artifacts. The corpus covers the workspace configuration, the five verified crates (shared
types, evidence records, the causal evidence graph, the claim registry, and the constitution
store), the TLA+ safety and liveness specifications with their model-checking
configurations, the Kani proof harnesses, the Lean 4 proofs, the test pyramid, the
continuous-integration workflow, the supply-chain policy, and the machine-readable status
artifacts.
Three reading notes. First, the Rust listings are implementation code, not pseudocode; the
crate and module names are the artifact's own. Second, the TLA+ and Kani listings are the
executable form of the invariants that Chapters 3–6 argue for in prose; reading them side by
side is the fastest way to see what “verified by execution” costs and buys. Third, the final
block is the completion seal quoted verbatim; like every identifier in this book it is a proper
name, retained for verifiability rather than style.

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#
# Este workspace contém 15 crates organizados em 5 camadas arquitecturais.
#
# Princípios:
# 1. Resolver "2" para unificação correcta de features
# 2. Dependências centralizadas em [workspace.dependencies]
# 3. Lints centralizados em [workspace.lints]
# 4. Metadata centralizada em [workspace.package]
# 5. Perfis de build centralizados
#

=== PAGINA 519 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology

//! # Arkhe Standards
//!
//! Tipos partilhados entre todos os crates do Arkhe AGI.
//!
//! Este crate define as abstracções fundamentais:
//!
//! - [`Category`] — classificação epistémica de uma afirmação
//! - [`Independence`] — nível de independência da evidência
//! - [`Status`] — estado de verificação (VERIFIED, FAILED, etc.)
//! - [`Gate`] — gates do pipeline de verificação (0-3)
//!
//! ## Exemplo
//!
//! ```
//! use arkhe_standards::{Category, Independence, Status};
//!
//! let category = Category::MeasuredEvidence;
//! assert!(category.is_falsifiable());
//!

/// Hash obtido.

/// Hash de um artefacto, com separação de domínio.
///
/// O `record_hash` é computado como:
///
/// ```text
/// BLAKE3( EVIDENCE_DOMAIN || metadata || content )
/// ```
///
/// # Invariantes
///
/// - `INV-EV-01`: Todo `record_hash` é verificável.
/// - `INV-EV-02`: Metadados e conteúdo não podem ser vazios.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct RecordHash([u8; 32]);
impl RecordHash {
/// Computa o `record_hash` de metadados e conteúdo.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Metadados vazios → [`EvidenceError::EmptyMetadata`].
/// - Conteúdo vazio → [`EvidenceError::EmptyContent`].
///
/// # Exemplo
///
/// ```
/// use arkhe_evidence::RecordHash;
///
/// let hash = RecordHash::compute(b"meta", b"content").unwrap();
/// assert!(hash.verify(b"meta", b"content").is_ok());
/// ```
pub fn compute(metadata: &[u8], content: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, EvidenceError> {
if metadata.is_empty() {
return Err(EvidenceError::EmptyMetadata);
}
if content.is_empty() {


=== PAGINA 531 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 531
return Err(EvidenceError::EmptyContent);
}
let mut hasher = Hasher::new_derive_key(EVIDENCE_DOMAIN);
hasher.update(metadata);
hasher.update(content);
Ok(Self(*hasher.finalize().as_bytes()))
}
/// Verifica um `record_hash` contra metadados e conteúdo.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Metadados vazios → [`EvidenceError::EmptyMetadata`].
/// - Conteúdo vazio → [`EvidenceError::EmptyContent`].
/// - Hash mismatch → [`EvidenceError::HashMismatch`].
pub fn verify(&self, metadata: &[u8], content: &[u8]) -> Result<(), EvidenceError> {
let expected = Self::compute(metadata, content)?;
if expected != *self {
return Err(EvidenceError::HashMismatch {
expected: hex::encode(expected.0),
actual: hex::encode(self.0),
});
}
Ok(())
}

#[must_use]
pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8; 32] {
&self.0
}
/// Retorna o hash em formato hexadecimal.
#[must_use]
pub fn to_hex(&self) -> String {
hex::encode(self.0)
}

///
/// # Domain separation

#[must_use]
pub fn compute_record_hash(
sequence: u64,
event_type: &str,
payload: &[u8],

hasher.update(&sequence.to_le_bytes());

hasher.update(payload);
hasher.update(prev_hash);
hasher.update(&timestamp.to_le_bytes());
*hasher.finalize().as_bytes()
}

pub fn append(

/// Verifica a integridade da cadeia.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Cadeia vazia → [`WormGraphError::EmptyChain`].
/// - Sequência quebrada → [`WormGraphError::SequenceBroken`].
/// - Cadeia quebrada → [`WormGraphError::ChainBroken`].
/// - Conteúdo adulterado → [`WormGraphError::ContentTampered`].
/// - Payload vazio → [`WormGraphError::EmptyPayload`].
///
/// # Exemplo
///
/// ```
/// use arkhe_wormgraph::WormGraph;
///
/// let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
/// wg.append("test", b"payload".to_vec(), 1000).unwrap();
/// assert!(wg.verify_chain().is_ok());
/// ```
pub fn verify_chain(&self) -> Result<(), WormGraphError> {
if self.events.is_empty() {
return Err(WormGraphError::EmptyChain);
}
let mut expected_prev = [0u8; 32];
for (i, event) in self.events.iter().enumerate() {
// 1. Verificar contiguidade de sequência (INV-WG-02)
let expected_seq = i as u64;


=== PAGINA 540 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 540
if event.sequence != expected_seq {
return Err(WormGraphError::SequenceBroken {
index: i,
expected: expected_seq,
actual: event.sequence,
});
}
// 2. Verificar payload não-vazio (INV-WG-04)
if event.payload.is_empty() {
return Err(WormGraphError::EmptyPayload(i));
}
// 3. Verificar ligação ao evento anterior (INV-WG-05)
if event.prev_hash != expected_prev {
return Err(WormGraphError::ChainBroken(i));
}
// 4. Recomputar record_hash do conteúdo (INV-WG-03)
let recomputed = GraphEvent::compute_record_hash(
event.sequence,
&event.event_type,
&event.payload,
&event.prev_hash,
event.timestamp,
);
if recomputed != event.record_hash {
return Err(WormGraphError::ContentTampered(i));
}
expected_prev = event.record_hash;
}
Ok(())
}

//! # Arkhe Claim Registry
//!
//! Registo de claims com verificação de integridade.
//!
//! ## Invariantes
//!
//! - `INV-CLAIM-01`: Toda claim registada tem `integrity_hash` verificado.
//! - `INV-CLAIM-02`: Claims com ID vazio são rejeitadas.
//! - `INV-CLAIM-03`: Claims com falsificador vazio são rejeitadas.
//! - `INV-CLAIM-04`: Os campos são privados (newtype pattern).
//! - `INV-CLAIM-05`: `deny_unknown_fields` rejeita campos extra.
//! - `INV-CLAIM-06`: `integrity_hash` é ignorado na deserialização.
//!
//! ## Exemplo
//!
//! ```
//! use arkhe_claim_registry::{Claim, ClaimRegistry};
//! use arkhe_standards::Category;
//!
//! let mut registry = ClaimRegistry::new();
//! let claim = Claim::new(
//! "claim-1",
//! "A statement",
//! Category::MeasuredEvidence,
//! "falsifier",
//! ).unwrap();
//! registry.register(claim).unwrap();
//! assert!(registry.verify_all().is_ok());

/// Verifica a integridade da claim.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Hash recomputado ≠ hash armazenado → [`ClaimError::IntegrityHashMismatch`].
pub fn verify_integrity(&self) -> Result<(), ClaimError> {
let expected = Self::compute_hash(
&self.id,
&self.statement,
self.category,
&self.falsifier,
);
if expected != self.integrity_hash {
return Err(ClaimError::IntegrityHashMismatch);
}
Ok(())
}

// CLAIM REGISTRY
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
/// Registo de claims.
///
/// # Invariantes
///
/// - `INV-CLAIM-01`: Toda claim registada tem `integrity_hash` verificado.
/// - `INV-CLAIM-07`: Claims duplicadas são rejeitadas.
#[derive(Debug, Default)]
pub struct ClaimRegistry {
claims: Vec<Claim>,
}
impl ClaimRegistry {
/// Cria um novo registo vazio.
#[must_use]
pub fn new() -> Self {
Self { claims: Vec::new() }
}
/// Regista uma claim.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Claim duplicada → [`ClaimError::Duplicate`] (verificado PRIMEIRO).
/// - `integrity_hash` inválido → [`ClaimError::IntegrityHashMismatch`] (verificado DEPO
↳ IS).


=== PAGINA 553 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 553
///
/// # Exemplo
///
/// ```
/// use arkhe_claim_registry::{Claim, ClaimRegistry};
/// use arkhe_standards::Category;
///
/// let mut registry = ClaimRegistry::new();
/// let claim = Claim::new(
/// "claim-1",
/// "A statement",
/// Category::MeasuredEvidence,
/// "falsifier",
/// ).unwrap();
/// registry.register(claim).unwrap();
/// assert_eq!(registry.len(), 1);
/// ```
pub fn register(&mut self, claim: Claim) -> Result<(), ClaimError> {
// 1. Verificar duplicado PRIMEIRO (evita erro confuso)
if self.claims.iter().any(|c| c.id == claim.id) {
return Err(ClaimError::Duplicate(claim.id));
}
// 2. Verificar integridade DEPOIS
claim.verify_integrity()?;
// 3. Só então adicionar
self.claims.push(claim);
Ok(())
}
/// Verifica todas as claims registadas.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Qualquer claim com hash inválido → [`ClaimError::IntegrityHashMismatch`].
pub fn verify_all(&self) -> Result<(), ClaimError> {
for claim in &self.claims {
claim.verify_integrity()?;
}
Ok(())
}
/// Obtém uma claim por ID.

SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 554

}
/// Número de claims registadas.
#[must_use]
pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
self.claims.len()
}
/// Retorna `true` se o registo está vazio.
#[must_use]
pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
self.claims.is_empty()
}
/// Retorna todas as claims.
#[must_use]
pub fn claims(&self) -> &[Claim] {
&self.claims
}
}

/// # Invariantes

/// - `quorum` e `timelock_seconds` são imutáveis após a proposta.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize)]
pub struct Invariant {

/// Ratifica o invariante.
///
/// # Fail-closed
///
/// - Quórum insuficiente → [`InvariantError::InsufficientQuorum`].
/// - Timelock não expirou → [`InvariantError::TimelockNotExpired`].
/// - Já ratificado → [`InvariantError::AlreadyRatified`].
/// - `now < proposed_at` → [`InvariantError::ClockSkew`].
///
/// # Exemplo
///
/// ```
/// use arkhe_governance::Invariant;
///
/// let mut inv = Invariant::propose(
/// "INV-TEST-01",
/// "Test",
/// 4,
/// 100,
/// 1_000_000,
/// ).unwrap();
///
/// inv.ratify(4, 1_000_200).unwrap();
/// ```
pub fn ratify(&mut self, approvals: u8, now: u64) -> Result<(), InvariantError> {
if self.status == InvariantStatus::Ratified {
return Err(InvariantError::AlreadyRatified(self.id.clone()));
}
// CORREÇÃO: verificar clock skew
if now < self.proposed_at {
return Err(InvariantError::ClockSkew);
}
if approvals < self.quorum {


=== PAGINA 566 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 566
return Err(InvariantError::InsufficientQuorum {
approvals,
required: self.quorum,
});
}
let elapsed = now - self.proposed_at; // seguro: now >= proposed_at
if elapsed < self.timelock_seconds {
return Err(InvariantError::TimelockNotExpired {
remaining: self.timelock_seconds - elapsed,
});
}
self.status = InvariantStatus::Ratified;
Ok(())
}
}

fn proof_append_rejects_empty_payload() {
let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
let event_type: String = kani::any();
let timestamp: u64 = kani::any();
let result = wg.append(event_type, vec![], timestamp);
kani::assert(
matches!(result, Err(WormGraphError::EmptyPayload(0))),
"Payload vazio deve ser rejeitado",
);
}
/// INV-WG-03: uma cadeia válida passa a verificação.
#[kani::proof]
#[kani::unwind(5)]
fn proof_verify_chain_succeeds_for_valid_chain() {
let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
let p1: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3];
let p2: Vec<u8> = vec![4, 5, 6];
wg.append("test", p1, 1000).unwrap();
wg.append("test", p2, 2000).unwrap();
let result = wg.verify_chain();
kani::assert(result.is_ok(), "Cadeia válida deve passar");
}
/// INV-WG-03: o record_hash é determinístico.
#[kani::proof]
fn proof_record_hash_is_deterministic() {
let seq: u64 = kani::any();
let event_type: String = kani::any();
let payload: Vec<u8> = kani::any();
let prev_hash: [u8; 32] = kani::any();
let timestamp: u64 = kani::any();
let h1 = arkhe_wormgraph::GraphEvent::compute_record_hash(
seq, &event_type, &payload, &prev_hash, timestamp,
);
let h2 = arkhe_wormgraph::GraphEvent::compute_record_hash(
seq, &event_type, &payload, &prev_hash, timestamp,
);
kani::assert(h1 == h2, "record_hash deve ser determinístico");
}

let statement: String = kani::any();
let category: Category = kani::any();

let result = Claim::new(id, statement, category, "");

);

K.6.2 — Lean 4 formal proofs (script)
-- ClaimRegistry.lean
-- Definição e prova de segurança para o ClaimRegistry.
--
-- Este ficheiro prova que as operações register, propose e ratify
-- preservam o invariante de segurança:
-- ratified ⊆ proposed ⊆ claims
import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Basic
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Tipos base
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
structure Claim where
id : String
statement : String
category : String
status : ClaimStatus
deriving DecidableEq, Repr
inductive ClaimStatus where
| proposed : ClaimStatus
| ratified : ClaimStatus
deriving DecidableEq, Repr
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Estado do registo
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
structure RegistryState where
claims : Finset Claim
proposed : Finset Claim
ratified : Finset Claim
deriving Repr
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Invariante de segurança: ratified ⊆ proposed ⊆ claims
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def SafetyInv (s : RegistryState) : Prop :=
s.ratified ⊆ s.proposed ∧ s.proposed ⊆ s.claims
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Operações


=== PAGINA 580 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 580
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def register (s : RegistryState) (c : Claim) : RegistryState :=
{ s with claims := s.claims ∪ {c} }
def propose (s : RegistryState) (c : Claim) : RegistryState :=
{ s with proposed := s.proposed ∪ {c} }
def ratify (s : RegistryState) (c : Claim) : RegistryState :=
{ s with ratified := s.ratified ∪ {c} }
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Teorema: register preserva SafetyInv
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theorem register_preserves_safety
(s : RegistryState)
(c : Claim)
(h : SafetyInv s) :
SafetyInv (register s c) := by
unfold SafetyInv at *
constructor
· -- ratified ⊆ proposed
intro x hx
exact h.1 hx
· -- proposed ⊆ claims
intro x hx
have hx' : x ∈ s.claims ∪ {c} := by
simp [register] at hx
exact hx
exact hx'
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- Teorema: propose preserva SafetyInv
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
theorem propose_preserves_safety
(s : RegistryState)
(c : Claim)
(h : SafetyInv s)
(hc : c ∈ s.claims) : -- pré-condição: c já registada
SafetyInv (propose s c) := by
unfold SafetyInv at *
constructor

exact hx
exact hx'
· -- proposed ⊆ claims
intro x hx

use arkhe_claim_registry::{Claim, ClaimRegistry};
use arkhe_evidence::RecordHash;
use arkhe_governance::Invariant;

#[test]
fn full_pipeline_with_valid_claims() {
// 1. Criar claim
let claim = Claim::new(
"claim-1",
"A statement",
Category::MeasuredEvidence,
"falsifier",
)
.unwrap();
// 2. Registar claim

registry.register(claim).unwrap();

let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
wg.append("claim-registered", b"claim-1".to_vec(), 1000)
.unwrap();
assert!(wg.verify_chain().is_ok());

"INV-TEST-01",
"Test statement",

1_000_000,
)
.unwrap();
inv.ratify(4, 1_000_200).unwrap();

)
.unwrap();
// Timelock não expirou

//! Benchmarks para o WormGraph.
use criterion::{black_box, criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};
use arkhe_wormgraph::WormGraph;
fn bench_append(c: &mut Criterion) {
let mut group = c.benchmark_group("wormgraph/append");
group.bench_function("single", |b| {
let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
b.iter(|| {
wg.append("test", b"payload".to_vec(), 1000).unwrap();
});
});
group.bench_function("chain_100", |b| {
b.iter(|| {
let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
for i in 0..100 {
wg.append("test", format!("payload-{}", i).into_bytes(), i as u64)
.unwrap();
}
black_box(wg);
});
});
group.finish();
}
fn bench_verify_chain(c: &mut Criterion) {
let mut group = c.benchmark_group("wormgraph/verify_chain");
for size in [10, 100, 1000] {
let mut wg = WormGraph::new();
for i in 0..size {
wg.append("test", format!("payload-{}", i).into_bytes(), i as u64)
.unwrap();
}
group.bench_function(format!("size_{}", size), |b| {
b.iter(|| {
black_box(wg.verify_chain().unwrap());
});
});
}
group.finish();
}
criterion_group!(benches, bench_append, bench_verify_chain);
criterion_main!(benches);

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Verificação de supply chain para o Arkhe AGI.
set -euo pipefail
echo "╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗"
echo "║ ARKHE AGI — SUPPLY CHAIN VERIFICATION ║"
echo "╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝"
echo ""
# 1. cargo-audit
echo "=== 1. cargo-audit ==="
if ! command -v cargo-audit &> /dev/null; then
cargo install cargo-audit --locked
fi
cargo audit
echo "␀ cargo-audit passou"
echo ""
# 2. cargo-deny
echo "=== 2. cargo-deny ==="
if ! command -v cargo-deny &> /dev/null; then
cargo install cargo-deny --locked
fi
cargo deny check
echo "␀ cargo-deny passou"
echo ""
# 3. cargo-vet
echo "=== 3. cargo-vet ==="
if ! command -v cargo-vet &> /dev/null; then
cargo install cargo-vet --locked
fi
cargo vet --locked
echo "␀ cargo-vet passou"
echo ""
# 4. Cargo.lock verification
echo "=== 4. Cargo.lock ==="
if git diff --exit-code Cargo.lock; then
echo "␀ Cargo.lock não modificado"
else
echo "␀ Cargo.lock foi modificado — executar cargo update"
exit 1
fi
echo ""
echo "╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗"

# Arkhe AGI
> A camada de verificação para agentes de IA.
[![CI](https://github.com/arkhe-os/arkhe-agi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https:
//gi
↳ thub.com/arkhe-os/arkhe-agi/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](LICEN
SE-M
↳ IT)
[![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.75%2B-orange.svg)](https://www.rust-lang.or
g)
## Visão Geral
O Arkhe AGI é um monorepo multi-crate que implementa a camada de verificação
para agentes de IA. A arquitectura segue três princípios fundamentais:
| Princípio | Descrição |
|:---|:---|
| **Fail-closed** | Rejeitar em erro, nunca permitir por omissão |
| **Status honesto** | `␀ VERIFIED`, `⚠␀ PARTIAL`, `␀ FAILED`, `␀ [NONEXISTENT]` |
| **Prove, do not promise** | Capacidades são declarações machine-checkable |
## Estrutura

## Invariantes
| ID | Enunciado | Crate |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `INV-EV-01` | Todo artefacto tem `record_hash` verificável | `arkhe-evidence` |

Appendix E — Consolidated Invariant Catalog
 This appendix consolidates, in one table, the invariant statements defended across the
chapters of this volume. It is a synthesis prepared for the reader, not a transcription of the
project's internal invariant file: the internal catalog (I-01 through I-20, model-checked in
TLA+) is an on-file artifact [28] whose exact wording is not reproduced here, and the
bioinspired invariants of Chapter 19 carry their own identifiers. Each row states the
invariant in machine-checkable spirit — an assertion about system behavior that either
holds or fails — together with the falsifier that would refute it and the chapter where the
argument is made. The catalog doubles as a review checklist: an implementation that
violates any row is not a weak instance of the architecture but a different system wearing its
name.

volume).

 Two remarks on use. First, the catalog is ordered by the pipeline rather than by
importance: the earlier rows are prerequisites for the later ones, and an audit that finds an
early-row violation need not check further. Second, several rows are deliberately about
what the system refuses to do — proceed on error, render pending as verified, accept
display intent as sign intent — because the incidents of Chapter 7 were all, at bottom,
failures of refusal. A governance body adopting the architecture can lift this table into its
ConstitutionStore as a starting invariant set, replacing the internal identifiers with its own
and amending under its own quorum rules, exactly as Chapter 13 prescribes.
Appendix F — Status Tokens, Epistemic Labels,
and Stamps
 A book about verification needs a visible convention for what its own statements are.
The volume uses three mechanisms, summarized in Table F.1. Status tokens are the
runtime vocabulary that Arkhe components emit: VERIFIED, PENDING, and the
deliberately stark [NONEXISTENT], which exists because the costliest failures in the
record — StablR and SUPERFORTUNE among them — were mislabeled pending states
treated as verified ones [6, 34]. Epistemic labels are the book's own marking discipline:
external claims are cited to verifiable public sources; claims that trace only to project
artifacts are labeled internal and listed as on-file with the authors [28–31, 45, 69, 70];
qualitative mappings and schematic figures say so in their captions. Stamps are the project's
convention for dated document identity of the form
ARKHE-OS-‹SUBJECT›-YYYY-MM-DD, of which the reader has seen
ARKHE-OS-HODGE-PLAN-2026-09-14 [69] and
ARKHE-OS-UNIVERSAL-LAYER-2026-09-15 [28].
Table F.1 — Conventions used throughout this volume.
Convention
Meaning
Where introduced

All four gates answered affirmatively at the stated time.
