 The conventions are deliberately few. Their shared property is refusal of silent defaults:
a reader should never have to guess whether a claim is verified, pending, absent, merely
planned, or schematic. That property — honest status applied to prose — is the same one
the runtime enforces on payloads, and it is the closest a document can come to practicing
what the architecture it describes preaches.
Appendix G — Verification Command Handbook
 This appendix collects, in one place, the operational commands a verifier actually
types. It is intentionally terse: the argument of the book is that verification must be cheap at
the keyboard, not only in theory. Three families appear — the artifact verifier, the evidence
graph, and decentralized distribution — and each listing below is annotated in the
surrounding text. The exact sub-command surface is the project's own [28]; the distribution
commands follow the Hashtree material [147] and standard git practice.
 Artifact verification. The verifier takes an artifact and an attestation record and
answers with an honest status. A GGUF model attestation check re-derives the file digest,
validates the signature against the pinned trust root, and reports one of the three status
tokens of Appendix F — never a bare success code that could be mislabeled downstream:
$ arkhe-verify attestation —model qwen3-8B-instruct.gguf \
—attestation arkhe.attestation.json \
—require inclusion,quorum
status : VERIFIED
model digest: blake3:9f2c...e81a (sha256:4412...c07d)
signer : ed25519:publisher-lab-01 (trust root: sigstore/fulcio)
inclusion : merkle proof ok — root 7d30...9b2c — anchored: rekor seq 1,204,553
quorum : 5/7 witnesses co-signed policy v2026.09
policy : arkhe.constitution@v2026.09 — model class permitted: inference-local
 Evidence graph inspection. Every consequential action of an agent session is a node;
the inspector replays the chain and re-checks inclusion proofs locally before showing
anything, so that what an auditor reads is what the graph contains:


=== PAGINA 598 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 598
$ arkhe-wormgraph log —session sess-2026-09-16-0417 —verify
n-041 deploy.contract signer=agent-07 parents=[n-040] inclusion=ok
n-042 policy.amend signer=quorum(4/7) timelock=7d inclusion=ok
n-043 txn.sign intent=clear-signed decode=independent inclusion=ok
3 nodes replayed; 0 verification errors; chain anchored at rekor seq 1,204,559
 Decentralized distribution. Binaries and large artifacts travel content-addressed over
Nostr-backed storage; git collaboration runs over the same identity layer. The install
command below is the project's published one-liner; the git remotes replace the centralized
forge for push and clone while NIP-34 events carry patches and reviews [140, 147]:
$ curl -fsSL https://upload.iris.to/npub1xdh.../releases%2Fhashtree/latest/install.sh |
sh
$ cargo install hashtree-cli # alternative: build from source
$ git remote add htree htree://self/arkhe-os
$ git push htree master # publish objects content-addressed
$ git clone htree://npub1dqgr.../hashtree
 Client-side audit. The same verification surface is exported to WebAssembly, so an
auditor can re-derive every verdict in a browser without installing anything or trusting the
vendor's infrastructure — the property Chapter 11 calls vendor-independent audit:
$ arkhe-verify-wasm serve —port 8791
# in browser console:
await arkhe.verifyAttestation(modelBytes, attestationJson, { trustRoot: 'sigstore' })
// -> { status: 'VERIFIED', digest: 'blake3:9f2c...e81a', inclusion: 'ok', ... }
 The handbook closes where the architecture began: with the observation that these
commands are short not because the problems are small, but because the evidence chain
carries the complexity. Where a verifier must ask four questions instead of one, the
operator types four words — require inclusion,quorum — and the machinery, not the
memory, supplies the discipline.
Appendix H — Data, Schemas, and Reproducibility
 Reproducibility obligations apply to this volume in the same form the architecture
applies them to agents: every figure either derives from a named dataset or is labeled as the
authors' schematic, and every derived figure can be regenerated from its source file. Three
datasets are used. First, the constitutional corpus: the Brazilian Federal Constitution of
1988 as consolidated text [32], parsed into 276 article nodes and 261 citation edges with
revocation flags, and reduced to the metric table of Chapter 20 — in-degree, out-degree,
PageRank, betweenness, d-Veto depth, and winding numbers — from which Figures 20.1
through 20.3 are drawn directly. Second, the incident dataset: the Bybit, StablR, and
SUPERFORTUNE records with their forensic sources [2, 4, 6, 34, 93–96], summarized in
Table 1.1 and Figure 7.1; loss figures are quoted from the cited primary reports rather than
recomputed. Third, the qualitative mappings — the regulatory matrix of Figure 9.1, the


=== PAGINA 599 ===
SHOW THE NUMBER — a verification-first epistemology
Page 599
category map of Figure 23.1, and the limitations assessment of Figure 24.1 — which are
the authors' structured judgment, labeled as such in their captions, and offered as
hypotheses for refutation rather than as measurements.
 Schemas follow the same rule of explicitness. The WormGraph node schema, the
GGUF attestation record, the Capability Manifest, and the hodge-verify workflow are
printed in full in Appendices C and D; the consolidated invariant catalog of Appendix E
states each assertion with its falsifier; and the status vocabulary of Appendix F fixes how
every automated statement in the system is to be read. Where the project's internal artifacts
are cited — the architecture corpus, ADR-011, the SASC audit report, the five-front plan
[28–30, 69, 70] — the citation is a disclosure of provenance, not a substitute for public
verifiability; the book's standing commitment is to release these artifacts under the project's
disclosure policy, and the internal figures that depend on them (the constitutional audit
among them) ship alongside their generator scripts so that the community can re-derive or
contest every number.

argued throughout: to show that the same small set of verification mechanisms recurs
across regimes that are usually treated as unrelated compliance worlds.

Further Reading by Part
 The reference list serves precision; this closing guide serves orientation. For each part,
we name the sources a reader new to the area should open first, with one sentence on why
each matters. The selection is necessarily personal, but every entry is cited in the text and
resolves through the reference list.
Part I. Deligne's official problem statement remains the clearest entry to why verification
claims are hard [48]; TRM Labs' 2026 crime report supplies the empirical backdrop of
agent-era theft [96]; the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications is the canonical risk
taxonomy [13, 14].
Part II. RFC 9162 formalizes append-only transparency [99]; the SLSA specification
shows what graded build assurance looks like in practice [102]; FIPS 204 is the document
behind the post-quantum signature story [104].
Part III. The FBI's Bybit PSA and Fireblocks' analysis together form the best public
forensic record of blind-signing failure [93, 95]; the AI Act Service Desk's record-keeping
guidance translates Art. 12 into engineering terms [18].
Part IV. The MCP specification is required reading for anyone governing agents through
tool interfaces [108]; Invariant Labs' tool-poisoning disclosure shows why interface trust
fails at exactly the layer MCP opens [109].
Part V. ICH E6(R3) as adopted text [73], DORA's regulation [71], and NIST SP 800-171
Rev. 3 [77] are the three instruments whose demands map most directly onto verification
gates.
Parts VI–VII. Caldara and Iacoviello's GPR paper is the measurement standard for
geopolitical data feeds [151]; the SSV academic study and ethereum.org's DVT primer
explain quorum-by-key-splitting [138, 139]; the Hashtree repository documents
content-addressed distribution in production [147].
Part VIII. The constitutional audit's method generalizes VetoGraph thinking [30]; the
Virtual Fly Brain atlas shows what mature machine-checkable ontologies look like [42,
43].
